Prince Harry says he would rejoin army as he warns of Russia threat

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 20:55:15 GMT

The Duke of Sussex, who carried out a surprise visit to Ukraine at the weekend, has said he would rejoin the military if asked, as he warned of the threat from Russia.

He told the Telegraph he thought people were right to be nervous in the current international political climate and said it was time to "double our support" for Ukraine.

There appeared to be warnings about President Trump - with Prince Harry saying there was a big separation between what the American public thinks about Ukraine and the administration's attitude.

Prince Harry, able to speak more freely than working royals, said he hoped after the US mid-term elections it would be "fantastic to have more American support" for Ukraine.

Speaking to the Telegraph's Dominic Nicholls, Prince Harry said he thought the threat to Europe had been there for the past 15 years - and he felt like it had been at war for the past decade.

"Just because there's not drones, bullets, and rockets flying at us, it doesn't mean that we're not at war," said Prince Harry.

Prince Harry had been in Lviv in Ukraine on Saturday and Sunday - and had told the BBC and journalists at events that he thought the "rest of the world will continue to support" Ukraine.

He had told his Ukrainian hosts, about a conflict with Russia that has already lasted more than four years: "You're going to win the war."

In his Telegraph podcast, he called for a similar unity that was being shown by Ukraine, and feared that Europe could be divided and could "turn on itself".

He addressed the shifting position of US President Trump in a way that is unusual for a royal.

"I think there's been a big separation between what American society feels regarding support for Ukraine, which I think is incredibly high and always has been, compared to a certain group, or in, in this case, an administration that was perhaps thinking about it differently," said Prince Harry.

"As of January, things are going to change, so I think we should all be looking forward to that," he said, referring to the US mid-term elections, which saw significant setbacks for President Trump.

Having served in the military in Afghanistan, he said he would return if needed for a future conflict: "If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel."

Prince Harry had received an enthusiastic welcome when he visited Lviv in Ukraine at the weekend, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.

There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women, some of the 150,000 seriously wounded war veterans in the country.

His visit had been carried out with a press blackout for security reasons - and the night before journalists arrived in the city to cover the visit, there had been air raid warnings that had forced Prince Harry's planning team to head for the shelters.

"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," Prince Harry had said, including inventing new ways of treating the growing number of injured casualties.

"War is a terrible thing," he said in Lviv, but hailed the resilience of the Ukrainians who had been badly wounded in their defence against Russia's invasion.

FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 20:55:01 GMT

Gianni Infantino has been leading Fifa since 2016

The Football Association has considered challenging Gianni Infantino's eligibility to run for a fourth term as Fifa president, BBC Sport can reveal.

But it believes any attempt to prevent him from standing in the election in March is likely to fail.

Infantino oversaw the introduction of a three-term limit when he replaced Sepp Blatter as leader of world football's governing body.

However, Fifa's council agreed in 2022 that his first period in office from 2016 to 2019 should not count as it was the remainder of his predecessor's interrupted final term.

Earlier this month, human rights campaign group Fair Square wrote to the FA claiming that the decision is open to legal challenge and was "contrary to the spirit and purpose" of Fifa statutes.

It urged the FA to ask Fifa's governance committee to bar Infantino from the election in March because he has already served the maximum three terms.

FA chair Debbie Hewitt has now replied, telling Fair Square that the governing body "has explored the possibility of challenging Mr Infantino's eligibility to run for a further term as the Fifa president but does not consider that such a challenge would secure the outcome sought".

In correspondence seen by the BBC, Hewitt adds: "Ultimately the process followed Fifa's governance and led to an outcome where Mr Infantino's part term was disregarded for the purposes of maximum term limits.

"Having considered the process in detail, we do not believe that a challenge would succeed."

In a statement, Fair Square said: "It's understandable that the FA has no faith in Fifa's internal processes to hold Infantino accountable for serious breaches of the rules, but it's a mistake to abandon these channels, not least because it sends a signal to Infantino that he can do whatever he likes.

"We will encourage the FA to leave its options open where this matter is concerned not least because Debbie Hewitt's position on the Fifa council puts her in a very strong position to demand clear answers on why Fifa discounted Infantino's first term."

Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - has said a national association or confederation may need to challenge Infantino's eligibility at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).

The FA was among a number of national associations to withdraw its support of Infantino in the wake of the crisis sparked by his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors.

European confederation Uefa has backed rival candidate Philippe Diallo, the president of the French Football Federation.

This video can not be played

Diallo announces FIFA president bid

Hewitt, who became a member of Fifa's council in 2023, also told Fair Square that the FA "remains opposed to Mr Infantino's re-election and is committed to providing its full support to Philippe Diallo as our preferred candidate in the upcoming Fifa presidential election".

Fifa has been approached for comment.

It has previously referred to the fact that in 2022 its council "unanimously confirmed its agreement with the view of the governance, audit & compliance committee that the period between 2016 and 2019 does not count as a term of office for the current Fifa president, who is therefore about to end his first term".

The FA declined to comment.

The UK government is asking for jailed rapist Russell Brand's YouTube account to be removed after his wife posted a video with a message from him claiming his innocence.

A justice minister has met with Google, which owns YouTube, as first reported by Sky News.

The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

On Sunday, his wife Laura shared a video on their YouTube channel, and read out a handwritten message from Brand, in which he claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening."

The message prompted an investigation into whether Brand broke prison rules.

Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

As things stand, the Brands' YouTube account is still active.

Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 20:14:57 GMT

Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.

Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.

The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.

The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.

Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.

Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.

It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.

Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".

Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.

In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.

Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.

A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."

"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."

A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".

Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.

Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.

One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second to the north in Gaza City, and the third in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.

The Israeli military said the first two strikes targeted "terrorists" and that it was not aware of the third incident, according to AFP news agency.

At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.

Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.

The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.

The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.

The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

William and Kate meet PM Modi as they wrap up India tour

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 20:07:08 GMT

The Prince and Princess of Wales have met India's prime minister as they ended their three-day visit to the country.

Narendra Modi thanked Prince William for bringing his Earthshot prize to the country during the couple's first international tour since 2022.

It comes a day after the royal couple gave out £1m prizes to winners of the environmental award, which was founded by the prince and remains one of his biggest personal projects.

Catherine also visited a maternity hospital, where she comforted a grieving mother who lost a baby after giving birth to premature twin girls.

On Wednesday, William and Catherine travelled from Mumbai to capital New Delhi for the final leg of their trip.

During a meeting at Modi's private residence, a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the royals and Modi discussed the "strength and importance of the UK–India bilateral relationship, reflecting on the deep and enduring ties between the two countries and the opportunities to strengthen their partnership in the years ahead".

The prince and princess also spoke "warmly" of their time in the country, thanking the prime minister and the people for their welcome, and saying how much they enjoyed returning to India, a decade after their last visit.

Modi called it a "pleasure" to meet them, and said he looks forward to "further strengthening" the UK–India partnership for the "shared prosperity of the people of our nations and the wider world".

When Prince William announced earlier this year that The Earthshot Prize ceremony was going to be held in India for the first time, he highlighted India's leadership in climate innovation, its biodiversity and its massive youth population as the key reasons for choosing the country.

The royal spokesperson said that the meeting with Modi touched on the success of the ceremony in Mumbai, and India's "growing leadership in environmental innovation".

The event, founded by Prince William in 2020, was hosted this year by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known filmmakers.

The couple last met the Indian prime minister on their official visit to India in 2016.

Ahead of their meeting with Modi on Wednesday, William met with film stars during a visit to a film production company, while Catherine visited a maternity hospital, where she met grieving mother Jyoti Karande.

Karande, whose other child remains in intensive care, is receiving treatment in the post-partum ward at Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital.

Catherine told the 29-year-old: "Stay strong. Well done. You've clearly been very, very brave."

William and Catherine's first official overseas trip in four years was short, but allowed them to combine personal projects - like Earthshot - with diplomacy.

As the future king and queen, they are viewed as a valuable diplomatic asset by the UK government.

And with Catherine recovering well and back on international duties following her cancer treatment, visits of a similar kind can be expected to fill their calendar.

Police chief says racists and misogynists working inside force

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 19:10:40 GMT

The chief of Wales' largest police force says he is working to root out racists and misogynists from his organisation as part of efforts to improve trust in officers.

Chief Constable Jeremy Vaughan had responded to a question from MPs about how he and other police chiefs were clamping down on staff misconduct "in a post-Sarah Everard era".

The South Wales Police chief said: "Do I think I've got racists, misogynists, working for me? Yes. Do I think my work is to find them and excommunicate them from policing? Absolutely yes."

He appeared in front of the Welsh Affairs Committee on Wednesday, along with Wales' three other police bosses, as part of its inquiry into the future of policing.

One of the issues being examined by the committee, made up of Welsh MPs from the UK Parliament, is a UK government proposal to reduce the number of police forces in England and Wales.

Committee chairperson, Newport West and Islwyn MP Ruth Jones, had asked the chief constables of all four forces how they were evaluating their forces' performance when it came to addressing misconduct.

Jones noted in her question that "we're still in a post-Sarah Everard era", referencing the 33-year-old woman who was abducted, raped and murdered by serving Met police officer Wayne Couzens in London in 2021, and that "there have been issues across Wales".

Vaughan said that 126 people had been dismissed from the force under his watch since he started his role six years ago, and that he believed it had been "significantly higher" than under his predecessor.

Saying he believed improvements to vetting and training meant his organisation was now "more upstanding than by-standing than ever before", he noted that 22 people within it were currently suspended - which he said was a "low proportion of the workforce".

He said that identifying and sacking racists and misogynists from within South Wales Police was a "whole-organisation leadership effort".

Dyfed-Powys Police Chief Constable Ifan Charles told the committee he had a number of people currently being investigated for gross misconduct, some of whom were currently suspended, and that "some of those are for misogynistic behaviours".

North Wales Police Chief Constable Amanda Blakeman said her force had "pursued individuals that should not be in policing" and had been "relentless in all aspects in terms of anti-corruption, information from the public, about how we'll deal with people who don't live up to" her force's standards.

Gwent Police Chief Constable Mark Hobrough admitted his force had previously had a "very different culture" with high-profile senior leaders "who did not represent the values of modern day policing" removed from it.

He said the force currently had 37 active misconduct cases and 14 people suspended.

He said a staff survey indicated high levels of confidence in reporting misconduct and that the force would deal with them.

Elsewhere in the committee the police chiefs were asked for their views on the UK government's policing White Paper published in January.

It proposes significantly reducing the number of forces in England and Wales by merging existing forces into larger ones. A review will propose the best way to organise the new forces and no final decisions have yet been taken.

Wales currently has four forces, but there has been speculation it could go down to one, as is the case in Northern Ireland and Scotland.

Blakeman told MPs she thought the current structure should remain in place.

"I'm genuinely concerned about the prospect of force mergers because of that difference that we see in north Wales, and I'm concerned about the impact that those mergers may have in terms of our communities and the service they get," she said.

"Anything that is centralised tends to see service reduced in our rural communities, of which there is a large scale across north Wales."

She said delivering for rural communities would be "significantly at risk" if Wales went down to one force.

"I'm concerned about the vulnerability and isolation that we would see in the furthest part of north Wales that's disconnected from the point of view of road infrastructure, ability to travel, and is more connected to the North West of England," she added.

Vaughan said a restructure of forces could deliver efficiencies but must be properly funded.

He said he broadly agreed with the "direction of travel" set out in the government's proposals.

But added: "It's quite hard to analyse the specifics because I don't know what they are yet."

The UK government has been approached for comment.

'Lip King unbothered' when mum collapsed after BBL

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:49:35 GMT

A man who carried out a cosmetic procedure which an expert said had led to a woman's death complained he was "exhausted" and seemed "unbothered" when paramedics arrived, an inquest has been told.

Mother-of-five Alice Webb, 33, collapsed at a friend's house in Gloucester on 23 September 2024 and died the following day after having a Brazilian Butt Lift (BBL).

Jordan Parke, known as the "Lip King", gave Webb seven times the recommended amount of filler before she collapsed. He was under investigation for gross negligence manslaughter when he died in 2026.

Earlier, an expert pathologist told Webb's inquest that a "gel-like" liquid had been found in blood vessels in her brain, lungs and heart.

Gloucestershire Coroner's Court heard Parke had already been banned from carrying out BBLs in Dudley and Salford following concerns about his procedures.

Parke had complained "I'm exhausted" and was seen laughing as Webb, from Wotton-under-Edge, recorded a video of the procedure.

Det Insp Adam Stacey, of Gloucestershire Constabulary, told the inquest the only first aid equipment at the premises was "some plasters".

Katy Skerrett, senior coroner for Gloucestershire, told the inquest an ambulance had been called at about 21:00 BST on the day Webb collapsed. Despite resuscitation attempts, she died in hospital during the early hours of the next day.

During the inquest, a jury was played a recording of a 999 call made by Parke.

He could be heard telling the operator that Webb had "literally just had [the procedure] done" and was not breathing correctly.

Allanah Kingston, a paramedic for South West Ambulance Service who responded to the 999 call, said Webb had been unable to manage her airway.

An ECG showed massive ischemia, "which showed part of heart was dying; we knew it was not good," Kingston added, before Webb went into cardiac arrest.

She told the inquest Parke had appeared "unbothered by the situation" and demonstrated a "lack of understanding that the treatment may have caused illness".

Parke, 34, lived in Manchester, where he ran a salon from his home address, and had a large social media following.

He was under investigation for gross negligence manslaughter but died earlier this year, meaning the criminal case was unable to proceed, Det Insp Adam Stacey, from Gloucestershire Constabulary, told the inquest.

Stacey said he had "no doubt" in his mind that Parke, who had received no professional medical training, conducted the procedure Webb underwent shortly before her death, given the video evidence available.

Of Parke's certificates found in Manchester, "none of them showed any degree of reassurance in degree of their formality", he added.

A number of cosmetic procedures had been carried out previously by Parke, who, in 2023, had been subject to investigation by Dudley environmental health officers. They issued him with a prohibition notice to not perform BBL procedures.

Concerns regarding basic first aid, lack of lifesaving equipment, and the use of anesthesia without prescription had also been raised, and another prohibition notice was issued to Parke in Salford in 2024.

He was not registered with the General Medical Council or the General Pharmaceutical Council, and the products he used were unlicensed in the UK. He also lacked a medical prescribing certificate.

Leadbeatter said he had not found any indication of clots blocking Webb's lungs, but did find a "gel-like material" in the fatty tissue and within muscle of her buttocks. It was also present in nearby nerves.

The material was also found in blood vessels elsewhere in the body, he said.

"I saw it in lungs, also within the section of the buttocks, and in small blood vessels in parts of the brain, in the heart and in small blood vessels in the thyroid gland and kidney," Leadbeatter told the jury.

He added there had been no evidence of an allergic reaction and a toxic pathology test found nothing in the blood that could explain Webb's death.

Webb had her own business, Crystal Clear Aesthetics, in Wotton-under-Edge.

Morgan Louise Townsend, Webb's sister-in-law, became tearful as she spoke at the inquest and said she had talked to her every day.

When asked if Webb had paid for the treatment, Townsend said she had paid for a training course but had to pay Parke £2,300 for the procedure he did on her.

Townsend said Webb had seemed "absolutely fine that day" and had kept her updated with pictures and videos throughout the treatment.

"At 19:31, she sent me photo of the filler that was going to go in her, I was shocked at how much there was," Townsend said.

"[Parke] said he was giving her 400ml for free, in total 1,400ml. She sent messages and said, 'OMG it kills'."

Townsend added Webb had sent a video of Parke giving her the treatment.

The last message from Webb to Townsend came at 20:12, she told the inquest, and consisted of just one word: "Painful."

Surgical BBLs involve inserting silicone-filled implants and/or removing fat from other parts of the body before injecting it into the buttocks, while non-surgical BBLs involve injecting dermal filler into the buttocks.

During the jury inquest, Dr Stephen Leadbeatter, a Home Office forensic pathologist, said he considered her cause of death to be "embolisation of hyaluronic acid from introduction into buttocks".

Embolisation is when something is carried in the bloodstream from one part of the body to another. Hyaluronic acid was the filler used in the procedure.

The inquest continues.

Council wins legal fight against flags on lamp-posts

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:19:34 GMT

Birmingham City Council has won a High Court injunction preventing unauthorised flags being attached to lamp-posts and other highway infrastructure across the city.

The authority sought the order after thousands of St George's flags and union jacks were put up by supporters of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours from summer 2025 onwards.

Council lawyers argued the displays created safety risks and fuelled tensions, while campaigners said the move would restrict freedom of expression.

Judge Emma Kelly said there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.

In her ruling, the judge said it would last until trial or further order of the court.

The order applies to Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge; Ben Cullen, who is also associated with the group; and persons unknown from attaching flags to street furniture and highway infrastructure.

It also grants a power of arrest against Bridge and persons unknown, meaning police could arrest someone without a warrant if they are suspected of breaching the injunction.

The council said anyone who breaches the order could be jailed for up to two years, fined or have their assets seized for contempt of court.

The local authority sought the injunction after thousands of St George's flags and union flags were attached to lamp-posts and bridges in Birmingham from summer 2025 onwards.

Lawyers acting for the council argued the displays could pose safety risks, obstruct visibility and contribute to tensions and disorder. The application also referred to reported incidents of alleged intimidation, harassment and obstruction connected to flags being put up in the city.

The court heard that, on one occasion, a man suffered a broken leg when he was struck by a cherry picker being used while flags were being installed.

The case followed similar legal action in Oxfordshire, where the county council secured a permanent injunction against four named individuals over flags attached to lamp-posts and other highway structures.

Bridge opposed the injunction, arguing it would interfere with rights to freedom of expression and protest under the European Convention on Human Rights.

His barrister, Liam Wells, told the court the campaign amounted to political expression protected by the convention and argued the injunction would have a "chilling effect" on those rights.

In her ruling, Kelly stressed the order was not a ban on displaying flags.

"The interim injunction needs to be understood for what it is," she said.

"It is not the court nor the claimant 'banning the union jack' or the display of Pride flags or anything of the like.

"Whilst the interim injunction order will cover flags of all types, it is limited in scope to the restraint of unauthorised flags attached to highway street furniture or infrastructure, and to the restraint of associated conduct, within the administrative area of Birmingham."

She added that concerns the injunction would unduly restrict free expression were "unwarranted" and said she was satisfied it was "just and convenient" to grant the order.

The injunction covers all unauthorised flags attached to street furniture, regardless of the type of flag involved.

Birmingham City Council's cabinet member for equalities, communities and social justice, Jane Baston, welcomed the ruling and described it as an "important step" in tackling unauthorised attachments to public highways.

She said residents remained free to display flags on their own property and said the council's approach had been "proportionate and evidence-led".

Councillor Robert Alden, leader of Birmingham local Conservatives, criticised the authority's decision to pursue the injunction, saying it should focus on resolving the city's bin strike and improving basic services.

Campaign group Brummies United Against Racism & Hate Crime welcomed the ruling, describing it as "a welcome decision and long overdue".

A further hearing is due to take place in Birmingham on Thursday.

Regulator mistakenly sent complaints about doctors to newspaper

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:48:10 GMT

The doctors' regulator the General Medical Council (GMC) has apologised after it mistakenly sent information about more than 220 doctors to a national newspaper.

The information included summaries of complaints alleging antisemitism or Islamophobia against the doctors.

For some of the medics involved, it was only when the GMC alerted them to the data breach that they discovered a complaint had been made about them.

The GMC says it is "very sorry" for the incident and has reported itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

The GMC - an independent body that regulates doctors, physician associates and anaesthesia associates to protect patient safety - sent the information about 223 doctors to a journalist at the Times newspaper.

While no names were revealed, GMC identification numbers were included, which would easily allow doctors to be found on the regulator's register.

Some doctors have also raised concerns that their ethnicity was included in the data breach.

All the medics involved have been the subject of a complaint involving either antisemitism or Islamophobia, dating from the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023 to September 2026.

The GMC says it has a legal and statutory responsibility to investigate such claims.

Meanwhile, the Times is understood to have promised not to make any of the leaked details public, but has said it will not delete the leaked information.

A spokesman for the doctor's trade union, the British Medical Association (BMA), condemned the leak.

"The BMA is aware that a number of doctors have received communication from the GMC to say that it erroneously sent personal identifiable data about them to the Times newspaper when responding to a media request," it said.

"The GMC must take action to ensure such a breach never occurs again."

The BMA said it would look at ways to support members affected and urged them to make contact via their website.

A doctors' campaign group, The Doctors' Association UK (DAUK), called for an independent investigation into the leak.

"If a doctor sent identifiable patient information to a newspaper, they could expect to be referred to the GMC," said Dr Matt Kneale, DAUK co-chairman.

"The GMC should hold itself to the same standard of confidentiality it expects from doctors. It owes every affected doctor a clear account of what it sent, how that happened and what it is doing to get the information deleted."

The doctors' regulator says around a fifth (20%) of the complaints made have already resulted in some sanction related to antisemitism, including two doctors who have been struck off the medical register.

Just over a quarter of complaints over Islamophobia - 26% - have led to disciplinary action.

But other complaints were closed, having failed to reach the threshold for investigation.

The GMC said it had contacted the doctors affected to explain what had happened, to apologise and provide information and support.

A spokesperson added: "We recognise the concern this will cause to both those impacted personally and other registrants and we are very sorry this happened.

"Our priority continues to be supporting those affected and taking steps to reduce the impact of this incident."

Grand Theft Auto 6 is a masterpiece, say critics

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:34:25 GMT

After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.

Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?

According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.

Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100 - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.

Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.

Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."

But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".

Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.

"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, but he added "there are also nits to pick".

For The New York Times one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.

Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.

But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.

The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".

And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics.

"They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".

Writing for Forbes, Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".

The Washington Post said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review.

"It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it.

"While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."

Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m).

Gaming journalist Jordan Middler is one of the lucky few in the UK who got early access from Rockstar and tells BBC Newsbeat it is the "game of a generation".

He'd played for about 100 hours by the time he hit the credits and says he still has so much to do.

Middler did spot one negative though - he found the game can "slow down" because of how much is going on.

He also says it is "long overdue" that there is a female lead in Lucia.

"The way previous GTA games have dealt with women has been a boys' club approach," he says.

"Introducing Lucia and not making her some kind of token character, she just fits in completely... and she will quickly become a fan favourite without question."

The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.

And despite having not released at the time, GTA 6 was the most-nominated title.

It will be up for eight prizes, including game of the year and best music.

The nomination of Manni L Perez in the best performance category confirmed wide speculation that she is the actress behind main character Lucia in GTA 6 - a fact Rockstar hadn't previously officially confirmed.

The jury for the event is largely made up of gaming journalists around the world, who would have received advanced copies for review.

Some, though, have questioned how a game that has just been released has garnered such positive reviews and award nominations.

There is a view in some online forums that the hype around the game has got out of control as, with one poster commenting: "I think everyone's tired of hearing about this game - I don't even want to play it anymore."

It appears so far, however, that is likely to be very much a minority view.

Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:00:04 GMT

There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.

For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.

With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.

Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.

"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."

The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground – accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.

Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air.

Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place. They have made breaches in the ground, and used welding tools to break through the thick steel.

The Russians were the first to exploit the pipe to infiltrate the nearby city of Kupyansk in September 2025. They have used underground pipelines before, during the capture of the city of Avdiivka in 2024, and last year in their bid to recapture areas of Russia's Kursk region.

But Ukrainian forces have slowly turned the tables.

A specially designed electric cart transports troops and supplies through the pipeline.

They call it the Kupyansk metro. It occasionally breaks down. We travelled on it for 40 minutes, heads bowed and legs crossed. There is a regular bump as you cross the welded sections of the pipe. It is like an austere fairground ride, without the fun.

Our destination was a break in the pipeline where Ukrainian troops have built dug-outs to store ammunition and equipment, with just enough room to stand. It is where the man they call Musician conducts the movement of troops and supplies. He has been living like a mole, his face engrained with dirt and earth.

Musician tells me he has spent the past three months there, with a few brief visits above ground to clean up or go to the toilet. From time to time we can hear the thuds of artillery rounds above. Musician tells me we are close to the line of contact: "But it's safe underground."

The cart continues its journey into the bowels of the earth. It returns about half an hour later with more troops covered in dirt. They have been fighting in positions on the surface.

There is a look of relief on their dust-caked faces.

"It's more comfortable in the pipe because drones don't fly here, and neither do artillery shells or glide bombs," says Vovochka, who has been fighting on the ground for the past three weeks.

But there has been fighting in the pipeline, too. Operation Veles, named after a mythical Slavic god of the underworld, began in April. Since then Ukraine has advanced 15km (9.3 miles) along the pipeline.

It has been painstaking, backbreaking work – with the ever-present fear of coming into contact with the enemy.

Back above ground we meet a few of the soldiers, from the 13th Khartiia Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard, who have taken part in the mission. Their first task was to clear the detritus, water and Russian barricades inside the pipeline.

The Ukrainian troops say some of the barriers were boobytrapped or piled with Russian bodies. "When we moved them or climbed over them, we had no idea what was underneath," says Chyzh.

The other danger, he said, was the ricochets from gunfire when they tried to advance. "You never know where a bullet is going to go or how it will bounce."

His comrade Kort says "we were all firing, we were pushing them back". Over the course of the operation Ukraine says it killed more than 100 Russian soldiers and took 30 prisoners. "Yes, there were bodies," says Kort. "I even had to sleep right next to them."

Their commander's former life as a miner helped prepare them for the physical and psychological challenges of operating underground.

From a building on the surface, Biashym keeps in regular contact with his men still in the pipeline. Behind him is a cabinet full of medicine.

Soldiers in the pipeline spend much of their time on their knees and suffer abrasions. Biashym admits some have had panic attacks from living in such a confined space. Others have struggled to breathe.

Hundreds of Colombian volunteers have also been involved in the operation, part of the RUG 23rd Assault Regiment.

Foreign fighters have helped boost Ukraine's depleted ranks. One of the Colombians, whose call sign is Gecko, tells me it took them 30 days to just clear 500m.

"It was difficult, it was hot and I had fear inside the pipe," he said. "But at some point I just thought, OK, just deal with it and let's advance."

The battle of the pipeline is not over.

Russian forces, like Ukraine's, have built fortified positions inside the pipeline. They still try to infiltrate Ukrainian positions, burrowing their way in and out of the pipe. From a control room above ground we watched Ukrainian drones target another Russian attempt to outflank them.

While some of the fighting taking place underground, there are still battles on the surface and in the air. It has been a combined operation.

But Zanuda, who is chief of the planning section of the 13th Khartiia Brigade, believes it is the best way to fight in the future. "Ground operations are now nearly impossible," he said, adding that "everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground".

There'll be more missions like this, he believes. "Pipelines run everywhere," he said. "You have to remember, back in the Soviet times, oil, gas and ammonia were being transported to Europe, with the entire transit route running through Ukraine."

In reality it has been brutal, gruelling and dangerous work in the harshest of conditions.

It has taken Ukraine seven months to clear 15km of the pipeline.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has hailed it as a success.

It has helped retake lost territory and been a boost for morale, but on its own it has not changed the course of the war.

Additional reporting by Moose Campbell, Volodymyr Lozhko and Rebecca Hartmann

Police investigate death of boy, 3, after nursery incident

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 16:51:58 GMT

An investigation has been launched into the death of a three-year-old boy following an incident at a nursery in Greater Manchester, police said.

The boy became critically ill at Cosy Toes Nursery in Middleton shortly before 16:00 GMT on Monday 2 November.

He was rushed to hospital, where he died three days later.

Greater Manchester Police said his family were being supported by specialist officers.

Det Ch Insp Claire Brennan said: "This is an incredibly tragic development in a deeply upsetting incident and our thoughts remain with the boy's family."

Police said an investigation had been launched in line with standard procedure following a child's death in a care setting.

No arrests have been made at this time.

A spokeswoman for Cosy Toes said they were "all heartbroken" by the "wonderful and beautiful" boy's death.

"Our thoughts and prayers are all with his family at this terrible time," she said.

"We will of course give our fullest possible assistance in every way possible to the enquiries that must rightly follow this tragic event."

Anyone with information about the boy's death is being urged to contact police.

Brennan said: "We are in the very early stages of our involvement and are carefully considering events and the evidence available to us.

"For now, we ask that the family's privacy is respected as they begin to navigate the unimaginable loss of their little boy."

Ofsted said it had taken the decision to suspend the nursery's registration in the wake of the incident, meaning the nursery will be closed for six weeks as investigations are carried out.

A spokesperson said: "Our thoughts are with the family of the young boy and everyone affected by this deeply distressing and tragic incident.

"We have worked closely with the police, and we have suspended the nursery's registration. We will continue to support the police and other agencies in their enquiries. We are unable to comment further while the police investigation is ongoing."

The sandpaper plot - who was there, who said what?

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 16:13:04 GMT

The Australia playing squad and staff were pictured before the third Test against South Africa in 2018

The sandpaper scandal, one of the biggest controversies in the history of Test cricket, continues to engulf Australian sport.

Fresh evidence from Cameron Bancroft - the culprit of the ball-tampering in South Africa in 2018 - has heaped pressure on Australia captain Pat Cummins, former coach Darren Lehmann and Cricket Australia.

In a detailed account of more than 4,000 words published in the West Australian newspaper, Bancroft alleges all the Australia players and coaches present in Cape Town eight years ago knew of the plot.

Bancroft's explosive testimony supports claims made by Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Chadd Sayers.

However, Cummins denied Khawaja's version of events in his own extraordinary news conference in Sydney last week. Cummins spoke to the media for 68 minutes in an address broadcast on live television.

Here, BBC Sport collects the most recent accounts of players and coaches involved in the saga that became widely known as sandpapergate.

TMS podcast: How does Bancroft's revelation impact 'sandpapergate'?

Batter Khawaja played all four Tests in South Africa and a total of 88 for Australia before retiring from international cricket earlier this year.

Revelations in his autobiography reignited debate around the sandpaper scandal and made headlines across the globe.

"It was all of us," Khawaja said. "Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.

"In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.

"Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game. I said, 'Take this as a team'.

"We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team, and so I was always of that stance."

Whole Australia team knew of sandpaper use - Khawaja

Warner was Australia's opening batter and vice-captain during the 2018 series. He, along with captain Steve Smith and Bancroft, were the three players punished for the ball-tampering.

The Cricket Australia (CA) investigation in 2018 found Warner developed the plan and that he instructed Bancroft to carry out the cheating.

After serving his ban, Warner returned to play a further 133 times for Australia across formats, including three Ashes series and the 2023 World Cup win. He retired from international cricket in 2024.

In response to Khawaja's book, Warner said: "I thank you for what you've done. It's 100% accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."

He also accused Cricket Australia of a cover-up, describing the CA investigation as "rushed" and botched".

"As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner said.

"If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?"

Warner accuses Cricket Australia of 'cover-up'

The Cape Town Test was the 13th of Cummins' Test career. A key bowler, he would go on to be named Australia's Test captain in 2021. It is a position he still holds.

Prior to Khawaja's book, Cummins and the other bowlers from Cape Town - Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon - had always denied knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper.

In an extraordinary news conference last week, Cummins called Khawaja's claims that the whole team knew about the plan "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".

"I said that consistently for the last eight years," Cummins said. "I did not know that was happening.

"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."

Asked if he knew of any plans at any stage to tamper with the ball during the series against South Africa, Cummins said: "No."

Cummins also said he did not remember a meeting where Khawaja had called on the team to take collective responsibility - something his former team-mate claimed.

This video can not be played

Complete and utter nonsense - Cummins

Opening batter Bancroft was playing his eighth Test in Cape Town, aged 25. He was the player caught using sandpaper on the field.

He played another two Tests after serving his ban and is still playing for Western Australia. He turns 34 this week.

In 2021, Bancroft said it was "self-explanatory" whether the bowlers knew of the plan, and on Wednesday he backed Khawaja's account, saying Cummins' news conference made him "feel angry, betrayed and alone".

Like Khawaja, Bancroft said sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before he was caught - and also said he had conversations with the Australia seamers about whether the ball was "swinging enough".

He said the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper. He also claimed that coach Lehmann and bowling coach David Saker were present in the initial discussions and that Bancroft's role was also discussed in a team meeting before day three.

In an account published by the West Australian on Wednesday, Bancroft wrote: "All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful.

"Is it going yet? It's not going yet, it needs more. So I would use the sandpaper more on the ball.

"There was even a time I was told to stop out of fear what I was doing was becoming too obvious."

Bancroft sandpaper claims heap pressure on Cummins

Lehmann was Australia coach at the time of the scandal. He was cleared by the CA investigation and said he had "no prior knowledge" of the plan to ball-tamper.

He resigned after the series and has been Northamptonshire coach since the start of the 2025 English season.

After Khawaja's revelations, Lehmann said: "I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball-tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years."

After Cricket Australia said it would hold an open forum, Lehmann said he has "nothing to hide".

Speaking on radio coverage of the third one-day international against England after Bancroft's account was published, Lehmann said: "I need to sit back, process it and work through each allegation.

"That's what I'll be doing over the next few days.

"I need to have a really good read of it. I need to make sure I'm saying what I want to say."

Smith, one of the greatest batters of his generation, was Australia's captain at the time of the scandal.

After serving a 12-month ban, he returned for the World Cup and Ashes the following year and has stood in as captain at times since.

He was found to have been aware of the plan to cheat and to mislead the public and match officials.

Smith, who broke down in tears when apologising at a subsequent news conference, as cameras captured the emotional toll of the moment, has not spoken publicly since Khawaja's book was published.

Speaking about the episode in September this year, he said: "That was a traumatic experience in my life and when I hear the flash of a camera it makes me revisit that in a way.

"I've tried to kind of erase a lot of 2018 and what happened. I can't remember a lot about the series. I've tried to block most of it out of my memory bank."

Marsh was bowling when Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball in Cape Town. As an all-rounder, he was not part of the 2021 bowlers' statement.

Marsh was captain during Australia's recent ODI series against England and refused to answer questions on the topic before the series opener.

"I am not here to share mine [story] today," he said.

"I respect Uzzie [Khawaja] has told his story; my focus is on tomorrow. I am not here to go back on South Africa."

Following the conclusion of the series, Marsh did not take part in his post-match news conference, with 26-year-old bowler Jack Edwards taking his place.

This video can not be played

'I've moved on' - Marsh bats away questions over sandpapergate

Paine was Australia's wicketkeeper during the South Africa series and was made captain when Smith was banned.

He served in the role until he stood down in 2021 over a historical investigation into sexually explicit text messages sent to a female colleague.

In his autobiography, Paine said the suggestion everyone in the Australia dressing room must have known about the sandpaper use is "rubbish" and claimed he first found out when images appeared on the big screen in Cape Town.

"Everyone out there was shocked when they looked up on the big screen and saw Cameron Bancroft with a piece of sandpaper in his hand," Paine wrote. "I was stunned. We all were.

"My heart sank, I was thinking, 'What the f***?' A sense of dread came over us all."

Bancroft said he discussed whether the ball was reversing with Paine during the second Test.

Saker was Australia's bowling coach during the South Africa series.

Bancroft alleged Saker was present for discussions about the use of sandpaper and told the batter he needed to do more to the ball.

Saker was also England bowling coach as recently as last month's tri-series in Pakistan. He was an influential part of England's 2010-11 Ashes win.

In 2021, reflecting on the sandpaper saga, Saker said: "Obviously a lot of things went wrong at that time. There was a lot of people to blame. It could have been me to blame, it could have been someone else. It could have been stopped and it wasn't, which is unfortunate.

"Cameron's a very nice guy. He's just doing it to get something off his chest… He's not going to be the last. You could point your finger at me, you could point your finger at Boof [Lehmann]. Could you point it at other people? Of course you could.

"The disappointing thing is it's never going to go away. Regardless of what's said. We all know that we made a monumental mistake. The gravity wasn't as plain until it all came out."

Starc was an integral part of the vaunted Australia attack in Cape Town and remains so in the present day. He is ranked as the number one bowler in Test cricket by the International Cricket Council.

Left-armer Starc repeatedly denied knowledge of the sandpaper plot, including in the statement released with Cummins, Hazlewood and Lyon in 2021, and in a news conference in the days after Khawaja's claims emerged.

Speaking on 10 November, Starc said: "Obviously, there's differing opinions of eight years ago. We were heavily grilled through the process at the time, and since, and I guess I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers, but where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed. My recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.

"I'll stick to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time, eight years ago. Clearly, there's different versions from different people, and I'll leave it where I left it back then."

Along with Cummins and Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon have remained part of Australia's first-choice bowling unit in the eight years since the sandpaper scandal, forming one of the greatest four-man attacks in Test history.

Seamer Hazlewood and off-spinner Lyon joined Cummins and Starc in releasing a statement in 2021, responding to an interview given by Bancroft to the Guardian newspaper when he said the bowlers' involvement in the sandpaper plot was "self-explanatory".

Neither Hazlewood nor Lyon has spoken publicly since the fresh claims from Khawaja, Warner and Bancroft emerged.

Their statement released with Cummins and Starc in 2021 said: "We pride ourselves on our honesty. So it's been disappointing to see that our integrity has been questioned by some journalists and past players in recent days in regard to the Cape Town Test of 2018.

"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands.

"We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."

A swing bowler, Sayers played his only Test for Australia after the sandpaper controversy erupted – the fourth and final match of the series against South Africa in Johannesburg.

Sayers, who retired from first-class cricket in 2021, spoke to Australian radio station SEN in the aftermath of Khawaja's claims, to corroborate the former batter's account.

Sayers claimed to have removed sandpaper from the field in the second Test against South Africa, the match before Bancroft was caught. He also backed up Khawaja's assertion that the entire Australia squad discussed the sandpaper issue after it was revealed in Cape Town.

Speaking on 15 November, Sayers said: "I am comfortable sitting here that I believe everyone in that side knew what was going on and what was being used.

"It was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in the changing rooms.

"After the occurrence in Cape Town, we all sat in the changing rooms after that day's play and, probably for 60 to 90 minutes, we talked about what had happened and I guess where to next."

Spinner Holland, who retired in 2021, was also a back-up bowler on the trip.

He also said there was a meeting held in the fallout from Cape Town about players taking responsibility.

"Once we got back to the hotel we did sit as a group [to discuss] what had happened and who was going to take the blame," Holland told newspaper The Australian.

"To Davey's [Warner's] credit, from what I remember, he did put his hand up and say he would take some of the responsibility, but not all of it.

"To be sitting there and seeing three blokes hung out to dry when you are supposed to be part of a team was a pretty hard watch."

Australia's Sayers 'took sandpaper from field'

Batter Handscomb was Australia's 12th man on the day Bancroft was caught, making frequent trips between the field and the dressing room.

Bancroft's account alleges Handscomb was told by Lehmann, via walkie-talkie, to "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".

Last week, following Khawaja's claims but before Bancroft spoke, Handscomb was asked for his recollections after making a century for Victoria in the Sheffield Shield against Western Australia.

On 11 November, Handscomb said: "I appreciate you have to ask these questions. I've had a nice day today, it's not really something that I want to comment on right now. I'll sort of just let the powers of be do their thing."

Former England batter Hick was part of the Australia backroom team on the South Africa tour of 2018.

Hick was made redundant by Cricket Australia as part of a series of cost-cutting measures in 2020.

Speaking to the Sydney Morning Herald last week, Hick said: "I have seen the various statements around the coaches, and I'm very disappointed with the broad nature of them.

"Khawaja puts it simply: 'It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us'. To me, what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false.

"In regard to any discussions around the ball-tampering in Port Elizabeth or Cape Town, I will say in true honesty that I did not hear or know anything.

"My first knowledge of all this was, like many, when it appeared on the big screen in Cape Town as I was sat on the outside balcony at the time."

The sandpaper plot - who was there, who said what?

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 16:13:04 GMT

The Australia playing squad and staff were pictured before the third Test against South Africa in 2018

The sandpaper scandal, one of the biggest controversies in the history of Test cricket, continues to engulf Australian sport.

Fresh evidence from Cameron Bancroft - the culprit of the ball-tampering in South Africa in 2018 - has heaped pressure on Australia captain Pat Cummins, former coach Darren Lehmann and Cricket Australia.

In a detailed account of more than 4,000 words published in the West Australian newspaper, Bancroft alleges all the Australia players and coaches present in Cape Town eight years ago knew of the plot.

Bancroft's explosive testimony supports claims made by Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Chadd Sayers.

However, Cummins denied Khawaja's version of events in his own extraordinary news conference in Sydney last week. Cummins spoke to the media for 68 minutes in an address broadcast on live television.

Here, BBC Sport collects the most recent accounts of players and coaches involved in the saga that became widely known as sandpapergate.

TMS podcast: How does Bancroft's revelation impact 'sandpapergate'?

Batter Khawaja played all four Tests in South Africa and a total of 88 for Australia before retiring from international cricket earlier this year.

Revelations in his autobiography reignited debate around the sandpaper scandal and made headlines across the globe.

"It was all of us," Khawaja said. "Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.

"In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.

"Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game. I said, 'Take this as a team'.

"We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team, and so I was always of that stance."

Whole Australia team knew of sandpaper use - Khawaja

Warner was Australia's opening batter and vice-captain during the 2018 series. He, along with captain Steve Smith and Bancroft, were the three players punished for the ball-tampering.

The Cricket Australia (CA) investigation in 2018 found Warner developed the plan and that he instructed Bancroft to carry out the cheating.

After serving his ban, Warner returned to play a further 133 times for Australia across formats, including three Ashes series and the 2023 World Cup win. He retired from international cricket in 2024.

In response to Khawaja's book, Warner said: "I thank you for what you've done. It's 100% accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."

He also accused Cricket Australia of a cover-up, describing the CA investigation as "rushed" and botched".

"As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner said.

"If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?"

Warner accuses Cricket Australia of 'cover-up'

The Cape Town Test was the 13th of Cummins' Test career. A key bowler, he would go on to be named Australia's Test captain in 2021. It is a position he still holds.

Prior to Khawaja's book, Cummins and the other bowlers from Cape Town - Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon - had always denied knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper.

In an extraordinary news conference last week, Cummins called Khawaja's claims that the whole team knew about the plan "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".

"I said that consistently for the last eight years," Cummins said. "I did not know that was happening.

"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."

Asked if he knew of any plans at any stage to tamper with the ball during the series against South Africa, Cummins said: "No."

Cummins also said he did not remember a meeting where Khawaja had called on the team to take collective responsibility - something his former team-mate claimed.

This video can not be played

Complete and utter nonsense - Cummins

Opening batter Bancroft was playing his eighth Test in Cape Town, aged 25. He was the player caught using sandpaper on the field.

He played another two Tests after serving his ban and is still playing for Western Australia. He turns 34 this week.

In 2021, Bancroft said it was "self-explanatory" whether the bowlers knew of the plan, and on Wednesday he backed Khawaja's account, saying Cummins' news conference made him "feel angry, betrayed and alone".

Like Khawaja, Bancroft said sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before he was caught - and also said he had conversations with the Australia seamers about whether the ball was "swinging enough".

He said the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper. He also claimed that coach Lehmann and bowling coach David Saker were present in the initial discussions and that Bancroft's role was also discussed in a team meeting before day three.

In an account published by the West Australian on Wednesday, Bancroft wrote: "All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful.

"Is it going yet? It's not going yet, it needs more. So I would use the sandpaper more on the ball.

"There was even a time I was told to stop out of fear what I was doing was becoming too obvious."

Bancroft sandpaper claims heap pressure on Cummins

Lehmann was Australia coach at the time of the scandal. He was cleared by the CA investigation and said he had "no prior knowledge" of the plan to ball-tamper.

He resigned after the series and has been Northamptonshire coach since the start of the 2025 English season.

After Khawaja's revelations, Lehmann said: "I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball-tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years."

After Cricket Australia said it would hold an open forum, Lehmann said he has "nothing to hide".

Speaking on radio coverage of the third one-day international against England after Bancroft's account was published, Lehmann said: "I need to sit back, process it and work through each allegation.

"That's what I'll be doing over the next few days.

"I need to have a really good read of it. I need to make sure I'm saying what I want to say."

Smith, one of the greatest batters of his generation, was Australia's captain at the time of the scandal.

After serving a 12-month ban, he returned for the World Cup and Ashes the following year and has stood in as captain at times since.

He was found to have been aware of the plan to cheat and to mislead the public and match officials.

Smith, who broke down in tears when apologising at a subsequent news conference, as cameras captured the emotional toll of the moment, has not spoken publicly since Khawaja's book was published.

Speaking about the episode in September this year, he said: "That was a traumatic experience in my life and when I hear the flash of a camera it makes me revisit that in a way.

"I've tried to kind of erase a lot of 2018 and what happened. I can't remember a lot about the series. I've tried to block most of it out of my memory bank."

Marsh was bowling when Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball in Cape Town. As an all-rounder, he was not part of the 2021 bowlers' statement.

Marsh was captain during Australia's recent ODI series against England and refused to answer questions on the topic before the series opener.

"I am not here to share mine [story] today," he said.

"I respect Uzzie [Khawaja] has told his story; my focus is on tomorrow. I am not here to go back on South Africa."

Following the conclusion of the series, Marsh did not take part in his post-match news conference, with 26-year-old bowler Jack Edwards taking his place.

This video can not be played

'I've moved on' - Marsh bats away questions over sandpapergate

Paine was Australia's wicketkeeper during the South Africa series and was made captain when Smith was banned.

He served in the role until he stood down in 2021 over a historical investigation into sexually explicit text messages sent to a female colleague.

In his autobiography, Paine said the suggestion everyone in the Australia dressing room must have known about the sandpaper use is "rubbish" and claimed he first found out when images appeared on the big screen in Cape Town.

"Everyone out there was shocked when they looked up on the big screen and saw Cameron Bancroft with a piece of sandpaper in his hand," Paine wrote. "I was stunned. We all were.

"My heart sank, I was thinking, 'What the f***?' A sense of dread came over us all."

Bancroft said he discussed whether the ball was reversing with Paine during the second Test.

Saker was Australia's bowling coach during the South Africa series.

Bancroft alleged Saker was present for discussions about the use of sandpaper and told the batter he needed to do more to the ball.

Saker was also England bowling coach as recently as last month's tri-series in Pakistan. He was an influential part of England's 2010-11 Ashes win.

In 2021, reflecting on the sandpaper saga, Saker said: "Obviously a lot of things went wrong at that time. There was a lot of people to blame. It could have been me to blame, it could have been someone else. It could have been stopped and it wasn't, which is unfortunate.

"Cameron's a very nice guy. He's just doing it to get something off his chest… He's not going to be the last. You could point your finger at me, you could point your finger at Boof [Lehmann]. Could you point it at other people? Of course you could.

"The disappointing thing is it's never going to go away. Regardless of what's said. We all know that we made a monumental mistake. The gravity wasn't as plain until it all came out."

The tightest survival scrap for years? Why it's not too early to worry

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 16:09:55 GMT

Is it too early for the Premier League bottom three to worry?

Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.

But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.

Two of the current bottom three, Crystal Palace and Manchester United, will resume their campaigns at the weekend with new managers after appointing Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino respectively.

Sunderland, wedged between the pair in 19th, have not pressed the panic button and have kept faith with Regis le Bris.

But is it too early to worry? We look at what the stats tell us about relegation battles in the past and what we can learn for the months ahead.

Looking at every Premier League season since it changed to a 20-team league in 1995-96, the current bottom three have cause to be concerned.

In 19 of the previous 31 seasons (61%), only one of the bottom three sides after 10 games managed to avoid relegation.

For fairness and accuracy, the 'bottom three' are the three sides with the worst record after 10 games, not simply those in the relegation zone after matchweek 10, since in some seasons a team had played nine games by that point.

Only in 10 seasons (32%) have two or more of the bottom three stayed up - and that has not happened in any of the past eight campaigns. The last time more than one team avoided the drop was in 2017-18, when all three survived.

That has only happened twice, although only twice have all three sides been relegated.

Overall, of the 93 previous teams in the bottom three after 10 games, 41 survived and 52 were relegated - a survival rate of 44%.

This is the third time that Palace have been bottom after 10 games. On both previous occasions, they did not just survive but thrived, finishing 11th.

They did so under Tony Pulis in 2013-14 and under Roy Hodgson in 2017-18. Both managers, like Frank, were appointed early in the season following poor starts under Ian Holloway and Frank de Boer respectively.

The 2013-14 season is the only previous time that Sunderland and Palace were the bottom two at this stage. The Black Cats also survived thanks to a great, late escape under Gus Poyet.

This is the first time United have been in the bottom three after 10 games of a Premier League season.

Given the size and resources of the club, it is unlikely they will go down, although the team in 18th place at this stage have been relegated in each of the past six seasons.

Fans of all three clubs will hope for a repeat of 2017-18, when not only Palace but the bottom three improved significantly to finish comfortably mid-table.

While history suggests only one of the bottom three will survive, there is also evidence to suggest that this might not be a standard Premier League season.

Palace have seven points, which is the most the bottom side after 10 games have had for 24 years. The bottom three all had eight points in 2002-03.

Sunderland's eight points is also the most that a side in 19th place have had for 16 years. Wolves had nine points in 2010-11 and survived in 17th.

In fact, only five points separate the bottom half of the Premier League, with Tottenham in 11th on 12 points and Palace bottom with seven – the smallest gap at this stage for 24 years.

The highest that a team in the bottom three after 10 games have finished the season is eighth - Bolton in 2003-04, Tottenham in 2008-09 and Everton in 2017-18 - which suggests it will be Conference League at best for Manchester United next season.

Then again, the table is so tight that only nine points separate Chelsea in fifth and Palace - the smallest gap at this stage for 16 years.

Given that fifth place has been enough to qualify for the Champions League in recent seasons, optimistic United fans may not be ruling it out just yet.

That means even sides who have started well could be involved in the relegation battle.

The most points a team have had after 10 games of a 38-game season and been relegated is 14 - Joe Royle's Manchester City in 2000-01.

The most recent team to start well but be relegated were Eddie Howe's Bournemouth in 2019-20, who were sitting pretty in ninth with 13 points at this stage but went down on the final day.

As mentioned, this season has both the 'best' bottom side in terms of points and the most compact bottom half of the table that we have seen at this stage since 2002-03.

In that season, West Ham were relegated on the final day with 42 points - the most a side have been relegated with in Premier League history.

Given the way this season is shaping up, 40 points might also not be enough to survive.
