Alcaraz continues winning run despite injury concern

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 16:01:47 GMT

Carlos Alcaraz was denied a first ATP Finals triumph by Jannik Sinner in last year's final

Carlos Alcaraz continued his sensational late-season form as he outclassed world number five Daniil Medvedev to all but confirm his progress at the ATP Finals.

But the 23-year-old Spaniard later said he had felt "a little problem" with his hamstring.

Alcaraz produced another sparkling display to control the contest throughout, despite ending the match with heavy strapping on his upper-left leg.

The issue did not disrupt the world number three, who led by a set and a break when he received treatment on the area, as he cruised to a 6-2 6-4 win in just 72 minutes.

"Right now I'm just feeling OK," Alcaraz said.

"We will see with my team and physio, but I think the rest of today and tomorrow are really going to be important days ahead of me."

It was an 11th consecutive victory for the seven-time major winner, following back-to-back titles at the Vienna Open and Paris Masters.

Alcaraz will qualify for the semi-finals before his last group match against Flavio Cobolli on Friday if Frances Tiafoe wins a set against the Italian later on Wednesday.

Asked what pleased him most about his performance, Alcaraz replied: "Everything".

"We could see in [Medvedev's] first match that he was serving very well. I returned really well, really aggressively, and really deep," he added.

"I think I just hit the ball in a sweet spot every time. I'm really happy about it."

Ruthless Zverev through to ATP Finals knockout stage

GB's Patten criticises ATP chairman and CEO for absence

Given the outstanding levels at which he is currently operating, it is easy to forget that Alcaraz spent four months out of action in the middle of the season.

The former world number one's rapid return from that wrist injury to his scintillating best has been astonishing.

Alcaraz has won three titles and lost just twice in 24 matches since making his return at the US Open in August, when his lack of match fitness appeared to catch up with him in a four-and-a-half hour epic against Ben Shelton.

Just 10 weeks on, he delivered one of the best indoor performances of his career in sweeping past 2020 champion Medvedev.

That came two days after he began his latest bid for a first ATP Finals title with a statement victory over Tiafoe - and later warned his rivals he has never felt better at this stage of the season.

Medvedev beat home hope Cobolli in straight sets in his opening match for his first win against a top-10 opponent since defeating Alcaraz at Indian Wells in March.

The Russian was no match for the Australian Open champion on this occasion, however.

A dominant seven-game streak ultimately decided the match, as Alcaraz ran away with the first set and then broke immediately in the second to take firm control.

The second seed did not face a single break point as he outmanoeuvred Medvedev, firing 16 winners and committing just 13 unforced errors.

It was a display which scored 9.5 out of 10 on the ATP's performance rating, which combines several statistics to measure a player's overall game, following a 9.6 in his opener.

That was despite Alcaraz playing the final seven games with the issue in his hamstring, which he will now work to overcome in the next 48 hours.

Parents jailed for torture and death of four-year-old girl in France in 1987

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 15:39:57 GMT

The mother of a four-year-old girl killed in central France and found along a motorway almost 40 years ago has been sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Halima El Bakhti, 72, was found guilty on Tuesday of "torture and acts of barbarity resulting in death without the intent to kill", French media reports.

The girl's father, 74-year-old Ahmed Touloub, was handed a 15-year sentence as an accomplice.

Four-year-old Inass Touloub was found along the A10 road in Suèvres in the Loir-et-Cher department on 11 August 1987. Her body bore multiple marks of abuse, including human bite marks, broken bones and burns with an iron.

She was buried in an unmarked grave near the location where her body was found. Unidentified for three decades, she was known only as the "Little Martyr of the A10".

Then, in 2018, she was identified after the DNA of her brother – tested in an unrelated case – matched with hers, leading to the arrest of their parents.

The trial took place in Loir-et-Cher Assize Court from 2 November, with the verdict delivered on Tuesday after several hours of deliberation.

During the trial, prosecutor Anaïs Allio emphasised that "not a single part of Inass's body was spared", and recalled the "sense of vertigo that overcame us all" upon viewing the "unbearable photographs" from the autopsy, France Info reports.

The jury concluded that the child's mother was suffering from impaired judgement at the time of the girl's death, which reduced the maximum potential sentence.

French media outlet France Info described the two defendants as sitting stoically in chairs before the court with their heads bowed as the reasoning behind the verdict was read out.

El Bakhti and Touloub have 10 days to appeal the verdict.

Inass's death sparked one of France's biggest ever investigations, with the girl's photograph posted in public places and an alert sent to more than 30 countries.

Divide and conquer - now maverick Erasmus plans online watchalong

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 15:02:01 GMT

Rassie Erasmus took the South Africa job after the departure of Allister Coetzee

Having been banned from the touchline for six matches, you will not find Rassie Erasmus at the Aviva Stadium when his South Africa side face Ireland.

Instead he will be hosting an online watchalong of Saturday's match, courtesy of a swiftly purchased domain name.

The South Africa head coach plans to stream his reactions live while watching on television from his team's Dublin hotel.

It is typical Erasmus. An unapologetic, unabashed show of defiance in the face of the authorities.

And he will not be short of virtual company.

Because, while Erasmus has run low of advocates elsewhere, his compatriots have rushed to his defence.

"Rassie was just asking questions," said former South Africa hooker Hanyani Shimange in the wake of Erasmus' ban for a scattergun series of complaints about the injustices suffered by his side.

"But you have to look at the facts. Where was the accountability for that refereeing performance [in the loss to France]?"

Naas Botha, legendary South Africa fly-half turned pundit, described Erasmus' punishment as a "debacle". "You can't tell me [officials] are untouchable," he said.

Supersport, which broadcasts South Africa's games domestically, published an article accusing Erasmus' critics of "pearl clutching", external and "shooting the messenger" with regards to the game's faults.

Despite slurring officials with a suggestion of match-fixing, Erasmus has the support of South Africa.

It is not surprising.

His feats with the team are astonishing.

South Africa were ranked sixth in the world when he took over in March 2018.

He arrived after a November tour in which they lost to Wales and were thrashed 38-3 by Ireland. New Zealand had racked up a record 57-0 win a few months earlier.

Erasmus turned the team around at speed, marrying their trademark up-front power with pace out wide.

They won the 2019 World Cup. The defended their title in 2023. They will go into the tournament in 2027 aiming for an unprecedented hat-trick. And few would bet against them achieving it.

Erasmus is relentlessly innovative.

Long before the sport's data revolution, he was coding game footage, picking up the technique from a friend who worked in the military. He has since developed Outfox, his own software which allows his teams to run through moves virtually on a screen away from the pitch.

Tactically, he has also been ahead of the curve. He pioneered the use of forward-heavy replacement benches, giving his team an edge in the final quarter of the match.

He saw the game-breaking potential of diminutive Sevens specialist Kurt-Lee Arendse and moulded Andre Esterhuizen into a genuine hybrid player, capable of playing in the back row and the backline.

Trick plays - forcing a scrum with a deliberate infringement off kick-off, or setting up a line-out in the middle of the pitch - have been part of Erasmus' arsenal.

Legally, he is across every possible loophole.

There was controversy before the match against France last weekend when he made use of the Nations Championships' looser regulations to swap his starting front row just over an hour before kick-off.

Previously, he demoted himself to water boy so he could run the touchline during the 2021 series win over the British and Irish Lions.

Former Springbok wing Bryan Habana worked under Erasmus at the Stormers in Cape Town.

"He is one of the master tacticians the game has ever seen," Habana told BBC Sport's Ireland Rugby Social.

"I don't always agree with how Rassie comes across, but I understand he wears his heart on his sleeve. He has got incredibly high standards.

"He's willing to be in the firing line to defend what he believes is right."

France's win over South Africa was only the Springboks' third defeat in 11 matches this year

But there is no doubt, by the letter of the law, that Erasmus is wrong - certainly in terms of the platform and terms he chose for his complaints.

In July World Rugby introduced new rules around criticism of officials. It specifically targeted "comments which, viewed objectively, a reasonable person would conclude were an attack on the credibility or competence of the match officials".

Mentioning "match-fixing" undermines the officials in exactly that way.

Considering Erasmus' previous, including an hour-long monologue bemoaning officiating of a first-Test defeat by the Lions in 2021 and a series of tweets after a loss to France a year later, he may be fortunate to only be banned for six matches.

World Rugby, perhaps pre-empting the reaction in South Africa, was clear that it was not punishing Erasmus for asking questions.

"Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches," it said in its judgement.

"Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official's integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse."

For many South Africans, though, Erasmus is still an outlaw hero.

World Rugby, based in Dublin, is seen by them as tilted towards the north.

Australian Brett Robinson, the current chairman, is the first figure from outside the Six Nations countries to hold the organisation's top job since it became an elected position.

The World Cup has been lifted by South Africa on four occasions, but held there only once.

Japan coach Eddie Jones, Erasmus' fellow maverick, recently suggested Ireland's political clout, external was behind his team's home game being staged in Australia rather than Tokyo.

South Africa were a powerful voice against the possible moves to "depower" the scrum - a key part of the Springbok game - at a February conference to discuss future law tweaks.

Erasmus' public pronouncements have fuelled conspiracy theories weaved from those threads. They have also made an all-time great team harder for outsiders to love.

Whether it is a deliberate ploy is hard to tell.

Certainly Erasmus is a repeat offender, but his offences have also come in his second language. He is an Afrikaans speaker.

Some also see instinctive honesty rather than a premeditated ploy in his public speaking.

"He also has almost no filters, so he will speak his mind without fully appreciating the consequences of what he has done," his biographer David O'Sullivan told BBC Sport in 2023.

Whatever the motivation, the consequences keep coming - for Erasmus, but also the rest of world rugby.

Referees Nic Berry and Wayne Barnes, previous targets of Erasmus' criticism, have detailed the effects it had on them.

Berry described "a character assassination" that caused "immeasurable damage". He has not refereed a South Africa game in the five years since.

Barnes' wife and children were threatened over social media.

South Africa's latest appeal to their supporters not to abuse officials, external may be too late for referee Andrea Piardi and his television match official Matteo Liperini, who oversaw France's win on Friday.

There is a wider question too.

For a complex sport, the image of a world champion coach publicly criticising officials does not little to dispel a wavering viewer's assumption that it is too intricate and confusing to justify their attention.

South Africa will always line up alongside their rebel chief.

But the patience of the rest of the rugby world with Erasmus' antics is wearing ever thinner.

The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 13:55:14 GMT

In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.

The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.

Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.

If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.

So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?

In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.

He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.

Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.

Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.

But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.

Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".

Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.

She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.

Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.

She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.

The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.

Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.

He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.

Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.

He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".

Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.

Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.

He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.

Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.

Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.

He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.

His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.

Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.

But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.

Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.

He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.

The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.

Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.

McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.

He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 13:17:06 GMT

Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to jump by £443 a year from January as the inflation rate rose to its highest level in a year.

A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, ahead of the official announcement next week.

Some households will get a £100 payment to help with the rising cost of living, a policy which was announced in the Budget.

Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices, official figures show.

Inflation has been driven higher in recent months as the US-Israel war with Iran has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.

In response to prices surging, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month, in a bid to slow inflation to its target of 2%.

Interest rates increased from 3.75% to 4%, and the Bank signalled a further rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.

Higher interest rates lift the cost of borrowing for some mortgages, loans and credit cards, but can also lead to a better return on savings.

Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was providing help for households with energy costs.

VAT has been cut on electricity bills to zero until next July and the government will also hand £100 to 20 million homes in January.

But with annual household energy bills forecast to reach £2,166, Cornwall Insight's retail markets principal, Craig Lowrey, said that "ultimately this support can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East".

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: "Affordability is my number one priority, and I will continue driving towards cheap, clean power."

Sophie, who manages a cafe in Brighton, told the BBC she watches her smart meter at home "like a hawk".

"I'm very conscious of the cost of energy, and it is having an impact on how we function in the home as a family," she said.

"I try to cook using the oven a lot less than I used to. We haven't got the heating on yet in our household. We're just like 'wear more layers'. We've got electric blankets on the sofa."

Shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, said four successive rises in the inflation rate was down to the UK's "soaring energy costs" and Labour's decision to "hike taxes and employment costs".

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS, said fuel prices were "once again a major contributor" to the increase in the inflation rate in October.

Rising energy prices can lead to more expensive food and staples for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs.

Earlier this month, the Bank of England said there had been "limited evidence" of this, with some firms absorbing cost increases and accepting lower profit margins.

But Fitzner said on Wednesday: "Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively."

Petrol prices rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October, the ONS said, with the average price last month hitting 174.7p per litre - the highest since August 2022.

Diesel prices, meanwhile, reached the highest price since records began 30 years ago, averaging 199.5p per litre in October.

But the ONS said price inflation in restaurants and cafes had slowed last month, and that prices had fallen on average for hotels.

And food price inflation rose by 0.9%, the slowest pace in five years.

Core inflation, which strips out energy and food costs, and services inflation were little changed on last month. The figure is closely watched by the Bank of England when setting interest rates.

It could mean the Bank opts to hold off on a further rate rise in December, though policymakers believe inflation could peak at 4.9% in the middle of next year and not return to 2% until 2028.

In an "adverse scenario", where the US-Iran war could escalate further and send oil prices higher, inflation could reach 6.2% in 2027, it has suggested.

A spokesperson for the Bank said it decided to raise rates two weeks ago to "limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2% target and stays there".

Additional reporting by Raphael Sheridan, economics producer

Heating bills, chocolate and cat food: What the inflation figures mean for you

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 13:10:01 GMT

Nobody will be celebrating the fact that prices in the UK are rising at the fastest pace for a year.

Add to that an expectation of higher household energy bills and sharpening price increases and things look grim for everyone.

But there are some signs of hope that may take the edge off the rising cost of living. Here's how.

That headline is not missing a decimal point. The latest prediction for the increase in domestic energy prices in the new year is, indeed, 26%.

Millions of homes in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap, which is set every three months. The next change for January will be officially announced next Wednesday, 25 November.

Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, which has a good track record with its predictions, suggests that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £2,166 a year - that's an increase of £443 from current levels.

Not all energy use for the year is between January and March, but a big chunk is owing to the cold, dark days and nights.

How much you pay depends on your use, with heavy users of gas likely to be the hardest hit.

The government has promised a £100 payment for people living in homes in council tax bands A to D in England to help cover winter energy costs. Other nations are planning similar support.

The latest inflation data shows that government assistance can have an impact on the general rate of inflation, as recorded by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Domestic energy prices rose by nearly 4% in October, but this was offset in inflationary terms by a cut in VAT on electricity bills.

While the rate of inflation in general was 3.6% in the year to October, food prices only went up by 0.9%.

So why the difference?

It is partly the result of intense competition between the supermarkets. Like many retailers, they are facing higher costs but are not passing that onto their customers in full.

There may be some scars from the recent cost-of-living spike here. Shoppers suffered a period during the big rise in inflation in 2022-23 when food prices rocketed.

Those higher prices are embedded. While food prices overall aren't coming down now, they aren't rising anywhere near as fast as back then.

The detail here is very interesting. Take chocolate: world cocoa prices are down since 2024, and now chocolate prices are falling - down 2.9%, according to the latest data.

But the ONS has also pointed to cat food as one, albeit small, driver of the faster rate of rising prices.

Should high energy and fuel costs - which are driving the rising rate of inflation - persist, there are questions over whether the cost of producing and transporting food also goes up, and the chances of that higher cost being passed on to consumers are greater.

Economists have been closely studying whether there are any signs of those so-called second-round effects - where an initial price shock spreads to wages, services and broader consumer prices. So far, there are relatively few.

Food is, of course, a necessity.

If prices rise then it takes a bigger chunk of people's income and so has a deeper impact on those whose finances are already stretched, so the latest data on food prices is good news for many people.

One set of economists who will consider whether there is evidence of second-round effects are the nine people who set interest rates, which heavily influences the cost of borrowing money - such as mortgages - as well as the returns people get on savings.

The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee meets again in December and, after that, in February.

Having just raised interest rates - for the first time in more than three years - to 4%, there's a widespread expectation among analysts that another hike is to come.

To be clear, we don't know if and when that will happen for sure.

The case for an increase would be if prices continue to accelerate. The Bank will want to slow that down.

The case against would be price rises remaining relatively confined to energy-related costs. Any easing of Middle East tensions could limit price rises without Bank of England intervention.

As far as wages are concerned, the latest official data suggests that rising prices are largely covered by rising pay.

That is an average - so is not true for everyone - but how long it remains the case may be key to how deep upcoming price rises cut into our personal finances.

Minister criticises media for 'amplifying' Russell Brand's prison message

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 12:11:39 GMT

Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell has criticised media organisations for broadcasting a message from the wife of jailed rapist Russell Brand on his behalf.

Laura Brand read out the message on the disgraced comedian's YouTube channel on Sunday, in which he said he was not guilty of the offences for which he is serving a 10-and-a-half year prison sentence.

The message has prompted an official investigation into whether Brand broke prison rules.

The clip of Laura Brand has been played on outlets including BBC Radio 4's Today programme, ITV's This Morning, Sky News, LBC and the News Agents podcast. On Wednesday, Education Secretary Powell said the media should not have "amplified" his words.

"I was appalled at that [message] and actually I think mainstream media shouldn't have transmitted that either," she told LBC on Wednesday.

"It's a platform I don't think should have been amplified, to be honest."

Powell went on to describe Russell Brand as "someone who's not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims".

She continued: "This is somebody who's been convicted and found guilty of very, very serious offences and rape."

In a statement, the BBC said the Today programme had played the Laura Brand clip "in error, due to miscommunication within the team", and had since removed it from catch-up service BBC Sounds.

BBC News has asked the other outlets named above for a comment.

ITN News chief executive Ian Rumsey told BBC Radio 4's The Media Show that the company's newsrooms, including ITV News and Channel 4 News, took the decision not to play the video.

He said: "You didn't need to show it. You could discuss, you could describe what it was, and I'm very pleased and proud that every area of ITN chose not to show it at all, and I think that's exactly the right decision."

YouTube said it is aware of the video and investigating, and that Brand's channel on the platform hasn't been able to make money since being suspended from its advert revenue scheme for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy" after allegations against him emerged in 2023. But the channel is still available to view.

Brand's social media accounts on Meta platforms - which owns Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - were disabled last week.

Earlier this week, Downing Street officials described Brand's message to his followers as "clearly appalling", adding that it was being urgently investigated.

No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.

"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."

Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin

BBC News Wed, 18 Nov 2026 10:53:21 GMT

The meeting hasn't even happened yet.

But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kremlin.

Whatever the outcome.

Think back to 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine President Putin was an international pariah. Western leaders were determined to isolate him and his country over the war in Ukraine.

Fast forward to 2026: Vladimir Putin has secured an historic meeting in Shenzhen. For the first time in history, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will sit down – just the three of them – for talks.

That puts Putin exactly where he wants to be: at the top table of global politics, rubbing shoulders with the leaders of the two great powers.

It allows him to boast that Western pressure on Russia has failed.

"We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure," Putin told a business forum of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation organisation.

That was followed by a meeting with Xi Jinping.

But the Kremlin says the "showstopper" event in Shenzhen will be Putin's trilateral with Xi and Trump.

It allows him to play global statesman, even as the Russian military continues to pound Ukrainian towns and cities, and the Kremlin continues to reject the idea of an unconditional, comprehensive ceasefire.

One short meeting is unlikely to reshape the world. But it's the optics that are key. The picture. The photo-op. Three leaders, three big powers, discussing big issues.

In a way, Vladimir Putin will use this meeting to send a holiday postcard to the rest of the world. Instead of "Wish you were here", he'll sign it: "Look: I'm here."

But what of those who are not at the table?

Among European leaders, and especially in Ukraine, there is concern that the three-way meeting might produce more than just a pretty picture, though not in a good way for Kyiv.

Donald Trump has already said that in Shenzhen he wants to discuss his "favourite subject" - the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin would likely welcome an opportunity to argue its case to Trump and Xi without Ukrainian officials or European leaders in the room.

Last month Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed concern that the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting might resemble the Yalta Conference of 1945. That is when the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States – Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt - met to re-organise post-World War Two Europe.

"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," said Zelensky.

It is unclear whether China would want the Ukraine war on the agenda in Shenzhen. In its official statements on the upcoming trilateral meeting, Beijing has talked more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".

In Shenzhen, Russia will make the most of the optics. But a diplomatic victory is not the same as a military one.

Nearly five years after President Putin launched his so-called "special military operation", Russia is still struggling to win its war on Ukraine.

Over this time, it has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.

And the Ukrainian strike on the road bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula – carried out on the eve of the summit - was a blow to Moscow's prestige. The attack severely damaged part of the multi-billion-dollar bridge built by Russia after it annexed Crimea from Ukraine.

The damage is not only a logistical headache for the Russian authorities.

It is a reminder that the Kremlin's "special operation" has not gone at all to plan.

The Shenzhen summit may give Vladimir Putin a big stage, and a bright spotlight.

It does not necessarily bring him closer to winning the war.

32 years of nominative determinism: New Scientist’s gift to the world

New Scientist November 18, 2026

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

That creaking sound you just heard was Feedback’s ageing joints as we painfully sat down to type out this commemorative column. We have been here for a considerable number of decades, to the point that our recollection of our earliest missives has become faded and confused.

Indeed, Feedback’s history is long and storied, to the point that it would defy the efforts of even the most conscientious biographer. We have been through many incarnations, most of whom went on to do far more felicitous things with their lives. It is a little-discussed fact, one not even known to reality, that a previous Feedback helped David Foster Wallace out by composing Infinite Jest over the course of a bank holiday weekend. We’re told that former Feedbacks also secretly performed the guitar solos on Stairway to Heaven and Killing in the Name.

Advertisement

For these reasons, most incarnations of Feedback were and are anonymous. Indeed, the identity of the current Feedback is known only to the king, the prime minister and the head of MI5. This anonymity has its drawbacks: our collective memory only stretches back so far. Thankfully, our editor took it upon themselves to venture into the New Scientist archive, in search of the first Feedbacks. It is difficult to fully convey what the archive is like, but if you imagine the warehouse at the end of Raiders of the Lost Ark and then insert a leaking roof and a surfeit of rats, your mental image will not be too badly astray.

Escaping with only a minor amputation and an urgent need to be vaccinated, the editor delivered to us pages from the very first New Scientist.

There is no Feedback, but there is a column called “It Seems to Me”, written by an anonymous person known only as “Geminus”.

This was the proto-Feedback, and it might best be described as a relic of a bygone age. There is an item about the best way to determine “the average speed of a record-breaking speed boat”, which is entirely predicated on a “haggle which took place in the correspondence columns of [British newspaper] The Times“. Today, it would be a Reddit thread.

And yet, that embryonic Feedback feels curiously of the moment. Notably, the first item is about the Suez crisis. For younger readers: the UK and others briefly invaded Egypt to gain control of the Suez canal, a vital freight route, but their attack was an embarrassing failure. Geminus argued that this had thrown the UK’s lackadaisical approach to energy security into sharp relief, and that “it was unwise – as events have shown – to lean too heavily on an imported fuel from the Middle East”. Uh-huh.

One theme that emerges from our trawl of the archives is the sheer number of words and phrases New Scientist (and occasionally Feedback) can take credit for. After poking around in the Oxford English Dictionary (with the aid of AI – don’t worry, we checked what it said), we found that more than 200 words and phrases apparently had their first known print appearance in New Scientist.

We think this must be an over-count from the OED – most surely emerged in technical journals unavailable to its compilers – but we have found two favourites, which we will be using from now on.

The first is acronymania, which apparently appeared in our pages in 1968, referring to an excessive enthusiasm for creating acronyms. The other is from 1959 and refers to a device for measuring bite force: a gnathodynamometer. We don’t know how or why we will use that, but we will.

Feedback is specifically going to take the credit for “RAS syndrome”, where “RAS” stands for “redundant acronym syndrome”. Feedback came up with this on 7 April 2001, to describe the phenomenon encapsulated by the term “HRT therapy”, where “HRT” is, of course, short for “hormone replacement therapy”, giving “hormone replacement therapy therapy”. See also: ATM machine, ISBN number and PCR reaction.

Depending how you pronounce RAS, it possibly ought to be “redundant abbreviation syndrome syndrome”, but let’s not concern ourselves overmuch with trivialities.

Some have also credited us with “nominative determinism”, used since 1994 to describe people whose names eerily match their jobs. This was originally prompted by, among other things, “an article on incontinence in the British Journal of Urology… by J. W. Splatt and D. Weedon”.

Today, nominative determinism has escaped Feedback and infests the rest of the magazine. Readers Rob Watson, Peter Mayer and Andi (no surname) all wrote in to flag a recent piece about recreating the conditions on the surface of our nearest star, which featured solar scientist Wei Sun.

We would like to make clear that we did not coin the term nominative determinism. In December 1994, a previous incarnation attributed it to Carl Richard (C. R.) Cavonius, a visual scientist and Feedback fan. All Feedback has done, in our many iterations, is to popularise it beyond all known limits.

Finally, we need to drop a small bombshell. A typo made it into print in the first Feedback to highlight Splatt and Weedon’s work, and it has been copied forward into several subsequent mentions. Hence we would like to offer a correction, 32 years after the fact: the first author of the incontinence paper was actually A. J. Splatt. Sorry about that.

Got a story for Feedback?

You can send stories to Feedback by email at feedback@newscientist. com. Please include your home address. This week’s and past Feedbacks can be seen on our website.

Are these the most spectacular and intriguing beetles in the world?

New Scientist November 18, 2026

What animal is older than the dinosaurs and accounts for nearly a quarter of species on Earth? It is the magnificent beetle, an insect whose wings rest underneath a hard, protective case that often displays beautiful colours and intricate ornaments. “Wherever you stand on the land surface of the Earth save only for Antarctica, you are never more than a few metres from a beetle,” writes Maxwell Barclay in Interesting Beetles, which showcases some of their stunning variety.

The main image shows the glorious flower chafer (Howdenypa gloriosa), a stunning opalescent green and blue. Its sleek flight from flower to flower, which takes place with the wing cases closed, unlike the clumsier flights of beetles with open wing cases, has attracted attention from aerospace engineers. They have fitted some flower chafers with tiny wireless transmitters to better understand how they manoeuvre while flying.

Below is the Colorado potato beetle (Leptinotarsa decemlineata), which has a destructive relationship with humans. After the potato was introduced to North America, this striped beetle started to prefer spuds to native foods and quickly became a worldwide pest.

Advertisement

Below, the carbuncle frog-legged beetle (Sagra carbunculus) shows off the buff hind legs that earned it its amphibian-inspired name and serve it well in battle – or when competing for an iridescent mate.

The specimens in these images are taken from the archives of the Natural History Museum in London, where Barclay is senior curator in charge of beetles. It was difficult, he writes in his book, to choose which to include, “because each of the 400,000 beetle species has an interesting story to tell”.

The violin beetle (Mormolyce phyllodes) shown below makes up for being an inelegant flyer by having a unique body shape that allows it to blend in with fallen leaves and winged seeds of trees in the steamy tropical rainforests where it resides.

Finally, the desert fog-basking beetle (Onymacris bicolor) shown below is another master of adaptation that can survive in places as arid and harsh as the Namib desert in southern Africa. Elegant in its black-and-white garb, this insect climbs to the top of a dune when conditions are right, points its head down and waits for dew to condense on special structures on its wings and then run into its mouth, keeping it alive.

Barclay writes that beetles can not only survive in all these habitats, from potato fields to tropical forests and deserts, but that they are an integral part of each of them. Without beetles as predators, pollinators, herbivores or scavengers, many ecosystems simply couldn’t function, he writes.

New Scientist is 70 years old – join us in celebrating

New Scientist November 18, 2026

Break open the bubbly, light the candles and get ready to party – New Scientist is 70 years old! Times have certainly changed since we published our first issue in 1956. Back then, some scientists had proposed that our carbon dioxide emissions were warming the planet, but the idea was controversial. Biologists were only beginning to unpick how DNA, whose structure had just been elucidated by Francis Crick, James Watson, Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, encoded the instructions for building organisms. The founders of this magazine couldn’t have envisaged the many ways that the web and smartphones would change daily life.

We are even old enough that what once seemed futuristic is now pleasantly quaint. Launching our first website, Planet Science, in 1995, we declared that, “As the technologies mature, quite soon and at a terminal near you, it may be possible to hear interviews with well-known scientists”. Our digital offering has expanded greatly since then, with these sorts of interviews now available across our podcast and video channels. That said, we also speculated that it might be possible to “manipulate three-dimensional models of molecules” on a future version of our website, which we still haven’t quite managed to deliver.

To mark our anniversary, we have put together a timeline of the biggest breakthroughs of the past 70 years. I enjoyed diving into our archives in search of how we reported era-defining moments. Our assessments haven’t always been on the money: after Yuri Gagarin’s space flight in 1961, for example, our correspondent declared “it is almost physically impossible for [the US] to beat the Russians to the moon”.

Advertisement

The secret to New Scientist‘s longevity is a devoted following of readers

A clear demonstration, if one were needed, that most predictions turn out to be wrong. But looking ahead is in New Scientist‘s DNA, so, bravely – or foolishly – we press on. The main feature in this special issue is a trip to the year 2096, seven decades from now, for an imagined article for our 140th anniversary. To make our predictions as informed as possible, Jacob Aron consulted a panoply of scientists for their views and wove it all together to create one plausible path for the future.

Sometimes, it turns out that fiction writers can see the future more accurately than scientists. Emily H. Wilson has trawled through 70 years of sci-fi in search of the most prescient predictions. Robert A. Heinlein, Ursula K. Le Guin, Octavia E. Butler and Cixin Liu are among those who have shown remarkable foresight.

Of course, the secret to New Scientist’s longevity is a devoted following who have been with us since the days of Daedalus, Enigma and Grimbledon Down. When we first started thinking about our anniversary, we wondered if there were readers who remembered our very first issue. We asked you for your stories about how you first encountered New Scientist and the role it has played in your life – and hundreds of you responded. It was a joy to read so many kind messages and wonderful stories. Most gratifyingly of all, we heard from a couple who met on our short-lived dating website in 2012 and are still happily married! You can read some of our favourite letters here.

Long-time readers may remember a couple of old faces who make an appearance in this issue. When I first joined New Scientist in 2015, I sat next to Andy Coghlan, a news reporter who had been on staff for almost as long as I had been sentient. Andy was hired in the days when job interviews took place in the pub and reporters away from the office had to file stories over the phone. He shares a few recollections about the huge stories he worked on, from Dolly the sheep to the world’s first face transplant. Meanwhile, in Almost the Last Word, former editors including Mick O’Hare reminisce about noble efforts to answer readers’ questions about noisy restaurants and champagne.

Finally, some fun and games. We thought you’d like a challenge, so we asked Nobel prizewinners to set some quiz questions. Barry Marshall, Jennifer Doudna and Saul Perlmutter gladly offered to test your knowledge of their specialist subjects: the bacteria that cause stomach ulcers, CRISPR gene editing and the expanding universe. We also have a special crossword that requires you to fill in the missing words from headlines that have appeared on our cover. Even Feedback is getting in on the action.

Despite all that has changed in the past 70 years, New Scientist remains one of a kind – a place where curious minds can feast on big ideas, baffling mysteries, hard-hitting journalism and the delightfully weird subjects of scientific inquiry. Thank you for being part of our story. It has been a great pleasure to put together this 70th anniversary issue – I hope you enjoy it too.

Sam Wong is New Scientist‘s anniversary editor

Our favourite reader questions of the past three decades

New Scientist November 18, 2026

Icycle

For New Scientist‘s 70th birthday, we wanted to look back at Last Word editors’ favourite questions. The Last Word launched in the 7 May 1994 issue of the magazine, with questions ranging from why some people sneeze in bright light to whether “damp” cold really is colder than “dry” cold. Since then, New Scientist readers and academic experts have been asking and answering what can only be described as an eclectic mix of questions. Here are the favourites of some of the editors who have taken the reigns over the years, along with a selection of answers.

Being asked to pick my top Last Word question is a bit like being asked which is my favourite child, but the one that stands out for me is: Why would anyone take a bicycle to Antarctica and what would they use it for? (Philip Crohn, Melbourne, Australia). Posed in the 6 July 2002 issue of the magazine, this was asked by a reader after they had watched archive footage of Ernest Shackleton’s historic expeditions.

Advertisement

The question of bikes in the Antarctic circles back nicely to the time when I first fell in love with Last Word, when I was working as a biologist at the British Antarctic Survey’s Rothera Research Station. Here, New Scientist was one of the prime offerings in the toilet magazine racks. Last Word was my favourite part of the magazine.

And yes, there was a bike on my Antarctic base too, which the radio operator avidly used to cycle through the snow.

Alison George, editor from 2020 to 2022

Robert HeadlandScott Polar Research Institute, University of Cambridge

Bicycles have been used sporadically in the Antarctic from the time of Captain Robert Scott’s fatal expedition in 1912. Indeed, one of the relics discovered in Scott’s hut at Cape Evans is a rusted bicycle. This was a gift from a New Zealand firm to the geologist Thomas Griffith Taylor, who later founded the Geographical Society of New South Wales and its journal The Australian Geographer. Prior to joining the expedition, Taylor studied in Cambridge, where cycling is a very popular form of transport. This undoubtedly explains his enthusiasm for bicycles.

This enthusiasm was soon snuffed out when he tried to make a 25-kilometre return journey to Turk’s Head from the Antarctic base camp and got into difficulties. He had to be rescued and later wrote: “I made a vow that the first bicycle ride in the Antarctic would be my last, and have every intention of keeping that vow.”

While I agree that bicycles are not a very practical form of transport in the Antarctic, they certainly have their uses – especially their wheels. Herbert Ponting, the famous polar photographer, used a cart that was fitted with bicycle wheels to take his equipment over the ice, hauled by a sledge dog. Antarctic researchers use bicycle wheels, fitted with cyclometers and attached to the back of sledges by a flexible link, to measure distances.

Bicycles rarely get a mention in expeditionary accounts, but they occasionally appear in photos, as in Shackleton’s Endurance expedition. Most are taken south by cycling enthusiasts but are generally more useful in ports visited on the way.

McMurdo station, a very large US installation in Antarctica, has several bicycles in use, mainly mountain bikes, that are used for both recreation and transport.

Squeezing outIn 2023, Last Word received a question that readers really threw themselves behind: What is the shortest space a parked car can get out of? Or a parking car can get into? (Toby Ebert, Ilfracombe, Devon, UK).

As editor of this section for three years, I learned that there are some things our readers particularly love: maths questions and sharing personal anecdotes. This offered the opportunity for both, and the answers poured in. Pure joy – although, despite one assertion that “this can probably be done with 50 millimetres or less of spare space”, my own opinion that I need at least 50 per cent longer than the length of my car was not changed.

Alison Flood, editor from 2022 to 2025

Hillary ShawNewport, Shropshire, UK

Since cars are essentially rectangular, the very shortest space a car can theoretically enter or exit, by Pythagoras’s theorem, is the diagonal from one front corner to the back corner on the opposite side, so 4.47 metres for an average car of 2 m × 4 m.

However, at this diagonal point, the (for example) left rear corner of the car is touching the kerb, the right rear corner is touching the car behind, the front left corner is touching the car in front and you have no space to manoeuvre to get fully in. Geometrically, if the car could rotate, you would need the same 0.47 m at the front to swing the car fully in, total space required 4.94 m. However, car wheels on an axle cannot physically turn by 90 degrees, so even this 4.94 m space would require an approaching-infinite-point turn to enter. You can spend approaching eternity to get in that space, or look for another space of maybe 5.5 m.

It is also possible to shift an adjacent car either by shunting or simply by nudging up and using your engine to overcome the other car’s brakes. But I don’t think this parking method is approved in the UK Highway Code.

Patrick ForsythMaldon, Essex, UK

Many years ago, when I was at school, a favourite trick was to get a gang of pupils together and lift a master’s Mini, wedging it between two trees. You only needed a couple of centimetres each end to get it in, but it could only be got out by more lifting. I think cars are heavier these days.

Blank skyWhile I’m relatively new to editing Last Word, having started with the 15 August 2026 issue of the magazine, I’m not new to loving it. It was genuinely challenging to whittle down my long list to just one favourite question, but it was also a lot of fun.

I landed on one from the 17 May 2025 issue – How would human civilisation differ if the sun, moon and planets were always obscured by clouds? (Simon Rockett, Debenham, Suffolk, UK) – as it combines my bias for anything to do with humanity’s story with a personal preference for more speculative Last Word questions. From empires to time-keeping and plant evolution, the responses take you on a thought-provoking journey – even if it is one that couldn’t rely on the sun and stars for navigation.

Sophie Berdugo, editor from 2026

Guy CoxSydney, Australia

Probably not much would have been different. If the stars and planets were always hidden, there would be no astrology – a plus.

We would still see day and night, and the seasons, so we would have calendars. Sundials are obviously out, but clepsydras (water clocks) have been used by ancient civilisations all over the world since at least 1300 BC, so we could tell the time.

The biggest difference would probably be that we couldn’t navigate by the sun and stars, so travel across large bodies of water wouldn’t be practicable. That wouldn’t stop humans from populating most of the globe, but it would have stopped colonial powers from taking over distant countries.

Alex McDowellLondon, UK

Navigation at sea would have been difficult because, prior to the invention of radio beacons, inertial guidance, satellite navigation and more, sailors used celestial bodies to navigate. They would have needed to rely heavily on dead reckoning.

Some argue that, before the magnetic compass, Vikings used crystals called sunstones to locate the sun in overcast conditions. Sunstones are able to take advantage of the fact that light scattered through cloud vapour is polarised, but light straight from the sun is not.

The first clocks were sundials, but these would be useless if we were always under cloud cover. But sunstones could be used to find which direction the sun was in, and when. One could use sunstones together with magnetic compasses to work out the time.

Perhaps these difficulties would have led to mechanical clocks being developed more quickly.

Astronomy would be delayed. Celestial bodies would be visible only if one could get above the clouds. If no mountain went above them, people would still be curious to know what was there, and this could lead to balloons and other aircraft being developed faster. Until people could get above the clouds, there would have been a lot of speculation about what was in and above them – and perhaps stories like Jack and the Beanstalk would have sounded credible!

Life would also have evolved differently. Plants may have developed a type of chlorophyll that uses more of the electromagnetic spectrum, absorbing even green light, and thus appearing black.

In the early days of Last Word, I used to put some questions to the test. For example, I remember buying a case of champagne and drinking it over the course of a week to disprove the fact that a teaspoon in the neck of the bottle keeps it fizzy (we needed a lot of controls). Such a hardship. It doesn’t, by the way; it stays fizzy for a long time if simply left alone.

Also, in the late 1990s and early 2000s, there was a penchant for voluminous restaurants in London with lots of wooden floors and steel fittings. We wanted to know if they were breaking legal workplace noise levels. So I got to eat at about 10 of them, taking a decibel meter with me, and we found that the noise way exceeded legal limits, meaning the staff should all have been wearing ear defenders.

As for favourite questions, I remember we asked why snot was green. Throughout my entire time at New Scientist, I was constantly asked that. But my fave question was from the 20 March 2004 issue: How fat do you need to be to be bulletproof? (Ward van Nostram, via email).

I always thought that was the perfect Last Word question: amusing, quirky, but having some scientific basis, and I was pretty sure somebody would have done the research. And it turned out they had. The US military had looked into it and found that you needed something like a 60-centimetre-thick layer of fat around your torso, thus rendering any soldier immobile and not very effective.

Mick O’Hare, editor from 1994 to 2018

The real reasons we keep seeing big tech outages – it isn’t just hackers

New Scientist November 18, 2026

In the past week, a Microsoft outage locked millions of people out of their email accounts, computer problems at a US bank stopped payments and a glitch in air traffic control systems grounded flights in the US. Even the US National Security Agency (NSA) reported that its secure intranet NSANet had fallen over, and Apple’s online services also went offline. The cluster of failures prompted rumours of a coordinated cyberattack by a foreign state or a hacking spree powered by AI.

Speculation about such ideas was so rife that the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, was forced to reassure people that the government had “zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind”.

But why are we seeing so many outages all at once? There are certainly hackers, including state-backed ones who stage coordinated attacks. For instance, a boss at the UK’s intelligence, security and cyber agency – Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ) – recently told New Scientist that Russia and China are staging “relentless” cyberattacks against the UK using AI. AI has also allowed even non-experts to uncover dramatic bugs in widely used software. But that isn’t what we have seen in recent days.

Advertisement

Rogue hacking AIs have changed the cybersecurity landscape

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) put its air traffic control outage down to “routine maintenance” in which copper communications lines were being upgraded to fibre-optic cable. The head of the FAA, Bryan Bedford, echoed Rubio in a press conference and said: “We see zero evidence of anything nefarious.”

Bank outages were put down to a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase. Microsoft blamed a trifecta of problems for its email issues: an old software bug, malfunctioning internal data connections and server capacity. As for the NSA glitch, the spy agency said only that problems arose “during scheduled routine maintenance”, and didn’t respond to a request for comment. Apple pinned its issues on an internal update.

The flurry of outages, then, is partly down to coincidence and partly explained by a chronic lack of investment in resilient infrastructure, says Daniel Dresner at the University of Manchester, UK. He says that not only is there no indication that these outages are linked, but there is no evidence that they are malicious hacks.

“Things are failing all the time,” says Dresner. “This stuff is really fragile.”

Free newsletter

Dresner says there has been an increasing trend – exacerbated by new AI models that can create computer code with unprecedented speed – to prioritise new features and updated interfaces over data validation and reliability.

“We all have what a colleague of mine called the ‘Big Mac mentality’: we want it with all the trimmings and we want it with speed. We’re happy because it’s working – until it fails,” says Dresner. “We wanted agility and we ended up with fragility.”

These sorts of failures aren’t rare, says Alon Hillel-Tuch at New York University. “The honest answer is that it isn’t really all happening now. Outages like these happen all the time. What’s unusual this week is that several big ones landed close together just as everyone started looking for a pattern. As for why it all seems to be happening at once, large outages are far more common than people realise,” he says.

Tim Stevens at King’s College London says that the technology sector has been developing profitable and desirable tools, but failing to build and maintain the infrastructure on which those tools rely. He says it is like a car firm selling sports cars when the roads are littered with potholes and dead ends. Spending money on fixing or improving infrastructure brings no immediate profit, so is overlooked.

Global race to update computers as AI discovers most disruptive hack yet

“This is what we built and this is what we have predicted for years and years and years. It’s coming home to roost,” says Stevens. “If you’re going to build an entire global system on demonstrably insecure networks and systems, then this is what you’re going to get. I don’t think there’s anything more than coincidence in the current set of events, it’s just they seem to have come in a short period of time.”

George Loukas at the University of Greenwich, UK, says that US government cuts to cybersecurity efforts like the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency will certainly have worsened matters overall, but that the real reason for the enormous disruption we see when services go offline is that we all tend to use a very small number of digital tools.

“We are depending increasingly on digital environments which tend to be an oligopoly. Five years ago, that wouldn’t be the case. We would have exactly the same event, but not the same impact,” says Loukas.

The growth of domestic solar installations opens the possibility of hackers targeting their smart inverter devices as a way to cause widespread power-system failures

In many industries, says Loukas, governments have stepped in and broken up monopolies, but he has seen less progress in the digital world. Until there are many thriving, competing rivals in every sector of technology, we will be vulnerable to enormous outages that bring everything grinding to a halt until staff at one company can find a fix.

Stevens says that AI has led to the discovery of a great number of software bugs, which have required lots of patches. That low-hanging fruit has now been picked and we are seeing a slowdown, he says, but that burst of activity is likely to have been a good thing overall for security.

However, there are huge hurdles between us and a more resilient online world, due to the “perverse economics of cybersecurity”, says Stevens. “If you’re going to test something to oblivion [to make sure it’s secure and resilient], then your competitors have already stolen the market. It is what it is, and I’m quite pessimistic about how to address this. It’s an uphill battle, particularly when the economic incentives point in the opposite direction.”

Homo erectus survived on mainland Asia 215,000 years longer than we thought

New Scientist November 18, 2026

Preserved teeth from two caves in southern China indicate Homo erectus lived on mainland Asia as recently as 184,000 years ago. That is recent enough for the species to have met later groups like the Denisovans.

It seems these Chinese H. erectus were living in a tropical rainforest – an environment where the species has not previously been found.

“We’ve got this late surviving population, and we’ve got this rich story of how they were living,” says geochronologist Kira Westaway at Macquarie University in Sydney.

Advertisement

H. erectus was one of the first species in our genus, Homo. It was also the first species of hominin we know for sure migrated beyond Africa. The earliest H. erectus fossils are from Africa 2 million years ago, but by 1.8 million years ago they were living in what is now Georgia on the border between Europe and Asia. Eventually the species spread further east into what is now China. They even made it to the island of Java.

The 85-million-year timeline of human evolution

The most recent fossils identified as H. erectus are from Java and are between 117,000 and 108,000 years old. However, it’s been thought the species vanished much earlier from mainland Asia. Until the discoveries from China announced today, the most recent securely dated H. erectus were from around 400,000 years ago.

Around this time, other hominin groups emerged, like the Denisovans who lived in East Asia. “The assumption would have been that erectus is basically no longer there, because they have evolved into a Denisovan population,” says molecular palaeontologist Frido Welker at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark.

Welker, Westaway and their colleagues investigated two caves in southern China. Baxian and Naxian are both limestone caves, about 15 kilometres apart. They were initially excavated by Chinese teams led by Yingqi Zhang at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing and Wei Wang at Shandong University.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Combined, the two caves contained more than 18,000 mammal fossils. These included nine hominin teeth: six from Naxian and three from Baxian. Based on their sizes and shapes, and CT scans of their internal structures, eight of the teeth were identified as belonging to Homo erectus. The ninth tooth, from Baxian cave, could not be clearly identified.

For further evidence to confirm the identity of the hominins, the team turned to molecular biology: they attempted to recover proteins preserved inside the dentine of the ancient teeth. Previously, only a handful of H. erectus specimens have yielded proteins – primarily those described in a study published in May. This time, Welker, Westaway and their colleagues were able to obtain proteins from five of the teeth, including the mystery ninth tooth.

The team focused on a protein called ameloblastin, found in the dentine. The four teeth identified as H. erectus turned out to have a telltale signature in the protein, only previously seen in other Asian H. erectus fossils and not in fossils belonging to other ancient hominins. This strengthened the case that these teeth did indeed come from the mouths of H. erectus individuals.

However, the H. erectus teeth also contained an unusual signature elsewhere in the protein, not seen in other groups. The team suggests that the teeth may be evidence of a genetically distinct population of H. erectus, probably separated from those we already know of by geographic distance.

“I can absolutely see how they came to the conclusion that this is a different population,” says Sheela Athreya at Texas A&M University. “They were careful to compare it to the entire database they could get a hold of.”

The remaining tooth, which could not be identified morphologically, had ameloblastin that could not be matched to a hominin – though that could be because most hominin fossils haven’t yielded preserved proteins. “We really cannot say at this stage what it is,” says Welker.

The researchers performed an array of experiments to determine the ages of the H. erectus teeth. They directly dated the teeth themselves, the sediments in which they were found and mineral formations in the caves. “They all date different events in the cave, and as long as you understand the events, they do all correlate really well with each other,” says Westaway. The team concluded the teeth are between 324,000 and 184,000 years old.

One of the first excavations to find extinct human remains took place on Java in the 1890s, and the original documentation reveals details about the mudflow that encased the fossils there

At the time, the caves seem to have been located in a tropical rainforest. The animal bones found at the site came from an array of rainforest-dwelling species, including extinct species of rhinoceros and elephant. The H. erectus population present at the cave was part of a food chain based on trees rather than grasses, according to analyses of carbon isotopes in the teeth. Other isotopic evidence points to humid tropical conditions.

The team also looked at strontium isotopes, which reveal where the H. erectus were living during their first few years of life while their teeth were still developing. “Their strontium levels do not match the area where they were found,” says Westaway. This suggests they travelled considerable distances within the rainforest.

“It speaks to the ecological flexibility of Homo erectus,” says Karen Baab, a palaeoanthropologist at Midwestern University in Arizona. She points out that the species existed for about 1.9 million years and spread from Africa to Java. “They seemed quite adaptable and flexible in general, because of the incredible range of niches they were occupying.”

Quantum trick lets you share your location super securely

New Scientist November 18, 2026

Financial institutions and critical infrastructure could be made far more secure in the near-future using quantum particles.

For years, researchers have predicted that quantum particles could enable someone to share their location, and to verify someone else’s, in a way that is exceedingly difficult to hack. This would allow one branch of a bank to confirm that a request for funds or client information is coming from another branch and not from a hacker. Likewise, hackers could be stopped from trying to remotely control a power grid, a nuclear plant – or even commercial freezers, which have recently been hacked across Europe.

Gautam Kavuri at the University of Colorado Boulder and his colleagues have now shown that quantum devices really can provide such location verification, offering a level of security impenetrable to most hackers.

Advertisement

Inside the company selling quantum entanglement

“From a security perspective, it’s sort of the gold-plated Rolls Royce of protocols. It’s got the best security you can have in principle, while making the least assumptions,” says team member Krister Shalm at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Colorado. “And you can actually do it.”

In the researchers’ experiment, two verifier devices had to confirm the location of a third device called the prover. Each device was in a different location: the verifiers were 195 metres apart in different labs and the prover was in a third location between them. Kavuri says it was important for these devices to be in different rooms on the NIST campus, rather than all in the same lab, because this is closer to a practical scenario in the real world. The devices were connected with electrical cables and optical fibres and could exchange quantum particles of light that had been connected into pairs through the inextricable link of quantum entanglement.

To begin the new quantum position verification (QPV) protocol, a verifier would send one photon from an entangled pair to the prover and, simultaneously, each verifier would also send a random number that instructed the prover on which particle property to measure. Next, the prover sent the outcome of that measurement to both verifiers. They used the time it took to receive this information to calculate the prover’s position.

Free newsletter

Several quantum tricks made this procedure more secure than any conventional one. First, quantum information, such as that carried by particles of light, can never be copied or cloned surreptitiously. Additionally, the researchers leveraged a procedure called a Bell test, which is specific to entangled particles, and would be failed if a hacker tampered with them. The net effect was that any conventional strategy for faking the position would set off one of these quantum safeguards.

In this way, the new work builds on past theoretical results that promise to make it nearly impossible for position verification to be hacked once you go beyond conventional communication and turn to quantum tricks, says Philip Verduyn Lunel at Sorbonne University in Paris.

“QPV is a possible ‘killer app’ for quantum networks,” says Wolfgang Löffler at Leiden University in the Netherlands. Although several outstanding problems will need to be solved to make this protocol fully practical, the new experiment is a big step towards doing just that, he says. Löffler says that it must have been a massive effort to get all the timings and device fidelities just right.

A network that connects quantum devices and a central server that spans Hefei, China, can allow multiple secure quantum chats at once

“They have really pushed all the experimental constraints to their limit,” says Verduyn Lunel.

Robert Malaney at the University of New South Wales Sydney says the new protocol is attractive for practical applications in part because it is compatible with conventional wireless communication infrastructure. But if several nefarious actors could quantum entangle devices that they use for hacking, they could still cheat the current implementation of the protocol, he says. This is because, in this case, the hackers could perform some computations without having to send each other extra messages.

Going forward, the protocol must also be adapted to work over longer distances, which could require new computational steps and devices, says Florian Speelman at the University of Amsterdam. This will be a challenge, but the new work still moves us closer to QPV being a reality, he says.

The researchers are now working on tweaking their protocol to make it more resilient to any photons getting lost as well as being more impervious to hackers looking to leverage quantum entanglement, says team member Yanbao Zhang at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

Nature DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11247-3

Selwyn residents who were undercharged for water will not receive backdated bills after an independent review uncovered millions of dollars in potentially unbilled charges.

Selwyn District Council released a PwC report examining historical drinking water, wastewater and trade waste billing.

The review found some customers had been undercharged and others overcharged.

The causes included gaps in how customers were set up, property, meter and billing records were linked and charging decisions were documented during a period of rapid growth for the district.

PwC estimated about $2.87 million in drinking water charges may not have been billed between July 1, 2024, and December 31, 2025.

About 1300 properties had missing or incorrect billing records, while about 2200 records showed billing had started late.

The figure was an estimate, not a confirmed financial loss.

Council chief executive Steve Gibling acknowledged the shortcomings.

“I’m making putting it right my top priority, and that work has already begun,” he said.

“Importantly, if you’ve had a bill from Selwyn Water, the amount on it is correct. This means everyone is now paying their fair share for the water they use.”

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

Selwyn Mayor Lydia Gliddon said the findings were disappointing but assured residents they would not face backdated bills.

“The time available to correct any undercharging through the Rating Act has passed. We also don’t think it would be fair when the mistakes were in Council’s own systems,” she said.

“We want these issues brought to us at the council table so they can be fixed. I know we can tackle it head-on and get this right for our ratepayers.”

The review also identified 32 properties that may have been charged the full wastewater rate when they should have paid half.

Further checks found 23 were being charged correctly, while the remaining nine are being investigated. Affected customers will be contacted directly if a credit is due.

The review also found that, historically, only the largest trade waste users were billed, with insufficient information available to calculate charges for other businesses.

The issues came to light during preparations to establish Selwyn Water, which took over water services from the council on July 1.

As of November 16, about 115 of the 1300 properties with missing or incorrect records still needed to be resolved, while all 2200 late billing records had been checked and incorporated into billing.

About 70 trade waste consent holders are now being invoiced and further work continues to identify and on-board other applicable customers. Affected businesses will be contacted.

Selwyn Water has committed to correcting every record and account by July 1, 2027.

“People are entitled to trust that the charges they pay are accurate and fair,” Gliddon said.

“That is why we are releasing the full report and being open about what it found and what we are doing about it.”

Customers with questions about their water bills can contact Selwyn Water on 0800 735 426 or email hello@selwynwater. co. nz.

Pilot whale dies after stranding on Pukehina Beach

New Zealand Herald November 18, 2026

Pilot whale found stranded on Pukehina Beach this morning. Photo / Mel

A pilot whale has died after stranding on Pukehina Beach.

Project Jonah community lead Louisa Hawkes said members of the public found the whale about an hour ago.

It was alive when it was first discovered but died shortly after.

Hawkes said the Department of Conservation was on its way to the beach to assess the situation.

She said the public was asked to keep an eye out for any other whales, in case more were nearby.

A juvenile whale, believed to be a humpback, was found dead at Pikowai Beach last week.

Residents Rex and Alyson Addenbrooke found the whale on Wednesday morning, and it was buried nearby after DoC and local iwi attended.
