Marlborough insect protein trial targets wine and aquaculture waste for animal feed

New Zealand Herald November 18, 2026

Grape marc could be mixed with mussel or salmon farm waste to ensure the protein and other nutrient levels are balanced. Photo / RNZ, Anisha Satya

By Samantha Gee of RNZ

Scientists in Marlborough are trialling a new way to turn wine and aquaculture industry waste into high-quality protein for animal feed.

A three-year pilot will test whether black soldier flies can convert organic waste such as grape marc into protein for fish and pet food.

The $2.6 million project is being led by the Marlborough Research Centre, with support from the Bioeconomy Science Institute, and has received $1.42m from the Waste Minimisation Fund.

Bioeconomy Science Institute business manager Abby Albright said Marlborough’s viticulture, aquaculture and fisheries industries produced large volumes of organic waste, and researchers had spent the past five years investigating whether it could be turned into a high-quality insect diet.

The project was focused on the black soldier fly, which Albright said was the “most widely farmed insect globally” because it grew “super, super fast”.

There was a global shortage of feed protein, but also an emerging insect agriculture sector.

“There’s a real opportunity here for us to underpin the quite ambitious growth trajectory of our aquaculture sector, and we can do that in a really beautiful circular way by rearing insects off of the side streams out of the wine-making and fisheries sectors.”

She said the juvenile insects used in the pilot would come from a Bioeconomy Science Institute research colony in Palmerston North.

The insect farm would not have lots of winged insects flying around, and the black soldier fly had no chewing mouthparts.

Instead, young larvae would be mixed with a slurry of organic matter and, in less than two weeks, they would reach harvestable size, be separated out, dried and milled into a high-protein product.

Albright said that, once the pilot facility was running at capacity, it was hoped the insects could process 250kg of organic material a day, resulting in about nine tonnes of insect biomass each year.

The leftover product – uneaten food, insect shells and excrement – is known as frass, a nutrient-dense product for which scientists are also exploring options.

“It’s got a great nutrient profile, it’s nitrogen-rich, and it’s also got a really high bulk density, so it actually increases the water-holding capacity of the soil that it’s added to, so we’ll be looking at how we can also create a value line item from the frass as well.”

Christchurch-based company Kōrure will raise, feed and process the larvae in two shipping containers in Marlborough.

Founder Ron Park said one container would be a fly-farm nursery, and the other would process the waste material.

It would run alongside an anaerobic digestion plant managed by bioenergy and waste-to-energy company Ecogas.

Park said the insects could process one tonne of organic waste a week.

The biggest challenge would be ensuring consistent organic waste across each season.

“Grape marc in summer versus winter will look really, really different, so we’ll have to mix grape marc with mussel or salmon farm waste to make sure the protein and other nutrient levels are balanced and optimal for the insects.”

Given that most of the feed stock used in New Zealand was imported, the pilot presented huge opportunities.

“For our country to be able to produce our own protein source for our animals, I believe that’s priceless.

“I’m very excited and very determined to make this work so that we can have a true circular economy here in New Zealand.

“We’ll be removing up to 70% or even more carbon emissions from the landfill by feeding [the waste] to insects, which is huge.

“We’re actually doing huge work towards our clean, green image and making sure that we’re not wasting materials in New Zealand.”

Mark Lucas, Marlborough District Council’s solid waste manager, said about 40% of the waste sent to the region’s landfills was organic matter. In the past year, its Emissions Trading Scheme liability was $1.4m.

Diverting some of that organic material would reduce the cost, and the pilot would test whether it was commercially viable to build a permanent facility in Blenheim, with the capacity to process up to 50,000 tonnes of organic waste each year.

Some industries were choosing to truck their organic waste out of Marlborough, where there were more sustainable options than sending it to landfill, and Lucas said that would change if there was an affordable and sustainable option within the region.

“We don’t know what legislation will change with the new Government when it’s decided, but with the current legislation that we have at the moment, we’re confident that it is going to be commercially viable, which means it will be cheaper for the people to get rid of their organics via the diversion option instead of sending it to landfill.”

Kaimoana Foods, an aquaculture feed and pet food manufacturer based in Manawatū, is the only company producing commercial fish food for salmon, kingfish and trout in New Zealand.

Director Joe Currie said his father started Denver Stock Feeds in 1997, which made poultry, dairy and calf feed, and the family decided to branch out into the aquafeed industry several years ago, as the stock used in New Zealand was all imported, mainly from Australia and Europe.

“We looked at that and thought, well, it’s kind of ridiculous, why can’t we make it locally, and so we’re trying to get into the market.”

Once the pilot was up and running, Currie said they would use a percentage of farmed insect protein in their commercial fish food.

“You can’t switch out all the fish meal for insect protein because then the entire composition of your pellet changes, but it’ll definitely take a percentage.”

He said it had been hard to make inroads with the larger producers, but the company supplied aquafeed for Mt Cook Alpine Salmon and the Earth Sciences New Zealand kingfish farm in Ruakākā.

“We’re not quite there yet, but our goal is to be at least 90% New Zealand-grown ingredients, which is why the insect protein has been of interest to us.

“We looked at it and thought, well, why wouldn’t you? Insect protein looks fantastic; it’s sustainable, you’re growing protein out of waste.”

The company used some imported anchovy meal in its formulations, which it was actively trying to reduce and replace with New Zealand products.

“Personally, I don’t see the point of shipping ingredients in from overseas if we can produce it locally. New Zealand’s great at growing things, so we might as well tap into our potential.

“We know we can grow it efficiently, and if it’s scalable, I think it’s a great addition to New Zealand’s sustainability story.”

Incoming Opportunity MP takes swipe at coalition’s climate record, calls out David Seymour

New Zealand Herald November 18, 2026

Opportunity Party MP-elect Kayla Kingdon-Bebb said the "dismantling of our Zero Carbon Act framework" persuaded her to enter parliamentary politics. Photo / Mark Mitchell

Opportunity Party MP-elect Kayla Kingdon-Bebb has called out Act’s leader and taken a swipe at the coalition’s record at an event for cross-party conversations on climate change.

Kingdon-Bebb, most recently the New Zealand chief executive of the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), was among those who spoke at an event launching the Members of Parliament Climate Consensus report in Wellington yesterday.

The report, based on interviews with 74 MPs, found most agreed that man-made climate change was real and that collaboration was needed, although there was disagreement on the right direction.

Kingdon-Bebb described climate change as “a really personal topic”, as her career in New Zealand had been in environmental policy and advocacy.

“It is my conviction, really, that unless those issues have a champion around the Cabinet table, they do not get attended to.”

She suggested the past three years had seen regression on nature and climate.

“At worst, we see backsliding. And the last three years, I think, is pretty clearly testament to that.”

What made her want to stand for the Opportunity Party was watching the “systemic dismantling of our Zero Carbon Act framework”.

She noted that the Zero Carbon Act passed with 119 votes to one: “Not naming any names, David Seymour.”

Seymour’s office responded: “David Seymour proudly voted one against 119 several times in his early years as the sole Act MP. On issues such as earthquake strengthening laws, rushed firearm law changes, and the Zero Carbon Act, the rest of Parliament has, in time, come around to making changes closer to his position.

“We hope Ms Kingdon-Bebb has the courage to stand alone on principle, then she’ll have earned the right to criticise those who have.”

Kingdon-Bebb said the Zero Carbon Act recognised climate change as a long-term challenge, and New Zealand needed more of the collaboration that saw it become law.

“It was really disheartening to me, as a New Zealander and as an environmental advocate, to see a lurch away from that in the last three years.”

Opportunity wanted to “rebuild the political centre” by collaborating across party lines and being willing to work with either side.

She said changes in government can see advocates for climate or nature lost from around the Cabinet table.

“Ideally, you have those people in all camps. Right now that’s not necessarily the case,” she told the audience, promising to be a “strong” voice on climate and nature.

She gave examples of “inter-generational problems” that needed cross-party conversations, including the infrastructure deficit and child poverty.

She suggested that cost-benefit analyses on policy changes were “impoverished” if they didn’t account for long-term impacts on future generations.

“Opportunity’s committed to getting our climate liability reflected on the Crown balance sheet.”

During the election campaign, Kingdon-Bebb was targeted by sexist remarks from New Zealand First MP-elect Michael Laws.

Politics was “not the nicest place to be, especially for women”, she said.

Azaria Howell is a multimedia reporter working from Parliament’s press gallery. She joined NZME in 2022 and became a Newstalk ZB political reporter in late 2024, with a keen interest in public service agency reform and government spending.

Public servants can be a handbrake on Government policy changes – Henry Olsen

New Zealand Herald November 18, 2026

Whatever coalition forms the next Government will need the public service to help it turn its policies into legislation. Photo / Mark Mitchell

Next week, the Electoral Commission will publish the full results of this month’s election. Whatever coalition is formed will need the public service to help it turn its policies into legislation.

Our representative democracy relies on politicians of any party and background being able to get professional advice from an apolitical public service. Without such assistance, elected leaders would be unable to effectively implement the policies for which they are accountable to voters.

In a new report for the New Zealand Initiative, No Minister: A free and frank analysis of the public service, my colleague Dr Benno Blaschke and I present our findings on culture and experiences of public servants. We found that the ideals of political neutrality and the provision of free and frank advice are at risk.

We interviewed 40 current and former officials, ministerial advisers, ministers, managers, senior leaders and others with experience with the system. We also surveyed 718 current and former public servants, asking questions about what they believed their role in our democracy was. We looked at published performance metrics for the public service as well.

Our survey suggests that most public servants want to support the Government of the day. However, fewer indicated willingness to make a wholehearted effort to implement policies with which they disagree. Seventy per cent of our respondents agreed that the public service should carry out the elected government’s programme whatever officials privately think, but only 59% agreed that officials should do their best to make a lawful policy they consider misguided succeed.

The managers and leaders we surveyed – those who oversee the production of advice and work closest to ministers – differed in their responses to our questions about culture and effort according to their political affiliations. Those who voted for left-wing parties were much less likely than those who voted for right-wing parties to say they would do their best to make a policy they disagree with succeed (58% to 84% respectively). While we cannot ascertain whether these results would reverse under a Labour-led Government, either way, they raise questions about the neutrality of the public service.

Officials also fail to be neutral when they act in ways that undermine the ability of elected governments to govern. We asked respondents what an official should do if they are convinced, in good faith, that a minister is wrong.

Providing advice to the minister and engaging the minister in debate, the kind of pushback the public service should offer, were the most popular options. However, 62% of respondents endorsed framing advice to steer the minister away from a decision and 55% endorsed briefing stakeholders and the media so that a minister’s policy becomes politically untenable.

The officials we interviewed described a similar culture to that indicated by our survey. Many know officials who want to serve the country but find such service difficult when it requires implementing policies they disagree with. Some interviewees reported cases in which officials worked against lawful political direction. Our interviewees’ experiences do not indicate the extent to which these practices occur but show how the culture suggested by our survey can lead to real action that diminishes the democratic character of our government.

We found that the provision of frank advice to ministers has issues as well. Based on ratings of policy papers that agencies post in their annual reports, the quality of advice is uneven across agencies. Some agencies average ratings of “Good”, while others barely clear the minimum acceptable standard.

The average ratings also show a modest but sharp declining trend, particularly in the share of advice receiving high ratings. Furthermore, independent reviews commissioned by the public service found that advice often lacks key information ministers need to make decisions, such as full implementation and options analysis.

There are at least two main reasons why agencies struggle to produce high-quality advice.

First, there are issues relating to organisational management. Many of our interviewees recalled excessive project management, unclear reporting lines and cases in which managers alter or soften analysts’ advice before it goes to ministers. Moreover, poorly managed restructures have plagued the service for decades, disrupting workflows, increasing stress for public servants and often pushing out the best and most experienced officials.

Second are issues relating to lacklustre political direction. Public servants need clear direction and feedback from ministers. Many of our interviewees cited conflicting demands, especially from ministers of different parties, making their work much harder. Ministers can also encourage the kind of managerialism described earlier. For example, a minister might order a department to “find savings” but leave it to the discretion of individual managers to determine how.

Our research suggests that the effectiveness of our elected government is constrained by a non-neutral public service culture, subpar advice and ministers who do not put in the effort needed to make policy work.

Many public servants and ministers do their best to help New Zealand succeed. Our future research will look at other issues in the service and ways to improve the situation for ministers and officials alike.

Note: our survey was a part of Curia Market Research’s regular national polls from June to August 2026. Respondents to each poll were drawn at random from commercial online panels, which together hold several hundred thousand New Zealanders. Those who said they were a current or former public servant were asked our questions, so respondents did not self-select into our survey.

Rotorua Museum short $5.6m exhibition funding before 2028 reopening

New Zealand Herald November 18, 2026

Construction to strengthen Rotorua Museum, housed in the heritage-listed Bath House building, has been completed. Photo / Rotorua Lakes Council

Almost 60% of the funding needed to fill the Rotorua Museum with exhibitions before its planned reopening in 2028 has yet to be found.

Rotorua Lakes Council is pursuing the sale of a mystery inner-city asset and seeking $2 million from the regional council to help plug the $5.6m gap, with Mayor Tania Tapsell confident the funding can be secured.

The museum has been closed for a decade as of this month.

The $73.35m construction phase of its extensive renovations was completed in September.

A further $9.51m was budgeted to develop its exhibitions.

A subsequent $2m Government grant made a “sizeable dent” in the museum’s exhibition funding shortfall, council chief executive Andrew Moraes told a September ceremony celebrating the finished construction.

At the time, he said the project was “very close” to being fully funded.

The council’s most recent museum update to councillors, in late October, revealed a $5.6m hole remained.

Tapsell told Local Democracy Reporting she was confident the money would be found without asking ratepayers to contribute any new funding, and within the timeline.

“The good news is that I believe we have a strong plan in place to be able to fund this,” she said.

She said the council was in the process of selling an inner-city asset, which would provide funding for the development.

That sale was expected to be completed by the end of the year.

The council would not disclose the asset because of commercial sensitivity.

The potential reallocation of inner-city revitalisation funding and a $2m request to the Bay of Plenty Regional Council’s new regional infrastructure fund were also possible funding sources.

Tapsell said the council remained committed to avoiding more ratepayer contributions where possible.

“We will be working as hard as we can to make sure we’re either reallocating or finding additional money elsewhere,” she said.

“It’s why we were quite deliberate in capping the contribution of ratepayers at $15.5m as we completed the rebuild.”

Council community experience manager Alex Wilson would not attach a value to potential funding pathways yet but said options were being progressed.

“But we cannot treat these as secured until we have gone through all the relevant processes,” Wilson said.

She said “no decision” had been made for ratepayers to cover any shortfall.

“If sufficient funding is not secured, council would need to consider available options and make decisions accordingly,” she said.

The uncertainty could also affect the project timeline, with Wilson describing funding as a “key programme risk”.

“The target reopening remains August 2028, but securing remaining funding within the required timeframe is important to achieving that.”

She said Moraes’ comment about being close to full funding in September related to those “potential funding” options, rather than anything secured.

It would be “premature” to comment on whether any unspent construction budget could be used for the exhibition, as construction accounts had not been finalised, Wilson said.

The museum, located in the heritage-listed Bath House building, has been closed since November 2016 after earthquake safety concerns emerged following the Kaikōura earthquake.

Once claimed to be New Zealand’s most photographed building, Tapsell acknowledged the museum would still have operating costs once it reopened, but believed it would be worth it.

“Museums all over the world don’t make money, but they are a very important community asset and facility that brings a range of benefits,” she said.

“But we do know that both domestic and international tourists are waiting for that building to reopen.

“You can already see that when you go to Government Gardens. Even though the museum isn’t open, the area has had its makeover and it’s very busy.”

Rotorua Museum is opening its doors on Saturday for a free community day, offering tours of its restored building and a preview of future exhibitions.

The open day will also provide another fundraising opportunity, with Watts & Hughes, the construction company that completed the restoration work, matching every dollar donated up to $10,000.

Wilson encouraged residents and museum enthusiasts to visit the building and support the donation options.

Mathew Nash is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist based at the Rotorua Daily Post. He has previously written for SunLive, been a regular contributor to RNZ and was a football reporter in the UK for eight years.

TaurangaNZ brand launched after two years and $1.28m development

New Zealand Herald November 18, 2026

The University of Waikato's Joseph MacFarlane (from left), Western Bay of Plenty Mayor James Denyer, Tourism Bay of Plenty general manager Oscar Nathan, TaurangaNZ head of partnerships Hayley Nelson, Ngāti Pūkenga chairwoman Kylie Smallman, Tauranga Mayor Mahé Drysdale, Priority One chief executive Dave Courtney and Tauranga City councillor Kevin Schuler at the blessing of Tauranga's new place brand. Photo / Ayla Yeoman

A new brand, TaurangaNZ, has been launched to promote the city and surrounding Western Bay of Plenty district.

The region’s first place brand was developed over two years as part of an almost $1.28 million locally led project using an Auckland design company.

It features a logo designed to “echo the tides and rhythms of life”.

The brand was developed with the aim of helping to promote the area to domestic and international markets as a desirable place to live, work, visit, invest and do business.

Tourism Bay of Plenty led the project, working with councils, mana whenua, Priority One and the University of Waikato.

Tauranga City Council put $1.01m into the project, and the Western Bay of Plenty District Council contributed $245,000 to support the brand’s development and launch.

The total budget of nearly $1.28m also included contributions from partner agencies.

The brand was blessed at Masonic Park on Wednesday morning before a launch event at the new Tauranga CBD library.

The brand package included a website – tauranganz. com – videos showcasing the region, new social media pages and content, and branded merchandise, including T-shirts to be sold at the new iSite in the library.

Western Bay Mayor James Denyer said at the launch the milestone was the beginning of a long-term investment in the region’s future.

“The real work starts now because this place brand will only succeed if it continues to be built through partnership across councils, iwi mana whenua, businesses and the community.”

He said the brand created a unified identity for Tauranga and Western Bay while allowing individual communities to maintain and celebrate their own identities.

Ngāti Pūkenga chairwoman Kylie Smallman said she was initially sceptical about whether one brand could represent the many identities of Tauranga Moana.

“As mana whenua, I’m very protective. It’s not just a home to us; it’s also a strong part of who we are.”

She said she was surprised by the final results and felt it successfully incorporated local identity and mana whenua perspectives.

“I see myself, my people and mana whenua in there.”

She said opportunities enabled by the brand included showcasing local culture, strengthening community belonging and pride, increasing awareness of local history and building partnerships.

Dave Courtney, chief executive of the region’s economic development agency, Priority One, framed the brand as an economic development asset.

He said its job was to “drive our region’s revenue line” and attract investment, business, skilled workers, visitors and entrepreneurs.

“We already have the ingredients that make this place great; this is the icing on the cake.”

He said success would depend on councils, businesses, tourism operators, education providers and communities telling a common story.

Tauranga Mayor Mahé Drysdale said the brand was a significant collaboration between the councils and a long-term investment in regional identity.

University of Waikato director of Tauranga campus development and operations Joseph MacFarlane said the brand helped strengthen connections between the university, Tauranga and Western Bay communities.

Having a “strong brand” to showcase the region’s identity would help “immensely” with the university’s aim to make the campus a welcoming destination for students from around the world.

The brand was crafted by Auckland design agency, Guardians, founded by Anzac Tasker.

Tasker said the brand was inspired by the tides, coastlines, mountains, islands, estuaries and peninsulas.

He said the design provided a platform for many different local stories to be told.

Tourism Bay of Plenty general manager Oscar Nathan said Guardians was chosen from a “rigorous RFP [request for proposal] process”.

“Ultimately, if you look up the Guardians, you’ll see that they are the absolute best in class at what they do.”

More than 2000 residents participated in the engagement and design phase in workshops, hui and other gatherings across the region.

TaurangaNZ head of partnerships Hayley Nelson said in a media release that ensuring local voices shaped its identity was fundamental.

“Through extensive engagement and collaboration, feedback opportunities and further refinement, the result is a place brand that beautifully represents the history and stories of our distinctive communities and their aspirations.”

She said the brand provided a platform to strengthen the city’s reputation, raise visibility and tell a compelling story about the region.

“As one of New Zealand’s fastest-growing regions, we’ve seized the opportunity to tell a more connected and consistent story about who we are, what we value and where we’re heading.”

TaurangaNZ features a recognisable shared wordmark designed to “echo the tides and rhythms of life” in Tauranga and the Western Bay of Plenty.

“It highlights five key themes – raw connection, natural innovation, replenishing growth, a tapestry of communities, and dual rhythm.”

Complementary wordmarks have been created for other communities in the region, such as Waihī Beach, Pāpāmoa and Te Puke.

People would see the new identity online, at libraries and community venues, on flags near Tauranga Airport, on the city’s digital kiosks and at major events such as this weekend’s World Triathlon Cup in Mount Maunganui.

‘It’s a disgrace’: Pike River families on 16-year wait

New Zealand Herald November 18, 2026

Police near end of probe into Pike River mine blast that killed 29 men. Photo / NZ Police

By Samantha Gee of RNZ

Pike River families say it is a disgrace that they are still waiting for a decision on whether criminal charges will be laid, as a result of the disaster that left 29 men dead 16 years ago.

In February, police said the criminal investigation into the disaster on the South Island’s West Coast mine on November 19, 2010, was nearing the final stages.

Eight months on, Police Assistant Commissioner Corrie Parnell reiterated that point.

“Operational security around the next phase of the investigation is critical and therefore it is not appropriate to comment further at this time.”

The investigation was reopened in 2018 and figures showed that since then it had cost more than $35 million, with about half of that spent on consultants, specialist fees and overseas travel.

In September 2022, police announced they were reopening the borehole drilling operation as part of the investigation and 10 boreholes were drilled, imaged and resealed.

Human remains were found in the mine in 2023. In November 2024, police said they were working with the Crown Solicitor and considering whether to lay charges over the disaster and it was hoped a decision would be reached in the first half of 2025.

In February, police said they had been working with the Wellington Crown Solicitor on the “legally complex” case for more than 18 months.

Crown Law referred questions to police.

Some family members of those who died in the disaster said it was not good enough.

Sonya Rockhouse, whose son Ben was 21 when he was killed in the explosion, said it was “bloody frustrating” and “absolutely ridiculous” to still be waiting for a decision.

Police had been in touch with her last week, but did not have any new information.

“I said to them, ‘You know, people are starting to die, it’s been so long’, and we just don’t understand the hold-up really – it just beggars belief.”

Lawyer Nigel Hampton, KC, who represented the miners’ union at the royal commission inquiry and the victims’ families, was gravely ill, as were others connected to the disaster.

“Anna’s [Anna Osborne, widow of Milton Osborne] living on borrowed time, her five years was up last year and thankfully she’s showing no signs of anything happening,” Rockhouse said.

“But you just don’t know. I’m getting older, I’m 68 next birthday, I could have a heart attack and drop dead tomorrow.”

Rockhouse told Morning Report that no one had been held to account and there had been no apology.

“You can’t kill 29 men in this country and just walk away, if somebody kills someone or murders someone they go to trial and you know we’ve had none of that – we’ve had nothing, no truth, no justice, no accountability.”

She said those deciding whether to prosecute “need to get their flippin’ act together and make the right decision”.

“We’ve warned them, we’ve told them that if we don’t get the result that we want, then they’re going to hear a hell of a lot more from us.

“If we’ve got to go back and protest and do what we did before, then we will – I’ll retire from work and we’ll go for it.”

On the 16th anniversary, Rockhouse said she and Osborne would be in Auckland for the 2026 New Zealand Screen Awards, where the feature film Pike River about the mining disaster had received 15 nominations.

“It’s better than last year on the 15th anniversary, we were meeting with Brooke van Velden and that was a flipping waste of time.”

She said they had not heard anything since meeting with the former Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety but still wanted to see a corporate manslaughter charge introduced in New Zealand.

Bernie Monk, whose 23-year-old son Michael died in the mine, said it had been a 16-year wait for redress. He said some of the families were told three months ago that a decision on charges was weeks away, but then nothing had happened.

“It’s a disgrace. We’ve got one of the biggest industrial homicides in New Zealand’s history and we’ve had to wait 16 years to get justice and accountability.

“We are never going to go away until something is done.”

Monk said on the 16th anniversary, he would be at the opening of the memorial at the mine site, which he expected would become a major asset for the West Coast and those wanting to commemorate the lives of the 29 men.

In response to questions from Kathryn Ryan on Nine to Noon about whether it was appropriate that families were still waiting for a decision on a prosecution, Parliament Speaker Gerry Brownlee said it was not, but that he had to be careful about what he said.

“What I will say is that it surprised me, I got there a few hours after it happened on the night, up on the mountain and from that moment – the police who should have been in charge and were in charge legally, had the [Pike River] company representative as a spokesman.

“At the time, I found that very odd because there had to be questions about what actually happened here. That’s all I’ll say about that.”

He said there remained questions over how the Pike River disaster was able to happen.

There was no ability for the methane to escape the mine before the explosion, he said, and it was his personal opinion that there should have been a second entrance into the mine.

“In the film footage you see on television of the stack, so-called breather stack, that’s 180 metres above the drift and there were flames coming out of that, so the intensity of that inferno was something wicked. Why wasn’t there a second entrance?”

He said he met the mine rescue crew that day with then-Prime Minister John Key.

“I met them on the night it happened and they weren’t going in there. They made it very clear, no – methane level’s too high, it’s dangerous.”

He and Key met them again the following Monday and asked each of them if they would go in, and they all said no.

Department of Conservation Greymouth operations manager Chris Hickford said the organisation had been working with the families on the memorial to commemorate the 29 men who died in the disaster.

He said details and photos of the memorial would be released once families had been to the site for an invite-only event for the 16th anniversary on Thursday.

The upper valley and memorial would remain closed to the public until visitor access, interpretation, and other facilities were completed – likely in mid-2027, he said.

It would be the first time since the disaster that members of the public were able to visit the portal.

- RNZ

A young supermarket checkout operator is being praised for his generous gesture towards a shopper caught short by paying for her groceries.

Staffer Hassan Munir, 21, who also plays professional basketball for the Wellington Saints, was scanning items at New World Hutt City in Lower Hutt yesterday afternoon when a customer realised she did not have enough money to cover her bill.

The customer wrote on a local community group on Facebook that she asked Munir to remove some of the items, but instead he stepped in and paid for the difference himself.

The anonymous shopper said they were particularly touched by the discreet way he helped.

“I also noticed he kept a low voice when all this was going on [so] as to not let other customers know of my failings and probably save what dignity I had left,” the customer wrote.

“I’m on my way home on the bus and hope his parents see this so they know about their son, Hassan.”

The post has attracted widespread attention online, prompting an outpouring of praise from locals.

Munir, who has worked at the store for three and a half years, told the Herald he didn’t think twice about helping.

“She had about $80 to spend,” he said.

“It was really only like $4.80 that I had to spend. It was like a Marmite, and I was like, ‘Nah, you know what? It’s just Marmite. It’s nothing, not a big deal’.

“I was just thinking about her, like, her kids might be wanting that Marmite or something. I just did it. It wasn’t really a big deal for me at the time, hey.

“I didn’t want her to feel bad or anything.”

New World Hutt City owner-operator Dan Williams said the team was proud of Munir, particularly the way he had handled the situation.

“What he did was incredibly kind, but what really stood out was the way he did it,” he said.

“He could see someone was in a difficult spot and quietly helped them out without making a fuss or embarrassing them.”

Munir, who is of Samoan and Pakistani heritage, works at the store part-time alongside pursuing his passion for basketball.

Wellington Saints chief executive Jordan Mills told the Herald Munir was a special young man who was well-liked by students and the wider community.

Alongside playing basketball, Munir is involved in the club’s coaching-in-schools programme, helping introduce young people to the sport.

Mills said he was “not surprised” to hear about Munir’s kindness, pointing to his “good upbringing”.

Munir acknowledged his parents and his faith for teaching him the importance of kindness and generosity.

“That’s really all from my parents that I am the way I am,” he said.

“Shout out to God as well. Thank you to God and my parents for teaching me about just being generous.”

He said he was grateful for the positive comments he had received online, but it was not the first time he had stepped in for customers who were short of money.

“I just try and help people out.”

Online commenters described him as an “outstanding human” with a “heart of gold”, as well as “incredibly considerate” and a “hard worker”.

One woman said she had shown the Facebook post to Munir’s supervisors while visiting the supermarket, and claimed they were not surprised by his generosity.

“He was so humble. He’s always so happy and polite when he serves me. I showed his supervisors the post, and they weren’t surprised,” she wrote.

“They said he does this all the time. What a dude!”

Williams described Munir as a humble young man who genuinely cared about those around him.

“Hassan is a really good young man – humble, switched on and someone with a strong moral compass who genuinely cares about people and his community.

“It’s lovely to see his kindness recognised like this. It certainly put a smile on all our faces.”

The world of The Gilded Age – the age itself, and the television series which borrows its setting, name and themes – could easily slide into the realm of soap opera, were it not for a persistent political thread that ties many of the show’s stories together.

Series creator Julian Fellowes’ turned Downton Abbey into a polished family drama that dabbled in class war, but the proximity of The Gilded Age to exploding American wealth and the age of robber barons has unexpectedly given it a little more political fire.

“Any time you do a period drama, you’re always in some way looking through the lens of your own time,” says Cynthia Nixon, who plays the once-penniless but now wealthy Ada Brook in the series.

“It is a moment that it is very similar to our period in the same way. Some of it is like women are still fighting for equality, African Americans are still fighting for equality, immigrants are still fighting for equality, working-class people are fighting for a bigger piece of the pie.”

Even more relevant to 2026, adds Nixon, is that “there are these people at the upper echelons of society who, through a combination of quirk and genius and being in the right place at the right time and determination, have made them so much money that they don’t even know what to do with it.

“As their wealth increases, everyone else’s wealth decreases. And this terrible imbalance has got to lead to a restructuring of society or a revolution. Those are really the only two choices.”

When the series opened, Ada Brook was the younger, unmarried sister of family matriarch Agnes van Rhijn, played by Christine Baranski. Their father had squandered the family’s wealth, so Agnes married the emotionally abusive Arnold van Rhijn and spinster Ada had come to live with them as part of the package.

But Ada’s fortunes would change; the show’s third and fourth seasons have seen her transform following the death of her husband, Reverend Luke Forte (Robert Sean Leonard), after discovering he came from a wealthy Boston family and his death left her with a massive inheritance.

The twist means, essentially, that Ada’s power in the structure of the household shifts, as Agnes’s recedes. (Cliff’s note for irregular viewers: Agnes’s son, Oscar [Blake Ritson], had lost the van Rhijn fortune to a swindler.)

5:04

Robber barons and revolution: the very modern point to The Gilded Age

Cynthia Nixon talks about working with Christine Baranski, wealth inequality, and the ‘original Mean Girl’ Mrs Astor

What does not change is that Ada and Agnes seem to operate as a kind of two-woman stage drama within the ornate frame of the show. Nixon and Baranski are veteran stage actresses, and Nixon says she relishes the screen time they share.

“When I was first cast in the show, the first thing I heard was [creator] Julian Fellowes, and that was very exciting. The second thing I heard was that it was the 1880s. That was very exciting. And the third thing I heard was Christine Baranski,” says Nixon.

“It’s such a delight to work with her and … she said something when our fortunes reversed – when Oscar lost all her money and then my husband made me a rich woman with his death – she said, the reversal in fortunes is a terrible thing for Agnes as a character, but it’s a wonderful thing for Christine as an actor.

“I think that so much of acting is you throw the ball as hard as you can and the other person catches it and throws it back,” Nixon says. “And when Christine is your acting partner, you don’t have to lob softballs. You can use everything you’ve got.”

The Gilded Age also offers a very specific spin on female power. While the wider world at the time was dominated by men and money, it subtly nods to ways in which women and minorities expressed their power and, in different ways, sometimes controlled their destinies.

“Because doors were closed to women in most professions, particularly women of a certain class were forbidden from working,” Nixon says. “So they took this seemingly ridiculous world of balls and tea parties and afternoon visits and calling cards, and they turned it into an industry that determined who was in and who was out and who had power.

“And having money was not enough,” Nixon adds. “[Shipping dynasty matriarch] Mrs Astor is sort of the original ‘mean girl’ deciding who’s in and who’s out. And god help you if you cross [her] because there’s no help for you.”

Before Nixon was Ada Brook in The Gilded Age she was grieving mother Becca Corbett in Rabbit Hole, a performance that earned her a Tony Award. She delivered an Emmy-nominated performance as Eleanor Roosevelt in the HBO film Warm Springs. And she will forever be connected to Miranda Hobbes, the New York corporate lawyer in Sex and the City and its sequel And Just Like That ….

All of those women, Nixon says, are never too far away, even long after the role has been laid to rest.

“I think particularly for a character that you’re still playing and still working on, on some level, your brain and your body are still thinking about them and still unpacking them,” she says. “I feel like they are definitely with me all the time.”

One very specific thing that surrounds and in some ways defines Nixon’s work is that much of her working life – certainly starring in Sex and the City, And Just Like That … and now The Gilded Age – is the architecture of New York City. For The Gilded Age, in particular, many parts of the city retain the heritage architecture that was built during the actual gilded age.

“Life is like a movie, and you think that the movie started playing when you walked into it, but the movie’s been playing for millions of years,” Nixon says.

“So, of course, I grew up with these amazing Stanford White-designed buildings, the New York Public Library, the Metropolitan Museum of Art [and though I knew his name], it never occurred to me when they were built, why they were built and who commissioned them.

“Now when I walk around, and I see these beautiful houses on Fifth Avenue and other places, I have a much deeper understanding that actually these weren’t just erected as public buildings. People used to, in many cases, live in them. And that is mind-blowing to me.”

The Gilded Age is now streaming on Paramount+.

Leanne’s ex was convicted of abusing her. A court mandates she co-parents with him

Sydney Morning Herald November 19, 2026

When Leanne* learnt the Family Court granted her ex, who was convicted of abusing her, overnight stays with their two young daughters, she walked outside and had a panic attack.

“I had a nervous breakdown ... I just screamed blue murder and hit my steering wheel,” she said. “I was so angry.”

The process has had an immense toll on Leanne’s physical and mental health, while the court gave confusing and extreme orders including mandatory therapy.

Scores of recent parliamentary inquiries, studies and reports have highlighted how the courts are contributing to further harm for people experiencing violence, while an investigation by The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age has revealed systems abuse, where perpetrators weaponise legal processes to continue domestic and family violence, is endemic.

Leanne still has a visceral reaction when she sees her ex, who was convicted of multiple offences including three counts of assault. He was fined and sentenced to a 12-month community correction order.

She was awarded sole parental responsibility, but must advise her ex on decisions about their daughters and facilitate handovers.

A judge ordered Leanne to attend therapy and submit proof to her ex and the court to keep her children. The reports had to include notes from a psychologist stating that Leanne understood that her ex posed no risk to the children. If she did not comply, the children would be removed from her care and placed with the father full-time.

Despite having no documented history of violence, Leanne was also ordered to complete a domestic violence prevention course.

While the Federal Family Circuit Court of Australia has implemented a raft of reforms to address domestic and family violence, including training for judges, screening parties for risk, and making family violence a consideration in the property and finance division, survivors and advocates argue more needs to be done to assist victim-survivors.

The Family Court is one of Australia’s most secretive jurisdictions, where publishing any identifying details of parties, witnesses, or children is illegal. Eighty-four per cent of parenting cases in the Family Court contain allegations of domestic violence.

We want to understand how systems abuse occurs and how to address it, and we’d like to hear from you. You can share your story with the reporter using the form below. By law, we cannot publicly identify parties to Family Court proceedings.

Leanne’s husband allegedly twice choked her in the weeks after she gave birth to their youngest child. While he was found not guilty of the choking charges, he was convicted of three counts of assault, one count of harassment, and twice breaching an AVO issued after his arrest.

In 2023, Leanne fled with their two young children to the US, where she had family, to escape further abuse. Her ex filed a Hague Convention abduction application, an international treaty drafted more than 40 years ago to address a spate of fathers taking their children abroad, which triggered an INTERPOL alert. Leanne returned with the children.

Upon returning, she unsuccessfully fought a ban on relocating abroad in the Family Court. Her mental health, which had been affected by the trauma of the abuse, worsened with the stress of court and the thought of losing her children to her abuser.

The AVO protecting her expired last year.

His legal team scrutinised her “fawning” text messages sent in the year after the abuse, questioning the legitimacy of her fear and using her mental health to challenge her fitness as a parent. He also admitted to pouring water over her head and verbal abuse.

Despite the convictions and further admissions of abuse, which a judge noted “raise serious concerns about father’s capacity to parent the children”, the court accepted the Independent Children’s Lawyers report that the children should have unsupervised time with the father.

Leanne said that before a final hearing, the judge told them to return to mediation, which was unsuccessful.

The court then granted final orders, giving the father increasing time with the children and required Leanne to submit psychological reports helping her accept he posed no “unacceptable risk” to their safety.

The judge also found her ex had “done nothing” to address his violent behaviour towards her.

Three appeal judges overturned the therapy order, calling it “vague”, “likely futile”, and “confusing”, and ruling that removing the children for non-compliance would be “sudden and extreme”.

The toll the proceedings had on Leanne was immense. She said she was hospitalised before the final hearing for a panic attack, had started taking antidepressants, and her hearing loss had worsened. “I shake … I have dizzy spells,” she said. “I’ve lost weight.”

She became fearful when she had to provide her address to the court and when he suggested home drop-offs. He now collects the children from locations close to her home. “That’s very, very scary,” she said.

Though eligible for legal aid, the former lawyer has spent thousands on court-ordered evaluations. She is often self-represented. Her ex spent close to $500,000 on legal fees.

A Family Court spokesperson said it couldn’t comment on individual cases, and declined to say whether the judge who made the initial orders requiring therapy was required to undergo additional training.

The spokesperson said the courts assessed safety before mediation, holding most electronically to manage risk where family violence made negotiating freely “unsafe or impossible”.

A 2023 review found the court exacerbated survivors’ trauma and routinely dismissed abuse claims, while a 2023 study on GPs treating domestic violence survivors found they were reluctant to seek necessary treatment from their GPs out of fear their clinical notes would be used against them in court. A 2015 study found mental health was used to limit child contact for 30 per cent of cases with mothers, but just 2 per cent of cases with fathers.

Meanwhile, Domestic Violence Commissioner Michaela Cronin said in September some judges still held horrendous views about women, with researcher Jess Hill noting an evaluation of the Family Court reforms had revealed some judges resisted domestic violence training. A 2025 study found family court judges reinforced gender bias.

Domestic Violence Action Centre chief executive Amie Carrington said women sometimes chose to stay in a violent relationship because they feared a court would award unsafe and unsupervised contact between the children and the perpetrator.

“They may choose to stay [to] remain supervising the child … as a protective mechanism for their children because they’re so afraid,” she said.

The resulting anxiety is then used to paint mothers as unfit parents, she said, with courts sometimes treating abuse as isolated incidents rather than a cumulative pattern.

Carrington said courts needed to start looking at patterns to distinguish coercive control from parental conflict. While there had been strides towards this, Carrington said there was more work to be done. “There needs to be stronger accountability for people who are using violence,” she said.

Reforms implemented in 2024 have included training for judges on domestic violence and expanded risk assessment screening, and removed the legal presumption of equal shared parental responsibility, focusing instead on a child’s best interests.

However, Carrington said a cultural approach still existed where children were treated as the property of biological parents instead of autonomous and victims.

DVNSW Deputy chief executive Pia Birac said protracted court proceedings could have an immense psychological impact on victim-survivors.

“There’s an idea that after a relationship ends, so too does the violence or coercive control,” she said. “Instead, many find themselves in proceedings that are not only hugely costly, but they have this ongoing relationship with the other person in the courts.”

Birac said the impact extended to children, too: “Children are not just exposed to violence; they experience it. They live with the consequences of a profound breach of trust by an adult who was supposed to keep them safe.”

Unless a perpetrator took meaningful action to address the drivers that led them to abuse their loved ones, Birac said, the risk was still present post-separation.

Birac said facilitating children’s time with an abuser could be construed as them not being protective, while not facilitating time meant they were viewed as obstructive. “Women in this process are caught in a double bind,” she said.

A 2025 parliamentary inquiry, which Independent MP Kate Chaney sat on, found the Family Court was ill-equipped to respond to family violence, and kept victims tied to abusers.

The inquiry found some judges even overrode state violence orders to grant perpetrators access to children. While the government backed 10 of its 11 recommendations, Chaney warned of “very little accountability” around implementing them.

“These reviews that talk about the deep systemic problems, and there’s very little accountability about what happens to those recommendations,” she said.

“[People in the court are] being further attacked by their ex-partner, who they’re trying to escape, by the very system that’s meant to help them resolve those issues.”

Chaney is calling on the government to implement time-bound, measurable reforms, as recommended by the Domestic Violence Commissioner.

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland acknowledged that, while there had been significant reform to address domestic and family violence, there was still a long way to go.

Rowland said training judges, lawyers and other court staff was a key focus of the government. Judicial staff must undergo annual training on domestic and family violence, while the government had also launched a national training program on coercive control.

The government had also agreed in principle to a 2022 Australian Law Reform Commission recommendation to establish a judicial commission as an oversight mechanism for the courts.

Leanne does not believe the Family Court is an appropriate mechanism for those who have experienced domestic violence, and gives too little weight to her former partner’s convictions.

“The court empowers [abusers] … they feast on it, and it will literally lead to more domestic violence.”

*Names changed for legal reasons.

The National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) offers support for emotional, physical and financial abuse. Support is also available from Kids Helpline 1800 55 1800; Lifeline 131 114; Beyond Blue 1300 224 636.

UK government reportedly asks for Russell Brand’s YouTube account to be deactivated

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 20:39:49 GMT

Justice minister makes request to Google representatives in wake of 51-year-old’s prison message, according to Sky News

The government has reportedly asked Google to deactivate Russell Brand’s YouTube account after he was able to publish a message claiming his innocence following his conviction for sexual offences.

A justice minister met representatives from the technology company to make the request after social media firm Meta disabled the former comedian’s profiles on Instagram and Facebook, according to Sky News.

Earlier this week, the Ministry of Justice launched an investigation into whether Brand, 51, broke prison rules after he shared a message claiming he was not guilty days after his conviction at Southwark Crown Court.

The actor was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years in prison for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

His wife, Laura Brand, read a message from her husband on Sunday in a video uploaded to their YouTube channel.

Prisoners are allowed to protest their innocence, meaning that no criminal offence was committed in the release of the video. However, convicts are not permitted to make statements from jail that cause distress to victims, and heavy restrictions apply to speaking to the media.

If he is found to have broken the rules, Brand could face sanctions ranging from an extension of his sentence to loss of privileges such as access to a telephone for a limited period.

It is understood a prisoner will be deemed to have broken the rules if they provide comments to a family member that they know will be published.

Responding to the video, the prime minister’s spokesperson called the comments “clearly appalling”.

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, also criticised broadcasters on Wednesday for “amplifying” Brand’s words by airing a clip of Laura Brand reading the message.

She told LBC radio: “I was appalled at that, and actually I think mainstream media shouldn’t have transmitted that either.”

Asked why she wanted to censor the message, Powell said: “It’s a platform I don’t think … should have been amplified, to be honest.”

The Ministry of Justice and Google were contacted for comment.

Google stopped Brand from profiting from YouTube content in 2023 after a media investigation revealed allegations of rape and sexual assault. At the time, the video platform said the decision was made “to protect” its users.

Birmingham council granted interim ban on union jacks on lamp-posts

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 20:32:58 GMT

High court judge issues order against Raise the Colours over flags on council-owned street furniture

The campaign group Raise the Colours has been temporarily banned from placing union jacks on lamp-posts and roundabouts in Birmingham after a legal challenge by the local council.

The high court judge Emma Kelly granted an interim injunction banning the placing of all flags on council-owned street furniture without prior permission in a judgment issued on Wednesday, Birmingham city council said.

The council, run by a minority coalition led by the Liberal Democrats, sought the injunction against seven people identified as supporting or participating in the affixing of flags in the city, including Ryan Bridge, a co-founder of Raise the Colours and “persons unknown”.

The application for an injunction, which attracted national attention and follows similar action by Oxfordshire county council, argued the actions of the flag activists had caused danger, alarm and distress.

People associated with Raise the Colours, which describes itself as a grassroots movement, have been placing union jacks and St George’s flags on public infrastructure across the country since August last year.

The group’s website states it is a “campaign to cover Britain in symbols of unity and patriotism”. However, others have accused the group of racism and spreading anti-immigration rhetoric – claims it has previously denied.

In its claim to the high court, Birmingham city council said the defendants had travelled across the city “unlawfully affixing flags” and had confronted residents who attempted to remove them.

“In doing so, they are engaging in tortious and criminal behaviour, which is both antisocial and dangerous,” the claim read, adding that the behaviour had caused “danger” and “alarm” to residents.

The council said residents of Birmingham had suffered “fear, anxiety, intimidation, harassment,” been put at “serious risk of harm”, and some had suffered physical injuries, including a broken leg.

The case was adjourned in early September after the judge said she was “troubled by the lack of clarity” from the council “against the individual defendants”, and a further hearing was scheduled at the end of September.

Bridge opposed the injunction and read a written statement to the court. He said: “For me, the union flag represents home, identity, belonging, national identity, British culture and patriotism.”

His lawyer, Liam Wells, argued that the injunction would have a “chilling effect” on human rights and that erecting union jacks and St George’s flags was an expression of his political views.

Wells said the interim injunction would risk “silencing people in their political views and expression of political opinions” and the council had failed to prove Bridge had acted unlawfully.

Three local residents, Adam Biggs, Mark Hudson and Tony Kaye, joined the case representing ‘persons unknown’ opposing the injunction bid, and expressed concerns it would ban people flying flags for pride and other campaigns.

The council’s cabinet member for equalities, communities and social justice, Jane Baston, said on Wednesday the local authority was grateful for the judgment and it was an “important step”.

“We have taken a proportionate and evidence-led approach throughout this case. Our priority has always been to protect public safety, supporting the welfare of our staff and contractors, maintaining community cohesion and ensuring public funds are used responsibly,” she said.

In a video uploaded to Facebook, Bridge said he was “gutted” and “devastated” by the decision, including the fact that the injunction granted power of arrest against him and others.

He said Raise the Colours was “not about race, colour, creed” but about opposing “illegal invaders breaking in our country, jeopardising our borders, on the rubber dinghies”.

At the Reform UK conference in Birmingham in September, Nigel Farage promised to help Bridge in his legal fight if the party was able to do so.

In response to the judgment, Reform’s leader in Birmingham, Jex Parkin, said the council had its “priorities entirely wrong” and had pursued an “ideologically driven case against residents proudly displaying our national flags – at huge public expense”.

The leader of the local Conservatives, Robert Alden, also criticised the injunction and said the council was “punishing ordinary Birmingham residents who simply want to show pride in where they live”.

He said: “Amidst a 23-month bin strike, loss of roads funding, and mounting litter on our streets, the council has chosen to make this court action a priority.”

The group Brummies United Against Racism, which campaigned for the injunction, welcomed the judgment. Members of the group told the Guardian earlier this year they had presented evidence of incidents involving Raise the Colours to the police and council officers.

The group said it was “not opposed to this country’s flag” and many of its supporters “see the flag as a symbol of celebration and unity”. “However, we are firmly opposed to those who seek to use the flag to further an agenda of hate and who dress up racism as patriotism,” a statement read.

A further hearing in the case will take place on Thursday.

Shabana Mahmood backs ban on police marching in pride events in uniform

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 20:03:50 GMT

Home secretary says ‘routine two-tier policing’ does not exist, but public trust in impartial law enforcement must be restored

Shabana Mahmood has backed a ban on police officers marching in pride events in uniform as she said there had been a “few examples” of two-tier policing.

Although she said there was no systematic or routine two-tier policing, the home secretary said “a new impartiality standard” was necessary to reverse the fall in the public’s faith in law enforcement.

She said one example had been when police officers took part in a pride event in Northumbria last year, which a court found had breached a duty of impartiality. Mahmood said: “The judgment found that they got the balance wrong … and that marching … was not acceptable and not impartial.

“Today at those marches, you will often have campaigners, on gender identity … and those issues are now contested … the marching alongside looks like a political act.”

Nik Adams, the deputy commissioner of City of London police who is also the LGBTQ+ lead for police chiefs, said: “Using the language about LGBTQ issues being contested makes LGBTQ people in policing and wider society feel less safe, makes their lives feel less valued.

“LGBTQ is a protected characteristic in law. The rights are hard won.”

Wiltshire police faces a court challenge next week for setting up a stall at a pride event in Swindon after claims it had exposed a lack of neutrality amid disputes over transgender rights.

Asked if she was accepting there was two-tier policing, Mahmood said: “There’s no systematic, systemic, routine two-tier policing in this country. I reject that charge.

One police leader told the Guardian this rhetoric was concerning as forces tried to navigate the culture wars buffeting Britain while serving all communities.

The Guardian view on the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting: it may be a first, but it’s not progress

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:35:14 GMT

A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies

“Historic” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement.

The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism.

Mr Xi looks like the power broker bringing Moscow and Washington together, and the gracious host, in a city which showcases China’s economic and technological progress and aspirations. The contrast between the glossy metropolis and a US currently beset by glaring tech failures hitting everything from flights to banking is especially flattering. For Mr Putin, who gloated about the “humiliation” of Europe in the run-up, this meeting is an even clearer win, making him look like a superpower peer rather than the leader of a pariah nation with a struggling economy.

Mr Trump has got a red carpet embrace, another “first” to promote – preferable to headlines dwelling on the Republicans’ midterms disaster – and the congenial company of strongmen. His nation has less to celebrate. Mr Trump seems to see meeting longstanding US allies as at best a chore. His bruising tariffs and nakedly transactional approach to security, as well as his love of autocrats, have pushed countries like the Philippines – which hosted the US president en route to China – into hedging their bets.

Mr Trump is not expected to raise Nvidia and suspected Chinese espionage – perhaps not least because his closeness to Jensen Huang, the company’s ousted CEO, makes the issue at least as discomfiting for him as it is for Beijing. The US president is unlikely to embarrass the two countries that are central to Iran’s ability to resist his disastrous and illegal war, or to press China over its facilitation of Russia’s war against Ukraine. Ukraine and Taiwan have reason to be anxious any time he speaks to Mr Putin and Mr Xi. But the US president is as likely to undermine them, whether deliberately or otherwise, in bilaterals or via a throwaway remark.

Comparisons to the 1945 Yalta summit of Joseph Stalin, Franklin D Roosevelt and Winston Churchill – which divided up Europe – grotesquely overstate the importance of a meeting scheduled to last less than an hour. Mr Xi does not do spontaneity, and is unlikely to be lured into sudden announcements. And despite the surface amity, the three still have strongly competing interests. China’s threat to rare earths brought a trade truce, but skirmishes continue. Mr Trump has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation. While China is arming itself at worrying speed, its arsenal is still dwarfed by those of the US and Russia.

Talking to rivals and adversaries is not inherently unwise. Under another US president, a closely focused and carefully prepared trilateral on, for instance, disarmament might even be fruitful. This is not that world. This will not be that meeting.

The Guardian view on ‘two-tier policing’: tackle the myth, don’t pander to it

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:34:59 GMT

Confidence in the system is being corroded by cynical campaigns and far-right propaganda – that is the challenge to be confronted

There are many areas of policy where public opinion diverges from evidence. Voters overestimate rates of crime, for example. Many will be sceptical of politicians who say today’s streets are safer than they used to be, although that is the reality. The challenge is to find methods of persuasion that don’t belittle the experiences of people who are afraid, and don’t like to be told their fears are unfounded.

But there is a different challenge that arises when the cause of public concern is a problem that doesn’t really exist. Many people are angry about “two-tier policing” in Britain, supposedly characterised by disproportionately severe enforcement against white people and leniency towards minorities. There is no evidence to support a systemic bias of that kind. By contrast, the data suggests an imbalance of fair treatment goes the other way. People of colour are underrepresented in the police, disproportionately targeted with stop-and-search policies and, if arrested, likelier to have force used against them.

The “two-tier” complaint has not arisen as the expression of millions experiencing anti-white policing. It is a function of campaigning by partisan media and radical rightwing politicians amplifying individual stories to construct a bogus narrative of official prejudice. Such was the case with Henry Nowak, for example, who was mistakenly arrested while dying from stab wounds inflicted by an attacker who falsely claimed to have himself been the victim of a racially aggravated assault. Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, urged the public to respond with “pure cold rage”. Elon Musk, the billionaire proprietor of X who routinely uses his platform to promote far-right activism in the UK, seized the incident as a cause célèbre. Protests turned violent. Politicians and media then cited “two-tier policing” as a mitigating factor, as if rioters were giving expression to a legitimate grievance.

It does not take many such incidents to irrigate a thriving digital ecosystem where it becomes entirely normal to believe something about the way UK policing works that is simply untrue.

Changing minds in that climate is not easy, although it is a task that Shabana Mahmood has set for police. Addressing the National Police Chiefs’ Council on Wednesday, the home secretary said the “corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing” had to be tackled “head-on”. While recognising that the problem was exaggerated by “motivated actors”, Ms Mahmood warned against “misguided course-correction” in dealing with minority concerns leading to “differential treatment”. She announced that a new “impartiality standard” would be set to reassure the public that all would be treated equally.

The ambition to change perceptions is the right one, but the method is flawed. Declaring the need for greater impartiality in the same breath as “two-tier policing” ramps up the salience of the phrase without tackling its underlying toxicity. The risk is that people who are convinced there is a conspiracy against them will feel vindicated, without trusting the politicians who offer a remedy. Advertising the falsehood is not a way to debunk it. The real challenge here is countering a vast machinery of far-right propaganda that contaminates British political debate on matters of race and social cohesion. That is a job that depends more on political imagination and courage than reworded police protocols. Impartiality should certainly be the standard. Facts and reality must also be the foundation of policy.

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:07:55 GMT

China’s Xi Jinping rallied Asia-Pacific nations against trade protectionism on Wednesday morning before heading to the airport to welcome Donald Trump, whose administration has just further restricted advanced chip exports, with a rare hug.

The Chinese president spent Wednesday’s opening day of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit switching lanes between multilateralist and big-power politics, culminating in a group photo where he stood central among fellow leaders. He was flanked by Trump and Vladimir Putin – whose blockbuster trilateral meeting will dominate Thursday’s proceedings as the summit gets to its business end.

Having all delegates in the photograph was a tightrope feat in itself, with potential Canadian and Australian refusals to stand with Putin over the war in Ukraine shelved out of respect for the host.

The Russian president did not arrive in a conciliatory mood, using his speech at the summit to call western powers “former hegemons”, state that Europe was in “a humiliating decline” and proclaim that sanctions no longer worked.

However, toasting his varied visitors at a welcoming banquet, Xi invoked “the grand plan for Asia-Pacific cooperation”. Thursday would see those gathered “discuss measures to expand mutual openness, explore pathways for innovation-driven growth, [and] broaden opportunities for pragmatic cooperation in various fields,” he said.

Openness was the main theme of his keynote address, presenting China as a stalwart of free trade and technological innovation.

“We find ourselves in a changing and turbulent world. Global growth lacks momentum, and unilateralism and protectionism are rampant,” he told the audience of business executives and Apec leaders. “We should firmly safeguard the WTO-centred, rules-based multilateral trading system, support free and open trade and investment, and keep global industrial and supply chains stable and unimpeded.”

Critics of Beijing have long accused it of hypocrisy on this point, noting the obstacles many foreign businesses face entering China’s vast market. But Xi’s messaging on open trade was echoed by other leaders who took to the stage after him, including South Korea’s Lee ⁠Jae Myung and Malaysia’s Anwar Ibrahim.

Putin meanwhile took aim at sanctions, claiming they had “largely run their course, having ⁠lost much of their intimidating power”.

That prompted a rebuttal from Canada’s Mark Carney, who told reporters Putin was “lying”. “Sanctions are very real and they’re going to continue to increase as long as this war goes on,” he said.

When Xi met Putin though, he called for closer political and military ties between Russia and China, in a continued demonstration of a tight relationship that has only deepened since Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2022.

Before Putin’s arrival in China, Russia sent nuclear-capable bombers to an airport in Vietnam, in a rare deployment interpreted as a pointed show of Moscow’s ability to project strength in the region despite being embroiled in the Ukraine war. Russian military aircraft had spooked air forces in both Taiwan and Japan on Tuesday as they flew past them while routeing south from Russia’s Far East region.

It was Xi’s reception of Trump, complete with an embrace, that broke with convention; the reception on the airport tarmac is believed to be the first by a Chinese leader in decades, although during Xi’s state visit to Washington in September, Trump had also taken the unusual step of greeting Xi on the tarmac.

Xi travelled to the airport despite the US announcing on Monday new interim rules to further restrict Beijing’s access to advanced semiconductors. That followed an awkward week of news after the chief executive of US chipmaker Nvidia resigned over an affair, reportedly with a woman some US officials suspect of being a Chinese spy.

Beijing’s “overriding objective” was “extending the fragile calm in the US-China relationship for as long as possible”, Ryan Hass, from the Brookings thinktank, told the AFP news agency. “[The reception] set a positive tone for Trump’s visit, marking a contrast from the swirl of news around the Jensen Huang scandal that preceded Trump’s arrival in Shenzhen.”

The state news agency Xinhua said Xi had noted “China is a nation with a tradition of courtesy that values reciprocating goodwill”, after Trump met Xi at the airport when he visited the US.

Trump and Xi will hold a bilateral meeting as well as talks with Putin on Thursday. On Wednesday, the Associated Press reported that Trump had said he and Putin would meet separately as well, citing an anonymous US official.

These meetings will dominate the day’s schedule and the news cycle, a fact that has at times seemed to bother China.

“The Chinese actually tried to have this meeting not happen … They kind of got jammed into it. Then, when it was going to happen, they just wanted statements,” the former US national security adviser Jake Sullivan said on The Rest is Politics podcast. “They are going to be deeply uncomfortable throughout this because this does not fit their narrative of a country that believes in multi-alignment, the United Nations, everyone around the table.”

Shen Weizhong, a former policy planner with China’s foreign ministry who now works for the Global Governance Institution, a Beijing-based thinktank, told the Guardian he would not be surprised if Sullivan was right and that China was “torn”.

“On the one hand, it will steal the spotlight. The outcome is not clear and there are no immediate deliverables,” he said. “But on the other side, it will help China’s image – it is the only facilitator who could do this, and if it can ease tensions on the world stage, that will be good.” He said he suspected enthusiasm from both Putin and Trump for the meeting could have ultimately swayed Beijing.

China is actively opposing the framing of the meetings as a new Yalta, the 1945 meeting between Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt that in effect carved up postwar Europe. “The global south will not like having a Yalta 2.0, and China is always taking the smaller countries into consideration,” said Shen.

Also potentially on Thursday’s agenda is an Apec joint statement that, an official told Reuters, delegates were “working around the clock” to find agreement on. “China as host will want something,” said Shen, though even Beijing is “not as obsessed with such deliverables” these days.
