Bacterial toxin produced by E coli leading suspect in rise in bowel cancer among under-50s

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:55:14 GMT

Scientists tell Commons exposure to colibactin in early life is potential driver of early-onset colorectal cancer

Exposure to a bacterial toxin in early life has emerged as a leading suspect in the rise of bowel cancer among those under 50, MPs have heard.

Cases of early-onset bowel cancer have doubled in many countries in the past two decades, and while rising obesity and a fall in physical activity are contributors, researchers believe other factors must also be involved.

Dr Karl Smith-Byrne, a senior molecular epidemiologist at the University of Oxford, told the Commons science and technology committee that known risk factors for colorectal cancer, such as obesity, smoking and alcohol, can explain only about half of the cases doctors diagnose.

He said he did not find it “plausible” that the rise in early onset bowel cancer could be entirely explained by risk factors that researchers were already aware of.

Last year scientists identified a toxin called colibactin, produced by some variants of E coli bacteria in the gut, as a potential driver of early onset colorectal cancer. Hallmark mutations caused by the toxin were three times more common in tumours from people under 40 than in those from people over 70.

More work is needed to understand whether colibactin actually drives bowel cancer, but it is a question scientists are now actively pursuing. “That’s probably the leading explanation at the moment,” Smith-Byrne told MPs.

Prof Mike Stratton at the Sanger Institute, who was not at the hearing, has said that colibactin causes mutations in some children but not others, with evidence of mutations appearing as early as infancy. By the age of 10, affected children can have a similar “mutational burden” to a 50-year-old, his work showed.

“If it is causing mutations, it’s causing mutations at a sensitive period earlier in life, and that can give that person’s colon or their rectum a head start on its journey towards being cancerous or developing these tumours,” said Smith-Byrne, who is himself a survivor of early-onset rectal cancer.

Some suspect that particular variants of E coli that normally live harmlessly in the gut have evolved in recent decades to produce colibactin. Prof Elio Riboli, a cancer epidemiologist at Imperial College London, told the committee: “This colibactin is essentially found in people born after 1960. Something has happened in the E coli bacteria … There must have been a mutation, and there is a new bacteria.”

Bowel cancer is the third most common cancer in the world, accounting for about one in 10 of all cases. The disease is still far more common in the over-50s, but global figures suggest diagnoses are rising steeply in younger people.

Prof Helen Coleman, a cancer epidemiologist at Queen’s University Belfast, told MPs that colibactin was “the first new clue that we’ve had in quite some time”, but that its potential role in bowel cancer was still under investigation.

“Even though we’re talking about adults that are being diagnosed with cancer between 18 and 49, it’s quite likely to be very early life exposures,” she said. “It could be something you were exposed to in very early childhood, possibly even in the prenatal period, and that makes it very difficult to study.”

Riboli said that while scientists needed to uncover the unknown drivers of different cancers, people should minimise risks that are already clear. In the UK and US, drinking and smoking are both falling, but obesity is rising and physical activity is in decline. “The quick win could come from applying what we know,” he said. “We could prevent about 60% of the cancers occurring now, but we are not applying in society what we know.”

Alexander Zverev notified of abuse lawsuit by ex-partner during ATP Finals

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:52:39 GMT

Men’s world No 1 allegedly violated terms of settlement

Lawyers say Zverev will ‘defend himself against lawsuit’

Alexander Zverev was officially notified of a lawsuit filed by his former partner during the middle of the season-ending ATP Finals on Wednesday. The latest legal case against the men’s world No 1 brought by the mother of the former couple’s daughter alleges that Zverev violated the terms of an out-of-court settlement between the pair after the woman accused him of assaulting her.

The lawsuit brought by Brenda Patea in Germany takes issue with Zverev reportedly saying in an interview with the French sports daily L’Equipe earlier this year that “it has been proven that the accusations were false” and “my innocence has been proven”.

Zverev’s Berlin-based lawyers, Christian Schertz and Anna Sophie Heuchemer, confirmed in a statement that they were formally served with Patea’s lawsuit on Wednesday.

“Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit,” Zverev’s lawyers said. “If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion” – which would be protected by the German constitution. They said there had been no breach of any contractual obligations.

Patea’s lawyer, Michael Scheele, said that Zverev’s claim over his innocence “triggered a veritable storm of criticism against our client”. He said the backlash was damaging to her business as an influencer and that she also felt her honour had been violated.

“Quite apart from the fact that Zverev’s claim is false, he was not permitted to make any public statements whatsoever, in any form,” he said. “Both Brenda Patea and Alexander Zverev had agreed to this in a settlement.”

Patea is seeking that Zverev be ordered not to repeat such comments and that he be fined up to €250,000 (£208,500) every time if he does.

Zverev faced a charge of causing bodily harm to Patea during an argument in Berlin in May 2020. He always denied any wrongdoing. The case ended in a district court in Berlin in 2024 after the settlement. The case officially declared no verdict and the settlement entailed no acknowledgment of guilt on Zverev’s part. Zverev agreed to pay fines to the state and charitable organisations.

The German player this month ascended to the world No 1 ranking for the first time. He also won his first two grand slam titles this year and is competing this week at the ATP Finals in Turin.

Zverev has not commented on the lawsuit.

Traces of filler found in heart and brain of woman who died after cosmetic procedure, UK inquest hears

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:42:22 GMT

Jury told Jordan Parke injected seven times amount of filler he was taught to use during Alice Webb’s ‘Brazilian butt lift’

A man known as the “Lip King” who carried out a “Brazilian butt lift” (BBL) on a woman who later died injected her with seven times the amount of filler that he had been taught to use, an inquest jury has been told.

Traces of the filler that Jordan Parke injected into Alice Webb, 33, were discovered in her heart, lungs, brain and kidneys, the inquest heard.

Police told the court in Gloucester they were confident they had a case against Parke for gross negligence manslaughter before he died earlier this year.

They said they had found many more who had “suffered negative experiences” and he had been banned from practising in two areas of the UK because of concerns about his safety record.

Webb, a beautician from Wotton-under-Edge, Gloucestershire, became unwell during the cosmetic procedure carried out by Parke at a beauty salon attached to a house in Gloucester in September 2024. She was taken to Gloucestershire Royal Hospital, where she died in the early hours of the next day.

Webb’s sister-in-law, Morgan Townsend, sobbed as she told the court Webb had paid £2,300 for the BBL treatment.

She said Webb sent her a photo of the procedure being carried out and she was “shocked” at how much filler was being used – 1,400ml and “loads” of local anaesthetic. Webb sent a message saying “OMG – it kills” and then simply “Painful”.

The jurors were shown a brief video clip of Parke carrying out the procedure on Webb. He was laughing as he injected her and told her: “Well done!”

Allanah Kingston, a paramedic who went to Webb’s aid when she collapsed, said she was surprised that Parke seemed “unbothered” by what had happened and “didn’t appear to understand the urgency”.

Kingston said Parke did not have personal details about Webb, such as her date of birth or emergency contact information. She added: “I found it strange [he] didn’t come to the hospital.”

The Home Office forensic pathologist Dr Stephen Leadbetter said the gel-like filler – hyaluronic acid – was identified in Webb’s lungs, brain, heart, kidneys and thyroid gland. He said it could have got into her system when a blood vessel was damaged during the BBL.

DI Adam Stacey, who led the investigation, said there was no formal training for BBLs in the UK but techniques were passed from practitioner to practitioner. He said Parke had no medical qualifications, but a doctor who had worked with him had recommended using 100ml of filler in each buttock.

Stacey said Parke had been banned from performing BBLs in two areas, Salford in Greater Manchester and Dudley, West Midlands, because of concerns that his methods were not safe, but he was able to carry on elsewhere.

“It’s an unregulated industry,” Stacey told the court. “We were confident we had a case of gross negligence manslaughter.”

Officers were about to go back to Parke to ask him more questions about what happened when he died earlier this year. Stacey said Parke’s cause of death was not yet known.

Asked if they had found other clients who had become unwell, Stacey replied: “There were many who suffered negative experiences.”

The inquest continues.

Kemi and Andy put another nail in the coffin of his consensus politics

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:35:35 GMT

The Tory leader is hardwired for conflict. It was futile for the PM to demand an end to her patronising tone

Well, that didn’t take long. When Andy Burnham first arrived in No 10, he said he was determined to do things differently. He wanted a new, consensual politics where he would work with other parties to put the country back together. Safe to say, that dream is already dead in the water. At least when it comes to his exchanges with Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions.

Andy might go through the motions of promising Ed Davey and various backbenchers a veneer of cross-party support that may or may not become reality – even Andy doesn’t have a clue which is which – but when it comes to Kemi, it’s now just a bloodless slanging match. Bloodless because there’s nothing really at stake. It’s all just a performance. Kemi has yet to land a blow on Burnham, so both leaders are merely playing to a gallery of their own backbenchers.

In fairness, it’s probably easiest this way. Even if Andy were to say: “You know what, Kemi? I think you’re right. Let’s try doing it your way,” Kemi would still find a way to say that would be the wrong thing to do. She is hardwired for conflict. And if there’s no one on hand for her to disagree with, she will happily round on herself. She is lost without someone to fight.

All of which leaves Andy and Kemi on cruise control, with PMQs a jeopardy-free zone. There were times when Keir Starmer was prime minister it felt as if he might fall apart on a Wednesday lunchtime. Not least when facing questions over his suicidal decision to appoint Peter Mandelson as ambassador to Washington. But Andy has no apparent weak spots. Certainly none that Kemi has so far identified. And she doesn’t seem particularly interested in doing much work to find them. So she goes into each session with no real idea of what she is hoping to achieve. Other than to have an argument that everyone will soon forget.

All of which suits Burnham just fine. He can tick off 12pm on Wednesday as a comparatively stress-free zone. So much so that he is even quite happy making fun of himself. In his traditional opening line of: “This morning I have had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others” he managed to add in an “according to ChatGPT”. A nod to one of his advisers being caught on a train last weekend using AI while drafting a speech.

Then we got the phoney war. Kemi chose to attack on welfare and Neets. It was what she had on her mind, so she might as well. When was the welfare bill going to come down, she asked. And why would everything the government did take at least 10 years? If Kemi had thought for a nanosecond, she could have answered the second question herself. It was taking that long because the Tories had done nothing about it for 14 years. Er … and if it was simple to fix, governments would have done it long ago.

Burnham initially chose to try to give Kemi a straight answer. The reason the welfare bill wouldn’t come down was because of the way the accounts were balanced. Some young people would get less in benefits but receive more in help to get them back to work. Then Andy looked up and saw that Kemi hadn’t been paying attention. He might as well have been talking to the hand. At which moment he rather gave up and resorted to the lowest common denominator: point-scoring. Kemi and her sidekick the shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, were just too dumb to understand anything. They wouldn’t be happy until they saw someone really suffer by having their benefits removed. Blood lust.

Now PMQs deteriorated into a charade. Kemi immediately countered by saying she understood everything perfectly and it was the prime minister who understood nothing. He just wanted welfare vibes, not welfare cuts. This was Kemi as “Disgusted of Saffron Walden”. Disgusted for the sake of being disgusted. For Andy, it was open warfare. Whatever else the Milburn review might be, it’s not just vibes. It was time for the Tories to show some humility. Kemi was guilty of choosing her facts selectively. Something he would naturally never do. Except he would. It may be a pointless fight, but it might as well be a dirty one.

There was still time for Kemi to misunderstand the deal with the EU: she assumed what had been agreed was 100,000 foreigners coming to the UK and no Brits going to Europe. By now, Burnham had had enough. Enough of the patronising tone, he said. He might as well have asked for time to stop. Patronising is what Kemi does. It’s almost a sign of endearment. Her way of expressing affection.

A few Tories liked to imagine that this was a major misstep on Burnham’s part. That to say something that has been blindingly obvious for a couple of years now was in some way a sign of weakness. That Kemi had got to him. In which case how many other truths are there that cannot be mentioned? The real point was that this was yet another PMQs where Burnham had come across as the more human, more likable politician. There’s a reason Labour is a long way clear in the opinion polls. Most people think the party is doing a decent job.

One cabinet minister missing from this week’s PMQs was the home secretary. Shabana Mahmood was at a police chiefs’ conference to give a speech on “two-tier policing”. Shabana is the government’s fall guy who willingly gets sent out to defend anything that might be seen as Reform adjacent. She wasn’t saying there was two-tier policing, but there again, she wasn’t saying there wasn’t. Maybe we could settle on police that target everyone. That’s something we could all get behind.

What stops us building the houses Britain needs

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:24:46 GMT

Emeritus professor Simon Price, Smart Growth UK’s Jon Reeds and former Labour council leader Steve Siddon respond to a column by John Harris

John Harris points out the utter inadequacy of Labour’s housing plans, despite Andy Burnham’s passionate advocacy for new social housing (Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream?, 15 November). And everyone agrees that we need many more houses. So what’s holding us back?

The problem lies in the fiscal rules. At first sight this is puzzling, as borrowing to invest is explicitly allowed (as opposed to borrowing to cover current expenditure). The explanation is the future debt target. Any capital investment increases public debt, and there is a binding debt-to-GDP ratio at the arbitrary and relatively close forecast horizon.

If you have a ceiling to taxation, this sort of makes sense. When you, for example, build a hospital, this has ongoing benefits and may well raise growth, but it also generates costs like salaries that have to come from somewhere, not to mention the debt service. It’s still true that if a project is worth doing, it should be done (and funded), but higher taxes are unpopular and the rule is there, and it seems we’re stuck with it.

But with housing, you get not only social benefits but also rent income that will pay for the investment, so this argument collapses. Debt that funds any investment that yields a financial return should be put in a separate accounting category and removed from the debt target. Let’s start with housing. Simon Price Emeritus professor of finance, Essex Business School

John Harris is right that building 1.5m new homes in the course of this parliament is a fantasy, but those of us campaigning to protect the planning system have always known that it was.

The 300,000 annual target was based on no assessment of need or capacity, let alone willingness to build. It stemmed from a 2015 House of Lords committee in need of a catchy headline that recommended raising it from 200,000. Housebuilders loved it because they knew they could persuade both Conservative and Labour governments to do more and more damage to the planning system in pursuit of it.

In reality, builders have no intention of chasing fantasy housing targets that apply both where and when markets are strong and where and when they’re not. And why would they bother trying to fulfil the Treasury’s 25-year dream of building so many homes that prices fall and iron out the ups and downs of the UK economy? Lower prices mean lower profits; a right to demand a 20% rate of return is one of many “reforms” they persuaded gullible ministers to include in planning guidance.

The latest victim is England’s green belts, where Labour has now allowed builders to demand huge chunks be recategorised as “grey belt”, though “cowpat estate belt” would be a better description. Jon Reeds Smart Growth UK

Following John Harris’s article regarding meeting social housing targets, and speaking as a retired Labour council leader, isn’t one of the solutions staring us in the face?

Allow councils to borrow money from the Public Works Loan Board at a reasonable interest rate to buy up housing currently for sale at the lower end of the market and rent it out to families on the housing waiting list.

This could have the benefit of creating instant council housing and, with that, cohesive communities, kickstart the private house-selling market and avoid the potential “stigma” of living on a council estate. It would also be self-funding. Steve Siddons Scarborough, North Yorkshire

BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:24:39 GMT

Clinicians should start with the patient in front of them to identify obesity, not rely on a 200-year-old method that was aimed at entire populations, says James Capon

Your report on a better way to diagnose obesity is welcome, though it is worth remembering how we came to rely on body mass index (BMI) in the first place (BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’, 11 November).

The index was devised in the 1830s by the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who wanted to describe the “average man” across whole populations. He never intended it as a verdict on any individual’s health, and it was largely forgotten until 1972, when the American physiologist Ancel Keys, most famous for developing the diet-heart hypothesis, revived it and gave it its current name. Again, it was for population studies.

Meanwhile, US life insurers had long priced policies on “build” – weight against height – drawn from their policyholders’ mortality; many now simply use BMI. Medicine absorbed the same logic. Weight relative to height became the yardstick, and BMI, needing only scales and a tape measure, became the standard. It was cheap, quick and showed deviation from the norm at a glance.

We measured what was easy, not what mattered, then overinterpreted individual results. A statistical tool for describing nations ended up deciding whether a muscular rugby player or a slim person carrying dangerous fat around their organs is “healthy”.

The Lancet Commission’s approach, adding waist measurements and tests of organ function, is a step in the right direction. Tellingly, though, it still begins with BMI. Habits formed over nearly two centuries are hard to break. If the aim is to diagnose individuals rather than describe populations, clinicians should start with the patient in front of them, not with Quetelet’s average person. James Capon Waterloo, Belgium

Why Palantir’s health tech is not the right fit for the NHS

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:24:21 GMT

The US firm’s health data system is based on an insurance model of healthcare, not the patient-centred universal service we have in Britain, says Prof Caroline Mitchell

The news that NHS England may have overstated the benefits of Palantir for improving efficiency will surprise few frontline clinicians (NHS England deletes ‘misleading’ claim 137 trusts benefiting from Palantir AI tools, 12 November)

Too often, global digital policy assumes that software designed for the fragmented, insurance-based US healthcare system can simply be adapted to a universal public service elsewhere. A legitimate concern is that algorithms underpinning AI decision-making may be immature in the NHS context, having been developed primarily for a very different US healthcare system.

A consultant in a local trust recently described having to work across seven bolt-on software systems for a single consultation, including one focused on billing functions. A senior US hospital administrator explained that the primary purpose of most US health data systems was to record care for reimbursement. He was astounded that, by contrast, NHS general practice records are designed to support lifelong patient care and safe prescribing, with an NHS app similarly focused on a coded healthcare rather than how much of an insurance allowance had been used up that year.

We should also ask why the NHS needs a US firm to manage its data when the UK has a strong record of healthcare-software innovation. Emis, developed with GP leadership, transformed primary care IT decades ago. Software built for an insurance market may simply not be the best fit for universal healthcare systems. Prof Caroline Mitchell GP, Sheffield, and professor of general practice research, Keele University

Blaming Ofsted inspectors for the system is unfair

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:24:10 GMT

Inspectors and educators alike have been placed under even greater pressure year after year, says Helen Kenny

As national officer for the FDA, the union representing a large number of His Majesty’s Inspectors (HMIs), I read Simon Jenkins’ piece with great interest (Ofsted’s menacing inspections are still disastrous. Schools should answer to the communities they serve, 13 November). Jenkins dismisses the work of HMIs as merely a “sniff” of the air and a stroll back to Whitehall, showing a lack of knowledge about their role. HMIs are former school leaders, with a deep knowledge and dedication to educating children and young people. They are as far from the typical civil servant (if there is such a thing) that it is possible to get, and in any case are not based in Whitehall.

Jenkins does at least suggest an alternative approach, unlike some who are calling for the abolition of Ofsted, but I really question whether he has thought it through. Parents value the provision of inspection, and most educators agree that assessments are fair – independent YouGov polling showed that 74% of educators believed their most recent inspection was accurate.

While an internal FDA survey of our HMI members shows that there have been improvements with the new inspection framework, could the process be better? Yes, further reform and resources are needed, as HMIs and educators alike have been placed under even greater pressure year after year, which has been evidenced through our own recent survey. But blaming the inspectors for the system is wholly unfair. They do not set government policy, but have an obligation to implement it, and ensure the quality of education expected by parents and pupils alike. Helen Kenny FDA national officer for Ofsted

The Quechua rapper and an artistic movement reclaiming language of the Incas

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:16:59 GMT

Renata Flores has gained global recognition for her music in Indigenous language whose speakers have faced social stigma

With her long black hair braided into beaded plaits, a delicate silver nose ring, and intricately patterned Andean textile draped around her chest above baggy, low-riding jeans, Renata Flores is a visual reflection of her music: a fusion of traditional and transgressive, old and new, rural and urban.

Nicknamed the “queen of Quechua rap”, Flores, 25, has earned global recognition for mixing Peru’s main Indigenous language and Andean instruments with the urban beats of trap, rap, hip-hop and reggaeton.

She rose to fame as a teenager singing covers in Quechua, the language used by the Incas and South America’s most widespread Indigenous language, with 8 million speakers along the spine of the Andes, half of them in Peru.

Her version of Michael Jackson’s The Way You Make Me Feel, which she translated into Quechua with the help of her grandmothers, became a viral hit on YouTube, launching her into the limelight at the age of 14.

Since that early start, she has molded her musical identity around Quechua, a language she chose to learn from her grandmothers, as her parents did not teach her due to social stigma and the fear that she could face discrimination.

“I feel happy and free when I sing in Quechua, with a strong sense of identity and empowerment,” she said. “Before, I’d say to myself: maybe I should sing in Spanish or English so that more people would listen to me. But I decided to carry on singing in Quechua.”

Her music now tackles darker, more complex themes: marginalisation, women’s rights and state oppression. It focuses on her identity as a Quechua woman and pays homage to the legacy of her forebears.

“I grew up hearing my grandmothers and my mother sing [in Quechua] but rap gave me the chance to say a lot of powerful, difficult things; to protest, too; and to tell the truth.”

Flores is finishing her second album, Kachnanikuraqmi, which means “we are still here” in Quechua. It is a message of hope, resilience and identity for the younger generation, she said.

Following Flores’s example, a vibrant and youthful Quechua-speaking artistic movement has taken hold in Ayacucho, nestled in the southern Andes, with many emerging artists choosing to reclaim the marginalised language.

“Renata is a major pioneer who represented – and continues to represent – our Quechua culture,” said Kayfex, an Ayacucho-born DJ and music producer, who won a Latin Grammy in 2023 and was later signed by Warner Music in the US.

“Music is very global these days and I think expectations are changing too,” he added as he mixed a booming bass track with the plaintive Andean harp and the chiming metallic clink of the iron rods used by traditional Quechua scissor dancers on one of Flores’s songs.

Ayacucho was at the centre of Peru’s bloody conflict between the fanatical Shining Path insurgents and brutal state security forces in the 1980s and 90s, during which nearly 70,000 people died. Tens of thousands more lost loved ones or were forcibly displaced, like Flores’s grandparents.

Patricia Rivera, Flores’s mother and her manager, said: “If you spoke Quechua, people assumed you were from a rural area, and if you were from a rural area you were a terrorist – it was like that. So the fact that people now sing and speak Quechua is a way of reclaiming the language. To say ‘we are Quechua’ with pride – we’re not terrorists.”

Flores is too young to remember that period, but political violence in Peru is by no means over. In December 2022, 10 people were killed and more than 60 injured when soldiers opened fire on protesters in Ayacucho during demonstrations against the government of the then president, Dina Boluarte.

“It was heartbreaking for many families,” said Flores, whose new album includes a song dedicated to the families of the victims. “Let’s say that I’m a transgressor and traditional – I like it when people tell me that I can be both,” she added.

World ‘held hostage by oil mafia’, says Panama minister at Cop 31

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:07:06 GMT

Key issues unresolved as summit enters final days, with 30 countries signed up to forge fossil fuel treaty separate to UN process

The world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia” and seems unable to break free, Panama’s environment minister has warned, as key issues remain unresolved in the final days of the UN Cop31 climate summit.

“We are in love with our kidnappers,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, at a press conference to announce 30 countries were now signed up to forge a new fossil fuel treaty, separate to the UN process. “We love the petroleum guys. We can’t live without them, and they are so smart they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.”

Expressing the frustration shared by scores of developing countries and thousands of civil society activists at these talks, he added: “They torture us for our own good, they destroy our planet for our own good. They destroy nature to help us, and they demand our unrequited, endless, unlimited, boundless love. And we are so stupid that we fall for it.”

Countries have only two official days of negotiation left at Cop31 to resolve key issues, such as whether the conference should recognise the need to “transition away from fossil fuels” and how to address the “overshoot” of global temperatures beyond the 1.5C of heating targeted in the Paris agreement.

The Australian presidency of the talks and the Turkish hosts convened a “divan” meeting of ministers on Wednesday evening. Named for the Ottoman empire’s term for a council or assembly, the aim of the meeting was to make progress on a revised draft of a possible outcome and find compromises on sticking points. Significant dividing lines remain on issues such as climate finance, how to ensure a “just transition” to clean economy jobs for workers in fossil fuels and helping poor countries adapt to the impacts of extreme weather.

The first draft of a “cover decision”, issued on Monday, contained 144 separate items, including several – such as the “transition away from fossil fuels” – that some of the nearly 200 countries at the fortnight-long talks find contentious. There are concerns that the Australian approach of including “everything” in the draft text may result in longer negotiations. A new draft is expected on Thursday morning.

A breakthrough from the “divan” meeting was not expected, but negotiators told the Guardian that countries were working together on compromises. Campaigners feared that the outcome would be feeble, however.

Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, accused rich countries of offering “crumbs” to a fund for the developing world to adapt to extreme weather. Only $50m has been pledged so far, compared with $135m last year.

“Rich countries are offering crumbs to the adaptation fund, while blocking the negotiations that should provide the money countries need,” he said. “Listening to ministers praise the adaptation fund before giving next to nothing, you have to wonder how they expect it to do the work they say is so important.”

There was anger, too, over the “just transition mechanism”, which is intended to help developing countries ensure workers in high-carbon industries can be retrained or helped, while they grow nascent green industries. “We’re seeing massive steps backwards on adaptation finance and just transition, relative to previous Cops,” said Brandon Wu, the director of policy and campaigns at the ActionAid USA charity. “In both cases, the blocking is being led by the EU.”

Irene Vélez Torres, the former Colombian minister who convened talks in Santa Marta in April on the phaseout of fossil fuels, said she was worried about a target to generate 35% of final energy from electricity by 2035, which is thought to have the explicit support of at least 60 countries, and the tacit support of more, including China. Like many campaigners, she would like to see provisions that ensure the electricity comes from renewable sources.

“I’m very scared that [the target] is not going to be explicit about clean green energy, because it may imply that they are going to lock us in future dependencies on gas and coal power. If we don’t explicitly declare that the electricity is going to be powered by green and clean energy, we may make a mistake,” she said.

Frustrated with the slow speed of the UN talks, some countries have been using Cop31 to further their own alternatives. Colombia has changed governments since Vélez convened talks on a “transition away from fossil fuels” in April, but the Santa Marta process carries on, with Tuvalu hosting the next meeting.

The Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, with 30 members, at whose event Navarro was speaking, is another attempt to create a “coalition of the willing” to phase fossil fuels out, as is the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance.

Ethiopia, which will host the Cop32 meeting next year, is leading a group of countries that want to go further than phasing fossil fuels out. The “group of negative emitters” aim to absorb more carbon than they produce, by using carbon capture technology or growing trees and restoring natural “carbon sinks”, such as wetlands and peatlands.

“Slashing emissions is essential but no longer enough,” said Ani Dasgupta, the president of the World Resources Institute thinktank. “We must also actively pull carbon out of the atmosphere, to bring temperatures back down.”

Samuel Addis Alemayehu, the Ethiopian ambassador, called for financial help for poor countries to follow through with their plans. “Ethiopia is expanding nature-based solutions [such as tree-planting] and calls for scaled-up support, adequate finance and access to technologies that reduce emissions,” he said.

Kelly Gough is simply astounding as Desire Under the Elms reaches the heights of Greek tragedy

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:00:04 GMT

Almeida theatre, London Part-Phaedra and part-Medea, Gough is mesmerising in Ebenezer Bamgboye’s stylised staging of Eugene O’Neill’s family drama

You would not know that Eugene O’Neill’s play was originally set on a mid 19th-century farm. This version by director Ebenezer Bamgboye brings modernity with its sleek storytelling, but also nods to the ancient Greek drama O’Neill was emulating in his 1924 play about illicit desire and the father-son fight for land.

It makes for a strange mix at first, beguiling and bewildering in equal measure. Bamgboye employs some of the striking theatricality that he brought to his magnetic adaptation of The Lonely Londoners two years ago. It is an original refashioning, the script sharper with less of the exposition that might date it, but the directorial flourishes come so thick and fast that it is stylised to the bone. Bamgboye has previously worked with Rebecca Frecknall (who staged the leaden O’Neill drama A Moon for the Misbegotten last year) and the first half seems to pay too big a debt to her style of work.

Ephraim (Antony Byrne) is an irredeemably tyrannical father and Eben (Zackary Momoh) his calculating son. Eben sees off his two half-brothers in hope to claim this farm, passed down from his late mother, as his own, when Ephraim brings home a young new bride, Abbie (Kelly Gough). “I can’t believe all this is mine,” she says, crowingly, when she sees the farm. So begins the fractious relationship between Abbie and Eben.

There is an attempt to tell O’Neill’s story on another level, with a racial element added. Set in the deep south rather than its original north-east, the dynamic is that of a white father and Black son through its casting. Eben speaks of his father’s slave-driving and his wrongful ownership of stolen land; Ephraim’s iron-rod rule begins to look like that of a plantation owner.

As in Frecknall’s production of A Streetcar Named Desire, music interprets emotion, from screams to sexual overtures and angry clashes. A live, roving trumpet and guitar interject in these moments, the musicians stalking the auditorium like musical ghosts, along with the spectre of Eben’s dead mother, singing languorously.

Movement is key, with sex or violence also transposed to dance, or jagged, jittery twitches. The effect is sometimes arresting but also overwrought. The sexual chemistry between Eben and Abbie is so choreographed that it does not give off enough heat. The ghostliness and gothicism seems over-egged with smoke rising from the blank canvas of darkness on Basia Bińkowska’s non-realist stage design.

But it rights itself and the overload of manufactured expressiveness gives way to something far more elemental in the second half when this production allows its actors simply to act. Momoh is good but Gough (whose sister Denise played the same role in a production 14 years ago) is off the scale. Part-Phaedra, part-Medea, she is a woman who has a purity of desire alongside her steeling ambitions and strength: she is the one to activate the attraction she feels towards Eben. Her unravelling is painful to watch, and her performance really does rise to the heights of Greek drama, intense and unstoppably tragic.

The tension takes on a vice-like grip as the music, movement and gothicism come together. This is artistic director Rupert Goold’s final production before his departure and is not perfect yet it rises to become incredibly powerful.

At Almeida theatre, London, until 23 December

Instant gratification is ruining our lives – and for me it started with my CD player’s shuffle button

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 16:35:47 GMT

Not even a compelling TV drama can stop me from staring at my phone. But this urge started 40 years ago, with what was at first presented as a useful feature

I blame the shuffle button. That’s what started me on the long road to a thoroughly scattered mind – generally unable to focus on anything for more than a few minutes or even seconds. I was always a bit like this, hence an ADHD diagnosis in later life. But back in the day I still managed to read a lot of books, watch long films and listen to whole records at one sitting. Now? Not so much. Actually, hardly ever.

Even something on television that I’m really engaged in – a drama or a football match – can hold me for only a few minutes before I find myself scrolling on my phone looking for I know not what. I don’t know whether it’s because I’m drawn to the small phone screen, or rather that I find absorption with whatever I’m watching on the big flatscreen just too much to bear.

I saw this process brilliantly summarised in a tweet by an American writer, Delia Cai, in which she berated herself for “another day of staring at the big screen while scrolling through my little screen so as to reward myself for staring at the medium screen all week”. That nails it. TV screen, phone screen, computer screen. Each somehow too compelling for us to focus on any one of them at the expense of the others. Ironically, of course, I came across this tweet while pawing away at my own small screen while (not) watching my bigger screen.

This has got to stop. It’s mad. And I trace the madness back to the shuffle button on my first CD player. This was 1989, towards the end of my student days. A record player, and many records, had cumbersomely accompanied me to the various dorms, flats and houses I’d called home. Now the era of the CD player had dawned and I wanted in.

Off I went to one of the dozens of hi-fi shops then plying their trade on London’s Tottenham Court Road. The bloke talked me through my options. Pointing at a shuffle button, he said: “Shuffling the tracks on your favourite album can breathe new life into it.” I remember him saying this very clearly.

On the way home I bought two CDs – an album I didn’t own, and an album I’d listened to, round and round on my turntable, a thousand times. I got back to my room, plugged things in, and lay on my bed listening to Shooting Rubber Bands at the Stars by Edie Brickell and New Bohemians. (My goodness, what a lot of words there are in that album and artist name. It’s a wonder I’ve managed to write them all down without losing focus.) I listened to it from beginning to end and quite enjoyed it.

Then I put on Dylan’s Blood on the Tracks and tried breathing new life into it by pressing that shuffle button. I didn’t much enjoy the experience. Disorientating. It felt like something had changed beyond the mere order of the tracks – the whole natural order of things perhaps. Something had shifted.

For the first 22 years of my life, listening to music had entailed dropping a needle on a record and listening to the whole of that side of the record. Yes, every now and again I’d stand up, go to the record player, lift the needle and drop it back down elsewhere on the vinyl, to listen to something again or even miss something out. But this was rare, if only because it was too much bother. So you’d listen to the whole thing.

Your enjoyment of your favourite track would even be enhanced for it having been preceded by a song you weren’t so keen on. Spared as we were in those innocent days from the dark forces of instant gratification, you’d stick with the track, knowing something better was coming. If You See Her, Say Hello, on side two of Blood on the Tracks, was so much better if you’d just put yourself through nine minutes of Lily, Rosemary and the Jack of Hearts, the track that preceded it. Sorry, Bob: not for me, that one.

The trouble with the shuffle button was that it was then but a short step to the skip button, which marked the end of music listening as we knew it, or at least as I knew it. Didn’t like a track? Just skip it. I’m not sure I’ve listened to Lily, Rosemary or indeed the Jack of Hearts since. But something more than a track had been lost. In fact, with Edie Brickell, all but one track on the album was lost. I liked Circle, track six, so before long it was the only track on the album that I troubled myself to enjoy. Skip, skip, skip, skip, skip, listen, end. Gratification: instant. Music-listening experience: diminished. Ability to concentrate: impaired.

Nearly four decades on, the skip button on a CD player feels archaic indeed. In fact, what’s a CD player? Just as the skip button made needle-lifting feel like a faff, music streaming on your phone makes pressing a CD’s skip button feel like hard labour. Who listens to whole albums now?

I asked this question on my radio show on the day the Ivor Novello award for best album was made. I wasn’t long looking for an answer before I realised I might be asking the wrong question: it’s less about who listens to a whole album, than who manages to get to the end of a whole song.

Spotify keeps tabs on who’s listening to what. And, encouragingly, for its end-of-year Wrapped feature, 2025 saw the introduction of a Top Albums metric. Great. But fascinatingly, depressingly, in Spotify’s words: “Albums make the list when you’ve listened to at least 70% of an album’s tracks, whether from the album page, within playlists, or any other place on Spotify.” So in other words, you only need ever (and then not all at once) to have listened to less than three-quarters of any given album. What’s that all about?

As for individual songs, as far as I can see Spotify keeps its data close to its chest, but a peer-reviewed study from 2020 has it that a quarter of songs are skipped within five seconds, and only around half are listened to all the way through.

Skip music, skip words, skip pictures, skip films, skip anything that dares to demand a moment of your attention. We’re skipping our way to species oblivion.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

Bancroft throws Cummins’ future into doubt after blowing lid off Australia sandpaper scandal

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 16:20:17 GMT

‘It was the whole team,’ says batter in explosive column

Comments mark devastating attack on captain’s integrity

Cameron Bancroft has shattered Cricket Australia’s attempts to draw a line under the sandpaper scandal by claiming that all players and coaches on the infamous tour of South Africa knew about a plot to tamper with the ball.

In an extraordinary 4,000-word first-person article for the West Australian that will raise doubts over the future of Pat Cummins, the former Australia opening batter launched a devastating attack on the current Test captain’s integrity, describing his 68-minute press conference at the Sydney Cricket Ground last week as an act of betrayal.

Bancroft has kept his silence since he was banned along with Steve Smith and David Warner, the then captain and vice-captain respectively, following an investigation by Cricket Australia after the South Africa tour of 2018, other than a 2021 interview with the Guardian in which he said it was “probably self-explanatory” that the bowlers were aware of the ball tampering, which led to Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon issuing a joint statement denying any knowledge or involvement.

Cummins stood by that line when grilled by journalists at the SCG last Friday in a remarkable press conference that Bancroft described as “the final straw”, which convinced him to tell his own side of the story for the first time.

“It was not just the three of us – Steve Smith, David Warner and I – who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa,” Bancroft wrote. “It was the whole team. When I was questioned during Cricket Australia’s investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account.

“I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others. I did this to protect Cricket Australia’s investigation and not implicate others around me.

“The recent release of Usman Khawaja’s autobiography, Sabr, has brought many of those memories back to the surface. But the final straw for me to write this account was ­Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins’ press conference.

“It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone. What I saw, experienced and lived with – not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa – is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time.”

Bancroft’s words were published within hours of Cricket Australia announcing the creation of a truth and reconciliation-style forum inviting players to provide their own confidential testimony on Sandpapergate without fear of sanctions in the hope of finally achieving closure on the matter, an initiative that now appears moot.

In response to Bancroft’s article, Cricket Australia said that process would continue, and that he would be welcome to contribute. “We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments,” a Cricket Australia statement said. “We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events. We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible.”

Cummins’ management also issued a statement on his behalf which reiterated his position from last week. “Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he’s been through there’s nothing in the statement that hasn’t been answered by Pat in his press conference,” it read.

Bancroft was banned for nine months for his part in the scandal, in which he took sandpaper on to the field to tamper with the ball in the third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town. Smith and Warner received 12-month suspensions, with the latter also banned from assuming any leadership roles for life as he was perceived to be the ringleader.

After eight years the controversy was reignited this month by the release by the recently retired opener Khawaja of his autobiography, in which he claimed that knowledge of the cheating went far beyond those three players, a version of events ­subsequently endorsed by Warner and the 12th man in Cape Town, Chadd Sayers.

In his account Bancroft claimed the ball-tampering began at the second Test at Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha, when Warner raised the possibility of using sandpaper to roughen one side of the ball during a team discussion involving players and coaching staff.

The 33-year-old said the then Australia bowling coach, David Saker, and the then head coach, Darren Lehmann, were present, while Smith entered the conversation briefly before making clear he wanted no part in the proposal.

Bancroft alleges he subsequently received regular feedback from Australia’s fast bowlers about whether his work on the ball was producing the desired reverse swing.

“I recall conversations with all the fast bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether it was reverse swinging enough,” Bancroft wrote. “All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful.”

Bancroft also claims the practice continued for the remainder of the second Test and into the third Test in Cape Town, where television cameras caught him attempting to conceal the sandpaper in his trousers. He claims Saker approached him during the Test at Newlands and instructed him to do more with the sandpaper to make the ball swing.

Bancroft claims that after he was caught, Saker specifically warned against identifying sandpaper as the material used, during the press conference, after he was spotted on the field with the ball-tampering agent. “We acknowledged ball-tampering while giving an inaccurate account of the material involved,” Bancroft wrote. “It was another lie. One told while we were supposedly taking responsibility.”

Lehmann left the ABC commentary box early at the final one-day international between Australia and England in Hobart when informed of Bancroft’s claims, while Marsh, the white-ball captain, did not attend the post-match press conference.

Bloomscrolling: the uplifting new way to waste your own time

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 16:05:40 GMT

Tired of your social media feeds being a bin fire? Want more beauty? Gen Z are training their algorithms – and it’s working wonders for them

Name: Bloomscrolling.

Age: The term has been floating around for a few years, but it has recently taken off on TikTok.

Appearance: Like social media, but – get this – not actively soul-destroying.

For the avoidance of doubt, you don’t mean doomscrolling? I do not. Doomscrolling is old hat. Everybody doomscrolls these days. What I’m talking about is fresh, exciting and new.

Well, consider me excited. In fact, bloomscrolling is the precise opposite of doomscrolling. Doomscrolling is where you sit for hours, wasting your life, thumbing through an infinite loop of algorithmically derived depressing posts.

Whereas bloomscrolling … Is where you sit for hours, wasting your life, thumbing through an infinite loop of algorithmically derived nice posts.

And how did this expression come about? It was initially popularised by Prof Ruha Benjamin to mean seeking out organisers, artists and educators whose work gave people reason to believe that things could change. But as it is used now, it comes from the author Lucy Bloom’s decision to delete her Instagram account and start afresh. She used her new account to only follow art-based accounts.

What happened? Well, her algorithm realised that she only liked art, so it started feeding her content about art, artist residencies and paint. She described feeling calmer and more motivated than when she was just scrolling through the usual bin fire of content.

I need to do this! Many already do. New research commissioned by the toy manufacturer Hasbro claims that 93% of 18-34-year-olds have curated their social feeds to make them a happier place.

How? It doesn’t need to be as drastic as Bloom’s approach. You might mute comments, or unfollow people whose incessant posting bothers you. But, really, the big thing is training the algorithm.

Is this a thing? Yes, it is. The faster you scroll through videos, the more TikTok learns that this is not relevant content for you. But if you linger on a video – let it replay a couple of times, even like it – then it remembers to serve you more of this in the future.

So you can train it to only show you nice things. That’s right, nice things. Or, in my case, an unbroken feed of Chinese women singing songs about how comprehensively their engine factory is stocked.

You’re weird. Hey, don’t algorithm-shame me.

Sorry. But why not go even further? Why not have multiple social media accounts, each tailored to a specific type of mood? You could have one account that is exclusively devoted to art, one to cute animals, and one to motivational messages.

Could I have one that’s just about insomnia and potholes, for when I get sick of this barrage of tweeness? I wouldn’t if I were you, but you scroll however you see fit.

Do say: “I use my social media for positivity.”

Don’t say: “All social media is a data-harvesting operation by the uncaring billionaire class.”

I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 15:50:46 GMT

A group of eight trainee parachutists did the jump, and not far from the ground, disaster struck. Rob Bugden describes how he rebuilt his life after the accident that changed everything

The skydive was going to plan. At 12,000ft, Rob Bugden jumped from the plane, quickly getting himself stable by arching his back to create a solid base. He checked for speed and altitude on his watch, and when he was low enough, pulled the parachute’s toggles. “I looked up. Good canopy.” But then: “Cut to black. And I’m waking up in a hospital in Phoenix.”

It was 21 January 2016, the final day of his Royal Air Force high altitude training in the US, when 30-year-old Bugden collided – mid-air – with his friend, Brook Stebbings. They were moving into the landing stack formation, a vertical queue of eight parachutists flying in a holding pattern at different altitudes, when, at approximately 1,000ft, Stebbings’ knee crashed into him, breaking his neck. They fell to the sand in the middle of the desert, entangled – looking, according to the team on the ground, “like we had a bag of washing above our heads”.

The special forces team ran over to stabilise them, checking for pulses and making sure they didn’t move and risk further injury. Stebbings was rushed to a hospital in Palm Springs where he was treated for a broken leg and torn kidneys; while Bugden was flown by helicopter to St Joseph’s hospital, where doctors did everything they could to save his life. He had metal fixations in his neck to stabilise the spine and his eye socket was put back together. He was paralysed, so received a tracheostomy to help him breathe on his own, a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube in his stomach to feed him, and a pacemaker, because his heart rate was dropping dangerously low.

When he woke up in a hospital room, groggy from all the medication, his first lucid thought, he says, was: “What’s my brother done?” Bugden’s brother was the one more likely to find himself in a hospital bed a long way from home, having served in the army in Northern Ireland, Sierra Leone, Kosovo, Bosnia, Iraq and Afghanistan. “Basically everywhere he’s been, he’s been shot at,” says Bugden. But when his sibling entered the room alongside their parents, who had hardly spoken since their divorce when Bugden was five, “it was: ‘Oh, what the hell have I done?’”

Bugden was born in Cornwall to a military family. Three of his grandparents were in the air force, his dad spent 22 years in the Royal Navy and his brother still serves in the army. “I always say it’s a bit like the family business,” says Bugden. “It was always going to happen.” But he wanted to give university and his athletic talents a chance first.

At university in Cardiff, he studied sports coaching, quickly discovering that academics weren’t his strong suit, and ran long distance for Great Britain under 23s. His claim to fame, he says, is that in 2006 he was “in the same British team as Mo Farah. He won the European cross country title for the first time that year. And the less said about my race, the better.” But when it was clear the Olympics weren’t on the cards, Bugden joined the air force.

He completed his basic training at RAF Halton in Buckinghamshire in 2008, then specialised as a physical training instructor. He did a four-month stint in the Falkland Islands, where his dad had been posted during the war in 1982, before deciding, in March 2015, to pursue a career as a parachute jumping instructor, despite a fear of heights. “I never got over it, but I think I faced it,” he says. “I jumped out of a plane at 20,000ft at night, and I didn’t hesitate.” Bugden says that he has never been calmer than the 10 seconds before leaving an aeroplane.

The weather in the UK wasn’t conducive to the kind of jumps the military wanted him to do – too wet and windy – so the air force relocated him to the trucker stop town of Blythe on the Arizona-California border for high altitude jump training, to be a training instructor. The dream had been to work with the special forces on missions like the Tristan da Cunha rescue in the Atlantic that took place in May 2026, he says, where six paratroopers and two medical clinicians were parachuted on to one of the world’s most remote inhabited islands to help a British national with suspected hantavirus. “It was so, so cool,” Bugden says about the operation. “I would have taught them to freefall.”

Unfortunately, that wasn’t to be. Three weeks after his final jump, following a hospital stint filled with tests, several operations, and medication that sent him in and out of consciousness, Bugden was medevaced back to the UK in a plane that flew low over the Atlantic Ocean so as not to compress his spine further. That’s when he found out the extent of his injuries. His spinal cord was severely damaged, leaving him a tetraplegic (where all four limbs are affected), and he would need to live with round the clock care for the rest of his life.

For the first four months, Bugden couldn’t move at all. “People would literally have to do everything for me: feed me, brush my teeth, comb my hair, wash my face.” But mobility wasn’t the only issue: he had three of the biggest problems related to spine injury – bladder, bowel and sexual function, so having children naturally will be difficult. He still struggles to regulate his temperature and his weight, which is hard to keep off.

It took Bugden 10 months in rehab to regain some independence: learning to flip his catheter so he could go to the bathroom on his own; to stand up with assistance to improve his bladder and bowel movements, prevent muscle spasms from sitting too long and feel his old height again, even briefly. “I’m 6ft 3in,” he says. “It’s quite nice being tall.”

Bugden started to feel like himself again at a military hospital in the Midlands, where there was a sense of camaraderie that he had missed from his air force days, and plenty of jokes. “I remember going into the cafeteria on one of my first days and there were two lads, both double amps, missing legs, and they were just going for each other – really taking the piss,” he says. “There was an injury hierarchy: I was going around calling [anyone] missing a leg a ‘flesh wound’, but obviously that’s a really serious traumatic injury.”

It was four years until he was discharged from rehab completely. “One of the biggest tools is patience,” he says. “Things don’t happen quickly, and that’s not just your rehabilitation.” There are psychological hurdles to overcome as well as the physical ones. “It’s peaks and troughs. You’ll do really well, then you’ll plateau, then you’ll dip, then you’ll come up a little bit and plateau. That’s just the way rehab and recovery works. It sounds really weird, but I enjoy it. Because when I was lying in a bed that was the worst time for me.”

Bugden now lives in an adapted bungalow in the rural Welsh village of Sigingstone in the Vale of Glamorgan, with his “lack of assistance dog”, Denzel. His health is stable and he operates his wheelchair with ease. The walls are covered in sporting memorabilia. There are England running vests from when he competed, and a signed shirt from the Cornish Pirates, his favourite rugby team, sent to him when he was in hospital. There are also images from his days training with the RAF. In the corner of the living room is a bar that Bugden says is looking a bit dry because his friends drained it watching rugby recently.

Much like before, Bugden’s life is filled with sports, pints and friendship. “I’m still me. I can still chat bollocks to the best of them,” he says. “And I can still get out and do things. I just have to do them differently now.” On the day we meet, Aaron and Mat, who were there at the time of the accident, drop by with their children. They both still train military personnel to parachute jump, but keep Bugden’s accident at the front of their minds when they do.

“I’m exceptionally fortunate with the support and help I’ve had all the way along,” says Bugden, as his friends wait for him so they can go to the beach for an ice-cream. “These boys, first and foremost, without them I would be a mess,” he says. But then again, “I would absolutely dig out blind for them. I think that’s a Celtic thing. And I think that’s a military thing as well.”

Early on, he remembers his friend feeding him, making airplane noises as you might do with a child. “I was just crying with laughter.” He likes that they don’t walk on egg shells around him. But he knows they would push him up a hill if he needed them to – because they have done. “There’s a few tears, a few beers, but in what was an incredibly difficult, dark time, there are these moments that were just unbelievable and so happy.”

After his accident, his friends set up a rugby team called Horus (named after the ancient Egyptian god of the sky) to bring military friends and families together, and raise money for charities that support injured veterans, like the RAF Benevolent Fund and Cakes for Casualties. “It was one of the most important parts of my rehab,” says Bugden about the game, which set the world record for the longest game of rugby 7s and 10s – played for more than 24 hours.

Bugden continues to cope with his accident with humour and a matter of factness. He still has hard times and it’s tough knowing that his career as he knew it is over – he was medically discharged from the air force after the accident, and now lives off his military pension. But he continues to work closely with the military and its associated charities.

He’s an ambassador for Sandville, a Welsh charity that helps people with life-limiting and life-changing conditions that can range from spinal injury to Parkinson’s and dementia; and the Royal Air Force Benevolent Fund, which he’s been a beneficiary of “and I’d be lost without”. He’s involved with Blesma, The Limbless Veterans, Help for Heroes, and the OppO Foundation, which give support to veterans and their families who are struggling with disability, mental health, or financial challenges. “We’ve got a long way to go for how things are set up for people in wheelchairs,” he says. “We’re a lot better than we were and we are moving in the right direction … but there are still certain places I can’t get in.”

In 2023, he competed in five half-marathons across Wales in a custom built sports wheelchair, raising £8,000 for five different charities that have helped him in some way. He spent months training his shoulders and biceps, using a ski machine to build strength in his arms. And he’s keen to take on more challenges in the future.

It’s not always easy, he says, but “life is this game of inches”. He’s quoting his favourite movie, the 1999 sports drama, Any Given Sunday, where Coach D’Amato, played by Al Pacino, gives his football team a pep talk. “We can stay here and get the shit kicked out of us, or we can fight our way back into the light. We can climb out of hell. One inch at a time,” the coach tells his team.

“Inches make metres, metres make miles, and miles make a lifetime,” adds Bugden.

The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets?

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 15:28:25 GMT

He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe

A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us.

And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof.

Nothing seemed to animate him much, which is why, when I asked, in slight desperation, about his recent experience as a consultant on a successful TV comedy show, I was amazed to watch the man come alive. Thrilled; he was absolutely bloody thrilled to revisit the excitement of being on set and get into it about the actors and the show-runners. And could I believe they were still writing an episode right up until filming (I could) and had I ever experienced anything like the buzz of a set? At the end of the day, all these poor men want is to get into showbiz.

I mention all this in light of the ongoing hoo-ha over Jensen Huang, the disgraced former head of Nvidia who, at the time of writing, will not, it seems, be allowed back as CEO after allegations surfaced of the 63-year-old conducting several extramarital affairs, one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with his own employees. If true, the spy thing is an unusual twist, but in all other respects, the story of Huang’s fall from grace tracks so exactly with the industry standard that it should be a mandatory module at business school. Namely: how to avoid becoming the next male tech billionaire to upgrade his wardrobe, ditch his wife of 40 years and tank the stock.

The surprising thing in the case of Huang is that, held up against the likes of Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, the co-founder of Nvidia was supposed to be a quieter, less obnoxious, more thoughtful billionaire, who put modesty at the core of his values. In a profile in the New Yorker a few years ago, Huang insisted on doing the interview at a branch of the fast food chain Denny’s, where – as he pointed out – he’d once worked as a dishwasher. You get the picture and are probably thinking of good old Bill Gates, as I am, a man whose dorky knitwear and long marriage to Melinda made him a forerunner in that same role of decent, quiet, uxorious – oh …

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

In Huang’s case, one glaring indicator that his humble persona was glitching was a wardrobe made up almost entirely of leather jackets, which speaks to a very particular moment in the billionaire’s life cycle. They do love a sartorial trademark, these men, to the extent that you wonder if they sit around brainstorming accessories to use as their new lewk. Beanie? Too casual. Fingerless gloves? Too weird. What if a jaunty waistcoat could be my thing? Huang reportedly has well over 30 leather jackets, including the $9,000 one from Tom Ford, the shiny crocodile-embossed one that looks like something your four-year-old daughter might wear to a party, and the cropped at the hip one to show off Huang’s trim waist, which, of course, takes discipline to maintain at his age.

And it’s discipline, not morality, we’re talking about. The leather jacket is harmless except as a signifier of a whole range of allegedly poor personal decisions Huang made that were not in the shareholders’ interests. What I find funny about this is that, when it really comes down to it, a group of people who describe themselves lovingly as “disruptors” are the most stultifyingly conventional people on Earth; all they want is to be popular, mostly with hot women, but also more generally with the cool crowd. Just look at Bezos this week, inserting himself with almost endearing irrelevance into the James Bond conversation: “It was me! I picked him! I bought the James Bond name and then I picked the new one because, at some level, and I hope you all understand this, I AM James Bond.” Of course you are, luvvie. You enjoy it.

Still, at least this famously unfunny crowd can occasionally give us a laugh, as Jensen Huang did this week in his statement, in which he said that, if it was deemed in the interests of the US, he would be “honoured” to return to Nvidia as CEO. Hahahaha, how noble of him, that’s actually a good one. Although, as we know, when it comes to companies as big as Nvidia, run by men with their minds elsewhere, the punchline – “whoops, there goes my pension fund!” – tends to fall most heavily on the rest of us.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

Sublime and ridiculous, but I love the wild experiments of Huddersfield’s contemporary music festival

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 15:05:11 GMT

The 49th edition of the new music festival begins this weekend. Where else can you indulge in a world of pure imagination, see the future – and chat over a curry with some of contemporary music’s biggest names?

The Huddersfield contemporary music festival – or hcmf, with contemporary-cool lower-case, as it’s styled – celebrates its 49th edition this month, turning the darkness of late November into a beacon of blazing new-music ambition in West Yorkshire.

It’s a festival with an extraordinary history. Nowhere else in the UK could you have bumped into Karlheinz Stockhausen and his entourage in a pub in the late 1980s; nowhere else could you have sat in the audience alongside Björk at the town hall; in no other town might you have stumbled on Pierre Boulez, John Cage, Olivier Messiaen and Yvonne Loriod chatting about the best place to have a curry that night. (Well, maybe I can’t guarantee the dinner discussion but all of the above have visited the festival over the past five decades.)

The festival was set up by the composer and academic Richard Steinitz in 1978 and, in the 20 years that Graham McKenzie has been artistic director, he has pushed its boundaries ever wider; it has featured music by creators from all over the world, including Ukraine, Lebanon and Estonia – but above all, by British-based musicians of all generations and genres.

One of the big problems with any “contemporary music festival” is defining what that phrase means. It’s the same problem with “new music”, or even that weird oxymoron, “contemporary classical music”. McKenzie’s answer is to be as inclusive and generous as his own musical tastes, and to burst open those definitions in every concert, whether it’s an urgently apocalyptic opera from Ukraine, or Seth Parker Woods playing an amplified ice cello. The festival has been especially interested in breaking down barriers between musicians who are improvisers – making music in the moment, and composers, writing down works for virtuosic musicians to play.

Genre is a largely useless way to think about what it is that happens at hcmf. Any festival that can feature pieces by Brian Ferneyhough alongside performances by Nwando Ebizie, improvisations from Heiner Goebbels as well as compositions by Wadada Leo Smith, is making a musical future in which the only commonality is adventure and vision.

In a single day at this year’s festival, you could start by hearing a 50-minute meditation by Lithuanian musicians on a long-forgotten 19th-century weather diary from America; then enjoy an afternoon at the bleeding edges of notated music and improvisation in a collaboration from Electric Circus and Juno 3. Your evening kicks off with a Finnish opera – Myself/Myself/Myself – for singer, actor and electronics that “follows a young woman, Didi, caught in a whirlwind of mental bombardment – fuelled by social media – who pushes herself against the world.” That’s an hour, allowing you time to move on to late-night Lithuanian experimentalism from the group Artisans, and their show, Synthetic Piss, featuring “the recycling of Lithuanian folk-music fetishisation in a joyful embrace of sonic trash”.

Just another Sunday in Huddersfield. Add in major UK premieres from new music luminaries James Dillon in the festival’s opening concert on 20 November, and Rebecca Saunders in the closing one nine days later, as well as a whole day of free events on 23 November, and it feels quite miraculous.

I myself saw Stockhausen in his orange jumper in the mid 1990s in the town hall – a musical myth made flesh, and have visited the festival whenever possible these past three decades. I was even lucky enough be guest artistic director in 2005, which still feels like yesterday. That’s the thing about hcmf: every performance has the power of prophecy, and when you remember festivals from the past, they still feel like visions of a future that are realised in wild and unpredictable forms. There’s also a surreal sense that all this music-making is a secret ritual of experimental arcana under the skin of a town in which Christmas bunting, parties and shopping are in full flow.

But what’s the point of adding contact microphones to plant pots? Or of sawing cardboard boxes to mine their sonic and cultural-critical potential? What about a piece that incorporates a boxing match and a live tattoo session? Even the provocation – is this music or rubbish? – makes an expressive point. The serious, but joyful, point is that all that innovation and questioning of what music is and what it means is profoundly playful, and playfully profound. Where else can you indulge more completely in a world of pure imagination, experiencing the limits of what music might be, than Huddersfield in late November?

The cast for English National Opera’s production of Philip Glass’s Einstein on the Beach was announced earlier this week. The operatic milestone comes to Manchester’s Aviva Studios next May (and travels to New York in September) and looks set to be a standout highlight of Glass’s 90th birthday year celebrations. Countertenor Anthony Roth Costanzo and singer and actor Zachary Smith will be at the heart of the cast – the two had starring roles in ENO’s acclaimed Akhnaten – another production directed by Phelim McDermott. Those tickets are going to be hot: the only time the extraordinary work has been performed in the UK was in 2012, at the Barbican, London. Whet your appetite with this 2014 staging, complete on YouTube, recorded at the Châtelet theatre in Paris.

This week, Tom has been listening to: Steven Osborne’s new album OK By Me – A Life in Encores. It’s a treasure trove of the pianist’s musical memories, from Grieg’s Butterfly to improvisations on Michael Tippett and Keith Jarrett, and his own composition – the title track. Osborne’s liner notes, too, are words of wonder about his life in music, and on how he’s put together the most personal album of his career. It’s entrancing.

Prem Rugby fires starting gun on 12-team expansion plan with £20m entry fee

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 14:30:03 GMT

Interested clubs have until 1 February to come forward

Prem chief is in US attempting to find potential investors

Prem Rugby has fired the starting gun on expanding to 12 teams by formally asking interested clubs to come forward by February. The chief executive, Simon Massie-Taylor, is in the United States attempting to woo investors, with the Prem determined to add two more teams to its ranks for the 2029-30 competition.

The previous top-flight sides Worcester Warriors, who won last season’s rebranded Champ, and London Irish – who have signalled their intention to return to the second tier as soon as next season – are among those expected to throw their hats into the ring, while the Welsh Rugby Union has sent a letter outlining a desire for clubs to join the Prem and create an Anglo-Welsh league.

To join the Prem, however, interested clubs would be required to buy a P share – valued at £20m – which explains Massie-Taylor’s charm offensive in the US. Coventry, Ealing and Cornish Pirates, who have already secured significant investment, are among the Champ sides expected to come forward before the 1 February deadline to register interest, after which a tender process will begin.

Birmingham Moseley, who play in the third tier, National League 1, are an attractive proposition because Birmingham City FC’s US investor, Knighthead Capital Management, is said to have expressed an interest. Insiders see multisport investors as those to target, with AFC Bournemouth’s US owner, Black Knight, recently taking over Exeter Chiefs. With Red Bull also investing in Newcastle and James Dyson doing so at Bath, Prem executives are confident of a further flurry of interest.

As well as investment in existing clubs, Prem Rugby is open to the creation of new franchises, particularly if it allows for a geographical spread. Yorkshire is considered fertile ground to break while Prem officials are watching developments at Wasps closely. The club have secured a 10-year option on land near Sevenoaks in Kent, the county with the second-highest ­number of players behind Yorkshire.

Amid interest from Wales, Prem officials are understood to be committed to welcoming English clubs to its expanded league. They question whether Welsh clubs would be willing to spend at least a season in the Champ – one of the key stipulations for interested parties – and whether they could afford a P share.

Prem Rugby has previously used the services of Deloitte and of Raine, the US bank that ran the sales process for cricket’s Hundred, while Massie-Taylor used to work in New York and is said to be a key player in attracting investment. Leicester, Harlequins and Gloucester are among the existing Prem clubs said to be gaining interest.
