A TikTok superstar bares all: Siorna Ashby’s best shot

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 14:27:03 GMT

Portraits often rely on the face and eyes to communicate. Here, I wanted to explore how much of Meg’s presence and personality could come through her body and gesture

I met Meg at a nude life-drawing class. I was struck by how free she seemed and how powerfully that came through in her modelling. I asked if I could photograph her for my project Body Like Mine. This series explores the difference between how our bodies are perceived externally and how we experience them ourselves. We see a body and we bring our own judgments and assumptions on to it, but the lived experience is very different.

Rather than portraying an idealised body, the project aims to explore what it feels like to inhabit your own body, and to see it as worthy of attention without asking it to become anything else first.

My photography is collaborative. I brought some visual ideas to the shoot, and Meg brought her own ways of moving and expressing herself. The photograph developed between us. I took references from art history: Jenny Saville’s nudes and Lucian Freud’s work have inspired me, along with the sense of flesh and physical presence in Rubens’ paintings.

I lit her in a painterly way and used a canvas backdrop. As I was photographing her, I found myself getting lower down. I wanted the body to have a real presence in the photograph, to become the portrait itself. It was Meg’s idea to scrunch her belly in that way. I asked her to look away so that her face wouldn’t be the first place your eye went. I love how fleshy the image feels. Portraits often rely on the face and eyes to communicate who someone is. Here, I wanted to explore how much of Meg’s presence and personality could come through her body and gesture.

Meg loved it and was delighted when the image was selected to be displayed in the National Portrait Gallery. Her nude modelling is only a small part of what she does – most of her time and energies go into raising awareness about overconsumption and the “tat” that fills our lives and ends up in landfill. She’s a superstar on TikTok!

“Fat women’s femininity is [often] stripped from them and … I am masculinised and called brave for just existing in this body. When I am life modelling, I feel the most feminine and deeply in touch with myself. I am proud to take up space and represent people who often are not,” she says.

My commissioned work specialises in boudoir and nude photography. Coming to this has been a personal journey. I was very critical of my body – I was one of those women who couldn’t look in a mirror. For me, being behind the camera was also a way of avoiding being in photographs. I liked having that control. I started out doing headshots, but when you run your own business, you need to be visible. I became frustrated with all the negative feelings I had about myself, and one day I stripped off and I took my own photographs of my nude body. And when I looked over the images I was shocked to realise that I didn’t hate them. In fact I thought they were beautiful.

And then I noticed a change in myself. I was walking down the street taller. I wasn’t wearing cardigans to hide my arms. And I realised that maybe I can help others. I don’t think a photograph can resolve someone’s relationship with their body, but it can be one part of seeing themselves differently, feeling more connected to their body, or recognising that they are worthy of being seen.

But there is a tension in my work between beauty standards and how women want to be seen. Much of the boudoir photography I do sits in that culture that shapes how women think they should look and what makes a body beautiful or desirable. But who decides what makes a body either of these things? Women’s bodies don’t exist to meet someone else’s expectations of beauty or desirability, which change over time. There is room for wanting to feel sexy, but whose idea of sexy are we working towards?

When I make or look at a nude photograph, I ask what the pose, light, colour and composition are communicating. Whose perspective is shaping the image, and how much say does the person being photographed have in how they are seen?

With Body Like Mine, I want to give more space to people’s own accounts of living in their bodies, particularly where those experiences differ from what others assume when they look at them. The next person I’m photographing lives with endometriosis, and another participant is experiencing memory loss. I want us to explore how those experiences might be expressed in a photograph, guided by what each person wants to share.

Before we photograph, I ask each person to choose a few words that describe what they would like us to express together. Those words give us a starting point for the images. Meg’s were “real”, “joyful” and “free”.

Body Like Mine is part of the Winston Taylor photo portrait prize exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery, London, until 17 January. siornaphotography. com; @siornaphotography

Born: Blackpool, 1983 High point: Having my photograph of Meg Foster, Body Like Mine, selected for the National Portrait Gallery’s Winston Taylor photo portrait prize 2026 exhibition. Top tip: Talk through boundaries before artistic nude or boudoir photoshoots, and keep checking in as you work. Make it easy for someone to change their mind, and be ready to adapt a pose, change direction or put the camera down.

‘I hope paramedics are on standby for the sex scenes!’ The wet and wild TV experience leaving fans dizzy

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 13:27:02 GMT

From icy squirts to bed-bouncing vibrations, erotic hockey drama Heated Rivalry just got even raunchier in ‘extreme sensory’ 4DX cinema screenings. But one scene proved too much – even for the super fans

I’m in the cinema foyer when I first spot them: hockey jerseys. Lots of them. “I’ve no idea what to expect!” giggles Chloe, who is wearing a black and yellow “Rozanov” jersey. Like me, she has never been to a 4DX screening before – but when Cineworld announced it would be showing episodes five and six of queer hockey drama Heated Rivalry in the novel format, she booked tickets immediately. “I actually had tickets for the 2D screening, but cancelled them for this,” she says.

Over the last two weeks, Heated Rivalry fans have been treated to big screen marathons of Jacob Tierney’s hit TV show, based on Rachel Reid’s bestselling book series, Game Changers. But 4DX is next level. The “extreme sensory” cinema technology is usually deployed for high-octane action flicks – films with epic battles or chase sequences. Still, with Cineworld offering the opportunity to “immerse yourself in the motion, wind, water [and] scent” of major league hockey’s raunchiest fictional romance, who could resist?

“I’m a big fan of Heated Rivalry; last weekend, I watched all the episodes at the cinema in one day – then they advertised the 4DX screenings,” says Ross. “I’ve never been to a 4DX screening before, so I thought this was the perfect opportunity.”

Will it be hot – literally? And steamy? Will it … vibrate? “The mind boggles!” says my seat neighbour, Ann – also wearing a jersey, this time in the red, white and blue of Shane Hollander’s Montreal Metros. She’s here with a group of Heated Rivalry megafans she met on the social media platform Threads, nine of them in total. They’ve been to a few fan events together, but 4DX is a first for her, too. “I hope they have paramedics on standby for the sex scenes!” she laughs. “I know there’s a bit in a swimming pool, so maybe we’ll get wet – whoah! We’re moving!”

The adverts come to a close and suddenly we’re off – thrown up and down in our seats, spritzed with water and blasted with cool air. I clutch my armrests and look for a seatbelt; there isn’t one. The screening is only half full – some men, mostly women – but soon everyone is hysterical with laughter. This, we realise, is going to be silly … and it’s going to be fun.

If you thought Heated Rivalry was all erotic tension and clandestine rendezvous, think again: 4DX soon makes it clear it’s actually all about texting. Every message – and there are a lot of them – sends a vibration through the seat. It’s like being sat on the sofa with someone in a particularly incessant group chat. Doors, too, now appear to be opened and closed more regularly, and with vibrational intent. When Hollander suffers a fractured collarbone and concussion on the ice, 4DX does its best to replicate the experience – and it is not exactly pleasant.

Plus, ice hockey is cold. Russia, where Ilya Rozanov’s family live, is really cold. And yes, when Shane and Ilya flirt by splashing each other with water in a lake, you end up damp.

Some of it makes more sense. As New York Admirals captain Scott Hunter beckons Kip Grady down from the stands in the penultimate episode’s heart-thumping climax, gentle seat movements make the moment feel genuinely dizzying. Someone behind me likens it to seasickness, but each to their own. Whether or not the inevitable bed-bouncing and, er, thrusting were in any way enhanced is also debatable.

“In reality, it was probably the thing that was least necessary to watch in 4DX – but that actually made it better because it was so daft,” says Alice, who I meet on the way out. She has come with her friend Hayley – both genuine hockey fans and season ticket holders who decided to book the screening while watching a game last week. “You can see the people who made it must have been thinking: well, what have we got? We’ve got doors, we’ve got cars, he’s in the snow for like 0.5 seconds, so let’s do something with that! We were crying with laughter.”

“Every time there was water on screen, you were just bracing yourself,” adds Hayley.

Indeed, when I ask cinemagoers about their favourite bits, most collapse into sheepish laughter. There is a particular scene that clearly springs to most minds – although, personally, it was one squirt of water I could have lived without. “That bit was quite the experience – I was absolutely mortified!” says Lindsey, one of the Threads group. She had a great time, though she concedes that “the effects maybe took away from the emotional aspect a little”.

As for Chloe, who swapped 2D for 4DX – did it live up to expectations? “It was brilliant!” she says, beaming. “I hope they do more. I’d definitely come again.”

Reid Wiseman, the astronaut shooting for the moon in F1 with Mercedes

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 13:00:01 GMT

Nasa crew member is fast seeing the similarities between flying Artemis II into lunar orbit and the F1 team’s drive for sporting brilliance

There are characters aplenty within Formula One, a sport that attracts the larger‑than-life, and at the sharp end it can be a parade ground for swaggering egos. Yet the newest addition to the paddock is a man whose quietly spoken, understated thoughtfulness and insight are compelling. Now part of the Mercedes team, Reid Wiseman has been to the moon and with it brings a perspective like no other.

Wiseman was one of four astronauts, alongside Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen, who completed the Artemis II lunar flyby in April. Last month Wiseman, the mission’s commander, became an ambassador for Mercedes’ F1 team, formalising a relationship that had been growing over several years, to the delight of his daughter, Katey, a fan of the newly crowned world champion, Kimi Antonelli.

“I saw Kimi [at the US GP], I just put my arm around him and I said: ‘Your life is kind of crazy,’” says Wiseman. “He said: ‘Yeah, but it’s all joy.’ If he can keep that spirit going, I think it’s perfect.”

It is hard to equate the easygoing, engaging 51-year-old in the Silver Arrows top in Mercedes hospitality with the steely-eyed missile man he most assuredly is, but Wiseman seems as at home in this environment as he is at Nasa. He brings a joyous enthusiasm to F1, informed by an experience shared between but a handful of people. He is one of only nine living humans to have seen the dark side of the moon.

“The four of us [Artemis astronauts] talk about it all the time. The thing that we most hoped that we would get again in our life is connection to our friends and family,” he says. “You understand how important it is to gather as humans, to do something with a shared vision greater than yourself, and to celebrate together these milestones in life.

“In F1 you look around and it’s parents with their kids, it’s youth getting excited about motorsports, about any sort of sports. They’re celebrating together, they’re sharing a bond. They’re with friends and family. It’s all the things that we wanted most to relate to from Artemis II.”

Wiseman, alongside his fellow Artemis astronauts, was the first to leave low-Earth orbit since 1972 and has travelled further into space – more than a quarter of a million miles – than any other human. He did not know what to expect or quite what a profound effect it would have on their lives.

“It actually enriched things like sport and life,” he says. “When you are looking back at this little, tiny Earth, truly the only thing you feel is hope, peace, joy. You feel lucky that that’s your planet.

“Watching the World Cup after coming back from Artemis II made me absolutely appreciate the different cultures of the world. You can get into these moments of division through sport but then at the end I think you can come together and you know you’re all humans, you’re all in the same place. So it actually brought it home, made it more important.”

That Wiseman has joined Mercedes is almost happenstance, almost but not quite. He grew up watching Nascar with his father in Delaware but had no connection to F1. In 2023 he was invited to the US GP and spent time with Mercedes and McLaren. A year later he met Antonelli, then Mercedes’ reserve driver, who was on a tour of the Johnson Space Center, but Wiseman already knew of the Italian prodigy.

Katey was a fan of the teenager before he even had a ride in F1. “She had been watching Kimi since he was a young driver in karting and she just loved the way he took all the corners,” Wiseman says. “Kids these days, they’re glued to the internet, they discover all the cool songs first and all the good drivers before any of us have heard of who they are. I’m not kidding. She found that kid a long time ago.”

Katey, who is backstage in hospitality completing her college work, certainly had an eye for talent, with Antonelli and Mercedes completing the drivers’ and constructors’ double this season. Wiseman opens stunning pictures on his phone from the Artemis mission of the moon and Earth with casual ease as if it were commonplace to harbour such treasures in a back pocket. Among them is a shot of him reading an email he received from his daughter while in space including a picture of Antonelli.

At Antonelli’s invitation Wiseman attended the Miami GP and spent time with the team last year – and they hit it off. “I never had an avenue to connect into Formula One until I met this team and then it was like a moth drawn to the light,” he explains. “I was completely impressed with the professionalism. There’s really no flash here, just a pursuit of excellence.”

There are obvious technological similarities between F1 and space flight but interestingly Wiseman notes that the former is far more cutting edge, constantly pushing the boundaries, while Nasa is, rightly, primarily occupied by meeting parameters to ensure the success and safety of the mission. However, they share structurally a huge number of people working together to a single goal, be it drivers or astronauts at the pointy end.

He highlights the importance of trust in the process, observing that it took a long time to build between the Artemis crew, a process they worked hard at and not without incident, as have Mercedes and Antonelli.

“Leading up to launch I ‘killed’ the entire crew in a simulator because I made the wrong decision,” he says. “In the end, that actually earned trust because of the way we debriefed that, learned from it, and we changed some of our operating principles as a crew.

“Kimi was a rookie last year and I think that was his year of developing trust with the team. Not every decision was great. But he developed that deep level of trust with the team and it’s paying off now when you watch him. Everybody trusts his decision-making, they trust what he’s going to do and they know all of his strengths and even though it’s probably hard to find them, they know his weaknesses, too.”

What, then, of that undefinable something that in early days of the space race set the astronauts apart – the right stuff? Does he see it in F1 drivers?

“When you’re a driver getting in a car, you are competing against yourself, probably more than anything else,” he says, after a pause to consider. “If I asked Kimi: ‘Who is he racing against?’ my guess is he’d say: ‘I’m racing against me. Everybody else is there but I’m racing against my own time.’

“In the astronaut world that’s how it started, that’s where ‘the right stuff’ started. If you’re alone in a spacecraft, it’s you and the machine. When the drivers get in the cars, they’re joking around with people but you can see that focus in their eyes. Get in the car and get to the task at hand. I feel that, I recognise that.”

Wiseman has proved hugely popular with Mercedes and in his duties representing them, and it is unsurprising that it is the team aspect to which he returns, with a pleasingly philosophical air he has surely earned as F1’s very own star man.

“I had Claude go and evaluate statements Apollo astronauts made after they came back and statements that [the] Artemis II [crew] made after we came back,” he says. “Claude said our statements were almost identical with one exception. Apollo astronauts said “I”, and Artemis II astronauts said “we”. That’s the only difference.

“I don’t know if that’s a cultural thing or if that’s kind of the premium that we now put on small team skills. Maybe it’s a change in humanity, right? Maybe we’re more invested in each other now?”

Doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby was barred from treating patients during trial

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 12:45:13 GMT

Exclusive: Jury was never told that Prof Peter Hindmarsh was barred from practising over concerns for patients’ safety

A senior doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby and who was held up by prosecutors as a pre-eminent expert was barred from treating patients during the trial over fears he posed a risk to their safety.

Prof Peter Hindmarsh, a specialist in hormones in children, was crucial to the crown’s argument that the British nurse had poisoned children by injecting insulin into fluid bags. But a Guardian investigation can reveal he was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023, five months before the end of the trial, by his employer, University College London hospitals trust (UCLH). Jurors were never told.

Among the reasons for UCLH’s decision was that his advice to child patients relating to insulin was not considered safe. A UCLH medical director told the General Medical Council (GMC), the doctors’ regulator, that the hospital could not “accept the level of risk Professor Hindmarsh appears to pose to children and young people”.

The GMC, which was already investigating Hindmarsh’s fitness to practise, subsequently applied for his registration as a doctor to be suspended. That could have resulted in his evidence in the trial of Letby – which was still in progress – being dismissed.

However, in April 2023 a medical practitioners tribunal – an independent panel that decides GMC proceedings against doctors – opted not to suspend his registration. Instead, it ordered that Hindmarsh be directly supervised in his work, to protect patient safety. That decision had no practical effect because UCLH had already barred him from practising at all.

While Hindmarsh’s ability to practise was being restricted, the trial of Letby continued at Manchester crown court. Her defence team was never informed that Hindmarsh’s hospital considered his professional judgment and practice so deficient as to be unsafe to child patients, or of the April 2023 tribunal ruling.

While Hindmarsh did inform the local police force, Cheshire constabulary, in December 2022 that he was subject to a GMC investigation, and in February 2023 the Crown Prosecution Service told Letby’s defence, her legal team was not made aware that he was later barred from practising on safety grounds.

Had they known, Letby’s defence team might have challenged his credibility as an expert witness and applied for the jury to be told or for his evidence to be dismissed.

Failures of disclosure are recognised as potential grounds for a referral to the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), the miscarriages of justice watchdog, and for convictions to be overturned.

The apparent lack of transparency could mean Hindmarsh breached legal rules requiring expert witnesses to disclose to the party instructing them any disciplinary proceedings against them and anything that may be considered to undermine their credibility. Hindmarsh declined to answer any of the Guardian’s questions about this, the hospitals’ concerns about him, or the GMC investigation.

Letby, who was a neonatal nurse at the Countess of Chester hospital, was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, and sentenced to 15 whole-life terms in prison. Court of appeal judges turned down her applications to appeal.

She has always maintained she is innocent, and her lawyer Mark McDonald has applied to the CCRC to send her case back to the court of appeal.

Since the convictions, dozens of leading UK and international medical experts have argued that the prosecution’s case, including Hindmarsh’s evidence, was wrong, and produced reports submitted in support of her CCRC application.

Dr Shoo Lee, a renowned Canadian neonatologist who argues that the prosecution misrepresented his research, last year made public the summary findings of a 14-member expert panel he had convened. They found unanimously that the babies died or collapsed due to natural causes and poor medical care on the unit, and that there was no evidence of murders, insulin poisoning or any other deliberate harm.

Seven experts have contributed to reports submitted by McDonald to the CCRC, contesting Hindmarsh’s opinions. They argue that Hindmarsh’s calculations and diagnoses of the babies’ medical conditions were factually inaccurate in many respects, and his opinion that insulin was infused via the fluid bags is not supported by the evidence. The experts also argue that blood tests known as immunoassays, relied on by the prosecution as definitive evidence of poisoning, are known to be fallible.

Lady Justice Thirlwall, who chaired a two-year public inquiry after the convictions, refused to consider the experts’ arguments that Letby may have suffered a miscarriage of justice, or to wait for the CCRC decision. She produced a report in September making a series of recommendations for the NHS, on the basis that Letby was guilty.

Hindmarsh was presented to the Letby jury throughout as a distinguished authority. The lead barrister for the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), Nick Johnson KC, described him to jurors as “the pre-eminent expert” on insulin.

Hindmarsh was a consultant paediatric endocrinologist – a specialist in hormones, including insulin, in children – at UCLH from 1991, and a professor at UCL, with an eminent reputation.

When Johnson introduced Hindmarsh at the trial, he asked if he was also an honorary consultant at Great Ormond Street. The jury was not told that four months earlier, in July 2022, Hindmarsh’s contract in that role at the children’s hospital had been terminated.

Hindmarsh asserted in his trial evidence that blood tests and the medical records of two babies being cared for at the Countess of Chester hospital showed they had been poisoned with insulin, most likely inserted into intravenous fluid bags. The prosecution alleged that Letby injected insulin into the bags, although there was no direct or forensic evidence that she or anybody else had done so.

Hindmarsh’s evidence alleging insulin poisoning was considered pivotal to the convictions. In summing up, the judge, James Goss, told the jury that if they were sure babies were being deliberately harmed, they could decide other babies were also being harmed, even if they were not sure about the precise cause.

Johnson presented the two cases of alleged insulin poisoning as incontrovertible evidence. The charges of attempted murder of those two babies were the first on which the jury reached guilty verdicts, and two of only three unanimous guilty verdicts.

The Guardian first revealed in March that the GMC launched an investigation into Hindmarsh on 25 November 2022, the same day he first gave evidence as an expert for the prosecution of Letby.

Great Ormond Street hospital had reported “multiple and wide-ranging concerns” to the GMC, including Hindmarsh’s “diagnosis and treatment of patients” and “cases where harm to patients has been alleged”. UCLH had been leading a formal investigation of its own into Hindmarsh, and in December 2022 it reported its similar concerns to the GMC.

Then in January 2023, while the Letby trial was still ongoing, a medical tribunal imposed orders that while the GMC investigation continued, Hindmarsh could only work at UCLH, and his clinical work had to be supervised, because otherwise he “may pose a real risk to members of the public”.

Until now, it has not been publicly known that UCLH reported further serious concerns on 15 March 2023, and informed the GMC it had excluded Hindmarsh from treating patients at all. This was less than three weeks after Hindmarsh had given his second and final day of evidence at Letby’s trial, on 24 February.

Documents seen by the Guardian show that a UCLH medical director, Dr Tim Hodgson, informed the GMC of the hospital’s decision. Hodgson wrote that Hindmarsh had breached the supervision order and given independent medical advice relating to three child patients, two involving insulin and diabetes. Hindmarsh’s medical colleagues had submitted “written concerns” about him, Hodgson said.

“On the grounds of safety UCLH are not presently in a position to allow Professor [Hindmarsh] to practice clinically even under supervision,” he wrote. “… I do not believe UCLH can accept the level of risk Professor Hindmarsh appears to pose to children and young people even with close clinical supervision.”

In two of the cases, Hodgson said Hindmarsh had independently advised the families that the children stop being given insulin at home. One of the children had an episode of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a critical, life-threatening complication caused by a severe lack of insulin.

“The patient had an episode of DKA and it’s not clear whether this coincided with the alleged advice from Professor Hindmarsh,” Hodgson wrote.

In the two insulin cases, Hodgson highlighted concerns that Hindmarsh was over-focusing on rare causes of hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) and diabetes (a cause of high blood sugar). In the first case, his colleagues believed Hindmarsh was not addressing more common causes of diabetes, and in the second, that he was “not treating high glucose levels appropriately”.

Had Letby’s defence team been informed of this, it could have strengthened the case for an application to inform the jury or exclude Hindmarsh’s evidence.

Experts who have provided reports for Letby’s CCRC application have argued that Hindmarsh’s opinion that the babies were poisoned via their fluid bags was an extremely unlikely explanation for their condition. They argue that Hindmarsh failed to recognise more common, identifiable medical causes.

Hodgson also said Hindmarsh had questioned the reliability of an insulin antibodies blood test result, sharing “his concern with the family that this was an erroneous, fallible test”.

This too could have been significant to Letby’s defence. At the trial, Johnson presented results from the immunoassay blood tests as definitive and said there was “no doubt” the two babies were poisoned.

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

Experts supporting Letby’s CCRC application say immunoassays are known to be fallible because they can react to antibodies in blood to give a falsely high insulin result. Hodgson’s report suggests Hindmarsh recognised that some blood tests were fallible, but he never made this clear at Letby’s trial.

The GMC responded to these new concerns by applying to the tribunal for Hindmarsh’s registration as a doctor to be suspended. Hindmarsh’s barrister argued strongly that although he would not be treating patients because UCLH had excluded him, he should be allowed to continue working as an expert witness. Suspension, she said, would impede his ability to do so.

The barrister argued to the tribunal that Hindmarsh had not breached the supervision order and “no harm has been caused to patients”.

The three-person tribunal said it could not determine whether the previous supervision order had “technically” been breached. “However, the tribunal felt that the three cases identified by UCLH did raise concerns about patient safety,” it said.

The tribunal decided that to suspend Hindmarsh would be disproportionate and explicitly allowed him to continue working as an expert witness, saying its order should not “restrict his non-clinical work”.

Instead, it imposed a tightening of the supervision requirement so that Hindmarsh from then had to be directly supervised when treating patients. This appears to have been a theoretical measure, however, because Hindmarsh was already restricted to only working for UCLH, and the hospital had barred him from treating patients at all.

Expert witnesses have a legal duty under the criminal procedure rules to tell the party instructing them – in Hindmarsh’s case, Cheshire constabulary – anything “that might reasonably be thought capable of undermining the expert’s opinion or detract from the credibility or impartiality of the expert”. This includes any disciplinary proceedings by a regulatory body.

The rules were introduced in 2014 to improve the reliability of expert evidence and guard against miscarriages of justice, after a series of wrongful convictions in the late 1990s and 2000s.

Lawyers have told the Guardian that under the rules, Hindmarsh should have told the police of the April 2023 tribunal ruling and that his hospital had barred him from clinical practice.

Tim Green KC, a specialist in disclosure, told the Guardian: “Whilst I cannot comment on the facts behind this complex and sensitive case, it is clear that the duty of an expert witness to make disclosure in a criminal or civil case of all material capable of undermining his opinion or detracting from his credibility is a continuous one.

“This duty extends after he has given evidence and through to the end of the proceedings. The duty continues through to any appeals, and arguably remains extant now, during the current considerations of the CCRC.

“Further restrictions imposed by a professional disciplinary tribunal on an expert’s right to practise, like those which can be imposed by the medical practitioners tribunal, are also disclosable in my view. Such restrictions are likely to be relevant to an assessment made by a jury or judge of an expert’s opinion evidence, competence and skill. For the same reasons, it also arguable that the information which led the tribunal to impose those restrictions in the first place is also disclosable.”

Lawyers have said Hindmarsh may have had a duty to tell the police and CPS initially, earlier in 2022, of the investigation into his practice led by UCLH, and that Great Ormond Street had terminated his contract. He does not appear to have done so.

When Johnson, the lead prosecutor, first introduced Hindmarsh in court on 25 November 2022, he sought to clarify that the professor had an eminent position at Great Ormond Street as well as UCLH. After two questions not answered clearly, Johnson asked Hindmarsh: “Are you an honorary consultant at Great Ormond Street hospital though?” Hindmarsh replied: “Yes. At that stage, yes.”

Hindmarsh did not say his contract at Great Ormond Street had been terminated four months earlier. That point was never clarified to the jury.

Hindmarsh was first informed of the GMC investigation into him on 30 November 2022. By this point, he had already made his first appearance in the Letby trial.

He told Cheshire constabulary two weeks later, on 14 December 2022. The CPS was informed two months later and told Letby’s then barrister, Ben Myers KC, on 20 February 2023, just four days before Hindmarsh was due to give his second day of evidence.

The CPS told Myers it would oppose the jury being told, because the GMC investigation into Hindmarsh had not reached a final adjudication. Myers did not then make an application to the judge for the jury to be informed.

On 23 February 2023, the day before Hindmarsh was due to return and give evidence, Johnson reminded the jury about him. “Professor Peter Hindmarsh will be here tomorrow to deal with the issue of insulin,” Johnson said. “And because he’s the pre-eminent expert in that narrow field, we will call him first.”

In July 2023, the judge referred to Hindmarsh’s evidence in his summing up. He did not mention Great Ormond Street at all, describing Hindmarsh as “emeritus professor of endocrinology at University College London and also a consultant paediatric endocrinologist at University College London hospitals”. Apparently unknown to the judge, UCLH had excluded Hindmarsh from practising as a consultant four months earlier.

Letby was convicted in August 2023. The GMC investigation into Hindmarsh never reached a final determination. In November 2024 Hindmarsh applied to remove himself from registration as a doctor. The GMC allowed this, a process known as “voluntary erasure”, which meant the investigation was stopped with no final adjudication.

The CPS has confirmed to the Guardian that it did not disclose to the defence anything relating to Hindmarsh being barred from clinical practice or the April 2023 tribunal ruling, because it had not been made aware of it.

Cheshire constabulary declined to provide information to the Guardian, so it is not clear whether Hindmarsh did or did not tell the police. Either way, it was not passed to the CPS, which would have disclosed it to Letby’s defence.

“Cheshire constabulary will not be commenting further in relation to this case,” a spokesperson said.

A CPS spokesperson said: “The CPS met all its disclosure obligations and no objections were raised by the defence at any stage in relation to expert evidence relied on by the prosecution.”

The CPS’ statement is made on the basis that it disclosed what it knew to the defence, and it had not been told about the tribunal ruling or that Hindmarsh was barred from treating patients. Johnson’s representatives did not reply to questions from the Guardian.

McDonald, Letby’s lawyer, said: “Peter Hindmarsh’s evidence was pivotal to the prosecution’s case against Lucy Letby. The insulin allegations were not simply another part of the prosecution’s case; they were its cornerstone, presented as scientific proof that she had deliberately poisoned babies and was capable of murder.

“It shaped the jury’s perception of Lucy and provided the lens through which they were invited to view every other allegation. This was not evidence that could be neatly confined to two convictions. Its influence permeated the entire trial. If the foundations of the insulin cases are unsafe, the consequences for the safety of the wider convictions cannot be overstated.”

The Guardian asked Hindmarsh detailed questions about the hospitals’ concerns, UCLH excluding him from clinical practice, and the GMC investigation, and put to him that he appeared not to have made adequate disclosure under the criminal procedure rules.

A representative for Hindmarsh replied: “He has no comment in relation to these questions and points.”

Netflix, Fox and the $2bn bid for the 2030 World Cup that could reshape live sports

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 12:01:00 GMT

The battle for the US TV rights to the tournament will pit the traditional broadcaster and the ‘whatever-it-takes’ streamer. It could be a tipping point in the industry

The awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but.

Media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn (£1.13bn) and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry.

There also appears to be a clear frontrunner. “I would put money on Netflix to win – they will pay whatever it takes,” one experienced media rights buyer told the Guardian.

Multiple sources have confirmed that Netflix would submit a bid before Thursday’s deadline for first-round offers, along with their fellow streamers Apple TV, Disney, Amazon, YouTube and Dazn, as well as the traditional broadcasting heavyweights, Fox, ESPN, NBC Universal and Skydance, although the last of these may find itself constrained by the budget cuts being made after its $110bn acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery. Netflix has already bought exclusive rights in the US for the 2027 and 2031 Women’s World Cups.

“There’s a huge range of buyers and therefore a broad range of possible outcomes,” one broadcasting veteran says. “All the media companies and streamers will bid. Fox will find it very challenging to retain the rights.”

In a significant change, Fifa is selling the English and Spanish rights together for the first time, a move that indicates it is seeking a single exclusive rights holder, which would suit the streaming companies. With Fox having paid $485m for exclusive English-language rights to the 2026 World Cup, and NBC Universal’s Telemundo paying $600m for the Spanish-language rights, the only certainty is that the 2030 price will be far higher, despite less attractive kick-off times for a US audience as the tournament is in Morocco, Spain and Portugal.

The impact of the time difference is hard to price, but may not prove to be that significant given the seemingly insatiable demand. NBC paid about $1.5bn for exclusive rights for the 2024 Paris Olympics and were rewarded with average daily viewing figures of more than 30 million, albeit with far more variation in programming than a World Cup.

Fifa awarded non-competitive extensions to Fox and Telemundo in 2015 as compensation for moving the 2022 Qatar World Cup to winter, a perspective that was strengthened on the back of this year’s record-breaking tournament. Fox’s live coverage of Spain’s extra-time victory over Argentina in the final was the most-watched soccer telecast in US history, with a peak audience of 51.685 million; five World Cup games brought in average audiences of more than 20 million; and the average viewing figure across all 104 matches was 7.7 million, twice the figure in Qatar four years earlier.

Telemundo’s coverage, available through NBC’s streaming platform Peacock, averaged a total audience of 6 million viewers per game, with Spain v Argentina and Mexico v England attracting peak audiences of more than 23 million, the highest-ever for Spanish-language broadcasts in the US.

The bumper audiences were extremely lucrative for the broadcasters, with figures from the advertising sales analysts Guideline showing that Fox and Telemundo generated a combined $1.19bn in advertising revenue alone during the tournament, almost three times the figure from Qatar four years earlier and more than their original rights investment.

Fox alone brought in $835m from World Cup advertising, with 30-second slots costing between $200,000 and $750,000 according to the Hollywood Reporter, and the six-minute hydration breaks generating between $2m and $9m per game.

Having left a considerable amount of money on the table because of the circumstances of the 2026 process, Fifa is determined to cash in this time around. Holding the auction only four months after the US hosted the World Cup appears a clear attempt to capitalise on the success of the previous tournament, which contributed the vast majority of Fifa’s $4bn media revenues over the four-year cycle to 2026.

The addition of hydration breaks will give bidders such as Fox more revenue to play with, although Fifa will expect the option for extra adverts to drive up the price and take its own cut this time around, having missed out in the summer. The two three-minute breaks in each half were only finalised last year and did not feature in the 2026 tender documents.

“Sports advertising is much more valuable than entertainment programming as it has a broader reach,” says François Godard, an independent media analyst. “And one-off events such as World Cups do not generally do particularly well for subscription services, who want year-round content.

“Fox in particular needs the World Cup and is heavily associated with it. They are the smallest of the legacy broadcasters and are reliant on sport, as well as news. Having said that, the market for sport amongst streamers is far more competitive in the US than in Europe. Netflix, Amazon and YouTube have all bought NFL rights, while Apple is investing heavily in Formula One, so I wouldn’t rule any of them out.”

after newsletter promotion

Adam Kelly, president of the global sports marketing agency IMG, has a seat at the table at many rights negotiations and has long predicted the rise of the streamers, viewing the 2030 World Cup as the potential tipping point when a premium event could be exclusively bought in a major market by a streaming service for the first time. IMG has the rights to sell more than 70 global sports organisations, including the Premier League, World Rugby and Wimbledon.

In addition to the exclusive rights in the US for the 2027 and 2031 Women’s World Cups, Netflix has secured exclusive 2030 World Cup rights in Spain. It must sublicense all of the Spanish national team’s matches, both semi-finals and final and at least one match per day to a domestic free-to-air broadcaster to comply with government regulations.

“These entities are the future of broadcasting, as they are the best companies in the world at turning attention into earnings,” Kelly says of the streamers. “Their model allows them to monetise better than their rivals due to their size, scale and the high consumption levels of their customers.

“Netflix in particular has built a sophisticated and lucrative advertising platform. They have the back-office capability and 2027 would provide a perfect test run. If they’re successful in the tender for the World Cup it shows they are potentially the future of sports broadcasting.”

Netflix’s diversification into an advertising business, which brought in $1.5bn last year with projections of $2.7bn this year, puts it ahead of Apple TV and Amazon and well placed to make a profit from an undertaking as large as broadcasting a men’s World Cup. The lack of stipulations in the US for free-to-air coverage makes this tender particularly attractive to Netflix, although if successful it could make some matches available to non-subscribers for promotional purposes, as Apple TV has done with Major League Soccer.

“As a company, Netflix’s unique offering is exclusivity, so why would they hand that to their rivals?” another broadcast source said. “There are no regulations in the US preventing exclusivity so I would expect Netflix to bid for and retain every game if they win.”

Given recent reports that Netflix is exploring tabling an offer for NBC Universal after withdrawing its $85bn bid for Warner Bros last year, a future partnership with a linear network cannot be ruled out if it is successful. Some sources have even suggested that the tender has been timed deliberately to attract a competitive bid from Netflix, as the streamer is short of sports content to promote during the 2027 Women’s World Cup. Others argue that Fifa would have been better advised waiting to build further on the interest created by that tournament.

The NFL’s decision to pause its media rights process as it seeks an early renegotiation of contracts that are due to run to 2034 is likely to have played a part in the timing, creating a window of opportunity for Fifa to go to market. While a second round of bidding is possible after Thursday’s opening round, the outcome is expected to be known within the next few weeks and could present a bounce for Gianni Infantino as he continues his presidential re-election campaign.

‘The sea washed away trees, then a whole row of houses. I knew it was time to get out’

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 12:00:58 GMT

Location: El Bosque, Mexico

Disaster: Sea encroachment

This is Guadalupe Cobos Pacheco’s story

The fishing village of El Bosque was the first community in Mexico to be recognised as climate-displaced. The inhabitants were moved in 2023. By then, coastal erosion and flooding had already taken many of the homes.

I was 12 when my family moved to El Bosque, and I never imagined ever living anywhere else. It’s where my children were born, and my grandchildren. My whole life was in El Bosque. I used to say I would only leave feet first – as in, straight to the cemetery.

El Bosque, which means “the forest”, was a fishing community. One hundred per cent of people lived from the sea.

The men fished out at sea, while the women would catch crabs and throw nets at the shore. We’d keep an eye on each other’s children or they’d come with us and play on the beach, so it was easy for us to work, and we contributed a steady source of income to the household. The older women would make food for the fishermen and tourists, things such as ceviche, fried fish and El Bosque’s famous empanadas: tortillas stuffed with crab or fish and deep-fried in lots of oil outside on a wood stove. People used to say: “If you went to El Bosque and you didn’t try some empanadas, you were never really there.”

I first noticed we were losing trees back in 2017, old ones that had been there for years. Then we lost the first house, that was in 2019, but I never imagined losing the community, not even in my wildest dreams.

I still remember the day that the climate scientist Dr Lilia Gama came to El Bosque, in 2022.

As soon as she stepped out of her truck, the very first thing I said to her was: “Doctor, tell me El Bosque is going to be saved.” She’s very gentle, but she said: “No, El Bosque is already irreparably broken. The coastal erosion is very advanced and it’s happening really fast.” She told us we’d have to leave; that it was a matter of when, not if.

By then, the sea had taken an entire street of houses, so we knew the sea was coming towards us but I still had faith it would stop. But Dr Gama said no, climate change was making the winds stronger and the water warmer, and we had no natural barriers left because of the construction and deforestation, and the oil platforms in the sea. She said that the next northerly winds might take another row of houses. And that’s what happened just a few months later. A storm on 7 November 2022 took my sister Cristina’s house and my mum’s. They were big houses, well built – my mum’s had been there for 30 years. That’s when I realised there was no turning back. I didn’t want to leave, but El Bosque was going to disappear.

We had been trying to organise as a community since 2019 but we didn’t know which door to knock on. I mean, how were we supposed to know? It wasn’t until organisations such as Conexiones Climáticas and Greenpeace came to El Bosque that we saw some light. But by then, it was too late: the sea was moving forward very fast, and relocation was the only option.

The first days of 2023 were horrible. Houses collapsing, the power going out – people lost everything, even their clothes. We started writing letters to the federal government, and we were in all the newspapers. In the end, the president agreed to help us, and the land to build Nuevo Bosque [New Forest] near the city of Frontera was donated to us by the Tabasco state government. They chose where we were going to live. Obviously, if they’d let us choose, we would’ve wanted to be close to the sea. But they put us here for safety, far from the sea, from the river, from the water.

We’re happy that we succeeded in getting the relocation, but city life is so different. Sometimes my blood sugar suddenly spikes and I get in such a bad mood that I just can’t take any more. Our entire day-to-day rhythm of life has changed. We’re stuck inside here, and everyone seems more irritable. I think we’re still grieving. I mean, losing our territory, our everyday life, our fishing, our sea, our river … It’s not easy to recover from that. This new place is fine, it’s nice, but it just doesn’t compare to what we had back there.

Our elders are really struggling for income and they get sick more, because they’re inside all day and can’t go down to the shore. The sea guarantees you food, and everything is so expensive here. Some of the women still go to El Bosque to help the fishermen, but it’s hard without your own transport. So this source of income, the fishing life for women, is fading away. Our whole day-to-day rhythm of life changed. But if you ask the women of El Bosque what they do, most will still say: ‘I’m a fisherwoman.’

I especially worry about the kids now – my God, what are they going to do? In El Bosque, fishing was a good trade. It’s something parents passed down to their children: fishing, love for the sea, the knowledge gained out at sea. My son, he’s a fisherman like his dad, it’s like an inheritance. But we’re losing that connection – the little one might not even learn to swim!

All along the Tabasco coastline the sea is right up at the shore, and when the erosion speeds up, who knows how many homes are going to be swept away. I really hope the authorities learn from El Bosque, because there are a lot of things that shouldn’t be repeated. For me, relocating coastal communities should be the last resort, because honestly, it’s horrible. I wouldn’t wish it on anyone. The government needs to act now, to build up dunes, plant trees. Mangroves are crucial. And communities should be at the centre of these discussions.

I know it’s not going to last for ever, that El Bosque is going to disappear when the sea and river come together. But we’re going to keep going back and fishing as long as we can, because we’re fishers. Look, I consider myself a person of the sea, and without the sea, I’m nobody.

We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 11:50:57 GMT

After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs

When I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI.

But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes.

Winning union recognition would be a huge step forward in securing a meaningful say over our conditions at Rockstar, but its significance would reach far beyond that. As one of the biggest and most influential game studios in the world, what happens here could open the door for other workers across the UK to imagine an alternative future for the industry – one in which workers’ voices are taken into account more.

Sometimes it’s hard to see the impact of these games when you’re working so hard on them. It’s only at times like this that the staggering scale of GTA’s success hits you. GTA V has sold over 230m copies, generating more than $10bn (£7.6bn) in worldwide revenue, surpassing any film in Hollywood’s history. This latest instalment is expected to break those records. Behind these numbers are thousands of people whose talent and hard work make the games possible. With a recognised union, we can ensure everyone, across every department, sees a fair share of the success we contributed to. Our games are industry-leading. Our wages, conditions and bonuses should be too.

While the highs of a game release like this can be incredible, game workers have also come to expect other, less welcome side effects: intense overtime in the buildup and mass redundancies in the aftermath. In previous years, Rockstar has faced allegations of “crunch culture”, where game workers are expected to do unhealthy amounts of overtime in the run-up to a launch. With a strong union we could make sure there is no return to this system. We have already seen the introduction of some overtime pay, and now we want to keep on pushing to ensure that every hour worked in our industry is an hour paid.

After the big day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it’s hard not to worry about what the future holds. Studios across the industry have been slashing huge portions of their workforces, with an estimated 24,000 roles axed globally over the last two years. It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised.

There’s another reason this is a pivotal moment for the UK’s biggest game studio to secure union recognition. The rapid emergence of AI is transforming how studios work and raising fundamental questions about the future of our industry. Across the sector, the skills that workers spend years developing risk being devalued as their creative work is replaced by AI. Rockstar has said it is committed to preserving jobs and it has been clear that our games will continue to be made by people. But with recognition we’d have a seat at the table to manage this industry-wide transition together.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

This vote will be many people’s first introduction to unions. It’s only over the past decade that game workers have begun to unionise, realising that to tackle the industry’s mounting challenges we need to come together. The IWGB Game Workers Union – which was first founded by Rockstar workers among others in 2018 – now represents thousands of members, across 300 UK studios. Encountering unions for the first time, people have a lot of questions. We’ve heard from colleagues who are nervous that the union is an outside troublemaking force that will threaten the company. But we’re not outsiders. We are hundreds of studio employees who live for Rockstar, its output, and the players. We want to see it succeed.

The vote will also coincide with the closing submissions of an ongoing employment tribunal over alleged union-busting at Rockstar, after the sudden firings of 31 of our union members last October. Rockstar insists the sackings were for gross misconduct unconnected with union activities. The company has said it makes “the best games possible by giving our talented teams world-class work environments and ongoing career opportunities” and that employee retention is above the industry standard.

No matter the result of the tribunal over the firings, the union at Rockstar has gone from strength to strength. We now just want employees across all departments to have a hand in shaping those “world-class work environments” Rockstar says we should have.

Whatever happens in this ballot, our union will continue fighting for a studio that works for every single person at Rockstar, and for workers across the industry. Unionising shouldn’t be something we simply admire from afar when dockers, miners or teachers do it. It’s something we can, and must, embrace for ourselves. The future of the industry shouldn’t be a game played over our heads.

Nestor Uriarte is an animation programmer at Rockstar Games

Fresh off recent wins, the left has a new goal: get AOC to run for president

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 11:00:57 GMT

With its policy priorities more mainstream than ever, the left is directing its momentum toward 2028

A week after the US midterm elections swept an unprecedented number of leftists into office across the country, about 600 people joined a Zoom call. The goal: to convince Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president.

On the call, organizers from Ready for AOC, a new group of progressive and labor organizers, wasted little time celebrating the Democrats’ electoral sweep. “People all over the country are ready for a much different and much better future,” said Genevieve Rand, an organizer with the group. “We are more ready than we have ever been.”

Ocasio-Cortez, the millennial New York congresswoman whose improbable defeat of an establishment candidate eight years ago helped usher in a renaissance for the US left, has not declared her intention to run, saying recently that she will take some time to decide “privately”. (She is also reportedly considering a primary challenge to the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer.) But the work to build a field operation behind her is already under way. On Saturday, at their biannual convention, the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, the insurgent group backing many of the leftist candidates who won office last week, also voted to encourage the longtime member to run. Within 24 hours of Ready for AOC’s launch last Monday, more than 10,000 people across 50 states had signed a pledge to support her, and nearly 4,000 had registered for organizing calls to jumpstart a field operation to get her elected.

“The goal is to get her to run,” said Ravi Sahai, an organizer with the group who also worked on the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani’s, odds-defeating campaign last year, who stressed Ready for AOC was an independent, volunteer operation with no affiliation to her team. “It’s clearly a very personal choice – and we want to respect that, but also demonstrate that there is real, widespread support behind such a run.”

In an age of soaring cost of living, seemingly endless wars and an ever-widening distance between a small set of oligarchs and everyone else, the left is having a moment. Calls for universal healthcare, affordable housing, free childcare and getting money out of politics have been on the ascent since Bernie Sanders’ history-making 2016 run. Today, they have never been more mainstream.

Eager to seize the momentum, not everyone is waiting for Ocasio-Cortez before lining up alternatives. Just two days after the midterms, the former democratic socialist congressman Jamaal Bowman and progressive activist Nomiki Konst launched a committee urging the California congressman Ro Khanna to run. Mamdani, whose winning endorsements of fellow democratic socialists have crowned him a kingmaker of the left, has been meeting with union leaders – including United Auto Workers (UAW) president, Shawn Fain, and Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA – to make the case for a leftist, labor-aligned leader to jump into the race.

But virtually no viable candidate on the left has Ocasio-Cortez’s name recognition, fundraising skills and deep relationships in Washington and within working-class movements.

“Her victory in 2018 shook national politics in a way that we hadn’t seen,” said Sahai. “There isn’t really anyone else that has that kind of profile.”

When she first ran for Congress, in 2018, Ocasio-Cortez said she wasn’t running “from the left” but rather “from the bottom”. As progressive and moderate Democrats swept to victory this month, that’s the grassroots, populist message her supporters are evoking, stressing policy – Medicare for All, the Green New Deal, raising the minimum wage – rather than ideology.

“The focus is on what we’re going to deliver for the American people, and that transcends whether it’s left or establishment,” said Sahai.

That approach may run up against the group most associated with this leftist resurgence. The DSA, the left’s largest national organization, is not always known for adapting its positions or rhetoric for a mainstream audience.

By January, six new democratic socialists, including pro-Palestinian activists and labor and community organizers, will join Ocasio-Cortez and congresswoman Rashida Tlaib. Four new democratic socialist mayors will join Mamdani at the helm of US cities. And more than 100 socialists will sit in state and local offices across the country. Buoyed by the wins, socialists who for years have prioritized down-ballot races and local organizing are increasingly urging that the time is now – maybe now or never – for a socialist president.

“In a time of rising fascism and historic levels of inequality, the stakes of the 2028 presidential election for the direction of US politics and world history are monumental,” read the resolution to back AOC, passed by the group’s New York City chapter over the weekend. “A winning presidential campaign creates enormous opportunity to deliver a democratic socialist agenda that puts working-class people back in control of their own lives.”

Whoever runs in 2028 will face a transformed political landscape. The DSA now counts more than 130,000 dues-paying members nationwide and more than 200 local chapters, and growing numbers of Americans are viewing socialism favorably.

“Democratic socialism is becoming part of the mainstream of American politics,” Eric Blanc, a professor of labor studies at Rutgers University and DSA member, said on election night. “Now, we have an opportunity to do something much bigger, and much bolder.”

The recent wins would have, not long ago, been unthinkable for a left that has historically existed outside the US’s bipartisan political system. While long-shot socialist candidates have run in presidential elections throughout US history, they have always done so on third-party lines. The biggest vote share a socialist candidate got was 6% – in 1912.

That candidate was Eugene Debs, a labor organizer, anti-war activist and founding member of the Socialist Party of America. From a peak of 120,000 members that year – a record the DSA surpassed this summer – socialism retreated to the margins of US politics, beaten down by repeated Red Scares, the cold war, runaway US capitalism, and the internal strife that often characterizes movements on the left.

It’s against that backdrop that the DSA was founded in 1982 by the longtime activist Michael Harrington. The vision was to promote a pragmatic approach to radical leftwing aspirations, what Harrington called “the left wing of the possible”.

DSA had limited political impact even as its members occasionally rose to elected office – David Dinkins, New York’s first Black mayor, was also its first democratic socialist one. Still, the group remained largely obscure.

Then came Bernie Sanders’ 2016 presidential run, which came within inches of the Democratic nomination with a raucous socialist, anti-billionaire message. Sanders was never a member of the DSA, but many within the organization view him as its political muse.

Sanders inspired young political newcomers such as Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani to launch their anti-establishment campaigns. Others followed their stunning upsets. The group’s once dormant membership soared with its wins.

“We have a world to win” is the DSA’s pitch to would-be members.

As DSA has grown in prominence, the group’s tensions have been on display – about pragmatism v ideological rigidity, Israel, policing and other issues. Even committed members including Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani, have at times distanced themselves from its more radical positions, such as abolishing borders or the US Senate.

And while the group is coalescing around Ocasio-Cortez, there is plenty of internal opposition. A faction opposes her on the grounds that she has compromised on some of the organization’s values, most notably on Israel. The national DSA, which has been more critical of Ocasio-Cortez and has not taken a position yet on a potential presidential run, rescinded its endorsement of her in 2024 over her failure to vote against funding for Israel’s Iron Dome and after she hosted a panel featuring supporters of the controversial IHRA definition of antisemitism. The NYC-DSA resolution to back her passed with 291 votes – but 123 delegates voted against it.

“The biggest danger is that DSA doesn’t live up to this moment that the left is not used to, engaging in mass politics, talking to millions of people and not just thousands of people,” said Blanc, the Rutgers professor and DSA member. “The biggest danger is that we don’t seize this moment and that we stick with the routines and internal, inward-looking purity politics of the last decades.”

It’s also not clear that the rest of the Democratic party is ready for a socialist presidential candidate. The DSA is not a political party – and the fact that DSA candidates are running as Democrats has irked party centrists and some of DSA’s own members who view the party as too compromised. Already, centrist Democratic funders fearful of the group’s impact on the 2028 election have pledged to spend millions to fight the group.

While the recent midterms may have been historic for the left, many of their wins came in solidly blue states, while more moderate Democrats broke through elsewhere. A successful presidential candidate will need a broader reach – at the very least in swing states.

In Michigan, for example, Abdul El-Sayed explicitly distanced himself from socialism and the DSA, even though he is broadly aligned with the left. In Florida, Angie Nixon, a progressive who joined DSA during the campaign, lost to the Republican candidate by a small margin. (Many blame the Democratic establishment for failing to rally behind her.) Francesca Hong, a DSA candidate who this summer came close to clinching the Democratic nomination for governor in the swing state of Wisconsin, also fell short.

“Of course, the growth of DSA in the last eight years or so has transformed the way that the left holds power in this country – and that’s not an insignificant thing,” said Sahai. “But this project goes beyond that, because what is needed to win on the national level is a coalition of the left, labor, progressives, liberals – a broad coalition that can bring all these groups together.”

Ocasio-Cortez is the only left candidate with “the ability to communicate to such a large group”, he added. “[She] has the kind of vision, experience, and connections to the movement that no other candidate has.”

This story was amended on 18 November 2026. An earlier version incorrectly identified Chuck Schumer as the Senate majority leader, and he is the Senate minority leader.

After 49 years, Nasa’s Voyager 1 is one light-day away from us. Can we save this ‘pale blue dot’?

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 11:00:56 GMT

Since the spacecraft’s 1977 launch, our wonderful and terrible species has done great damage to our planet. Voyager has offered us a clear view of ourselves

Imagine traveling nonstop for 49 years, alone in the dark with no destination in sight, powered by curiosity and engineering.

Further imagine making that journey not at bullet train or jet plane speed, but much faster: at 37,800 miles per hour, free from friction in a vast sea of cold, soundless space, bombarded by radiation and cosmic rays yet still able to communicate with folks back home.

Today, 18 November, that intrepid traveler – Voyager 1, a robotic space probe the size of a Mini Cooper – is exactly one light day away from us: 16.1bn miles.

No other human-made object has ever gone this far. Radio signals from Earth (traveling at the speed of light, 186,000 miles per second) now take 24 hours to reach it, and another 24 hours to return. The return signals are so weak that scientists at Nasa’s Deep Space Network must use a massive satellite dish to hear them.

Nasa launched Voyager 1 in early September 1977, just weeks after the first Star Wars movie hit theaters with Luke Skywalker and his charming sidekick droid, R2D2. It took photos of the planets Jupiter and Saturn, then continued onward.

In 2012 it exited the sun’s protective shield of charged particles and magnetic fields, crossed a boundary called the heliopause, and entered interstellar space. That’s when it became a message in a bottle.

That message consists of a 12in, gold-plated copper disk engraved with information to showcase human culture and the diversity of life on Earth, should any advanced civilization discover it. The disk contains photos and greetings in 55 human languages, music by Mozart and Chuck Berry, the sound of a baby crying and a whale singing. It also has a time stamp and a map that orients the position of our solar system to 14 pulsars – dense remnants of massive stars – that rotate rapidly and emit beams of radiation like flashing cosmic lighthouses. The message says, in essence: this is where we live and who we are. We thrive on connection. Come see us sometime.

The astronomer Carl Sagan chaired a committee that designed the disk. In the late 1980s, as Voyager 1 hastened through the outer solar system, he tried to convince Nasa to turn the probe’s sensitive cameras back toward home.

Nasa resisted, concerned about the risk of instrument damage. Finally, on Valentine’s Day 1990, the cameras turned. The result was one of the most profound images ever captured in space exploration. Sagan called it the “pale blue dot”, wherein Earth appears as a fraction of a pixel, “like a mote of dust caught in a sunbeam”.

At that moment, Voyager 1 began to probe us, forcing us, from a great distance and with great irony, to take a close look at ourselves.

“From this vantage point,” Sagan said, “the Earth might not seem of any particular interest. But for us, it’s home … On it everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives.”

On this small planet and against all odds, molecules composed themselves into organic matter that over billions of years evolved into complex living organisms. Geologic epochs came and went. Continents moved. Species thrived and perished, with one, only very recently, standing upright and coming to dominate all others.

That’s us: a remarkable biped capable of love, compassion and war; of making music, felling forests, creating literature, burning oil, building probes and exploring space.

Scientists today say humans have “gravely altered” the chemistry, biology and physical structure of Earth’s land and water, with much of that damage occurring since Voyager 1 left us. We (or some among us) have destroyed countless habitats and damaged ecosystems to where wildlife populations are now collapsing worldwide. Building a global economy on fossil fuels has so warmed and toxified our planet that few places – if any – are pristine any more.

“Dear Future Generations,” the author Kurt Vonnegut said shortly before he died in 2007. “Please accept our apologies. We were rolling drunk on petroleum.”

It wasn’t always this way.

For most of human history, long before we stared at our computer screens and cellphones, we sat around campfires and studied the night sky. We found patterns in the stars, named them, and told stories.

Much later, we invented science and turned our rational minds toward a better understanding of ourselves and everything around us. It is science today that tells us we are made of star stuff; that every element in us was forged in the fiery furnaces of stars.

“When we look out into space,” says the professor of astronomy, Brian Cox, “we are looking into our own origins, because we are truly children of the stars.”

When astronauts orbit Earth (many of them for months on end), they see no flags or national boundaries or competing interests. Instead, they see a single home shared by billions: spaceship Earth, a blue world wreathed in clouds and surrounded by a cold, sterile darkness.

One of those astronauts, Ron Garan, concluded that if humanity intends to flourish far into the future, it must shift its priorities from economy-first to planet-first, followed by society, then economy. Without clean air, fresh water, stable ecosystems and a suitable climate, society and the economy mean nothing. They collapse.

If we get things right and survive our technological adolescence, thousands of future generations will enjoy this still beautiful, bountiful planet: a world of suitable temperatures and robust (though rapidly diminishing) biodiversity.

Much damage has been done, mostly by ignorance and greed. Global warming is accelerating, and hard challenges lie ahead. But this crisis and others can be mitigated if we set our hearts and minds to it; if we learn to live together and strive to belong, not to dominate.

Sometime soon, probably in the 2030s, Voyager 1 will lose all power and go silent. But it will sail on, carried by inertia, headed not for Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to us after our sun, but toward the constellation Ophiuchus. In roughly 17,600 years, it will be one light year from Earth.

And beyond that?

Is anybody out there?

“It has been said that astronomy is a humbling and character-building experience,” wrote Carl Sagan. “There is perhaps no better demonstration of the folly of human conceits than this distant image of our tiny world.

“To me, it underscores our responsibility to deal more kindly with one another, and to preserve and cherish the pale blue dot, the only home we’ve ever known.”

Kim Heacox is the author of many books, including The Only Kayak and Jimmy Bluefeather, both winners of the National Outdoor Book Award

David Beckham’s perfume, Poundland – and a mighty, mighty stink

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 11:00:56 GMT

The Beckhams have made an art of monetising their every move. But apparently there are limits to where they’re prepared to sell their wares

Thoughts and half-price prayers with Poundland, please. The discount chain has been on the verge of collapse for a while, and its future looks bleak. Now, to add to the ignominy, David Beckham is kicking it while it’s down.

Not literally, by the way: I suppose I should spell that out since we’re dealing with a litigious billionaire. I did not mean to imply or cause a reasonable person to infer that Sir David is standing on Brixton high street kicking a Poundland. Rather, DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, is causing a bit of a stink about the fact that the football legend’s fragrance range was found on sale in the discount store as well as at other purveyors of budget goods. It is now suing the perfume company, Coty, which it further accuses of under reporting sales, for $41m (£31m).

“DB Ventures … ensures that all of its brand licensing partnerships maintain the lifestyle and luxury image of the brand that Sir David has carefully cultivated for decades,” court filings stated. “Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station. How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.” Coty has denied that it had ever sold the fragrances in Poundland.

Either way, the lawyer who wrote this exquisite paragraph is wasted in the legal profession and should really think about a marketing career. They’ve managed to distill the essence of the Beckham brand in just a few words: desperation and greed.

I’m not saying that Victoria and David Beckham, who are now worth an estimated £1.2bn, aren’t talented and hardworking, etc. But at a certain point monetising every second of your life, and wringing every possible penny out of your famous name, gets a bit naff, doesn’t it? While celebrity-backed businesses and endorsements are obviously commonplace, the Beckhams have taken things to an extreme, slapping their name or image on everything from whisky to Walkers crisps to AliExpress. Even 15-year-old Harper Beckham is launching a skincare brand. They’ve become the British Kardashian-Jenners.

Not everyone in the Beckham family seems quite so keen on the family business, however. “My family values public promotion and endorsements above all else,” Brooklyn Peltz Beckham, who has been in a bitter feud with his parents, lamented in a statement published in January. “Brand Beckham comes first.” You’d think that a public feud with their son would have taught Posh ‘n’ Becks that there are certain things money can’t buy. For everything else, there’s Poundland.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist
