Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 11:00:55 GMT

With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre

Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI?

In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it.

For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building.

For a long time you really are two-bit criminals on the run, getting in with every dirtbag petty thief and drug-runner you come across in order to scrape some cash together and stay under the radar. You meet hillbilly pill-heads and biker gangs, friendly conspiracy theorists, a shady doctor, Lucia’s former prison friends and their lowlife boyfriends. By the time I actually got to Vice City – a glitzy den of sin, the centre of all Leonida’s pleasures and all its most extravagant criminality, where the gangbangers hustle on social media and even the narcos are obsessed with their Instagram clout – I had been playing for 30 hours. It took me 70 hours to finish the game and I could have taken longer.

Leonida is so lifelike that at times it beggars belief, so vast that it feels overwhelming, and outside the story missions you can do whatever you please. There are nightclubs, gyms, flea markets, malls, restaurants, clothes shops, basketball courts, shooting ranges, aircraft hangars, projects and mansions, places to hunt and fish or go kayaking, gas stations and thousands of individuals engaged in conversation as you pass by. Interesting things are always happening in your peripheral vision. You might witness the cops chasing someone down to plant drugs on them, or overhear an interesting confrontation, or see a car speeding away and wonder where it’s going – though interesting things always seemed to happen when I was driving a stolen car at high speed towards a discerning buyer, or otherwise unable to stop and follow my nose. Thankfully, another opportunity would always present itself.

I often felt that the only thing messing up Rockstar’s perfect simulation was me. All this detail and realism comes with some disadvantages, namely complex controls and a tendency for the game’s systems to collide with my intentions in unexpected and sometimes annoying ways. Here I am, driving at high speed through the city before clipping the kerb and flipping my car, causing a massive pile-up. Here I am pressing the wrong button and accidentally punching a random passerby rather than greeting them as intended, kicking off a ridiculous skirmish in which I have to knock out half the customers at a restaurant before running from the cops. Here I am again pressing the wrong button at a bike rack and ending up pinned beneath a tumbling row of bicycles. Missions can go south very quickly and for reasons that aren’t always obvious. In every street race I wiped out spectacularly by crashing into something I couldn’t properly see, while my opponents magically recovered from every collision and sped ahead. This can be a frustrating game at times: unpredictable, laborious, unwieldy and, occasionally, unfair. That is because you are not the master of the game world. You simply exist within it.

Like most compelling crime fiction, Jason and Lucia’s story involves an escalating series of messy events that pull them further and further from where they started, and have you constantly wondering how on earth they’re going to get out of the newest trouble they’re in. To avoid spoilers, substantive discussion of this story can only happen in the coming weeks. But I will say that I was rooting so hard for Jason and Lucia by the end that I felt quite sick with worry about what was going to happen to them, pacing back and forth in front of my TV throughout the final missions. Among all the expectations I had for GTA VI, I did not expect it to make me so emotional.

The key to this is the bond you form with Jason and Lucia. After tens of hours in their company, watching them together – how she smiles fondly at him when they dance together, their playful banter, the stick-ups they pull off as a duo, their resilience and faith in themselves and each other in the face of escalating disaster – I found it impossible not to care for them. They are our avatars in GTA VI’s world but they are not blank stand-ins for the player: you decide their actions but not their personalities. They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim. It made me care about them much more. When the story gave me opportunities to decide what would happen next, what came to mind for me was what they would do, not what I would do.

This is indicative of a tonal shift for Grand Theft Auto that became more obvious the more I played. This series is famous for its violence, misanthropy and pitch-black humour. I have been invested in its characters before, have even rooted for some of them, but I have rarely liked them or related to them. This is the first GTA that wants to encourage some measure of empathy alongside its trademark violent chaos. I was astonished to discover that the game offers you small incentives for acts of kindness, such as texting your partner a selfie, doing your neighbour a favour or throwing your rubbish in the bin rather than dropping it on the ground. Jason and Lucia are not extravagant caricatures, but two people trying to make it in a world totally stacked against them. Pretty much everyone in this Floridian fever-dream is a total crook, on the take or mixed up in some bullshit scheme. It’s so easy to get away with crime in this city, and so difficult to do things the right way. The events of this game might be totally outlandish but these characters and their motivations keep things at least somewhat grounded.

If you thought this newfound heart might tone down GTA’s 18-rated provocativeness, however, you would be very wrong. The protagonists may be surprisingly relatable but they exist in a world that is absurdly foul-mouthed, filthy and over-the-top offensive in every imaginable way. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating. Barely a half-hour ever goes by without someone snorting coke off a knife blade, or some full-frontal nudity. There are missions set inside a pornographer’s mansion and a small-town strip club; you can visit those clubs and get a private dance (as either Jason or Lucia, for what it’s worth, or together). At one point Lucia opens the wrong hotel room door to see a woman in a corset wielding a golf club, thwacking balls at a guy’s testicles. On the in-game TV there is a reality show about horny geriatrics. It does not so much push the boundaries of taste as ignore the existence of taste. It contains every perverted scenario you could imagine and several more that would never occur to you.

Sometimes it is a little jarring to emerge from a really pivotal and moving scene between Jason and Lucia into a virtual city where the billboards read things like “WANTED for shitting everywhere: THE SHIT BEAST.” But I found these two sides of GTA’s personality surprisingly easy to accommodate. It’s not as though the story is without its many moments of absurd levity and humour, too: at one point I was taking a bunch of terrifying gang leaders with face tattoos on a real-estate tour, where they sincerely admired the outdoor space with brick pizza oven, and another time I was chasing a man wearing nothing but an alligator thong through a well-to-do suburban neighbourhood. A game this huge can accommodate both pathos and lewdness, and much more.

I did find, however, that Lucia – Grand Theft Auto’s first female protagonist – changed how a lot of this landed for me. GTA has never been particularly kind to women (or men, for that fact, but in past games it has exclusively been the women who were sexualised). There is still a lot of sexism in GTA VI’s world, but now we have Lucia to react to it. This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story, from up-and-coming rappers to Lucia’s mother, from a jaded strip-club worker to a badass middle-aged drug-runner whose custom purple carbine rifle is her prized possession. This is a game in which women can be as violent, visibly tough and deeply messed-up as the men. And without wanting to give too much away: there are male strippers in Leonida, too.

I am not about to make a case for GTA VI as a feminist game – there is much to be offended by here, if you are so inclined – but I will say that as a woman who has played and enjoyed every GTA game while also often rolling my eyes at their casual sniggering misogyny, GTA VI hits different for me. I liked it more because the women aren’t always the butt of a joke. Also for the first time, I did not find the violence gratuitous or overblown, despite the fact that this is a story about crime and criminals. There is nothing here like GTA V’s infamous torture mission, which made me feel sick. It says a lot that of all the immoral opportunities afforded to me in Vice City, the only thing I straight-up said “no” to was getting involved in a metaverse scam. THAT would be going too far.

I keep reaching for something that sums up GTA VI, as much as it’s possible to sum up a game as vast as this, and the closest I come is the nightclubs. These show GTA VI at its most extravagant: hundreds of virtual people under the pulsing lights, all dressed up to go out, dancing to a fastidiously curated soundtrack featuring some of the real world’s most famous artists as the controller pulses to the bassline in your hands. These big nights out are an opportunity for both Vice City’s sleaziest denizens and Rockstar’s developers to flash their cash: they are the game’s most ostentatiously expensive and showy scenarios. But at the centre of it all, there are Jason and Lucia, dancing together, focused on each other in the midst of all this chaos and excess.

Grand Theft Auto VI is out 19 November; £69.99 / €79.99 / A$159.95 / $79.99

‘Worst decision in cinema history’: Guardian readers shaken and stirred by the casting of Robert Pattinson as Bond

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 10:00:47 GMT

‘Deliciously dark’! ‘Not sexy enough’! Opinion is split on whether the star of Twilight and The Batman is the right choice to play 007. Here’s what some of you thought

So it’s official, Robert Pattinson will be James Bond. The long-awaited announcement of who would be stepping into 007’s tuxedo came as a surprise, and has divided opinion, judging by the more than 700 responses the Guardian received to a callout on the topic.

Readers were split on whether bosses at the franchise’s owner Amazon were right to give the role to the star of Twilight, Tenet and The Batman. Here are some of their views.

Brilliant casting! And with Denis Villeneuve directing, I’m expecting something deliciously dark. Pattinson has that perfect “is he a good guy or a bad guy?” face. There’s something mysterious and slightly sinister about him. Definitely not Austin Powers. I’m absolutely thrilled and applaud this direction for Bond. Tatara, US

His face is such that it always adds some mysterious vibe to whatever he is expressing as an actor. I do think this will add more depth to the Bond character. The other candidates were more within the predictable bubble, Robert has something extra beyond that and hopefully it will deliver high quality to the next Bond films. Well done! Kris, the Netherlands

I have never felt this much rage in my life. This is the worst decision in all of cinema history. Since the age of five I’ve been watching James Bond. I have seen every film four, maybe even five times. Never in my life have I been more disappointed by a casting decision. This is an abomination. Robert Pattinson does not have a good appearance for the role. He lacks the heroic, flirtatious, life on the edge aesthetic. In my opinion, he is is also simply not sexy enough to be a Bond. He should have been a villain, that I would watch. Gemma, Australia

Casting Pattinson as Bond is a huge letdown. It feels like a lazy, play-it-safe studio decision lacking any real depth or vision. They missed the mark entirely – this goes against everything that defines the character of Bond. Nemanja, 34, Bosnia and Herzegovina

I was delighted to hear about Pattinson’s casting. I am a long-time fan of Bond; my mother took me to see Skyfall in the cinema when I was 10 (I think she had a bit of a crush on Daniel Craig). My favourite Bond is Timothy Dalton, I think Pattinson could bring the same dark intensity to the role. My favourite director is Denis Villeneuve, and Pattinson is one of my favourite actors, to have them working together on the next Bond film feels like a dream come true. Joe, 24, Brighton

Boring! Don’t get me wrong, I’m sure Robert Pattinson will be amazing in the role but he has been in every movie under the sun the past couple of years and it would just be nice to see someone else’s face on the screen and given a chance. I was really rooting for Nicholas Hoult. Rebecca, 26, London

Many of us assumed the next Bond would be a fresh-faced actor in his late 20s. Pattinson is 40, so the tone shift isn’t about youth. That may be a strength. A 40-year-old Pattinson can be seasoned and unsettling without being a young boy playing at being a killer. Where Craig’s Bond was a blunt instrument with a broken heart, Pattinson brings something stranger: unpredictability and a faintly dangerous charm. Villeneuve clearly sees something similar. The two have already worked together, and Pattinson plays the villain Scytale in Dune: Part Three. If Villeneuve can make Bond as immersive and unnerving as Arrakis, we’re in for something special. Jayjay, London

I don’t like it simply because it’s so weird as a movie lover to see Batman as Bond. I know actors obviously take different roles but two iconic characters in the same timeframe! Is there really such a lack of talented actors who can perform in Hollywood? Josh, teacher, 33, Sheffield

This is a missed opportunity. Pattinson is a good actor but too established in other roles. Also, too old for a reset role. A grave miscalculation. Bond has always been most successful when the actor has been a blank slate on whom the audience can project its fantasies of Bond. Pattinson is too established. I also wonder whether he can bring the necessary camp touch – the knowing, self-referential, theatrical excess. Martin, lawyer, Bordeaux, France

My initial reaction wasn’t especially positive. R-Patz, Bond? Cedric Diggory from Harry Potter, the Twilight pin-up, a Batman?! I thought he was too well known to mould himself into 007. It felt like a dramatic and high-profile curveball. But perhaps that’s why it makes perfect sense. I had been rooting for Jack Lowden, but Pattinson has proven in recent times how good an actor he is – I am now intrigued to see what he can bring to the famous character. The casting will undoubtedly draw a lot of attention and scrutiny, and put bums on seats for his films. Davy, tour guide, 32, Perthshire

Childhood neglect, unmet needs, mental health struggles: this is the making of a Neet

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 08:00:36 GMT

As a researcher for the Milburn review, I’ve seen how we’ve failed a generation – then castigated them. Britain must break this vicious cycle

Mark Mon-Williams is chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Leeds and professor of psychology at Bradford Institute of Health Research

Alan Milburn and Peter Fonagy have, between them, expertly diagnosed the UK’s illness. Their reviews show we don’t just have a Neet crisis. Or a school absence crisis. Or a Send crisis. We have a neglected childhood crisis that will wreck the country’s long-term prosperity if we just keep patching over these symptoms.

The solution to any problem starts with understanding its causes, and Milburn and Fonagy provide a thoughtful analysis. I have worked closely with both of them, being a topic group member for Fonagy’s independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism, and supporting Milburn with data analytics. Their reviews have followed the evidence, all of which shows a system neglecting children at scale. We have decreased benefits and slashed the support provided to children: today 4.5 million children are living in poverty. When these children grow up and are diagnosed with anxiety and depression, impeding their ability to work, they are often castigated as feckless snowflakes. It is easier to do this than admit that we have failed a generation, and that this is the predictable consequence of political decisions.

Born in Bradford, our longitudinal birth cohort programme launched in 2007 to follow the development of 13,500 children and their families, has been tracking these changes in real time, and our Child of the North consortium has synthesised the national evidence. Our findings show how childhood disadvantage accumulates into young adulthood. The science is extensive and methodologically complex, but the findings can be readily grasped through the life of an archetypal child who we will call Tracey.

Tracey is a young person desperate for education, employment or training. Like many others, she has special educational needs, anxiety and depression. We might think Tracey is Neet because she lives in a rundown area without transport links to education, employment, or training. But most young people in Bradford lack good transport, so this is only part of the story.

This is where our connected datasets are so powerful, as they allow us to travel back in time and piece together Tracey’s life from birth. Tracey’s mum was anxious and depressed and living in poverty when she was pregnant. These risk factors are known to hinder children’s development, but the signal was ignored. In fact, Tracey’s mum got less support than her middle-class peers because she couldn’t get to an antenatal group, while health visitor support was being slashed for expectant mums.

Tracey was born prematurely with health complications. Fortunately, our brilliant NHS ensured that her medical needs were met. Unfortunately, information about Tracey wasn’t shared with the other public services that would deal with the consequences of her early health problems downstream. The NHS also couldn’t address the impoverished environment in which Tracey spent her early years.

It turns out that brain science can be surprisingly easy to understand. Children need healthy environments for healthy brain growth. If children grow up in impoverished environments, they won’t develop the core skills needed to achieve and thrive in education. This means they will, by definition, have educational needs that go beyond the pedagogical support required by children whose families can access developmentally supportive environments.

The impoverished preschool environment means that Tracey starts school without the core skills needed to thrive. This is not a surprise to our Bradford researchers, who can see her history of risk factors. But it is a surprise for her teachers, who did not receive any of this information from Tracey’s mum or other public services.

Tracey struggles in primary school and her needs are not well supported: her mum cannot navigate the complex processes needed to secure the clinical diagnosis that would trigger support for her neurodevelopmental and educational needs.

It should be no surprise that Tracey struggles when she arrives at secondary school. But it is a surprise to the secondary school, because it wasn’t provided with the recorded information that screams Tracey needs love, understanding and help.

Tracey doesn’t feel included at secondary school or that she belongs there. Once more, brain science can be surprisingly easy to understand. The brain generates feelings of anxiety when faced with environments that feel hostile, and feelings of depression when hope is eroded.

Tracey attends a school with an outstanding Ofsted rating, but her own results are not helping its league table position. The school gently encourages her away from class and Tracey starts to miss school on an increasingly frequent basis. Before Tracey can sit her GCSEs, the school suggests that perhaps she should find another school or be educated at home. This is an unscrupulous yet perfectly rational response within an education system that rewards attainment over inclusion. Unfortunately, the science shows an unequivocal relationship between school absence and becoming Neet, so there is no surprise when Tracey ends up not in education, employment or training.

This all appears inevitable when viewed in hindsight. But it isn’t. Patterns in data are not fixed outcomes. We know that schemes like Sure Start in England, mercilessly cut by the coalition government, can transform children’s lives and help them enjoy healthy, productive futures. Our Bradford research shows an earlier diagnosis of neurodevelopmental issues is associated with lower risk of teenage mental health problems, and that “inclusive” schools show lower Neet rates. Early risk factors are signals for intervention, not fatalistic trapdoors. Young people don’t become Neet overnight, and every day offers an opportunity to either reduce childhood risks or let them accumulate.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Why Tracey? Our hypothetical child is homage to Tracey Emin. Her work Why I Never Became a Dancer uses art to capture these scientific truths and shows how one child overcame childhood trauma to become a world-leading artist.

Compassion shines from the Milburn and Fonagy reviews. We must share their compassion. Our children need love, understanding and a national commitment to overcome the UK’s neglected childhood crisis.

Tracey’s story is not only about poverty or adversity but also about system failure. The social safety net is cut without consideration of the long-term consequences. Health services treat medical problems, but cannot see or address living conditions. Information isn’t shared between services. Schools are rewarded for exam results, rather than helping children. Support, rationed by thresholds, only arrives at crisis points.

The answer cannot be another sticking plaster for young people transitioning into adulthood. We need to reimagine how we support children from birth so our young people and economy can thrive. This means reshaping the public sector around improving children’s lives, while tackling the deprivation that creates adversity in the first place.

Andy Burnham is right when he says that this demands a generational response. We must all get behind a national commitment to transform childhood, recognising that the anxiety, depression and lost opportunities experienced by too many young people are not inevitable. They are the consequences of choices we have made as a society, and choices we have the power to change.

Mark Mon-Williams is chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Leeds and professor of psychology at Bradford Institute of Health Research

Jack Grealish recalls a golden age of mavericks – but football has moved on

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 08:00:36 GMT

Everton forward has magical talent and popularity to burn, but has come up against hard reality of the modern game

Thomas Tuchel has never called up the player he once claimed to love “everything about”. The reason for Jack Grealish’s omission from Tuchel’s first England squad in March 2025 was given as “he simply has no rhythm”.

Catch a falling star? Last month Grealish was suspended by Everton for three matches after “a breach of club discipline”. Suggestions his loan from Manchester City might be cancelled were calmed by David Moyes. Last week, Grealish played in a behind-closed-doors friendly against Derby before issuing an Instagram statement: “I want to apologise to the fans and everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks.” Amid tabloid tales of karaoke nights and extended socialising, how close is the former boy wonder, now 31, to blowing it?

By many definitions, Grealish’s is an outstanding career. From teenage hometown hero with Aston Villa, an emblem of their revival as a Premier League club, to record £100m signing and treble winner with City. All while maintaining a popular public persona, an everyman quality to accompany the looks and the lifestyle.

Even in the Republic of Ireland, the nation he forsook to play for England, Grealish is nothing like the pariah figure Declan Rice is for having taken a similar decision. Yet Grealish is fast becoming a tale of charms unfulfilled, talent inelegantly wasted. The trophies he won at City were as a functioning cog, the “rest station” of Pep Guardiola’s machine, not the expressive soloist who won hearts for those rippling leg muscles.

At Euro 2020, as Gareth Southgate’s England ground through the gears in the group stage, Wembley crowds bayed for Grealish to come on. English football is forever seeking its new Paul Gascoigne, the ball-carrying maverick breaking through heavily fortified enemy lines. Garrulous, fun-loving Grealish threw back to memories of football bad boys who made red‑top headlines while remaining idols on the terraces.

The tradition was deep-set, from the 1950s heyday of Len Shackleton, the “Clown Prince” of the north-east, to the 1970s, when an era of cloggers and roughhouse football was lifted by the characters who later inspired The Mavericks, the late Rob Steen’s 1995 book. “We treasure them because they embraced risk, because they dared not to give a damn, because, most of all, they dared on our behalf,” wrote Steen.

Peter Osgood, Alan Hudson, Stan Bowles, Frank Worthington, Charlie George and Tony Currie were household names who enjoyed a 1990s revival in the era of Loaded and Fantasy Football League, when football and debauchery were freely coupled. In 2026 there is an entire cottage industry of podcasts and YouTube channels recalling golden days when the pub was as prevalent in a footballer’s life as the training pitch.

In 2026, the elite modern footballer’s existence is a near‑monastic one. On Sunday, the Brighton head coach, Fabian Hürzeler, described the disciplines Pascal Gross follows to remain a high-functioning Premier League player: “So much work in the shadows, recovery, preparation.” The “refuelling habits”, to use the euphemism Graham Taylor attached to Gascoigne, are not workable for a required body-fat percentage between 8% and 12% or the muscle repair from a target of eight to 10 hours of proper sleep.

Technical ability is the barest minimum. Focused application is a necessity, particularly when player wages continue to climb. Jadon Sancho has winners’ medals in the Europa League and Conference League and played in a Champions League final but, at 26, has not found a club willing to take on a player released at the end of his Manchester United career.

The paradigm player of this age, officially after his Ballon d’Or, is Harry Kane. He and Grealish made breakthroughs in 2014-15; Kane as the new king of White Hart Lane, Grealish as the teenage star of Villa’s run to the FA Cup final. Grealish, spoken of with hushed tones in Birmingham and Irish youth football circles, was the greater talent. Kane’s rise came via a drive to continued improvement from a lower base level.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

As Kane received his individual prize at the London Palladium last month, Thierry Henry, the co-compère, made an unscheduled intervention. “Harry Kane is a perfect example that work ethic is a talent, working hard is talent, not only pure skill … this guy had to suffer.” Henry was criticised for comments depicted as elitist, though his point drove at the pair’s diverging paths.

It also recalled the philosophical battle of the 1970s, when cavalier players such as Bowles and George, with five and one England cap respectively, were ignored by the roundhead England managers Alf Ramsey and Don Revie. Succeeding George Best, the exemplar of talent unfulfilled, in being British football’s biggest star was Kevin Keegan, whose playing style was all about hard work and energetic running, such that an innate, deep talent was masked.

Best received plenty of second chances. His appearances for Hibernian in the 1979-80 season allowed him to receive a share of Easter Road gate receipts. That same season at Nottingham Forest, Brian Clough tried to get a spin out of both George and Bowles. All three ventures were soon curtailed.

How many chances remain for Grealish? On joining Everton, he appeared renewed. Moyes said after a match-winning performance at Wolves in August last year: “He probably needs a bit of love and attention.” In December at Bournemouth, Grealish returned the sentiment: “I love David Moyes to pieces.” More behaviour of the kind that he was suspended for and that love will be dashed on the rocks. The maverick tradition Grealish was born to follow and its attendant behaviours belong in football’s past.

UK will miss climate targets if it weakens EV sales rules, advisers warn

The Guardian Wed, 18 Nov 2026 00:01:26 GMT

Analysts say mooted move to let more petrol and diesel vehicles be sold would wreck plan to reach net zero by 2050

Weakening the UK’s electric car sales rules would probably cause the government to miss legally binding climate targets, according to advisers tracking Britain’s progress to net zero.

The analysis by the Climate Change Committee (CCC) suggests the policy would blow a hole in the plan for achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 – prompting concerns that Andy Burnham’s government will have to slash the UK’s carbon emissions reduction targets, known as the carbon budgets.

In a letter published on Wednesday, the CCC said the UK is “likely to miss” its climate targets if it confirms plans to allow more sales of petrol and diesel cars and vans in the next four years.

Those changes could result in an extra 8.4m tonnes of CO2 pollution a year from the UK by next decade.

The electric vehicle rules are the single biggest contributor to those climate goals, meaning the government will have to find other major carbon emission reductions, unless it amends the budgets to allow more pollution.

Carmakers must sell a bigger proportion of electric cars each year under the rules, known as the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, or face fines of £12,000 per vehicle.

However, the industry has lobbied intensively for months to cut the headline targets from 80% electric by 2030 to as low as 50% or 60%, arguing that the mandate was putting them under too much financial pressure.

Electric cars were 26.6% of UK new car sales during the first 10 months of 2026, well below the 33% headline target. However, carmakers are expected to comply with the mandate using a series of loopholes known as “flexibilities”.

The committee’s chair, Nigel Topping, wrote to Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, to oppose any reduction of the targets.

Such cuts would, he said, “put the government’s commitment to tackling climate change at risk, miss an opportunity to reduce costs for a typical household by about £800 a year, increase the UK’s exposure to volatile oil markets by up to 15m barrels of oil a year in 2030, and damage long-term competitiveness as our main export markets rapidly transition to electric vehicles”.

Some in government have become alarmed in recent months about the impact the government’s various changes could have on the UK’s ability to meet its climate commitments.

The government has just cut funding for installing heat pumps, the second-biggest decarbonisation policy. Burnham has also alienated some Labour MPs by waving through gas extraction from the Jackdaw gasfield, and considering approval for the massive Rosebank oilfield.

MPs voted earlier this year to approve a new set of carbon reductions for the years 2038-42.

However, the Guardian has learned that one cabinet minister in the Keir Starmer government wanted the government to go back to parliament to scrap those planned reductions and enact a more conservative target instead.

The idea did not come to fruition though, with other cabinet ministers mostly opposed.

An industry source with knowledge of discussions in government said that serious consideration was still being given to changing the carbon budgets in the run-up to the UN’s Cop31 climate conference, subject to parliamentary approval.

The source said it was not clear if the proposal was still being discussed. A government source strongly denied that it was under consideration.

The changes to the mandate also mean the UK is unlikely to meet the carbon budget covering 2033 to 2037.

after newsletter promotion

Several analysts said the government will struggle to find emissions reductions elsewhere, given the scale of pollution from petrol and diesel cars and vans. The policy could also face opposition from the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, each of which have their own carbon budgets.

Burnham on Thursday told Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, that he was “proud to support this Cop’s focus on electrification” and urged people to choose electric cars and heat pumps.

Doug Parr, chief scientist at Greenpeace UK, said: “The Burnham government cannot talk of climate leadership on the international stage while doing a U-turn on ZEV targets at home.”

Topping added: “Weakening the zero-emission vehicle mandate would miss an opportunity to reduce the cost of living for people, undermine Britain’s competitiveness and leave us more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices.

“People are buying electric vehicles in record numbers because they are cheaper to own than the alternative.

“The mandate gives those up and down the supply chain the certainty they need to invest, supports thousands of jobs, and keeps the UK on track to meet its climate commitments.

“British drivers deserve better than a backtrack on such critical policy.”

The car industry criticised the CCC’s analysis. Mike Hawes, chief executive of the Society for Motor Manufacturers and Traders, said: “A successful EV transition needs a strong market and a competitive industry.

“The CCC, however, ignores the damaging cost of the targets it defends: billions in unsustainable discounts and millions more in government incentives.

“Contrary to the CCC’s claims, the mandate is deterring local investment, as however much manufacturers export, without a strong local market there is no business case to build here.”

A government spokesperson said: “We remain committed to the phaseout of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets.

“Our consultation on the mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition.”

UK backs idea of new levies on polluting sectors to pay for climate action costs

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 17:59:41 GMT

Britain joins other signatories to statement urging introduction of targeted taxes on heavy emitters

The UK has signed a statement that backs levies on polluting sectors to pay for the impacts of the climate crisis, in a strong political signal that could pave the way for frequent flyer and crypto taxes.

Signing the statement at the UN climate summit means the UK joins a group of governments urging Cop31 to look at “the potential of targeted, small levies to ensure a contribution to the costs of climate action from polluting sectors”. The other signatories so far are Kenya, South Sudan, Spain, Timor Leste, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.

Although no global “solidarity levies” have yet been put in place, a taskforce backed by the French government has suggested making a small charge on flights for the most frequent flyers and passengers in business class, and charges on crypto-currency transactions as potential ways of raising revenue.

Analysis last year by the Dutch environmental consultancy CE Delft, commissioned by the Global Solidarity Levies Task Force, showed that a levy on tickets that began at €10 on short-haul flights in economy, rising to €30 on long-haul flights, and €20 for short-haul business-class tickets, rising to €120 for long haul, would produce revenues of about €106bn a year.

However, these ideas have been hard to put into practice. A proposed levy on the carbon dioxide produced by international shipping, overseen by the International Maritime Organization, has been postponed after opposition from the US under Donald Trump.

The UK government told the Guardian it was “committed to leading developed nations in mobilising at least $300bn per year by 2035”.

“In that context, the UK supports looking beyond the traditional flows of donor financing, to exploring much wider and deeper types of financial flows, from emerging markets, from private actors, and through financial innovations that can channel much greater levels of climate finance.”

Signing the letter does not commit the UK to any immediate actions.

The government added that it was carefully considering the “solidarity levy” proposals. “However, tax is an important matter of domestic sovereignty, so we will need to consider whether proposals are in the national interest,” the Treasury said.

NGOs welcomed the move. David Hillman, co-convener of the Make Polluters Pay International Coalition, said it was a “clear sign that the politics are shifting”.

“This is hard-won progress. But signing a statement is only the beginning,” he said. “The UK must now use its G20 presidency next year to turn words into action – putting taxes on polluting industries firmly on the agenda and building international support for measures that make the biggest polluters pay their fair share.”

Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, Ami McCarthy, said: “It’s good to see the UK finally looking at new ways to pay for the escalating costs of extreme weather. Right now, global funding for adaptation is just a 10th of what’s needed to survive worsening floods and heatwaves, and this Cop has barely moved the dial.

“With public finances as tight as they are, it’s madness to keep handing the bill to taxpayers and the people struck down when extreme weather hits. It’s time to make the polluters pay – starting with the fossil fuel giants swimming in record profits.

“As next year’s G20 host, the UK needs to turn this statement of intent into cold, hard cash.”

Developing countries have been disappointed at the Cop31 negotiations on climate finance so far, as no substantial amounts of new money are likely to be pledgedat the summit. Rich countries have committed to providing $300bn a year to the developing world by 2035, to help poor countries adapt to the impacts of extreme weather and cut their greenhouse gas emissions.

However, many current finance pledges run out within the next three years, and many countries have yet to put new pledges in place, which creates uncertainty for recipient countries. Analysis seen by the Guardian showed that although the developed world is broadly on track to meet the $300bn target, mostly through contributions channelled through the multilateral development banks such as the World Bank, the delay in fleshing out future finance commitments is making it difficult for countries to plan.

Several countries that are already planning an exit from oil and gas also want to see a final agreement in Turkey that takes forward governments’ previous pledge to “transition away from fossil fuels”.

Maina Talia, the climate change minister of the low-lying Pacific nation of Tuvalu, said: “We must get serious about transitioning away from fossil fuels.”

He said roadmaps that countries were developing to move away from fossil fuels were “only a concept until you see it travelling forwards”.

Denmark’s climate minister, Samira Nawa, said: “If we truly want to confront these issues, we have to address the root cause. Our dependence [on fossil fuels] is a root cause for most of our global challenges.”

Spain’s minister for ecological transition, Sara Aagesen, said: “The world cannot wait and neither can our societies. They are the ones demanding action and living through fires, heatwaves, floods, droughts. They are the ones paying the bill for dependence on fossil fuels.”

U. S. School Districts Weigh Breaking Up With Google Search Over A. I.

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Google’s refusal to unbundle A. I. features from search for students prompted a backlash. Now schools are looking for alternatives.

By Natasha Singer and Dana Goldstein

Natasha Singer reported from Los Angeles, and Dana Goldstein from New York City.

Three of the largest U. S. school districts, New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago, are considering using alternate search engines after Google this month refused to remove artificial intelligence from search tools used by students, officials said.

Starting next year, Google said, its A. I.-related products, including Search and its Gemini app, will be turned off automatically for schools, and administrators can choose to turn those A. I. tools on. But there will be no version of search available without A. I. chatbot features, meaning schools that want to forgo A. I. will lose access to an important learning tool.

Google’s approach created a firestorm of criticism from lawmakers, government officials, education leaders and parents, some of whom said the tech giant was trying to force its A. I. into public schools.

Now, some schools across the United States are blocking Google’s A. I. in search — or considering alternative providers.

“If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options,” Kamar H. Samuels, the chancellor of New York City schools, said in a statement. “We refuse to accept the false binary Google has laid out.”

Google’s new use-it-or-lose-it stance on A. I. in search underscores how the tech giant’s interlocking ecosystem of Chromebook laptops and apps like Gmail and Docs has become essential classroom infrastructure. The company’s search engine is a go-to product for teaching students how to do research and find primary sources.

But some educators worry that the generative A. I. that Google has embedded in its search engine for consumers could hinder students’ critical thinking, undermine learning and present safety risks. Some students have used the chatbots embedded in search to cheat, they have said, or scanned A. I.-generated search summaries instead of reading historical documents and news sources.

Educators are balancing those concerns with the reality that A. I. has already become an important tool in the work force, that a majority of U. S. teenagers already use chatbots and that many students will need to use A. I. in their future jobs.

Medical associations have also warned that developing relationships with chatbots could have negative mental health effects on young people. Earlier this month, two parents in North Carolina sued Google, saying their daughter had developed a plan to die by suicide after prolonged chats with the company’s A. I. on search on her school Chromebook. (Google said it had built safeguards into its A. I. features in search to help young people find emergency resources and was reviewing the claims in the lawsuit.)

Now districts like Chicago Public Schools, the fourth-largest U. S. school system, are urging Google to provide them with a version of search without A. I. features. “If such an arrangement can’t be reached,” Chicago Public Schools said in an email, “the district will look to other search solutions.”

Among the search engine alternatives for schools: DuckDuckGo and Microsoft’s Bing. Both offer options to disable A. I.-generated answers.

Google argued this month that it would be providing schools with more options to control student A. I. access — not fewer. Administrators could give students access to A. I. Mode, a chatbot-like function in search, as well as A. I. Overview, which summarizes search results, the company said. It is also pilot testing Guided Learning, a new chatbot widget intended to break down academic questions for students without providing easy answers.

“We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers,” Google said in a statement, noting that next year the company would turn off its Gemini app and search engine for schools “until schools decide which services to enable.”

Over the last three years, the company has made building generative A. I. a top business priority. And Google has integrated its Gemini A. I. chatbot throughout its software suite.

The fight over Google’s A. I. products has been brewing for months, with district leaders and teachers across the country approaching Google employees at meetings and online to request greater control over how students interact with generative A. I.

School tech directors in four states said they and their colleagues had repeatedly pressed Google this year to let schools decide which A. I. tools, if any, might be appropriate for students in different grades. And they warned that Google’s all-or-nothing approach to search essentially overrode more nuanced school policies on student A. I. use.

“We need to be able to control our own pace,” said Chris Warden, the technology director at Central R-3 School District in Park Hills, Mo., “not have Google tell us what the pace of A. I. adoption is going to be.”

In September, the New York City Department of Education and the Los Angeles Unified School District announced moratoriums on student use of generative A. I.

At the start of this school year, Google’s education team helped Los Angeles schools turn off A. I. mode for students logged into their school Google accounts, according to school board members. But Google said during its announcement this month that its A. I. features were so “deeply integrated” in search that it could not provide schools with a chatbot-free search engine.

Google’s decision prompted groups of parents to protest last week in front of the company’s Boston, Boulder, Chicago, New York and Portland offices.

In Chicago, several dozen parents and educators chanted slogans like, “Hey, Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini.”

“We don’t want corporations determining what is happening in our kids’ classrooms and how our schools are run,” said Cassie Creswell, the executive director of a parent group called Illinois Families for Public Schools, who helped organize the Chicago rally.

Parents and students also protested in Venice, Calif., carrying signs like “We don’t need Alphabet to teach the alphabet.”

At a meeting of the Los Angeles school board’s A. I. committee two days later, Jack Kelanic, the district’s chief information officer, was applauded when he said, “We have choices” as to which company’s software to use. “We can change the default search engine literally overnight,” he added.

This week, Jenn Brown, a Google program manager, offered an explanation for the company’s refusal to provide schools with a chatbot-free search engine for students. Google now considers search to be fundamentally an A. I. product, she said during a monthly Google Meet for school tech leaders, according to a school administrator who attended the discussion.

New York City, Los Angeles and other school districts said they were using a combination of software controls and filters to independently block student access to A. I. in Google search. Even so, some New York City parents have found students can still easily access A. I. Mode at home when signed into their student Google accounts.

New York City has declined to participate in the pilot of Google’s new chatbot feature for students, according to the district. Instead, the district is conducting its own research of five other A. I. tools for potential use at the high-school level.

In the absence of A. I. controls from Google, some smaller school districts are also working to independently disable chatbots in search. In Missouri, Mr. Warden said his rural school district, which serves about 2,000 students, had signed up for a new service from Lightspeed Systems, an online student monitoring service for schools. The software is designed to block student access to A. I. Overview and A. I. Mode in Google search.

The backlash against Google has complicated some school districts’ plans to teach students how to use chatbots effectively, said Nick Melvoin, a Los Angeles school board member.

“Ironically, it undermines the goal of trying to get some A. I. into schools,” Mr. Melvoin said.

Matthew Haag contributed reporting.

Natasha Singer has covered tech in schools for The Times for more than decade. She is currently focused on the groundswell of parent concern about school laptops and A. I. chatbots.

Dana Goldstein covers education for The Times.

Senator Bill Cassidy Blocks Trump Pick to Head Science Agency

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

A venture capitalist and Peter Thiel acolyte, Jim O’Neill faced bipartisan concern over whether he would stand up for science.

By Adam Sella and Sheryl Gay Stolberg

Reporting from Washington

The chairman of the Senate health committee on Wednesday blocked President Trump’s nominee to lead the National Science Foundation, prolonging a leadership vacuum at an agency that has been rocked by the administration’s efforts to reshape research funding.

The committee was scheduled to vote Wednesday on the nomination of Jim O’Neill, a science and technology investor who served briefly as a top deputy to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and had been tapped months ago to lead the science agency.

But moments after convening the committee, the chairman, Senator Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana and fierce critic of Mr. Kennedy, abruptly announced that the panel would not consider Mr. O’Neill’s nomination after all.

A White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss a personnel matter, said Mr. Trump had not withdrawn the nomination. It is unclear whether it can move forward without Mr. Cassidy’s support.

Mr. O’Neill “did not do enough to stand up for science” in previous roles in the administration, Mr. Cassidy said. He noted that several committee members had concerns about Mr. O’Neill’s independent judgment in light of his “role in the firing” of the former director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Susan Monarez.

After Dr. Monarez was pushed out in August 2025, Mr. O’Neill briefly became acting director while continuing to serve as Mr. Kennedy’s deputy. Then he himself was replaced, and nominated to lead the N. S. F. amid a reorganization of the top ranks of the health department.

“I like Jim personally, but this time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right,” Mr. Cassidy said.

The panel’s refusal to consider Mr. O’Neill came just hours after the White House withdrew another Trump nominee. Dr. Heidi Overton, tapped to run the Food and Drug Administration, and Mr. O’Neill were among five nominees to be considered on Wednesday morning. At the last minute, however, the health committee distributed a revised agenda with their names crossed off.

Mr. Cassidy, a physician, lost his primary earlier this year to a Trump-backed challenger and is in his last weeks as a senator. He has faced intense criticism from public health leaders for casting the deciding vote to confirm Mr. Kennedy.

A White House spokeswoman, Allison Schuster, stood by the nomination later Wednesday, saying in a statement that the N. S. F. “needs the leadership of Jim O’Neill, who has spent over a decade in the private sector helping to identify and finance cutting-edge technologies of the future.”

The science foundation, an independent agency that funds basic research, has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since April 2025, when Sethuraman Panchanathan, an appointee from President Trump’s first term, quit amid an administration-led effort to cancel hundreds of active grants and slash agency funding.

In the interim, the Trump administration has sought greater control over the N. S. F. From withholding over $1 billion in congressional appropriations to attempting to defund the social sciences division, the Trump administration has reshaped the agency to align with its priorities.

The changes at the science foundation are part of a broader push by the Trump administration to overhaul federal research funding.

Like some top science officials in the Trump administration, Mr. O’Neill’s background is in venture capital, not science. Mr. O’Neill has a degree in the humanities from Yale University and worked extensively with the Silicon Valley billionaire Peter Thiel before joining the Trump administration.

With Mr. O’Neill’s nomination dashed, it is unclear who will lead the agency next year. Last month, the N. S. F.’s chief of staff, who has led the agency since Dr. Panchanathan quit, announced that he would retire by the end of the year, according to an internal memo reviewed by The New York Times. The N. S. F. declined to comment about its leadership plans.

Adam Sella covers breaking news for The Times in Washington.

Sheryl Gay Stolberg is a correspondent based in Washington for The Times, covering Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and President Trump’s health agenda.

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Supported by

The Israeli military said it was conducting a limited raid into territory controlled by Hamas to address a threat. The militant group accused Israel of violating the truce.

By Natan OdenheimerIyad Abuheweila and Abu Bakr Bashir

Israeli forces advanced on Wednesday into an area of the central Gaza Strip controlled by Hamas, making a rare incursion into territory outside the area held by Israel since a U. S.-brokered cease-fire agreement was reached at the end of last year.

The Israeli military said that its troops, conveyed by tanks, moved into the area with engineering machinery to destroy a Hamas tunnel that “posed an immediate and direct threat” to Israeli forces in a joint operation with the Shin Bet, an Israeli intelligence agency.

The military added that the raid was a limited effort, suggesting that a large assault was not underway, but it did not offer details on what was being targeted or how long the operation would last.

Earlier Wednesday, the Israeli Air Force struck Nuseirat in the central Gaza Strip, killing at least one person, according to a statement from the Al Awda Medical Complex, which said it also treated two people injured in the strike. The Israeli military said the strike targeted a Hamas commander and was separate from the ground operation.

Ahead of the incursion, the Israeli military issued evacuation orders to residents of the area, saying Israeli vehicles would be traveling along Salah al-Din Road, a main artery, and it would be closed to Palestinians.

Hamas called the Israeli actions “a blatant violation of the cease-fire agreement” and said that by “herding citizens into a narrow strip of the territory,” Israel was making a humanitarian catastrophe worse.

Mahmoud Basal, a spokesman for Gaza’s civil defense, an emergency service under the Hamas-run interior ministry, said that more than 5,200 people were displaced by the Israeli operation.

While Israel has often carried out airstrikes in Gaza since agreeing with Hamas to halt the war, the incursion marked the first time Israel has deployed heavy armored vehicles far across the cease-fire line separating the areas under Palestinian control from those held by the Israeli military.

More than 1,600 people have been killed by Israeli fire during the cease-fire, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.

Many Palestinians in Gaza hoped Israel would cease its aerial attacks after Hamas agreed in July to an American framework for decommissioning and storing weapons, intended as the first step toward rebuilding the war-torn coastal enclave. But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said the plan fell short of true disarmament and refused to halt the strikes, which at times have come daily.

Though the Israeli military said the ground operation is limited, Palestinians said they worry it might signal that Israel is increasing its attacks.

“I thought my life was over,” said Muhammad Yasin, 50, who works at a bakery on Salah al-Din Road, recalling the moment he saw a cloud of dust kicked up in the distance by Israeli tanks and heard gunfire.

He said he and about 40 family members then fled their tent for another camp. “We really hoped this war was over for us already,” he said.

Natan Odenheimer is a Times reporter in Jerusalem, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs.

Trump, Xi and Putin Will Sit Down for the First Time. It Won’t Be Like Yalta.

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Trump’s Trip to Asia

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

While the three leaders would like to project the image that they are guiding the world order, they are unlikely to settle major issues at their gathering in Shenzhen, China.

By David E. Sanger and Peter Baker

David E. Sanger and Peter Baker have covered five American presidents and their relationships with their Russian and Chinese counterparts. They reported from Shenzhen, China, where they are covering President Trump’s trip.

The meeting Thursday between President Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir V. Putin marks the first time in history that the leaders of the United States, China and Russia — possessors of more than 90 percent of the world’s nuclear weapons — have sat down together.

But not every first in history results in a significant accomplishment — or any accomplishment. And as Mr. Trump landed on late Wednesday in Shenzhen, the chip-making, telecommunications, software and robotics heart of China, it was already clear that this meeting was unlikely to live up to the many comparisons being made to Yalta, the end-of-World-War-II conference where Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin divided up the globe.

Together, talking largely in secret, the Yalta participants laid the foundation for a postwar order that lasted nearly half a century, while leaving millions of people trapped behind the Iron Curtain.

There are many reasons that Yalta is a poor analog when thinking about the Shenzhen summit. Yalta stretched over eight days, with a bevy of diplomats and generals working the back rooms to turn the visions discussed by the three leaders into action plans. The meeting involving Mr. Trump, Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi is set to last around an hour or so — essentially a glorified photo op, by comparison, and not one in which major issues are likely to be settled.

And instead of a conclave of three allies on the verge of a joint victory over a mutual foe, this meeting features three leaders who have not been partners in a great venture, and are unlikely to be any time soon.

The three men have major differences on issues as far-ranging as China’s fast-growing nuclear arsenal, the regulation of artificial intelligence, the future of space weapons, the war in Ukraine and the war in Iran — a conflict that has haunted Mr. Trump, enriched Mr. Putin and angered Mr. Xi.

So they will not enter the room expecting that they will have time to raise, much less resolve, many critical issues.

But even photo ops can linger as important symbols. And the one that may appeal to all three men is the message that they are the true global deciders, engaged in a project to shape world order.

After enduring a resounding electoral defeat this month, that image may be particularly appealing to Mr. Trump, who makes no secret of his admiration for strong leaders who do not have to put up with pesky legislatures or an intrusive press.

For Mr. Putin, the meeting serves to help readmit him to the world community, and to recognize that he remains too powerful to ignore, even after losing half a million soldiers in a nearly five-year-long battle for Ukraine.

And Mr. Xi gets to play the role of global convener, albeit of a gathering with an exclusive list of participants.

Among those not at the table: Japan, India, South Korea, Australia, Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Brazil, Canada, Mexico, South Africa and, perhaps most notably, Ukraine and Iran.

Still, Mr. Trump, Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi clearly have conflicting agendas. Mr. Trump has repeatedly said in recent days that his No. 1 priority is to take on “denuclearization,” his somewhat sloppy way of referring to arms control. Mr. Putin likely wants to talk about Ukraine, potentially figuring that Mr. Trump wants a peace deal and will not be especially picky about the details.

And Mr. Xi, who was wary about holding any meeting without a predetermined outcome, will be looking for ways to leverage his role in the service of becoming the world’s largest military, economic and technological power by 2049 — the 100th year of Mao’s revolution.

The three men have deeply complicated relationships. The Chinese and Russian presidents have met roughly 50 times, and famously declared five years ago a “partnership without limits.” While that partnership falls well short of a true alliance, they are unified in a mutual desire to diminish the scope of American power. That was evident on Wednesday, when Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin met together.

In their one-on-one conversation, Mr. Xi told the Russian leader, who he has at times referred to as his greatest friend, that relations between China and Russia had remained as “steadfast as a rock through wind and rain,” according to Chinese state media. Mr. Xi called for the two sides to advance the “democratization of international relations,” a term he often uses to describe a world order in which the United States is less dominant.

For his part, Mr. Putin appears happy to possibly be perceived as out of the penalty box for his brutal invasion of Ukraine.

“He’s at the big boys table with the other great superpowers,” said Alina Polyakova, the president of the Center for European Policy Analysis. “For Putin, it’s credibility, it’s legitimacy. He sees himself as the tsar of an empire rather than the president of a frankly declining” country.

Mr. Trump’s national security policy refers to an updated “Monroe Doctrine” aimed at keeping foreign powers out of the Western Hemisphere. Mr. Putin talks about restoring much of the empire of Peter the Great, starting with Ukraine — but perhaps not ending there. Mr. Xi has expanded his military operations in the Pacific, building bases out of artificial islands in the South China Sea, confronting the Philippines over ownership of some of its islands, and running near-constant military exercises that encircle Taiwan.

It all feels very much like the late 1800s, the peak of the “spheres of influence” approach to world governance by a few dominant nations. In January, asked whether he believed in a spheres-of-influence approach to the world, Mr. Trump said, “It’s not necessarily where I want it to go.” But he added that as he looked around the world, “it’s where it’s going.”

It is clear that none of the three superpowers want to be limited to their own neighborhoods, even if their maps are expansively drawn. China may be focused on the Pacific first, but it wants access to copper mines in Peru and Ecuador. The United States may talk the talk of withdrawing from the world, but it wants to retain influence across the Middle East, which is why it has kept the bases that Iran attacked in the Gulf in recent months, forcing some to all but shutter. And it is not about to give up its presence in Japan or South Korea.

Russia has ambitions that also reach into space and cyberspace, as well as the Arctic and Africa.

Still, there is a serious imbalance among the three nations that will be represented at the meeting. While the United States and China are the two leading global powers, Russia pales by comparison in most respects, other than its residual nuclear arsenal and its energy resources.

While the United States and China are racing to develop artificial intelligence, Russia is at best a bit player in that field. Other than its nuclear capacity, Russia’s military has been shown over the past four years to be far weaker than Mr. Putin projected.

And economically, Russia cannot compete with the other two countries at the table. While the United States and China are the world’s largest and second-largest economies, respectively, Russia places only eighth. Its economy is barely one-eighth of the size of China’s, and one-eleventh the size of the United States’. It manufactures almost nothing of value for much of the rest of the world, other than military hardware — and vodka and caviar.

So for Mr. Putin, the meeting allows him to project the illusion that he and his country are more important than they actually are, to claim a certain geopolitical swagger unjustified by reality.

The meeting is also a way for Mr. Putin to snub Europe and essentially say that he does not need to deal with those countries, because he can sit down with the leaders of the two most important powers in the world.

“Demonstrating Europe’s irrelevance is very important to Putin at this point,” said Michael Kimmage, the director of the Kennan Institute, named for George Kennan, the famed American diplomat who designed much of the strategy around the Cold War.

“I think nothing is going to come of it, and it will be fairly quickly forgotten,” he added. “But still, to go from the Treaty of Versailles to Yalta to this shows that Europe is being erased.”

Ukraine may be discussed, as Mr. Trump indicated shortly before leaving the United States for Asia. But many Americans and Europeans close to the peace talks have concluded that Mr. Putin has no interest in making a deal to end the war. His government’s current proposal largely repeats the same maximalist demands it made before the full-scale invasion of 2022, conditions that were unacceptable to Europe and Ukraine then and remain so today.

Michael McFaul, a former ambassador to Russia, said Mr. Putin had made plain he was not seeking peace. “If he really thought this was an event for peace, the last thing he would be doing would be bombing the bridges in Kyiv that is now crippling the capital of Ukraine,” Mr. McFaul said. “I don’t think he thinks of this as a genuine effort to advance peace. He gets the photo op and he gets to call it Yalta 2.0.”

Still, some foreign policy veterans said that the meeting could not hurt — and in some ways, could probably help — by opening lines of communication among three powers that are crucial to issues around the globe.

“Even if the summit yields no concrete results, it will nonetheless have been worthwhile,” Charles Kupchan, a Georgetown international affairs professor and former national security aide to Presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama, wrote in Foreign Affairs. “Trump, Xi and Putin are paving the way for their successors to advance great-power cooperation across ideological lines and stabilize a fragmented world.”

David E. Sanger covers the Trump administration and a range of national security issues. He has been a Times journalist for more than four decades and has written four books on foreign policy and national security challenges.

Peter Baker is the chief White House correspondent for The Times. He is covering his sixth presidency and sometimes writes analytical pieces that place presidents and their administrations in a larger context and historical framework.
