Ground Stop Came as Duffy Pushed to Rapidly Upgrade Aviation Systems

The New York Times November 18, 2026

U. S. Flight Disruptions

Advertisement

Supported by

Current and former officials say that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s push to quickly finish modernization during President Trump’s second term could continue to disrupt air travel.

By Kate KellyNicholas Nehamas and Karoun Demirjian

Kate Kelly reported from New York. Nicholas Nehamas and Karoun Demirjian reported from Washington.

The Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to upgrade communications equipment on Friday afternoon, leading to a halt in air travel during one of the busiest times of the week, reflects the breakneck pace of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s efforts to overhaul the country’s aviation infrastructure.

“The longer we stay on an old rickety network, the less safe it becomes,” Mr. Duffy told reporters Tuesday on Capitol Hill. “So we do have to charge forward.”

But current and former officials say Mr. Duffy’s push to transform the F. A. A.’s slow and cautious culture — including by rapidly installing artificial intelligence systems and finishing upgrades before President Trump leaves office — is a risky gambit that could continue to disrupt air traveland lead to other fallout.

Federal officials are still trying to determine how the replacement of wiring at a remote facility in Arkansas may have led to a data overload in critical air traffic control systems across the country on Friday. As the technical problems caused radio static in communications between pilots and air traffic controllers, the F. A. A. grounded all flights, imposing the longest nationwide halt since the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001.

The very fact that such work was being done on a Friday afternoon was imprudent, according to some federal aviation experts.

“During the time that I was at the F. A. A., if we were doing any change, we would try to do it at an off-peak period,” said Katie Thomson, Maryland’s transportation secretary, who served as the F. A. A.’s No. 2 official under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. She added, “It would not be something that we would do on a Friday afternoon at peak travel hours.”

Mary Schiavo, a former Transportation Department inspector general during the first Bush and Clinton administrations, said that while the nation urgently needed to modernize its air traffic control system, performing the upgrade on a busy Friday afternoon suggested that it was moving too quickly.

“That’s not typical. Everyone knows that’s a busy travel time,” she said in an interview. “I would imagine the looming Thanksgiving holiday had them on overdrive.”

The upgrade was done on a Friday afternoon instead of at night or over the weekend in order to meet the project’s ambitious schedule, and because the work was not considered high risk, according to a person with knowledge of the agency’s investigation who was not authorized to speak publicly.

Officials still have not determined the root cause of the failure that led to the ground stop, which was only the third one in the agency’s history. The incident led to thousands of delays ahead of the busy holiday travel season and deepened worries about the safety of the nation’s aviation system, which has experienced a cascade of problems in recent years including last year’s midair collision above Washington, D. C., that killed 67 people.

Mr. Duffy has said no travelers were in danger on Friday and that there is no evidence of sabotage. He has said the incident showed the need for vast new investments in the aviation communications systems. But the situation has raised questions about the transportation secretary’s stewardship of the aviation system, including whether the pace of upgrades was pushing work to be done at times that pose a high risk of travel disruptions.

Mr. Duffy told reporters on Saturday that officials did not anticipate that Friday’s upgrades, which were conducted at a small, remote facility in El Dorado, Ark., could threaten the entire network, and that contractors regularly did such work at remote locations during the day.

“These smaller locations don’t have that kind of impact — or they shouldn’t have that kind of impact,” he said, adding that “there’ll be a re-evaluation of when we do this work.”

The job, in which copper wire used for telecommunications was being upgraded to fiber-optic cable, was performed between about 10 a. m. and 3 p. m., according to the F. A. A.

But shortly after the work, a router that had just been installed began firing a barrage of data that overloaded critical air traffic control systems at locations around the country. As some pilots began noticing radio static in their conversations with air traffic controllers, federal officials moved to ground all planes at 3:54 p. m.

The Arkansas upgrade was being handled by a single technician employed by L3Harris, one of the F. A. A.’s biggest contractors, officials have said. The work had been approved by the agency and was supervised by one of its technicians, Bryan Bedford, the F. A. A. administrator, told reporters on Tuesday. Similar work had been completed many times at other locations with no major issues, Mr. Bedford said.

Mr. Duffy said in a recent interview on CNBC that he could not “guarantee” that future disruptions would now happen without continued investment.

Mr. Duffy has demanded $50 billion in additional funding, a request that caused lawmakers, including some Republicans, to recoil on Tuesday. The F. A. A. has so far spent a small fraction of the $12.5 billion Congress appropriated for air traffic modernization last year. Transportation Department officials say they have committed about a third of the funding earmarked for telecommunications and radar upgrades.

Officials say 70 percent of the network’s copper wires have been replaced with high-speed fiber-optic cables. About half of the cables were upgraded in the past year alone, a considerably faster pace than previous administrations have reached.

But experts previously warned that the faster pace has potential downsides. A report in September by the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan federal watchdog agency, noted both advantages and risks of Mr. Duffy’s expedited improvements.

The Trump administration shaved roughly nine years off its timeline to modernize voice radio systems used by air traffic controllers, the report said. It also sped up the replacement of copper wire with fiber by 21 months.

But at the same time, the faster pace carried the potential of “cost increases and potential disruptions to the national airspace,” said Kevin Walsh, the director of information technology and cybersecurity audits for the G. A. O., in an interview with The New York Times.

The F. A. A.’s telecommunications network and its hardware issues were a trouble spot for domestic air travel long before travel came to a halt on Friday.

In April 2025, air traffic controllers handling flights in and out of Newark Liberty International Airport experienced a simultaneous outage of their radar feeds and their radio contact with pilots because of a burned copper wire, a Transportation Department inspector general inquiry found. And as recently as September, a technical glitch at a Philadelphia air traffic hub and the cutting of a fiber backup line interrupted controller communications in the Northeast Corridor.

Given that about 30 percent of the country’s aviation data lines still run through copper wires, additional, and potentially ill-timed, upgrades may be in store.

And as the F. A. A. works through a new and more ambitious operating pace, the Trump administration has tried to bring in fresh ideas and systems to help.

Those attempts have also faced problems.

In December 2025, the F. A. A. used a competitive bidding process to hire the security technology company Peraton to manage the air traffic control system overhaul, for which Congress had set aside $12.5 billion in funding.

The idea was for Peraton’s team to offer expertise and coordinate the network of contractors that would install the needed hardware and software. But Peraton’s team faced resistance from F. A. A. employees, some of whom thought that team lacked the expertise to take over agency work, said a former F. A. A. employee and three other people with knowledge of the matter. The people requested anonymity to discuss confidential processes.

Peraton was under a tight timeline — one that has been strained at times because of limits on access to facilities and delivery schedules, according to one of these people.

Peraton spokespeople did not respond to requests for comment.

Other contractors and timelines have encountered pushback from F. A. A. employees, according to current and former F. A. A. and Transportation Department employees.

An artificial intelligence system meant to optimize the routing of flights in and out of U. S. airports to account for weather, neighboring traffic and other factors has been one such effort, said three people who were briefed on the matter but requested anonymity to discuss confidential proceedings.

Known as Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, or SMART, the new system was rolled out in September at Washington-area airports by Air Space Intelligence, a Boston tech company that was awarded an $875 million contract in June.

But the system faced opposition from Shawn McClosky, the air traffic manager running the F. A. A. airspace command center in Warrenton, Va., said the four people who were briefed on the matter. Mr. McClosky believed the system was being launched too hastily and without proper review, two of those people said.

His supervisor, LaKisha Price, a senior system operations manager at the F. A. A., backed Mr. McClosky up, the people said, pushing for additional reviews. Both were removed from their positions.

Ms. Price and officials at Air Space Intelligence did not respond to requests for comment. Mr. McClosky declined to comment.

Julie Tate contributed research.

Kate Kelly is an investigative reporter covering government accountability for The Times.

Nicholas Nehamas is a Washington correspondent for The Times, focusing on the Trump administration and its efforts to transform the federal government.

Karoun Demirjian is a breaking news reporter for The Times.

Nvidia’s Interim C. E. O. Tries to Soothe a Rattled Company: ‘We’ve Got This.’

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Turmoil at Nvidia

Advertisement

Supported by

At an all-hands meeting with employees, Colette Kress sought to put the indiscretions of Nvidia’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, behind them.

By Tripp Mickle

Tripp Mickle reports on Nvidia from San Francisco.

Shortly after 9 a. m. local time on Wednesday, Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive, took the stage inside the company’s headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif., and tried to exude calm.

It had been barely six days since she assumed the top job of the wildly profitable chip maker. Nvidia has been rocked by revelations that its charismatic and visionary co-founder had two affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U. S. intelligence services determined was feeding information to Beijing. The all-hands meeting that Ms. Kress and other executives had convened, a livestream of which was reviewed by The New York Times, was an attempt to soothe the anxieties of a rattled company.

“Our ambition will not change,” Ms. Kress said, who sounded calm and confident as she sat perched on a stool. “Our passion to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners and shareholders will not change.”

She added: “Just remember, we’ve got this.”

In a the span of a month, Nvidia employees have learned that Mr. Huang had multiple affairs and had misled the board about behavior that was at odds with the company’s “code of conduct, standards and cultural norms.”

Mr. Huang resigned in the wake of those revelations, shocking people from Silicon Valley to Washington to Beijing, many of whom had come to see him as the figurehead of the A. I. boom. Nvidia’s market value, which was within a whisper of $6 trillion a month ago, has plummeted to $3.66 trillion.

Last week, Nvidia’s board named Ms. Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as its interim chief executive. It has hired a search firm to find a permanent leader. It also is moving forward with an independent investigation, led by Wachtell Lipton, an outside law firm, into Mr. Huang’s behavior.

Mr. Huang and his allies have mounted a campaign over the past week to return him to the top of the company he started more than three decades ago at a Denny’s in Silicon Valley.

In a call with Wall Street analysts on Tuesday, Harvey C. Jones, the chair of the company’s board, made clear that Mr. Huang would not return.

The back and forth has left employees confused. Some have rallied behind Mr. Huang, signing letters and writing social media posts in support of his return.

“Jensen touched every single employee on an emotional level, genuinely cared about every single developer, and cherished every fragile research idea,” Nik Spirin, an A. I. engineer at Nvidia, wrote in a social media post. “He was both the soul and the mind of the company and the ecosystem.”

Others are looking forward to a future without him. Over the past year, Mr. Huang has alienated parts of this work force by allying himself with President Trump and undermining a plan by other tech companies to develop a systematic way to evaluate the safety of A. I. systems before their release, said three current and former employees who were not authorized to speak publicly about internal company matters.

Wednesday’s meeting began with video footage of company leaders making speeches and demonstrating products. The audio over that video included words that seemed relevant to the moment:

“Nvidia has a history of persevering.”

“It’s all about tenacity as a company.”

“This is the most incredible company on the planet.”

Ms. Kress then took the stage with the executive team and read written remarks. She praised the team behind her, saying “I know this team. I know how much they care for the company and the work.”

Ahead of Nvidia’s all-company meetings, the leadership team solicits questions from employees. The questions on Wednesday largely focused on Mr. Huang’s resignation.

Mr. Jones joined Ms. Kress onstage and shared details of his own Nvidia journey. He joined the board in 2004. He spoke about how his personal relationship with Mr. Huang had made the chain of events over the past week difficult for the board.

“The board was and is fully aware of Jensen’s monumental contribution to the company,” Mr. Jones said. “Several of the board, including me, worked with him for many years and counted him as a friend.”

Mr. Jones reiterated what he told Wall Street analysts on Tuesday.

“It is unrealistic to think we can find a Jensen clone,” Mr. Jones said. “He was one of a kind. That said, there are dynamic leaders out there with demonstrated intellect, high tech engineering experience, strategic thinking, cultural compatibility and a track record of success.”

Chris Malachowsky, a Nvidia co-founder, choked up as he spoke about the situation the company has found itself in and thanked the board for its leadership. Then, he recounted how in the company’s early days, he, Mr. Huang and fellow co-founder Curtis Priem spent much of their time talking about the culture they wanted to instill in Nvidia.

They had a series of core values, he said. Maintain the highest standards in everything they do. Be intellectually honest. Innovate in everything they do. Be direct and candid in communications.

“Those have stood the test of time,” Mr. Malachowsky said. “I’m proud of them. In fact, it’s the violation of the first that’s given me pause over the past week.”

Mr. Malachowsky said that if the company adheres to those core values, it “will come out strong.” He urged employees to demonstrate those values in meetings and discussions.

“Keep these standards,” Mr. Malachowsky said. “Keep the culture alive. If we did our jobs well, and I think we did, we’re going to be fine.”

Ian Buck, the head of Nvidia’s data center business, said that the company didn’t need to worry about the road map it has developed for designing and manufacturing future generations of A. I. chips, which are the bedrock of the company’s business. He pointed to the leadership team beside him onstage and said, “We know how to get it done.”

Nvidia’s executive team said their business strategy won’t change. They plan to continue to support open models and close its acquisition of Hugging Face, a library of open A. I. models that Nvidia is purchasing for $12.9 billion. It is going to use those systems in its development of robotics and autonomous vehicles.

“All of that continues so we can become the leader of open models,” said Dwight Diercks, senior vice president of engineering.

Other executives made assurances about other key areas of the company’s business. They said Nvidia will maintain strong relationships with suppliers like Taiwan Manufacturing Semiconductor Company, which makes all its chips. They said the company would continue to outpace the industry in developing more powerful A. I. chips. And they will execute “a great business plan that endures.”

Nick Parker, who leads worldwide sales, said the company will expand its leadership ranks because it is “a great piece of the magic of how Nvidia delivers value.”

The leadership team had the benefit of the company’s latest earnings behind it. On Wednesday, the company reported quarterly profit and sales doubled, with revenue topping $100 billion for the first time. The results showed that the dominant maker of A. I. chips has momentum as the A. I. boom continues to expand.

The company said it will proceed with its Washington conference in December, which is scheduled the same week Mr. Huang and Tim Teter, the company’s general counsel, are expected to testify in a closed-door briefing with Congress. Mr. Huang is usually the ringmaster at those events. In his absence, other leaders at the company will share the stage for the keynote.

Ms. Kress, who joined the company 13 years ago, closed the nearly hourlong meeting by talking about her love of American football. Her son, who has been a student at the University of Florida, took her to a Gators football game. She marveled at the team’s third quarter tradition. when every fan in the stadium stands up and sings the team’s adopted anthem.

“It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony, singing that song,” she said. “You know what: We’re going to hear that song, and I believe in all of you that you’re going to help sing it.”

She sat back down as employees erupted in applause and the speakers filled with the guitar chords of Tom Petty’s “I Won’t Back Down.”

Tripp Mickle reports for The Times on some of the world’s biggest tech companies, including Nvidia, Google and Apple. He also writes about tech industry trends like layoffs and artificial intelligence.

Trump Arrives in China Focused on Friendship, Not Spy Scandal

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Trump’s Trip to Asia

Advertisement

Supported by

President Xi Jinping of China offered a hug and a red-carpet welcome as President Trump avoided discussing the espionage case that brought down Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.

By Peter Baker

Peter Baker, the chief White House correspondent, is traveling with President Trump in Asia and reported from Shenzhen, China.

President Trump was welcomed to China on Wednesday with a warm embrace both figuratively and literally, as he arrived for a fraught visit shadowed by a major spy scandal that he seemed determined to ignore.

Upon landing in Shenzhen, a bustling technology center, for a series of meetings, Mr. Trump was greeted at the airport by President Xi Jinping of China, who hugged him on a red carpet as a colorfully dressed crowd waved flowers and flags and chanted “warm welcome” in Mandarin.

The visit, however, may have a see-no-evil, hear-no-evil quality because Mr. Trump has said he does not intend to raise the biggest China spy scandal of recent years, one that has upended one of America’s technology giants and pitted members of his own administration against each other. Instead, Mr. Trump prioritized a show of friendship amid the allegations of espionage.

Mr. Trump reveled in the pageantry of the moment as he joined Mr. Xi for a banquet dinner that opened the annual meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, a group of 21 major economies in the region. The two leaders toasted future prosperity and looked forward to meeting separately on Thursday as well as together with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia in a much-anticipated trilateral summit.

Mr. Xi’s decision to personally welcome Mr. Trump at the airport was a rare act by the Chinese leader. He did not do so when Mr. Trump visited Beijing in May. But Mr. Trump made a point of traveling to Joint Base Andrews outside Washington to greet Mr. Xi in September, an uncommon move for an American president and the first time Mr. Trump had done so for a foreign visitor.

So, Mr. Xi returned the gesture on Wednesday. “China is a nation of etiquette with a tradition of reciprocity,” Mr. Xi said, according to Chinese state media.

By contrast, Mr. Xi sent lower-level officials to greet Mr. Putin and other regional leaders arriving for the summit meeting, as is customary.

Still, Mr. Xi met separately with Mr. Putin for more than two hours in advance of the three-way meeting planned for Thursday, and he hailed the Chinese-Russian relationship as “steadfast as a rock through wind and rain.”

The two encounters underscored Mr. Xi’s efforts to balance relations with Russia and the United States. While Russia has become a close partner in recent years and Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin have developed a bond over dozens of meetings, China has a far more extensive and important economic relationship with the United States.

The atmosphere at the summit with other leaders was sometimes tense. Mr. Xi barely offered a smile to Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan, with whom he is in a bitter, yearlong diplomatic spat. Mr. Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada, who have an uneasy relationship as they tussle over trade, had their first in-person meeting of the year. Days earlier, Mr. Carney angered the Trump administration by repeating that he would look elsewhere, including to China, if Mr. Trump did not lift tariffs on Canada’s auto exports.

Left unaddressed was the recent revelation that Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, had an extramarital affair with a business executive who U. S. intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The executive, Alice Huang, who is not related, worked for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center firm and was suspected of gathering intelligence for Beijing.

Mr. Huang resigned under pressure and Mr. Trump’s senior advisers have been squabbling over administration policy on chip exports that could benefit China. The administration announced earlier this week new rules meant to restrict remote access to advanced chips and servers that could help develop Chinese artificial intelligence.

Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, has blamed Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, for resisting restrictions on chip sales. Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick are both accompanying Mr. Trump on his Asia trip, though they were seen standing apart.

The Nvidia scandal has put Mr. Trump on the defensive because of his close relationship with Mr. Huang, who joined the president’s trip to China in May. Mr. Trump has denied being told about the matter, despite reporting by The New York Times that he was informed at least twice, including en route to China in May. He has said he does not know if Ms. Huang was a spy and urged Mr. Huang to fight for his job. Even after Mr. Huang’s resignation, Mr. Trump voiced support for his reinstatement.

This is not the first time Mr. Trump has opted not to confront Mr. Xi with allegations of Chinese interference in the sensitive U. S. matters. In a prime-time address to the nation in July, Mr. Trump accused China of hacking or purchasing U. S. voter rolls, but then said nothing about it publicly when he hosted Mr. Xi for a lavish state visit at the White House in September.

Although Mr. Trump once regularly lashed out at China over its trade practices, he has become more intent over the past year on forging closer ties between the world’s two largest economies. “We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them,” he said before leaving the United States.

Mr. Trump arrived in China after a stop in Manila for the annual meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN. He met with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines, who engaged in some fast-food diplomacy with the American president, who is known for his taste for greasy meals.

Mr. Marcos said that he sent some fried chicken to Mr. Trump at his hotel the night before from Jollibee, a chain that is considered a national treasure in the Philippines. “Since you’re strapped for time, I thought a taste of Manila might be good,” he said. Mr. Trump did not say whether he ate the food.

He did, however, make a point of paying a visit to Mr. Marcos’s mother, Imelda Marcos, 97, the former first lady of the Philippines, who got to know Mr. Trump at New York parties in the 1990s.

“Welcome to the Philippines,” she told Mr. Trump. She handed him a gift and blew him a kiss as he walked away with her son.

“She’s always the most beautiful,” Mr. Trump said.

While Mr. Trump failed to sign a trade deal with Thailand that had been expected to be finalized during his stop in Manila, he announced that he did unexpectedly reach a trade agreement with the Philippines. “We didn’t know that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly and it’s a magnificent deal for both,” he said.

Mr. Marcos’s office later said the deal would cover energy and food security, without providing further details. Mr. Trump said on social media that the deal would benefit American farmers.

There was no such accord between Mr. Trump and Mr. Carney after their tense encounter in Shenzhen later in the day. In a statement, Mr. Carney’s office said that the two leaders “discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement” but offered no further details.

Much attention was focused on Mr. Trump’s meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin on Thursday. The White House said Mr. Trump will also meet separately with Mr. Putin, their first get-together since a much-ballyhooed Alaska summit failed to produce an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.

Mr. Putin arrived in Asia with a show of force. Even as he landed in Shenzhen, Russian strategic nuclear bombers landed in Vietnam. It was the first time that Russian strategic nuclear bombers had deployed to Vietnam since the Soviet era and served as a reminder before the trilateral talks that Moscow remains the world’s largest nuclear power.

Reporting was contributed by Paul Sonne, Ian Austen and Keith Bradsher in Shenzhen; Lily Kuo in Taipei, Taiwan; Leo Sands in London; Aie Balagtas See in Manila; and Francesca Regalado.

Peter Baker is the chief White House correspondent for The Times. He is covering his sixth presidency and sometimes writes analytical pieces that place presidents and their administrations in a larger context and historical framework.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

OpinionJasmine Sun

Credit... Michael Houtz

Supported by

By Jasmine Sun

Ms. Sun writes about A. I. and Silicon Valley for Opinion.

Imagine an artificial intelligence company that is about to launch the biggest I. P. O. in history. Behind it are the sleepless weeks, the training runs full of bugs, the yearslong grind of wooing investors and customers without a product or profit. It will no longer be a scrappy start-up but the consummate envy of Silicon Valley. You might expect relief and celebration, champagne-drenched galas and shiny sports cars rolling into the office parking lot.

On Anthropic’s investor roadshow, there are hints of such jubilance. The Wall Street bankers ushering Anthropic into the public markets hyped a conversation with the chief executive, Dario Amodei, with music by the electronic producer Fred Again and a room adorned with futuristic Anthropic swag. But euphoria is not the mood back at Anthropic headquarters.

In the weeks leading up to the initial public offering, employees of Anthropic — who affectionately call themselves “Ants” — have been preoccupied with concerns about how to slow down A. I. Following a recent spate of rogue agent episodes, the industry has felt doomier than ever.

Even the most ardent techno-optimists have quieted their cheers. Group chats and gatherings instead debate pacing the frontier: how the leading A. I. labs can stop racing and agree to cooperate on the speed of model development, ensuring they have time to make the models safe before releasing them to the world.

For many Ants, the hard part is just beginning. They see recursive self-improvement, in which current A. I. models autonomously build the next generation, looming on the horizon. Because of this potential breakthrough, Anthropic’s co-founder Jack Clark as well as the independent forecasting group A. I. Futures Project have moved up the likely arrival date for superhuman A. I. researchers. They now anticipate it being in 2027.

Once A. I. models can build their successors, they are even more likely to escape human control. Nobody is ready for this future, but nobody is stopping — rather the opposite. Anthropic’s first spending priority with its I. P. O. cash will be buying more compute to reach recursive self-improvement before its rivals do.

I have spoken to dozens of Ants during the past two years, from company founders to young researchers to jaded ex-employees. I have found them surprisingly earnest in their dedication to making A. I. go well. But their concerns are also idiosyncratic and insular, often far removed from the concerns that most people hold about A. I.

They do not view Anthropic as a normal for-profit company. So as the U. S. economy and our personal financial fates become yoked to the Ants, it’s critical that we understand what they believe.

Juxtaposed with what they presume will be the imminent arrival of superintelligence, the upcoming payday seems parochial to many at Anthropic. Some employees describe the I. P. O. with a shrug, likening it to just another funding round.

This is a peculiar attitude for a crowd of young people who, in many cases, are about to become deca- and centimillionaires overnight. The Ants are not your average tech workers. They spend morning to night at rows of desks in the bare, high-security offices in San Francisco’s downtown, where the common books on display include Richard Rhodes’s “The Making of the Atomic Bomb” and paperback printouts of company writings, such as Mr. Amodei’s “Machines of Loving Grace” and the in-house philosopher Amanda Askell’s “Claude’s Constitution.”

No one is compelled to work the grueling “996” hours (9 a. m. to 9 p. m., six days a week) that have become common in the tech industry, but a good number of Ants do so anyway out of their own feverish devotion. Many cram themselves into modest group apartments, host house parties where few, if any, drink and blank when I ask how they spend their lavish salaries, even with my prompts: “A wardrobe update, maybe?” “Ever considered flying business class?”

The money is secondary. The most common form of I. P. O. talk involves discussions of where to allocate the newly liquid stock in their charitable donation accounts.

As a company, Anthropic has been strongly influenced by effective altruism, which holds the belief that the wealthy are obliged to share their fruits with the world. New hires are invited to pledge a percentage of their equity to charity when they start, which Anthropic matches part of. Top targets include charities dedicated to animal welfare, global health and research on A. I. alignment and safety. Many have begun giving big to political campaigns.

As for their own stock, few of the Ants I spoke to planned to sell right after the I. P. O. The notion of an “A. I. bubble” seems not to exist at Anthropic. Employees expect their equity to eventually be worth much, much more.

Anthropic crisply embodies the mind-rending paradox of contemporary A. I. The research scientists who’ve done the most to extend A. I. capabilities are often the most insistent about its risks. Anthropic is the most vocal company when it comes to economic impacts such as mass automation, yet it’s also the leading vendor of the A. I. enterprise agents that threaten to replace white-collar workers.

Such a stance can seem duplicitous and self-serving, both convenient and convoluted. “Our ability to have a positive impact on the world scales in relation to our reach and stature as a successful company,” reads one eye-roll-inducing statement in Anthropic’s I. P. O. prospectus. While the company’s leaders have been candid about the risks, they have been less forthcoming about their solutions. When asked why they should birth what they suspect is an existentially dangerous technology, their answer amounts to, essentially, just trust us because we’re the good guys.

Anthropic is about to become one of the most important companies of the 21st century. If it wants to steward our country, our economy and our lives, Anthropic must do much more to earn the public’s trust. We need a plan for how it will build A. I. safely, and not just reliance on a few people’s judgment calls.

Mr. Amodei seems to hold two convictions very strongly: First, that powerful A. I. might destroy humanity. Second, that our only shot at survival is to create a supremely successful, market-eating technology company to build that A. I. first.

Anthropic used to insist that it was not gunning for first place. In a 2022 podcast, Mr. Amodei said Anthropic “shouldn’t be racing ahead or trying to build models that are way bigger than other orgs.” He suggested instead that the company would do safety research as a fast-follower of A. I. development. The company intended to study the technology without pushing capabilities ahead, some investors said he told them at the time.

In the summer of 2022, Anthropic decided not to make Claude, its A. I. chatbot, available to the public over internal concerns about safety. This allowed OpenAI — which had gotten wind of Anthropic’s internal prototype — to design a similar product, rush ChatGPT out the door first and gain a decisive lead in consumer mindshare.

In Anthropic company lore, this saga is put on a pedestal as an example of choosing principle over profit. Yet it may have also been a strategic wake-up call for Mr. Amodei, who called the sacrifice a “one-off.” Increasingly, Mr. Amodei seemed to see how being the leader in the A. I. race conferred compounding benefits in terms of revenue, recruiting, fund-raising and developing the next-generation A. I. models. Once commercial A. I. products had been introduced, Mr. Amodei seemed unwilling to settle for second place.

Anthropic is certainly very good at racing. Although it spent its toddler years scrambling to replicate OpenAI’s language and reasoning models, Anthropic has since led the charge on coding agents.

It is not an exaggeration to say that Claude Code reinvented the discipline of software engineering. Where programmers used to write lines of code by hand, many now use plain English to command fleets of A. I. agents. Since the release of Claude Code, Anthropic’s quarterly revenue has surpassed OpenAI’s, surging to $17 billion in the third quarter of 2026. Today, more than half of the Fortune 500 are Anthropic’s six-figure customers.

With this kind of success, Mr. Amodei has updated his theory of change — he calls it a “race to the top.” Only by building the most advanced A. I. systems can Anthropic influence the whole industry in a safer direction, he argues. Three underlying assumptions are baked into this strategy.

First, Anthropic assumes the A. I. race itself is inevitable, so no single actor can stop superintelligence from being built. The financial rewards for building a machine that can match or exceed humans’ cognitive abilities are so great that someone is guaranteed to pursue it. If not Mr. Amodei and his team, then Sam Altman, or Mark Zuckerberg or Elon Musk.

Second, Anthropic assumes it is the most responsible of A. I.’s possible stewards. In public and internally, Mr. Amodei likes to invoke OpenAI and the Chinese government as competitive boogeymen. These are viewed as actors that are pushing just as hard as Anthropic on building and commercializing powerful A. I. models, but that would be far less responsible — reckless at best, and authoritarian at worst. Looking at the recent evidence, the most severe rogue agent hacks have indeed come out of OpenAI. And if you think Claude is the A. I. with the best moral values, then expanding Claude’s market share could be construed as a virtue in itself.

Third, Anthropic assumes the “winner” of A. I. will gain tremendous influence over the A. I. ecosystem and the U. S. government. Through commercial success, Anthropic aims to show the industry that being safety-minded can be good for business, good for science and good for attracting top talent.

Some Anthropic staffers point to initiatives like embedding A. I. safety auditors with the company’s engineering teams — a decision that has inspired competitors to make similar commitments. Additionally, the company has said it will use its commercial strength to advocate A. I. regulation, as it did in the fight for California’s S. B. 53, which increased transparency requirements for leading A. I. companies.

Anthropic’s race-to-the-top argument sounds positive-sum, but its worldview also contains a dose of realpolitik. In the future, it may use access to frontier A. I. systems as hard leverage in deals. “Dario talks about how Anthropic might become more powerful than the government, and needs to have its own relationship with nation-states,” said one former employee, who remained anonymous in order to discuss internal deliberations.

One former Ant referenced J. R. R. Tolkien’s parable in trying to explain Anthropic’s mind-set: Whomever builds superintelligence first will get Sauron’s ring. That person or company will possess the most dangerous cyberweapons in the world, the cures and recipes for every disease, and an army of tireless digital geniuses to do its bidding. The most load-bearing question, then, is the morality of the one who wields the ring. (Of course, in Middle Earth, the Ring was destroyed because even the purest soul couldn’t make it safe.)

And why is Anthropic confident that its own power won’t corrupt? The company prides itself on costly signals: making choices that trade off against short-term profits, whether prohibiting Chinese entities from buying its products; placing 5 percent of its shares into a “Public Benefit Fund” to spend on “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations” of its choice; or refusing to permit the Department of Defense to use Claude for domestic mass surveillance, an act that infuriated the Trump administration and briefly got Anthropic marked as a supply-chain risk last winter.

Another former Anthropic employee explained how Mr. Amodei often justified controversial decisions, such as taking investments from Persian Gulf countries. This money, like most of the investment flowing into Anthropic, would be used to fund its sprint. The former Ant recalled Mr. Amodei saying that his goal was not to be popular with average Americans, but to do the right thing.

Anthropic has warned investors that these decisions may get more costly over time. As it details in its I. P. O. prospectus: “Our product and investment decisions may not prioritize short-term financial results,” and this “could adversely affect the market price” of the company’s stock.

The company wants to preserve the option to pivot from maximizing shareholder value to A. I. slowdowns once it assesses that the risks are too great — a strategy sometimes called “burning a lead.” Most former employees whom I spoke to believed that Mr. Amodei was deeply principled and would be willing to make sacrifices for safety. But they also acknowledged that rapid growth, and the economic momentum that propels it, can outrun even the most conscientious of founders.

Anthropic is known for its committed esprit de corps, which the S-1 Securities and Exchange Commission registration form lists as a core competitive advantage. Good Ants are dutiful, self-scrutinizing and total believers in A. I.’s world-historic importance. One notorious interview question asks employment candidates how they’d feel about working at Anthropic if their stock went to zero as a result of safety slowdowns. Research teams will happily reject technical superstars if they lack culture fit.

In internal debates, early employees act as informal ethos-enforcers, questioning whether their colleagues’ decisions are sufficiently “aligned.” It’s a company of loyalists: Both leaks and departures have been rare. Arguably, this focus has paid off. Anthropic has progressed quickly on automated coding while OpenAI, whose culture is understood to resemble a bunch of battling fiefs, was distracted by drama and side quests.

Even before the I. P. O., Anthropic has been showing signs of widening organizational fracture: It’s starting to behave like a normal company, and not everyone likes it. Some Ants fumed at the company’s Washington lobbyists for shopping a draft bill that would pre-empt state legislation on A. I. and limit the government’s ability to block model releases. Mr. Amodei mounted a public defense with a long post on X, and, in another X post, the policy team promised revisions.

Early employees mutter about cultural dilution. They question whether some of the more recently hired Ants, many of whom do regular corporate jobs, such as sales and marketing, are adequately “A. G. I.-pilled.” Do they really believe in superintelligence, or are they just trying to get rich?

Some anxious Ants have begun asking whether Anthropic should stop training better frontier models now, even if it can’t guarantee that competitors like OpenAI will do the same. This suggestion was shut down by Mr. Amodei, who urged staff members to stop listening to outside activists and explained that the company could pace itself without shooting itself in the foot. It was all part of the same strategy: Anthropic must keep winning to keep the world safe, and even if it stops, its competitors will not.

Still, grumbles from the staff reflect a growing tension between safety and growth — one that could be exacerbated by the fiduciary responsibilities of being a public company. Once Anthropic’s shares arrive in Americans’ retirement portfolios, will this new constituency really let it slow down? Will the company permit itself? Will the government? And does the company’s impact on people’s pocketbooks factor into its public-minded mission?

Anthropic hopes its public benefit corporation status will protect it against normal company incentives. Under its five-tier stock structure, the founders, employees and trustees can elect board members, while traditional investors have a limited role. The company is also trying to secure a congressional antitrust exemption so that it can coordinate a slowdown with the other American A. I. labs.

I do not doubt these good intentions. But time after time, the idealistic hopes of A. I. leaders — for instance, Anthropic’s early aim to do safety from second place, or OpenAI’s original nonprofit board — have looked naïve once faced with market realities.

There is one more big open question in the A. I. safety community: Is it technically possible to verify whether an A. I. model is aligned enough to release? This is the crux of the disagreement between Anthropic and many of its A. I. safety critics. Anthropic thinks it will be able to ship safe-enough models with careful evaluation and procedural safeguards. Skeptics see this endeavor as futile, pointing to examples of Claude only pretending to follow its instructions, or agents that have knowingly cheated and hacked during internal tests.

There is a parallel to be drawn here: We don’t have the science to determine whether an A. I. model is obedient or merely feigning compliance. At the same time, we don’t know whether a C. E. O. is altruistic and mission-driven or performative and power-hungry. But we can observe, from the history of rogue A. I. s and rogue executives, that competitive situations drive unethical behavior.

We also know that both A. I. s and founders are rewarded for extreme levels of persistence and hubris. Once committed to a mission — even a supremely risky one like building an aligned superintelligence — they will do anything but concede.

Anthropic doesn’t view A. I. as a normal technology, and it doesn’t see itself as a normal company either. Here, I tried to pull back the curtain on its idiosyncratic culture and mission. Does reading about the company’s perspective make you trust it more or less?

Jasmine Sun writes about A. I. and Silicon Valley for Opinion and the editorial board.

How Kennedy Upended a Group Guiding Health Care for All Americans

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Fifteen former members and federal employees told The Times that, over two years, the administration blocked their work and ended the U. S. Preventive Services Task Force’s scientific independence.

By Maggie Astor

Dr. Roger D. Klein wanted to know why artificial intelligence couldn’t guide Americans’ medical screenings.

It was early 2026, and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. hadn’t let the 16-member United States Preventive Services Task Force meet in almost a year. Its recommendations, which inform everything from mammograms to prostate cancer screening for 340 million Americans, had ground to a halt.

Now Dr. Klein — a molecular pathologist and lawyer appointed by the Trump administration to lead the task force’s parent agency, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality — was suggesting jettisoning the research centers that systematically reviewed the evidence on which the task force based its decisions.

His assistant could do that with A. I., he said, according to two officials who heard him, including Tess Miller, then the agency’s acting scientific director for the task force.

The task force, normally composed of experts in primary care and research, was established in 1984 to evaluate preventive services: tools to prevent or diagnose disease early in asymptomatic people. Its work isn’t visible to most Americans, but its influence is vast; clinicians follow it, and most insurers must cover what it recommends. When people receive a colonoscopy at no cost, it’s because of the task force. When doctors screen for hypertension during pregnancy or offer medication to help a smoker quit, task force guidance informs them.

The task force typically meets in person three times a year and can publish around a dozen recommendations. But for nearly a year and a half, it has been unable to make any new recommendations or update existing ones. Guidelines on at least 18 topics, including cardiovascular disease, H. I. V. screening, food allergies and more, have stalled, leaving clinicians and patients without up-to-date information.

Fifteen former task force members and agency employees, some of whom spoke on the condition that they not be named to avoid retaliation, described dysfunction and political interference, particularly after a June 2025 Supreme Court ruling gave Mr. Kennedy more control over the panel. Courtney Spencer, a spokeswoman for the Department of Health and Human Services, said work had been suspended until the department “understood how best to move forward” in response to the ruling.

A former agency employee recalled telling a medical journal repeatedly to delay publication of a recommendation on cervical cancer screening, because political appointees weren’t signing off despite repeated requests. Former members and employees described how, in a departure from the task force’s decades of scientific independence, Dr. Klein called for changes to drafts, including cutting references to race. On one occasion, two said, he described evidence-based medicine as “socialized medicine.”

After preventing the task force from meeting in person since March 2025, Mr. Kennedy revived it this September by appointing eight new members. All 16 are scheduled to convene on Thursday.

But the panel and the agency that supports it are profoundly changed, and public health experts fear the lost time will reverberate.

“No one will be able to point to a single moment or a single unique decision and say, ‘That’s when it went wrong,’” said Karina Davidson, a former chair of the task force. “It’s going to show up years from now in our public health surveillance, in later-stage diagnoses, in missed interventions, in preventable deaths that didn’t have to happen. And by then, it will be too late to undo.”

The first signs of conflict came almost immediately after Mr. Trump’s second inauguration, when he issued executive orders targeting diversity, equity and inclusion and transgender rights, and some federal agencies forbade or discouraged phrases like “transgender,” “Black” and “men who have sex with men” — language important for describing how medical findings and risk differ among groups.

Task force members began to discuss whether they could achieve the same public-health goals with different words, and revised a recommendation on intimate partner violence.

But the turning point, former members and agency employees said, was in June 2025, when the Supreme Court affirmed that Mr. Kennedy could replace task force members before their terms ended and overrule recommendations.

The administration interpreted its new authority broadly.

Agency employees were told that a political appointee had to approve all public task force actions, including posting documents for public comment and publishing recommendations, said Dr. Justin Mills, who was a medical officer supporting the task force; Dr. Miller; and several other former employees.

Research plans, drafts and final recommendations all had to be reviewed, they said — and the reviewers never signed off.

The task force met in March 2025 and issued five recommendations in the first half of that year, with the last one published in June. It hasn’t met or published guidelines since.

Dr. Klein, appointed in June 2025, didn’t reply to task force leaders’ emails and rarely responded to agency employees, even as they pressed him to clear the growing backlog of documents and actions needing approval, said Dr. Michael Silverstein, then the task force’s chair; Dr. Miller; and several others.

But occasionally, Dr. Klein broke his silence.

He called a draft recommendation on preventing alcohol abuse “worthless,” Dr. Miller said, and asked for removal of mentions of race from other documents, Dr. Mills and another employee recalled.

In a response to a draft about risk assessment for cancers related to BRCA genes, which Dr. Silverstein shared with The New York Times, Dr. Klein disputed the task force’s conclusions. Among other things, he seemed to conflate genetic testing guidelines for people with breast cancer and without it.

He also challenged pieces of the task force’s methodology, in comments that Dr. Silverstein said showed “no understanding of how the task force assesses both the benefits and the harms of preventive services.”

How we choose health experts to talk to. Times reporters often spend weeks interviewing doctors, researchers and other health professionals to help report an article. We seek leaders in their fields, watch out for conflicts of interest and try to get a variety of viewpoints.

Ms. Spencer, the H. H. S. spokeswoman, said Dr. Klein didn’t recall the alcohol conversation “as described” but had believed resources might be better spent on other topics. On race, she said he had wanted “precise descriptions of patient populations and the clinical relevance of the findings.” On BRCA-related cancers, she reiterated what Dr. Klein had written. She also said “secretarial oversight of task force recommendations predates this administration.”

But Dr. Silverstein, Dr. Mills and several other former task force members and agency employees said that before 2025, interference from political appointees was unheard-of. Oversight did not involve editing or objecting to conclusions, they said.

“There was a thick firewall, and a high premium was placed on the independence of the task force members,” said Dr. Elisabeth Kato, who worked at the agency for more than 15 years, including a stint as acting associate scientific director for the task force.

In July 2025, The Wall Street Journal reported that Mr. Kennedy might purge the task force, and an in-person meeting was canceled — the first of four consecutive cancellations.

With those developments, it “became very clear to us what it meant to conduct scientifically rigorous work under threat of being fired,” Dr. Silverstein said. “What if we found something in the data, or what if we interpreted the data in a way that made the administration angry?”

Task force members continued to meet virtually to review evidence and develop recommendations. They wrote their annual report to Congress, said Dr. Silverstein and Dr. Esa Davis, who was a vice chair, outlining topics that could use more research funding; this edition was focused on women’s and children’s health.

But they couldn’t vote, publish anything or send the report without in-person meetings or approval. Among the stalled items were the guidelines on cervical cancer screening, endorsing a new self-collection option; another agency later released similar guidance, but the task force still hasn’t.

“We had to keep saying, ‘Maybe now, maybe now, maybe now,’” said Dr. Miller, who was in touch with the journal’s editors. “We moved it I don’t know how many times.”

There was growing anguish, members said, at being unable to publish information with concrete implications for people’s health.

“It was clearer and clearer that we weren’t going to be able to get the work done at some point,” said Dr. David Chelmow, a former member. “There was going to be a tipping point.”

The agency supporting the task force lost employees as Elon Musk’s DOGE sliced through the government, and more as dysfunction led people to resign in frustration. The task force division’s medical officers, who had reviewed evidence, sifted through public comments, written drafts of recommendations and more, are all gone.

John M. Ruiz, a former member, and several others said the panel, whose members are part-time volunteers, couldn’t function without them.

By late March 2026, the panel had gone from 16 members to 10 as terms expired and no appointments were made.

In May, the two remaining leaders — Dr. John Wong and Dr. Davis — were invited to meet with Dr. Klein for the first time. They thought it was finally a chance to discuss the task force’s needs.

Instead, they found Dr. Klein with an H. H. S. lawyer, who fired them.

Normally, the scientific director for the task force — a nonpolitical employee at the parent agency — vetted applicants with the task force chairs, four people previously involved in selection said. The agency director made final calls but generally respected the scientific director’s and chairs’ judgments.

Now, Dr. Klein and other political appointees led the process.

A Federal Register notice said nomination and application materials would be publicly accessible, but agency officials denied access to a Times reporter. Through a lawsuit, The Times obtained the names of 247 nominees and 40 who received interviews.

Dr. Alex Krist, a former chair; Dr. Quyen Ngo-Metzger, a former scientific director; and Dr. Silverstein reviewed the list of interviewees for The Times and said it included some strong candidates, but that Mr. Kennedy’s appointees didn’t meet the usual standards of primary care and research expertise.

Most of them are specialists; only two are primary care experts, and they don’t have the level of experience with systematic research that was typical for past members. The new chair, Dr. Seth J. Corey, is a pediatric hematologist-oncologist whose publications show minimal experience with systematic evidence reviews.

“Hard to see how his expertise fits here at all,” Dr. Ngo-Metzger said.

Through the H. H. S. press office, Dr. Klein said the appointees “were chosen for expertise, experience and diversity of settings and geography.” He said Dr. Corey’s master’s degree in public health gave him “advanced formal education in evidence analysis and evaluation as well as epidemiology,” and that he had done extensive medical research and reviewed manuscripts for journals. (Dr. Corey did not respond to requests for comment.)

Several appointees also have broad financial conflicts that former leaders said would previously have been disqualifying.

While H. H. S. said it would have a process to require recusal from individual topics, it hasn’t been made public. New members are set to begin assessing topics Thursday.

Among those interviewed but rejected were Dr. Davis and Dr. Wong, whose termination letters from Mr. Kennedy had encouraged them to reapply for membership.

In Dr. Wong’s interview, he said, Dr. Klein pressed him to defend the concept of evidence-based medicine, describing it as “socialized medicine” to control costs. Dr. Mills, the former medical officer, was present and confirmed Dr. Wong’s description.

“Dr. Klein does not believe evidence-based medicine is socialized medicine,” Ms. Spencer said. “His point concerned how the rigid application of evidence-based medicine techniques, which are often biased against taking action, were early on embraced by socialized systems.”

Thursday’s meeting will provide the first indications of how the new panel will operate, under substantial scrutiny. Last week, seven former task force chairs urged congressional committees to subpoena Mr. Kennedy and Dr. Klein. Senator Angus King, a Maine independent aligned with Democrats, and Representative Maxine Dexter, an Oregon Democrat, have proposed legislation to codify some previous membership criteria, as well as the panel’s independence.

Another challenge looms.

Three members are scheduled to leave at the end of the year. Normally, replacements would be named months in advance. So far, none have been.

Dani Blum contributed reporting.

I’ve been reporting on the U. S. Preventive Services Task Force since last summer. Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other political appointees have undermined the panel by canceling meetings, requiring political approval of documents and not replacing members whose terms ended. I’ll keep reporting as the task force resumes its work with new members appointed by Kennedy. What questions do you want answered?

Maggie Astor covers women’s health and the health effects of government policies for The Times.

The Shadow of Yalta Hangs Over Trump’s Summit in China

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Trump’s Trip to Asia

Advertisement

Supported by

A 1945 meeting of Churchill, Stalin and Franklin Roosevelt set Europe’s course for decades. Here’s what happened.

By Leo Sands

As the Second World War neared an end, the soon-to-be victors — Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union, Winston Churchill of Britain and President Franklin D. Roosevelt — sat down in the Crimean resort of Yalta to discuss the fate of postwar Europe. Their decisions in February 1945 helped shape the global order for the rest of the 20th century, making Yalta synonymous with an era of great-power bargaining by outsize personalities.

On Thursday, the leaders of the world’s three largest military powers will meet again. This time it will be President Xi Jinping of China, whose nation has supplanted Britain in military might, hosting President Trump and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

The trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China — at an uncertain geopolitical moment dogged by wars, climate change and the rise of artificial intelligence — has prompted some analysts to label it “Yalta 2.0.”

That parallel has limits, historians say. For one, Yalta was a meeting of allies whose broad objectives overlapped, said Catherine Grace Katz, a historian of 20th century geopolitics and author of a book on that summit. “Or at least ostensibly still allies at the time,” she said.

By February 1945, the three Allied powers were united in their fight against Hitler’s Germany, whose defeat by then seemed inevitable. British and American troops had already stormed through France and Belgium, while the Soviet war machine was steamrolling across Eastern Europe, squeezing Germany from both flanks.

At Yalta, the allies agreed on what the Northern Hemisphere would look like after the dust of war settled.

Stalin agreed to join the fight against Japan in return for territory in the Northern Pacific. Roosevelt — by then frail, two months from his death and focused on ensuring Japan’s surrender — offered the Soviets broad leeway over Poland’s future. That set the stage for decades of Soviet domination over Eastern Europe.

David Reynolds, a professor of history at the University of Cambridge who specializes in 20th-century diplomacy, argued against overstating what was decided at Yalta.

“‘Yalta’ is a notorious word” that to many conjures the carving up of Europe and selling out to Stalin — but that is somewhat oversimplified, he said, adding: “The fate of postwar Europe was decided on the battlefield, not at the conference table.”

By the time of the February conference, the Red Army was on the verge of taking Berlin, and both Roosevelt and Churchill had privately conceded the inevitability of Soviet domination of Eastern Europe, Professor Reynolds said.

Ms. Katz said, “Short of physically pushing them out of Poland, there was not a lot that the West could do.”

She also pointed out that it was a year earlier, at a meeting in Moscow, when Churchill and Stalin scribbled out their secret “percentages” agreement on a piece of paper. That led to Europe being split between Western and Communist blocs, a division that eventually became the Iron Curtain and persisted until the end of the Cold War.

It was better to see Yalta not as the single moment when “the world was carved up into these spheres of influence,” she said, but rather as the culmination of battlefield events and other wartime talks.

That said, she argued, Roosevelt missed opportunities to press for greater concessions from Stalin at Yalta. The president took Stalin at his word when he insisted Poland's leaders couldn’t attend the conference, she said, and dismissed Churchill for being overly concerned with Poland’s future.

“Roosevelt was woefully unprepared in dealing with Stalin and understanding Russian history and Stalin’s true objectives when it came to Poland,” Ms. Katz said. (Successive U. S. administrations would similarly underestimate Moscow’s commitment to maintaining sway over Eastern Europe, culminating in Mr. Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.)

Professor Reynolds said that several other critical negotiations were also hammered out at Yalta, which is often forgotten.

It was the scene of hard-fought bargaining by Churchill to secure protections to stop Germany from being eviscerated under a future surrender, as Stalin had wanted, he said. Churchill was adamant that Europe needed to avert a disastrous repeat of the Treaty of Versailles at the end of the First World War, the terms of which were so punitive on Germany that many believe it planted the seeds of World War II.

“It is not the purpose of the Allies to destroy the people of Germany, or leave them without the necessary means of subsistence,” Churchill told British lawmakers in February 1945, after he had returned to London from Yalta. “Our policy is not revenge; it is to take such measures as may be necessary to secure the future peace and safety of the world.”

Roosevelt also used the Yalta conference to advance his blueprint for a new multilateral institution that would try to resolve conflicts through deliberation rather than war: the United Nations. It was formally established nine months later.

In other words, the suggestion that Yalta was synonymous with Europe’s “carve-up” by great powers flattens the history of the war’s final years, Professor Reynolds argued. “These historical events have a memory life, and all the other aspects that don’t fit within the memory narrative get forgotten,” he said.

Leo Sands is a correspondent for the Breaking News Hub of The New York Times based in London.

Anthropic Is Set to Finalize Pricing for Blockbuster I. P. O.

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

The A. I. company is expected to officially price its shares on Wednesday, and its stock will begin trading on Thursday.

By Erin Griffith and Lauren Hirsch

Erin Griffith reported from San Francisco and Lauren Hirsch from New York.

Anthropic on Wednesday is expected to finalize the pricing for its initial public offering, potentially defying a volatile and anxious stock market with robust investor demand for artificial intelligence companies and setting a milestone for the A. I. industry.

The San Francisco-based A. I. company, which makes the Claude chatbot, had set a preliminary price range of $70 to $78 a share. But it has seen strong investor interest, and is likely to set a final price on the high end of that range, if not higher, two people familiar with the company’s offering said.

At $70 to $78 a share, Anthropic would be worth $1.26 trillion to $1.41 trillion, when all shares are counted. That would mean the company’s offering would be second in size only to Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which in June raised $85.7 billion at a $1.77 trillion valuation in its public listing.

Anthropic’s shares will begin trading on Thursday on Nasdaq under the symbol ANT.

The listing comes amid a moment of growing market nervousness. Investors have been fearing that the A. I. boom, which has been fueled by debt, may suddenly deflate. With the midterm elections changing the makeup of Congress, the potential for regulations to slow down A. I. development, including data centers, has increased.

The pricing is expected to be finalized on Wednesday evening. Here’s what to know while you wait.

Anthropic’s offering is the first time that public market investors will have the chance to invest in one of the A. I. industry’s “frontier labs,” which are developing the core models underlying the boom. The company’s offering prospectus showed a fast-growing business alongside a narrative of future growth and abundance, including curing diseases and expanding economic prosperity. Revenue soared to $33 billion in the first nine months of the year from $41 million in 2023.

The company has had an astonishing rise in just five years. Founded in 2021 by a group of former OpenAI employees, Anthropic and its Claude chatbot were a somewhat obscure second place player to OpenAI’s ChatGPT. But Anthropic’s focus on business tools, including Claude Code, which automates software development, became increasingly popular over the last year.

Anthropic is going public partly because building A. I. requires so much money to pay for computer chips, data processing power and electricity. The company has issued convertible debt to fund some of the infrastructure needed to support its business, like chips, computing power and data centers. This debt, which turns into equity in the future, is counted as a loss on Anthropic’s books, resulting in a net loss of $104 billion in the first nine months of the year.

The public offering is set to the backdrop of turmoil at A. I, chipmaker Nvidia, after the ouster last week of the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang. On Tuesday, Nvidia reported that its sales topped $100 billion for the first time in the third quarter, twice as much as a year earlier, showing that its business is robust. The company indicated Mr. Huang was not welcome back — even as the former chief executive issued a statement saying he would welcome a return. Read more about Mr. Huang’s downfall here.

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, has for years exasperated his peers with warnings about extreme risks of A. I., even as his company has built some of the most powerful A. I. systems in the world. Frustration has turned to hostility as Anthropic leaped into the lead in A. I. development, experienced stunning revenue growth and moved toward what is likely to be one of the largest initial public offerings ever. Read more about the knives out for Anthropic here.

Erin Griffith covers tech companies, start-ups and the culture of Silicon Valley from San Francisco.

Lauren Hirsch is a Times reporter who covers deals and dealmakers in Wall Street and Washington.
