Jeff Bezos Said Drone Delivery ‘Will Happen.’ This Town Said, Not Here.

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Amazon wants to offer faster delivery. Residents want quiet skies. A Massachusetts suburb wages an epic battle for control of its airspace.

By Juliet Macur

Photographs by Sophie Park

Juliet Macur reported from Westborough, Mass., and watched more than a dozen hours of public meetings about the issue of drone deliveries in the town.

In a font that begged for a magnifying glass, right below the newspaper’s classified ads, there it was: Notice of Public Hearing.

Christine Farmer, a longtime resident of Westborough, Mass., normally skipped over legal notices in the weekly Community Advocate. But this time, she caught it by chance — a public hearing in mid-September on Amazon’s request to build a drone hub for its new delivery service. The project, which involved a staging area and launch zones, would be based at the company’s warehouse less than two miles from Ms. Farmer’s home.

It was the first time Ms. Farmer, a 63-year-old executive coach and business consultant, had heard about plans for drone deliveries in the region.

Like many of her neighbors in Westborough, Ms. Farmer loved Amazon. A few months earlier, she had nearly hugged an Amazon driver to thank him for bringing her a package — by electric van — that she needed that same day.

But the drone deliveries felt startling and unnecessary, she thought — an existential change.

Were delivery drones really something Westborough needed, zipping over its ponds and parks, hiking trails and tall, tall trees?

Ms. Farmer’s decision to attend the meeting eventually led her to a place she never expected to be: in the thick of a growing rebellion against Amazon and its plans for drone delivery dominance across America.

In 2013, Amazon introduced the concept of widespread drone delivery as if it was a fait accompli, with its founder, Jeff Bezos, saying that it “will work, and it will happen.” The reason for it was simple, the company has said: customers demand ever faster service.

Amazon now has 20 drone hubs, and in August, and the company said that it aimed to expand drone deliveries to nearly 500 U. S. towns and cities, including more than 60 hubs, by the end of the year. Some local governments have readily approved the company’s plans.

“As residents learn more about it and see it for themselves, Prime Air is a welcome addition to communities,” said Lindsay Hamilton, an Amazon spokeswoman, adding that the drone program reduces traffic on the road and brings highly skilled jobs.

But some residents, like Ms. Farmer, are dreading an influx of 83-pound flying machines that seem straight out of “The Jetsons.” Zooming across the sky at up to 74 miles an hour, they look to some residents like colossal interplanetary insects and sound like a supersized swarm of locusts.

Opponents of the drones are fuming at the Federal Aviation Administration for ruling that commercial delivery drones would not significantly affect “the human environment” and that each location did not need a full environmental review. (The F. A. A. declined to comment.) And they are furious with local authorities for not doing more to push back against the impending changes to the sights and sounds of everyday life.

If Amazon drones come, Ms. Farmer asked, what would stop Walmart drones from following? Or DoorDash? Target? Home Depot?

“We will be living under a drone highway, and who would want that?” said Ms. Farmer, who raised two daughters in Westborough, a town of about 23,000 people, 30 miles west of Boston.

She continued, “I really just can’t imagine living in a world where the skies just aren’t quiet anymore.”

Before the Westborough planning board meeting in mid-September, Ms. Farmer went out of her way to say a prayer at her church. She asked for guidance because she considered the drone issue to be “a tipping point for our country.”

At the board meeting, she found only a handful of other residents, mostly there for other, more quotidian issues. They seemed surprised, Ms. Farmer thought, when Tareq Wafaie, an economic development manager for Amazon, delivered a presentation about Amazon’s Prime Air program. It would be the first drone delivery service in New England.

Mr. Wafaie explained that the drones are about five feet wide and five feet tall, have six arms with propellers, and can carry a single package that is five pounds or less. Customers opting in can get deliveries in 30 minutes or less, he said, with the drones dropping packages onto people’s yards or driveways from 13 feet up, without humans guiding them in real time.

The F. A. A., which governs the nation’s airspace, had cleared Amazon’s drone hub for up to 1,000 flights per day, from “about sunrise to sunset,” Mr. Wafaie said, and the drones can fly as far as 7.5 miles before circling back to their home base.

Ms. Farmer grabbed her phone and started calculating: If there were, say, 600 drone deliveries in 12 hours, that would mean almost one delivery every minute.

Several residents seemed to be thinking along similar lines. “The risk does not match the want,” Jen Parent, a teacher, told the board. “We’re at this point in our human history with technology, just because we can do it, doesn’t mean we should do it.”

One man said he couldn’t imagine the drones being quiet. Another said that drones were “cool,” but worried about privacy because their cameras could peer into yards.

A nervous Ms. Farmer fumbled with the microphone before taking it off its stand.

In a voice gentle enough to read bedtime stories, she explained that she had grown up in Winthrop, a town near Boston’s Logan Airport. Every day, all day long, she heard planes overhead.

“I just want to advise and really just say, you open the door to this and more will come,” she said to the planning board. “I implore that you continue to consider the sounds and the visuals. I love to walk. We love the nature.”

She added, “That’s why I moved here.”

The planning board postponed its decision. When Ms. Farmer got home, she told her husband, “Honey, this is not our wheelhouse. But we can’t stay silent.”

Steeped in the issue for what she called “a whole 30 seconds,” Ms. Farmer began posting about the drones on social media, to tell her neighbors.

At a Sept. 22 meeting of the select board, the town’s policymaking body, the public was allowed to speak about the issue and Ms. Farmer got up — twice — to oppose Amazon’s plan.

Once Amazon begins its service, “there’s no turning back,” she warned, citing communities in Louisiana, Michigan, Nebraska and Texas, where residents say they feel trapped after their cities approved Amazon’s plans.

The next day, Amazon held an informational session at a local hotel. Ms. Farmer sat in a corner to listen to other residents speak, amazed that a coalition against the drones had grown so quickly.

More than 200 people squeezed into the room, including residents from nearby towns that would be affected.

For nearly three hours, Mr. Wafaie, of Amazon, took questions from the crowd, saying that the drones were safe, popular and unobtrusive. He said the operation would start with about six of them (a decrease from the 10 to 12 he had discussed with the town in mid-August).

“We do hear a lot of feedback from our customers that we’re not fast enough, so that is the exact problem we’re trying to solve,” said Mr. Wafaie, who did not return an emailed request for comment. “Our customers are demanding this service.”

A lot of those, he added, are “single mothers who need diapers because they’re home with a sick child, and they can’t go out.”

The crowd groaned.

When Mr. Wafaie compared the drone noise to the sound made by someone holding an electric toothbrush, a high-pitched buzz filled the room. Someone had brought an electric toothbrush, and held it up. “That’s annoying!” said one woman.

“All day long, horrible!” another said.

For a second, Ms. Farmer laughed. Having watched many video posts of Amazon drones flying, she felt that the toothbrush came nowhere close to how loud they were.

Ms. Farmer has been sensitive to noise since sustaining a head injury in a car crash nearly a decade ago. When her neighbors mow their lawns or clear leaves with a blower, she has to run to the other side of her house. But at least those sounds fade quickly, she told herself. The drones would be relentless.

No one in the crowd spoke in favor of the drones. Instead, residents badgered Mr. Wafaie about safety, privacy and home values. Would Amazon fly more drones and bigger ones? Could residents stop this program if they didn’t like it?

Several times, he said that they would not like his answer.

Amazon backing out of a drone hub wherever people don’t want it, he said, “would probably not happen.”

“We have a program that we are scaling,” he added.

Dan Kline, a Westborough resident, said in an interview that he assumed the company would have that stance. Scaling business, he said, is “what Amazon does.”

“There’s an air of arrogance that, ‘We’re Amazon and we’re going to this no matter what anyone says, or no matter what anyone wants,” he said. “But this is our town, not Amazon’s.”

The day after that informational session, Ms. Farmer and one of her old Westborough friends, Rod Jané, talked on the phone, in a panic.

It turned out that even before that first public meeting that Ms. Farmer attended in September, Amazon had already received a key ruling from the town.

Westborough’s building commissioner, William Hezlitt, had decided that Amazon’s proposed drone hub — which would replace parking spaces at their distribution center — was allowed by law, because it was an “accessory to the primary use,” as innocuous as, say, adding a carport to a home.

Mr. Hezlitt did not return a request for comment.

Mr. Jané, who works in economic and real estate development, and Ms. Farmer thought Mr. Hezlitt’s designation made no sense because the drone technology was wholly new. They thought Amazon should be required to obtain a special permit to use its property to fly drones. That would force the company to make a case for its drone hub, and the public would have a say.

They decided to contest the decision. By law, they had 30 days to appeal it. And they were on Day 29.

With the town hall closing at noon the next day, Mr. Jané and Ms. Farmer shifted into hyper speed. From their desks across town from each other, they began typing up and tweaking drafts of an appeal, sharing them by email.

By 5:30 a. m., they had an almost final version. They thought it would be smart to show that other residents supported it, so at 7 a. m., Ms. Farmer left home with a copy of the document and began flagging down people — in their cars, after morning Mass, on the street, jogging — to gather signatures. Twenty-five people signed.

Just after 10 a. m., she and Mr. Jané met outside of the town hall and walked together to the town clerk’s office, meeting their deadline with time to spare. “We did it,” he exclaimed, and both let out a long exhale.

The appeal hearing was scheduled for November, and Amazon’s project would be on hold until then. Other opposition was also gathering. With hundreds of residents now rebelling — many involved with Mass Blue Skies, a nonprofit started by Ms. Farmer and Mr. Jané and about 10 others — the town of Westborough made its own move to stop Amazon’s plans.

Some residents, including Mr. Jané, helped the town draft a bylaw that would restrict ground operations of any unmanned aircraft, “to protect the health, safety, privacy, peace, quiet enjoyment, property rights, and general welfare” of residents. It would bar drone launchpads, staging points and drop zones.

In October, more than 500 people packed the high school auditorium to vote on the bylaw.

There was a retired mechanic in his 70s. A homemaker in her 30s. Tech workers and cashiers. Longtime residents living in houses from the 1800s, and new neighbors in apartment buildings.

In interviews at the meeting, nearly two dozen people said that the vote meant more than just trying to stop Amazon.

The residents said their votes stood for quiet weekend mornings hiking the Charm Bracelet trails that encircle the town. And peaceful afternoons sipping tea on their neighbor’s picnic table. And lolling in the privacy of their backyard, maybe even sunbathing nude.

The bylaw passed, 510-13.

As residents left the high school, Ms. Farmer had tears in her eyes as she grabbed people — some complete strangers — to hug them.

The Massachusetts attorney general said it has until Jan. 20 to decide whether to approve the new bylaw. But the vote already has had an effect.

At the end of October, just days before a hearing on Ms. Farmer’s and Mr. Jané’s appeal of the decision on accessory use, Amazon asked the town to withdraw its application for the drone hub, but asserted the right to come back with a new plan. The building commissioner then withdrew his own decision.

For now, it remains Westborough, 1, Amazon, 0.

In the past several months, I’d been hearing a rumble from towns and cities across the country that residents were fighting Amazon’s delivery drones. Many of those people were surprised when they saw the drones buzzing across their skies, saying that the deliveries had started without much, or any, notice. So, what could residents do to stop them? I went to Westborough, Massachusetts to find out.

Juliet Macur is a national reporter at The Times, based in Washington, D. C., who often writes about America through the lens of sports.

Trump Grows Frustrated With Vance Over Iran War Critique

The New York Times November 18, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The tension comes at a critical juncture for the vice president, who is considering whether to run for president in 2028.

By Tyler Pager

Reporting from Washington

At first, President Trump appeared notably unfazed by Vice President JD Vance’s post-election analysis blaming the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm wipeout.

“I think it’s largely true,” the president told reporters after Mr. Vance posted a lengthy missive on social media in which he also critiqued much of the administration’s messaging in the run-up to the elections.

But over the past two weeks, Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with how his vice president framed his assessment of what went wrong, complaining to aides and allies that Mr. Vance should have made a point of saying the president made the right decision in going to war with Iran, according to people with knowledge of the president’s comments.

At the same time, Mr. Trump has continued to praise Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, in private conversations and suggesting that he could be a strong presidential candidate, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe discussions going on behind closed doors. Mr. Trump’s allies have noted that Mr. Rubio has repeatedly said the president’s move to attack Iran was essential for the country’s national security.

Mr. Trump has hinted at his irritation with Mr. Vance in public, saying earlier this month that the vice president should have “made one other statement.”

“If you had it to do again, would you do it again? The answer is yes,” he said, laying out what he believes was missing from Mr. Vance’s analysis.

The tension comes at a critical juncture for Mr. Vance, who is considering whether to run for president in 2028, a campaign in which Mr. Trump’s support could be critical to his ability to secure the Republican nomination. The president’s favorable comments about Mr. Rubio are the latest example of how Mr. Trump has been weighing the strengths of the two men as the question of his successor grows more urgent.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Mr. Vance’s office declined to comment, pointing to recent interviews the vice president has given.

When asked on Fox News this week about his post-election commentary and whether there was any “daylight” between him and the president, Mr. Vance said, “I think there’s no daylight between the president or any other senior member of the administration.”

On Wednesday, Mr. Vance canceled a planned appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit, citing meetings in Washington to address the recent tech outages.

Since Mr. Trump brought him aboard as his running mate for a second term, many Republicans have assumed that Mr. Vance, a former senator from Ohio, would be the front-runner for their party’s nomination in 2028. But Mr. Trump has waffled publicly and privately on his vice president throughout his tenure, and Mr. Vance says he has not decided whether to run for president.

“I haven’t made a decision,” he said on Fox News. “We’ll figure it out sometime next year.”

Allies of Mr. Vance, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations, say he is genuinely undecided about his political future. They point to his young family (his fourth child was born in July) as one reason he might not mount a White House bid in 2028. They also note his obsession with political analysis and data and suggest that if he does not see a path to victory, he may sit out this race.

The fallout from the war with Iran — and its unpopularity among voters — could be a significant factor, too. Some allies of Mr. Vance say that if the president decides to resume major combat operations in Iran, it would drastically reduce Mr. Vance’s chances of running.

The vice president, who endorsed Mr. Trump in 2023 saying he would not drag the United States into new wars, expressed reservations about the conflict privately inside the administration. But after the huge G. O. P. losses in this month’s midterms, he went public, laying out in blunt terms what he said went wrong.

“The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in his lengthy social media post the day after the midterms.

Mr. Vance made the point of adding that Mr. Trump had also said as much — though the president has blamed Republicans’ losses on many factors, chiefly that he was not on the ticket.

For Mr. Vance, it appeared to be an attempt to separate himself from the administration’s policy without criticizing the president. But Mr. Trump soon announced that he was pulling his vice president from engaging in peace talks with Iran, an effort that Mr. Vance had intensified shortly before the elections. Mr. Trump said he wanted Mr. Vance to focus on investigating allegations of fraud in Democratic-run jurisdictions.

Alyssa Farah Griffin, who worked in Mr. Trump’s White House during the first term and is now a co-host of “The View,” said that comment from Mr. Vance reminded her of a comment that Kamala Harris, then the vice president, made on the ABC show during the 2024 campaign. When asked if she would have done anything differently from President Joseph R. Biden Jr., Ms. Harris said, “There is not a thing that comes to mind.”

“JD Vance is in the impossible position that any Trump V. P. inevitably ends up in,” Ms. Griffin said. “He can’t have any separation or daylight from the president.”

Mr. Vance’s “daylight” comment this week “may have seemed insignificant in the moment, but it will live in campaign ads,” she added.

Mr. Vance’s allies say a competitive primary, not a coronation, will benefit the next Republican presidential nominee, and they cite Ms. Harris’s loss in 2024 as evidence of that theory. Ms. Harris quickly secured the Democratic nomination after Mr. Biden dropped out of the race, despite some Democrats’ calls for a more formal nominating process.

But Mr. Vance ultimately could find himself in a similar situation to Ms. Harris, who many voters saw as an extension of Mr. Biden, political strategists said. Even as she privately signaled she had concerns about Mr. Biden’s handling of the Israel-Hamas war, she was unable to figure out how to separate herself from the unpopular president.

“It’s very hard to get me to say that I have any amount of sympathy for JD Vance because he put himself in this position,” said Rob Flaherty, a Democratic strategist and former deputy campaign manager to Ms. Harris. “But you do have to feel for him because he’s stuck. When you’re the vice president, you’re stuck. In the Harris situation, there was not much you can actually do to separate yourself.”

Mr. Vance now must wrestle with that complex dynamic as he assesses the future of the Republican Party and in which direction he would try to lead it. His path to the vice presidency — from a “never Trumper” to Mr. Trump’s vice president — suggests that he could go in different directions.

Mr. Vance was an avowed critic of Mr. Trump in 2016, calling him “unfit for our nation’s highest office.” He then became a supporter of Mr. Trump and sought the president’s endorsement when he ran for a Senate seat in Ohio in 2022. He received the endorsement and won that race.

Many Republicans believe Mr. Vance would need the explicit, or at least implicit, support from Mr. Trump to win a Republican primary. But that is far from a guarantee. The president has always relished competition among his aides, and his advisers say he is in no rush to endorse a successor.

And after Republicans’ disastrous results in the elections this month, in which Democrats won the largest midterm victory for either party since the post-Watergate elections, other Republicans see an opening, too. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas and Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida are among those considering possible bids.

Then there’s Mr. Rubio. He has said he would support Mr. Vance and dismissed reports that he is going to leave the administration to run for president. But some of his allies said he would run if Mr. Trump encouraged him to do so — and Mr. Trump has not been shy about lavishing praise on him.

“How hot is Marco, right?” Mr. Trump said Tuesday at the ASEAN summit in Manila. “Is Marco doing a great job? He’s been fantastic.”

While Mr. Vance has remained in the United States, as the vice president does when the president travels abroad, Mr. Rubio is playing a prominent role on the president’s trip. On Tuesday, he addressed public fears about the multiple technology outages in the United States, seeking to reassure Americans that there was no evidence of cyberattacks.

Mr. Rubio’s defense of the Iran war, in particular, has earned him good will with the president.

In a recent interview with The Times, Mr. Rubio said Mr. Trump “deserves a tremendous amount of credit” for authorizing strikes against Iran.

“Ultimately, that is the price of leadership — is the willingness to do things that may not be politically popular or expedient but are necessary for your country and its long-term future,” he said.

The distinct approaches of Mr. Rubio and Mr. Vance underscore a broader debate in the party — should the next Republican presidential candidate align themselves with Mr. Trump’s legacy?

Chris Christie, the former Republican governor of New Jersey, who himself is considering another run for the White House, said Mr. Vance’s challenges transcend his unique position as vice president.

“I don’t think anyone that was part of Trump 2.0 will be able to win in the fall of 2028,” he said. “They will be billed as another four years of Donald Trump, and that will not be salable to the American people.”

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

The Greed of Youth Sports Has No Limits

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

By Jessica Grose

Opinion Writer

It’s middle school draft day at Legendary Prep Academy, a private baseball-focused middle and high school in Scottsdale, Ariz. The school is the center of new reality show on Paramount+ called “Team Moms: Baseball,” which follows several families with children enrolled at the academy.

The brief event is meant to mimic Major League Baseball’s draft, although here the two teams play against each other, the winners mainly get internal bragging rights and the losers have to paint their toenails in the school’s colors. The academy’s chief executive explains why this activity is necessary: “It helps them understand the future that they’re looking at. Like, baseball turns into a business.”

Much of the drama of “Team Moms” swirls around the parents, who look and act like off-brand Real Housewives (the show is produced by Kim Kardashian, among others). Each family’s outsize devotion to their children’s athletic career — parents want their sons to go pro, so they act less like mothers and fathers and more like asset managers — is the show’s selling point. “There is money to be spent in baseball,” one of the moms says a minute into the first episode, though exactly how much is never related. Later on a dad explains: “We have a different mind-set. This is your job.”

Legendary Prep’s website boasts that “this is not a normal school.” A typical schedule has three hours of training in the morning, a “chef catered” lunch, two hours of “classroom,” followed by more training. The parents appear to put baseball prowess above everything, including their children’s health and social development. When the kids get injured, the parents often have little sympathy and want them back on the field ASAP. “You’re here to train,” one mom tells her son. “These kids aren’t your friends.”

These kids are 13 and 14 years old.

Maybe you’re dismissing this as over-the-top, made-for-TV preening. And it certainly is dramatized for our viewing pleasure. But unfortunately, the youth sports industrial complex has grown out of control. “Team Mom” exposes a rapacious system that has ensnared millions of American parents.

Youth sports are now a $40 billion business, and private equity is sinking its claws in, according to my colleagues Joe Drape and Ken Belson. Private sports academies like Legendary Prep are just one small and expensive part of a huge industry. “About 60 million children play sports, and the average U. S. sports family spent $1,016 on its child’s primary sport in 2024, a 46 percent increase since 2019,” they noted in July 2025, relying on data from the Aspen Institute’s Project Play. Recreation and church-based leagues have been hollowed out, and there are few low-cost options for older kids.

I have observed investors become increasingly shameless about bilking parents for new kinds of services since I started writing about how money is ruining youth sports a few years ago. The chief executive of Fastbreak AI, a company that handles operations for youth, amateur and professional sports, said in an interview that he hopes to start offering charter flights for youth sports in the next few years.

“As ridiculous as that sounds, the economics actually work in your favor if you’re filling up an entire 737 or 757 or 777,” Fastbreak’s chief executive, John Stewart, told Buying Sandlot, a newsletter about the youth sports business, in October. “You can give the athletes on the plane a better experience,” he added.

This month, The Boston Globe wrote about how travel sports are contributing to absenteeism in Massachusetts schools, because more and more students are missing class for far-flung games. This doesn’t affect just these students, who may be sacrificing learning for an edge on the court or playing field. Parental investment in travel and club sports also makes school sports less accessible.

“The wealthier students who can afford the extra time on the court or field have a better shot at making varsity, leaving fewer spots for kids who can’t afford the clubs but need an extra incentive to come to school,” The Globe’s Christopher Huffaker and Marcela Rodrigues explain.

I do not blame individual parents who want to give their children these athletic opportunities. Many of us are trapped in what the sociologist Nina Bandelj calls, in her book “Overinvested,” “the emotional economy of parenting.” Being an “excellent parent” in 2026 often means filling children’s time with character-building, physically healthy activities, rather than just letting them guide themselves and experience boredom.

Parents are easy marks for profiteers who tell them they need to shell out for the well-being of their kids. So we get sucked in, Bandelj told me over the phone, and then “we keep supporting our children and keep paying this money because down the line this money becomes an expression of devotion and love.” (I indict myself here: I swore I would never pay for club sports, but then my older daughter fell in love with volleyball. I’m an adoring chump just like everybody else.)

Because spending money on sports has been wrapped up in our identities as “excellent” parents, it can feel impossible to opt out. That’s why my friend and former colleague Jay Caspian Kang, the author of the forthcoming “The Endless Tryout: Reclaiming Childhood From Relentless Competition,” has suggestions for systemic fixes.

Above all, Kang thinks that we need to reinvest in public school sports, which are often on the chopping block when district budgets are trimmed. Robust public school sports options provide all children with the opportunity to play, including ones who don’t have the money for club teams or are simply mediocre athletes. School teams benefit the community: They allow students to have rivalries with other schools, to feel the confidence of being part of a team, and to have a respite if things aren’t going well at home or academically.

The same can’t be said of club sports. They’re not attached to schools and so kids hop to different teams based on which they think will get them the best opportunities in college or in the pros. Club sports and specialization at early ages may even be burning out the best athletes before they can get to higher levels; 70 percent of youth athletes stop participating in organized sports by age 13, according to a 2024 study published in the journal Pediatrics.

Other solutions Kang mentions are legislative. In May, a handful of Democrats in the House and Senate introduced the Let Kids Play Act, which would ban private equity investment in youth sports and compensate families for “junk fees” and predatory contracts.

That bill is stalled, but I have minor hope that the new Congress may do something, because the anger at the state of youth sports appears to be bipartisan. In July, the conservative commentator Matt Walsh posted on X about how youth sports “went completely insane at some point over the past several years,” and added, “I actually think the ‘everybody’s a winner, the score doesn’t matter’ approach was preferable to this. Bring back the participation trophies if this is the alternative.”

Reality TV’s greatest strength is revealing uncomfortable truths about American society that many of us would rather pretend are garish exaggerations. “Team Moms” is coming back for a second season next fall. If nothing else, it should force us to confront what we’re putting ourselves and our kids through and figure out some way to pull ourselves out of the abyss.

Nina Bandelj helped me understand why we parents are such marks for companies that are trying to get us to spend money on extracurriculars: Our love for our children and our identity as good parents is all wrapped up in these opportunities. Have you felt pressure to spend on sports outside of school? How much have you spent over the years and has it been worth it?

The Times’s Vivian Yee has a fascinating and disturbing profile of a “sorority influencer” who has been getting cosmetic procedures since she was in high school, and appears to spend every waking hour on her appearance.

Two University of Arizona sorority members have the following conversation about whether one of them should get a “lip flip,” a kind of lip injection to change her smile. “I don’t necessarily need it, but it’s like, everyone else at this school has it,” one says.

Yee explains further: “Both procedures are available at a local med spa, where until a couple years ago, undergraduates could use Cat Cash — student bursary funds, generally replenished by parents — to pay for fillers by swiping their student IDs. The spa takes Cat Cash only for non-injectable beauty services now, but lips keep getting flipped.”

I’m more committed than ever to going full crone.

“South Park” has an incredible parody of club sports parents and their absurd commitment and one-upmanship: “You’re so lucky you only have one kid. We spent the week getting up at two in the morning to get our three kids to 50 different cities and stay at nine hotel rooms at the same time!”

Feel free to drop me a line about anything here.

An earlier version of this newsletter misstated the publication status of a book. “Overinvested” by Nina Bandelj was published in January; it is not forthcoming.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Jessica Grose is an Opinion writer for The Times, covering family, religion, education, culture and the way we live now.

Google Buys Worker Data From Spirit Airlines in a New Market to Feed A. I.

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

A flight attendants’ union challenged Google’s plans to protect personal information in the data in court, saying the company’s measures were not enough to protect Spirit’s employees.

By Rebecca Davis O’Brien

Rebecca Davis O’Brien writes about labor.

When Spirit Airlines shut down in May, its assets went up for sale: a small fleet of airplanes, coveted slots at LaGuardia Airport and decades of internal workplace data, including employee records, tax forms, 100 million emails and half a billion Microsoft Teams messages.

Google had the winning bid, $10 million, for those employment records, a novel asset class the company said it would use to improve its artificial intelligence products. Imagine what a large language model could glean from the recruiting and timekeeping files of such a large company, or from workers’ snarky chats about their bosses.

But in August, a union representing 5,500 flight attendants affected by the bankruptcy filed an objection in federal court, saying that de-identifying measures promised by Google and Spirit, largely related to the protection of consumer data, were not enough to protect Spirit’s employees.

“If it was not for our union, this would have just happened in a fire sale in the middle of the night,” said Sara Nelson, the president of the Association of Flight Attendants. “This is a brand-new frontier for workers’ rights. It’s making people’s lives, their entire privacy, a commodity.”

Last week, Google agreed to new limitations on the employee data. In a hearing on Tuesday, a bankruptcy judge in federal court in New York State accepted the revised sale terms, and the flight attendants’ union dropped its objections. A spokesman for Google said the company was happy with the result but declined to comment further until the court posted the full language of the agreement.

Spirit said it was pleased that the court had approved the sale of data that would go through a “court-supervised exclusion and de-identification process” before its transfer to Google.

“This approval follows months of productive dialogue between Spirit, Google, the consumer privacy ombudsman, our labor unions and the other key stakeholders who have engaged constructively to ensure the sale is conducted in line with data privacy regulations and best practices,” a Spirit spokesman said.

Data has been sold before in bankruptcies that have raised consumer privacy concerns, like the 2025 bankruptcy of 23andMe, a genetic testing service. And there are examples of a failed company’s records becoming public. After Enron, an energy company, collapsed in 2001, federal investigators released a trove of company emails. They have been mined for case studies and research.

But only recently have companies sought access to a failed company’s internal work force data. There is a market developing, largely out of sight, for the carcasses of dead companies to be turned into feasts for large language models with insatiable appetites for written communication. SpaceX’s A. I. unit has considered buying data from struggling start-ups, Bloomberg reported in September.

The Spirit case appears to be the first large-scale example of using “corporate detritus” to train large language models, said Greg Ewing, a partner at Spencer Fane, a law firm. The idea is to teach A. I. how humans speak in the workplace.

“This is a whole new world, where all that data is so valuable to A. I. companies,” Mr. Ewing said. “We are going to see whole marketplaces arise out of it.”

Eric Chafetz, a partner at Lowenstein Sandler, a law firm, said the Spirit case was the first large bankruptcy sale in which a buyer had said it was motivated to build A. I. models. “We have recently received numerous unsolicited inbound inquiries from entities purporting to want to buy similar types of data,” he said. “Parties do believe there’s real value in trying to purchase a failed or failing company’s data.”

This has consequences for employees, Mr. Chafetz said: The bankruptcy code’s privacy protections were designed for consumers. “Employees aren’t in that picture at all,” he said.

Ms. Nelson said personnel files, even if they were cleared of identifying information, could be used to connect private data to a specific employee. A woman’s leave for reproductive care could one day be traced back to her. A pilot’s detailed background check, later uncovered, could expose sensitive personal details.

The flight attendants’ union, which is part of the AFL-CIO, wants to enshrine worker privacy protections into contracts and the law, she said.

“These are standards that can be put into law right away because we already have a major company working on the advancement of these A. I. models, who can comply with these very high standards of protections for workers,” Ms. Nelson said.

The union was joined in its efforts by other unions affected by the Spirit bankruptcy; in all, Ms. Nelson said, about 17,000 workers had been affected by the data privacy issue. In October, more than 120 congressional leaders sent a letter to Google and Spirit asking them to include more protections for employees.

The revised agreement makes clear that certain information is not to be part of the sale, including employee medical and disability records, flight crew fatigue reports and payroll records.

Last week, lawyers for GE Aerospace and CFM International, parts suppliers to Spirit, asked the bankruptcy court to exclude data related to their companies, too, including information related to engine maintenance and avionics systems.

“The data sale poses significant risks to parties that provided such information to the debtors over the years, because Google may use or disclose it through its A. I. products,” they wrote.

Rebecca Davis O’Brien covers labor and the work force for The Times.

Democrats Nominate Jeffries as Speaker, Making History

The New York Times November 18, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

The vote put Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York in line to become the first Black lawmaker to win the post second in line to the presidency.

By Annie Karni

Reporting from the Capitol

House Democrats on Wednesday nominated Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York to be speaker, voting overwhelmingly over resistance from the left to put him in line to become the first Black lawmaker to hold the post.

The election by secret ballot came just over two weeks after Mr. Jeffries, 56, who has led House Democrats since 2022, presided over sweeping victories for his party, which won a historically large majority in the midterm elections.

The vote was 251 to 11, with two Democrats abstaining, according to a person who attended the confidential session and detailed the results on the condition of anonymity. The margin demonstrated the breadth of Mr. Jeffries’s backing in a large and ideologically diverse caucus.

Accepting the nomination, he paid homage to the civil rights hero and long-serving Representative John Lewis of Georgia, who frequently exhorted people to get in “good trouble” fighting injustice.

“It’s a ‘good trouble’ moment in America,” Mr. Jeffries told the assembled Democrats.

He will still have to be elected on the House floor in January, when he will need a majority of members in the chamber to rise and say his name to formally win the post that is second in line to the presidency. But the lopsided secret-ballot vote suggested he will have more than enough support to do so.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

Mr. Jeffries’s nomination was almost a foregone conclusion; no Democrat emerged to challenge him, and even some of his loudest critics ultimately did not want to publicly oppose the man in line to be the nation’s first Black speaker.

His frictionless ascent counted as a rarity in the House, where party leaders often rise through tumultuous challenges.

“It’s a good day,” said Representative Steny Hoyer of Maryland, the former No. 2 Democrat, as he headed into the closed-door session. “I served with the first woman speaker of the House. Now we’re going to elect the first African American speaker of the House.” Mr. Hoyer said it was a testimony to the country’s progress.

Inside the room, according to a person who was present, Representative James E. Clyburn, Democrat of South Carolina, gave the final speech nominating Mr. Jeffries, invoking Mr. Lewis, who died in 2020, as he reflected on the significance of elevating a Black man for the job.

Still, Mr. Jeffries faced loud grass-roots resistance from progressives fed up with the Democratic Party establishment who see Mr. Jeffries, a reserved moderate and prodigious fund-raiser, as an avatar of the status quo who is beholden to corporate interests.

Progressives who want Democrats to cut off U. S. aid to Israel and who champion “Medicare for all” said they were concerned that Mr. Jeffries, a longtime supporter of the Jewish state who they view as too closely aligned with AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobbying group, would stand in the way of their demands.

In a statement, a group of newly elected democratic socialist lawmakers said they voted against Mr. Jeffries because their constituents sent them to Congress with a “mandate” to deliver change on “Medicare for all, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics” and “ending the genocide in Gaza.” While the group acknowledged some “meaningful progress” in their conversations with Mr. Jeffries, they said they still opposed him.

The group included Representatives-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York; Adam Hamawy of New Jersey; Frederick Haynes of Texas; Melat Kiros of Colorado; Donavan McKinney of Michigan; and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania.

Mr. Jeffries, who in recent days met with almost all members and newly elected Democrats as he sought to wrap up his nomination with as little opposition as possible, is known for his cautious and highly disciplined style.

He likes to host listening sessions and have a caucus “family discussion” before telegraphing his stance on any issue. But he also appears willing to move in response to broad calls for bold action.

On Tuesday, for instance, less than 24 hours before his nomination, Mr. Jeffries endorsed a broad expansion of Medicare to cover more Americans and a wider variety of services, edging closer to the Medicare for all proposal championed by progressives.

It was a sign that with a larger majority giving him more room to maneuver and progressives pressing him to take up a bolder agenda, he saw the need and opportunity to take a more ambitious approach.

Mr. Jeffries, who grew up in a working-class home in the Crown Heights section of Brooklyn in the 1980s, first ran for the State Legislature at 29. He was always viewed by people around him as a potential national leader, though he had been hesitant to reflect on the significance of his place in history until he had the vote wrapped up.

“Over the last four years, that pressure has already been on me,” he said in an interview earlier this month, when asked if he felt the weight of breaking a racial barrier. “Failure is not an option.”

Despite the sweeping electoral victories, Mr. Jeffries has been facing loud resistance to his leadership. Many lawmakers said their phone lines had been blowing up with constituents demanding a new face to lead the party as it takes control of Congress. But even amid that pressure, many of the progressives in Congress said they thought Mr. Jeffries deserved a chance to lead them in the majority.

House Democrats on Wednesday also nominated Representative Katherine M. Clark, Democrat of Massachusetts, to serve as the first female majority leader next year. And they nominated Representative Pete Aguilar, Democrat of California, to serve as the whip. Ms. Clark and Mr. Aguilar, who have served as the Nos. 2 and 3 House Democrats since 2022, were nominated by a unanimous voice vote for their positions.

Annie Karni is a congressional correspondent for The Times.

The Anti-A. I. Campus Movement Is Growing

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Some students are refusing to use A. I., and others are starting petitions to limit it across entire campuses. Colleges have taken notice.

By Dana Goldstein

Last March, a handful of students at Transylvania University created a petition, attempting to slow the advance of artificial intelligence on their campus. It asked the administration to cancel chatbot licenses with A. I. giants and instead invest the money in “human-centered education.”

About a third of the college’s students signed on.

Transylvania, in Lexington, Ky., is tiny, with under 1,000 students. But across the country and the globe, there has been a swell of campus resistance to A. I., including a growing group of conscientious objectors who refuse to use A. I. at all.

Polls show the vast majority of American students use chatbots for school work. College leaders have generally embraced A. I., saying it is key to preparing students for the work force.

But as A. I. use grows, more students and faculty are sounding alarms and trying to slow it down.

Much of the opposition comes from the political left, and focuses on how A. I. could harm the environment, diminish the power of workers or be used in warfare. Some of the loudest voices in opposition are studying the arts, where human creativity is paramount, or the law, as tech companies face lawsuits over potential copyright and privacy violations.

But there are also deep concerns that A. I. degrades the experience of college itself, by removing the productive struggle of learning.

Resistors from California to Sydney to Paris are increasingly publishing manifestoes that lay out demands: that colleges not partner with A. I. companies; that professors not be required to use generative A. I. in lessons or grading; and that students be allowed to refuse to complete assignments that require the use of chatbots, without any impact on their grades.

At the University of Kentucky, a research employee who described himself as a humanist successfully applied for a religious exemption from using A. I.

Alice Beatty, 22, helped lead the Transylvania petition drive as a senior last spring. The student newspaper had called attention to the $120,000 the university paid to purchase licenses to ChatGPT and Gemini, chatbots from OpenAI and Google. And Ms. Beatty had participated in a discussion group formed by several A. I.-skeptical professors.

She noted that even before Transylvania provided free access to chatbots, A. I. had been everywhere on campus. Students used it to summarize readings, break down physics problems and compose discussion-board posts and papers that they were supposed to be writing the old-fashioned way, on their own.

Yet when Ms. Beatty and some classmates stood near the dining hall to collect signatures on the petition, almost everyone they spoke to signed.

“I use A. I.,” she recalled some peers telling her, “and I am ashamed I use it.”

A spokeswoman for Transylvania University declined an interview request but said that professors were free to either embrace A. I., limit its use or ban it entirely in their classes.

For students, ethical and practical questions about A. I. will be part of the world they enter after graduating, she said by email.

Vague and confusing college A. I. policies have helped create the conscientious objector movement, said Hollis Robbins, an English professor at the University of Utah who writes often about A. I. and education. She suggested that colleges stop grading take-home assignments that are easy to cheat on with A. I., and shut down online courses that have become rife with academic misconduct in the A. I. era.

If institutions took those steps, she argued, students might be more curious and hopeful about the technology.

“There is silence about these major tech issues,” she said. “Students just seeing grown-ups being inconsistent and letting them down.”

Georgetown University began offering students and faculty free access to Gemini in March. At the time, like many institutions, Georgetown generally allowed each professor to set their own A. I. rules.

Yet in focus groups on A. I. conducted by the university, students asked for clearer guidance. They were worried about cognitive offloading, cheating and A. I. providing false information. Forty percent of the student sentiment was cautious or negative toward A. I., according to the university, compared with 25 percent that was positive or hopeful.

Georgetown’s student newspaper published an editorial criticizing the Gemini license, arguing that it tacitly pushed students toward technology that is often used to plagiarize and avoid academic effort.

This fall, the university is changing its approach. Under a new president, Eduardo M. Peñalver, it announced it would form a faculty committee to come up with clearer principles on A. I. use. For Georgetown, a Jesuit institution, Pope Leo XIV’s recent encyclical on the risks of A. I. will be an important influence.

Dr. Peñalver said in an interview that Georgetown would seek to make course expectations around A. I. more transparent and provide more tech-free spaces on campus. Oral presentations, discussion groups and in-person tests would become more important, he said, to protect “from the intrusion of this technology.”

Still, the university will continue to expand free access to A. I. tools, which he said had the potential to do good.

“We’re not interested in pushing people to use A. I. in ways that don’t align with their values,” Dr. Peñalver said. “But I certainly encourage people to learn about it.”

“Even if you’re opposed to this technology,” he added, “that awareness and understanding is important to the success of your project.”

Many conscientious objectors, though, say they try to avoid generative A. I. as much as possible, blocking it from their devices and not experimenting with it in their own work.

Emily Tucker, executive director of the Center on Privacy and Technology at Georgetown Law School, has been a leader in organizing resistance to A. I. use on campus. She has also signed an open letter with 1,300 other educators “who refuse the call for generative A. I. adoption in schools and colleges, and reject the narrative of its inevitability.”

Law students have told her they feared that if they didn’t use A. I. to speed their output, they would be outpaced in class and at work by those who did. But Professor Tucker said that using A. I. degrades a student’s ability to read and analyze dense legal texts, and risks incorrect citations of case law.

“It’s not useful,” said Professor Tucker, who said she rarely uses A. I. herself, though she acknowledged it might help in some tasks, like seeking specific information within a large set of documents.

At Cornell, Shimon Edelman, a psychology professor who holds a Ph. D. in computer science, has also signed the anti-A. I. letter. He lets students decide whether or not to use A. I., though he warns them it could degrade deeper learning.

He said he had been dismayed to see the Cornell administration greet A. I. warmly, as an “essential tool,” instead of warning more forcefully against its risks. In October, Cornell announced free access to chatbots, A. I. coding tools and agentic A. I.

“It’s unthinkable,” Professor Edelman said of using A. I. in his own research, even when he faced having to read 800 documents for a recent book project.

Emmali Simmelink, a senior studying classics and religion at Whitman College in Washington State, said students on her campus sometimes plug classroom discussion prompts directly into ChatGPT.

“If you can’t generate a coherent thought without ChatGPT, I genuinely lose a lot of respect for you,” she said. She added, laughing, “I am really insufferable about this.”

She said she brings up concerns about the environmental impact of A. I. as soon as she hears somebody say, “I asked ChatGPT.”

The topic can be divisive socially, so much so, several students said, that friend groups often develop a shared view of A. I.

Preston Hicks, 26, is studying history and education at Rider University in New Jersey — a second degree, after he worked previously as a software developer. He said many of his friends are artists who instinctually oppose A. I., a view he often shares.

But he can also imagine using A. I. in his future career as a teacher, to handle paperwork and other logistical tasks.

“I am more nuanced,” he said. “If I see a good use, I will use it.”

Dana Goldstein covers education for The Times.

After 49 Years, Voyager 1 Is a Mind-Blowing One Light-Day From Earth

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Launched in 1977, the hardy spacecraft is still sending messages back home from a staggering distance in interstellar space.

By Nadia Drake

After nearly half a century in flight, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft has crossed an invisible threshold — a boundary measured by time rather than distance. Today, our farthest-flung creation is one light-day from Earth, beaming messages home across an expanse that takes photons a full 24 hours to traverse.

“It is truly a staggering feeling, to know that Voyager 1 is one light-day from Earth,” said Nicky Fox, NASA’s associate administrator for the science mission directorate. “That makes us pause and think about just how vast our universe is.”

In a sense, today’s boundary crossing represents a change toward a more interstellar mind-set, said Jordan Bimm, a space historian at the University of Chicago. “It’s a rhetorical shift we are making to signal our hope and ambition for future space missions that go faster and further,” Dr. Bimm said.

It’s also a reminder of the lonely undercurrents of exploration. Launched in the summer of 1977, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2 set off on a journey to surveil the outer solar system’s giant planets. They ended up becoming humankind’s most enduring pair of spacecraft, and now, 49 years later, both of them are relaying information about their travels through interstellar space.

Neither spacecraft was ever meant to come home, and the farther they go, the harder it gets for them to trade messages with their builders.

The radio transmissions we use to communicate with spacecraft travel at light-speed — about 186,000 miles per second. That’s fast, but space is big, and there’s no way to get around light’s limit. Each conversation we have with our space-faring explorers is laggy, and the delays grow with distance.

Depending on the relative positions of the planets, messages to Mars can take as few as three minutes or as long as 22 minutes to arrive. That’s why it’s impossible for people on Earth to drive a Mars rover in real time; engineers instead send packages of preprogrammed commands. It can take nearly an hour for transmissions to reach NASA’s Juno spacecraft, which orbits Jupiter.

And Voyager 1? At its light-day distance, even a simple check-in takes 48 hours.

“You wake up on a Monday morning and say hello to the spacecraft, and on Wednesday morning it says hello to you,” said Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager mission project manager at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California.

The Voyagers’ dispatches from the cosmos are a big part of the reason they are so beloved and celebrated today. As they looped through the solar system on a sort of 20th-century odyssey, they revealed a lively array of worlds big and small.

Some of them seemed almost too fantastic to be true — like Jupiter’s icy moon Europa, which improbably appeared to harbor a vast, alien ocean. And Io, tucked in next to the giant planet, turned out to be so intensely volcanic that some scientists initially suspected well-organized mischief.

“My first thought was, No, the Caltech students have pulled a prank and they’ve gotten into the feed,” recalled Alan Cummings, at senior research scientist at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena, Calif. “It just didn’t look real. It looked like a poorly rendered pizza.”

After coloring in our solar neighborhood, the Voyagers set their sights on the uncharted waters of interstellar space. Their new goal: to emerge from the heliosphere, a protective cocoon created by the sun’s magnetic field and solar wind, and explore the galactic wilds.

In the 1970s, no one knew exactly where the bubble’s edge lay, or how long it might take to reach. Turns out, it would take 36 years of hurtling through space at some 38,000 miles per hour before the Voyager 1 team reported a telltale shift in cosmic radiation that signaled its passage beyond the solar bubble. Voyager 2 crossed over in 2018.

“When we crossed that border, we were all humbled by the experience,” said Stamatios Krimigis, a space scientist at the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory who is the oldest active principal investigator on the Voyager team. “We realized that we were essentially a delegation from humanity, going away from our home planet and our own solar system, and we ventured on into the unknown. I can’t get over it, all these years later.”

But while the speed of light is an immutable constant, the Voyager mission is not. Eventually, both spacecraft will run out of power and fall silent. Yet they will press on into a cosmos only they can know. And in five billion years or so, when the sun swells into a red giant and obliterates Earth as we know it, the Voyagers will still be there.

“The Voyagers were the first to do a lot of things, but they will also be one of the last pieces of evidence that humans on Earth have ever existed,” Dr. Cummings said. “That boggles my mind.”

Each spacecraft carries a Golden Record etched with the sights and sounds of planet Earth, along with instructions for how to play that record, should it ever be found. For the rest of their existence, the twin spacecraft will carry these relics of their creators, bearing our hopes and dreams into the stars.

“Voyager is humanity’s gift to the universe,” Dodd said. “Go boldly, Voyager. Godspeed.”

Fish and High Prices: How Mary Peltola Triumphed in Alaska’s Senate Race

The New York Times November 18, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

Beleaguered by high fuel costs and wary of overfishing, Alaskans were drawn to the Democrat’s hyperlocal pitch.

By Kellen Browning and Emily Schwing

Emily Schwing reported from Anchorage

In the end, Mary Peltola may not have needed two Dan Sullivans on the ballot after all.

A final batch of votes pushed Ms. Peltola, the Democratic former congresswoman, across the threshold to victory against Senator Dan S. Sullivan of Alaska late on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press. Ms. Peltola’s victory secured a 56th seat in the Senate for her party in a midterm election that Democrats swept.

She won by over 12,000 votes, more than the roughly 4,700 earned by Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher whom Democratic operatives had recruited into the race in an apparent effort to confuse Republicans and siphon their votes from an incumbent with the same name.

Around the country, the presence of that other Dan Sullivan on the ballot dominated coverage of the race. But in Alaska, Ms. Peltola laid the groundwork for a dominant victory over the incumbent through more conventional means, attacking him on the cost of living and positioning herself as a working-class champion.

Like other Democrats who flipped G. O. P. seats this month, Ms. Peltola capitalized on voter anger over high gas and diesel fuel costs, the war in Iran and an unpopular president. But in Alaska, where regional matters and politicians’ personal brands play an outsize role, Ms. Peltola’s win also reflected her success running as a broadly palatable challenger steeped in local concerns. By the end, seemingly everyone knew Ms. Peltola’s campaign slogan: “Fish, Family, Freedom.”

“They had a good strategy,” said Ashley Reed, a nonpartisan state lobbyist who, like many supporters of the incumbent, begrudgingly acknowledged that Ms. Peltola’s attacks had hit home. “They just hammered away, and one of the things that worked real well is the Sullivan campaign did not counter some really harsh claims.”

While the senator focused on communities in the Mat-Su Valley and the Kenai Peninsula, conservative areas outside Anchorage, Ms. Peltola was trekking to tiny rural villages in far-flung parts of the state, many of which are reachable only by boat or small plane. She flew in and out of distant towns for days in a row, covering thousands of miles. She reached some of them by snowmobile.

“It matters who shows up,” said Gloria Burns, the president of the Ketchikan Indian Community in southeastern Alaska, who supported Ms. Peltola. “That attracted me, because I have to be thinking about who pushes for and supports policies that are best for my people.”

Ms. Peltola’s travel seemed to pay off. An analysis of voting data by district showed that the remote rural regions of Alaska shifted the most toward Democrats when compared with 2024. And although turnout was down across the board compared with the presidential election that year, the rural districts generally saw the smallest turnout declines.

Outside money and other resources flooded the state, aiding both candidates. The state’s Democratic machinery went into overdrive, with the AFL-CIO knocking on more than 28,000 doors of fellow union members, according to Bronson Frye, the group’s secretary-treasurer — far more than the roughly 10,000 the union might knock in a normal year.

From the beginning, Ms. Peltola’s allies knew that toppling a two-term incumbent would be difficult. Mr. Sullivan was seen as a low-key and relatively uncontroversial figure, and he had forged deep relationships with various constituencies in the state, including certain Alaska Native corporate interests and those working in the oil industry. The Democrats saw opportunity, however, in the senator’s understated persona, capitalizing on his struggle to differentiate himself from Mr. Trump.

“He didn’t know what to do in a campaign where the Republican brand wasn’t going to save him,” said John-Henry Heckendorn, an Alaska political strategist who worked with super PACs supporting Ms. Peltola.

Mr. Heckendorn said a moment crystallizing that struggle came in late October, when thousands arrived in Anchorage for the 60th annual Alaska Federation of Natives convention.

It was a high-profile opportunity for political candidates to sway a crucial swing bloc just before the election, and attendees were eager to watch the top two candidates face off in a forum. But Mr. Sullivan didn’t show up, giving Ms. Peltola the stage to herself to talk about how to reduce large-scale commercial fishing and bring down high costs, and to link Mr. Sullivan to Mr. Trump.

The senator had delivered a solo speech earlier at the convention. A senior adviser for his campaign disputed the idea that the decision not to appear onstage with Ms. Peltola was an unforced error. The adviser, who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe internal campaign strategy, argued instead that the national environment was the main culprit in Mr. Sullivan’s loss.

The adviser also acknowledged, however, that Democratic attacks against Mr. Sullivan, which had begun even before Ms. Peltola entered the race, appeared to have left a mark. He said Democrats’ efforts to recruit potential spoiler candidates including Daniel J. Sullivan, which were revealed in a New York Times article in October, had aided Ms. Peltola’s campaign beyond just vote tallies, by dominating news headlines and deflecting attention from her.

Mr. Sullivan did find opportunities to go on offense. He pushed Ms. Peltola to engage in more televised debates. And Ms. Peltola at times proceeded with caution, skipping chances to engage with her opponent and avoiding the national media spotlight. Mr. Sullivan derided her as “No Show Peltola.”

Still, Ms. Peltola had become well-known in Alaska after campaigning statewide three times for the House. A former commercial fisher who later served in the State Legislature, she also led a commission that served as an intermediary between Alaska Natives and outside agencies that enforced rules on fishing.

She focused heavily this year — as she always has — on her opposition to large-scale trawlers, which compete with subsistence fishers seeking to fill their freezers before Alaska’s long winters.

Ms. Peltola’s message began feeling increasingly relevant, Alaskans said, as the fishing crisis grew more acute, and as skyrocketing prices of diesel and other goods were putting the state on edge. (Mr. Sullivan also opposed trawling, focusing particularly on Russian and Chinese fleets, but he didn’t make the issue a centerpiece of his campaign.)

Four years ago, “she was a little bit alone in this critique of the way Alaska’s managing this resource,” said Joelle Hall, the former president of the Alaska AFL-CIO, the state’s largest labor union. “As time goes on, more and more people realize, ‘Oh, what’s going on?’”

Art Hackney, a veteran G. O. P. strategist in Alaska who worked for super PACs backing Mr. Sullivan, said the senator’s campaign assumed that voters knew about his legislative record, which allowed Ms. Peltola to drive a “relentlessly dishonest” narrative that he was not working to address the cost of living even as his family business had continued to make profits.

“I don’t think Dan’s campaign inoculated himself well” against the attacks, Mr. Hackney said. He added: “People just wanted to punish anyone in Trump’s realm,” and Ms. Peltola “was just riding the tide.”

Ms. Peltola was also on the defensive at times. In September, The Times reported that she had been verbally abusive to her employees, used offensive slurs and even shoved a former aide. Her campaign denied some of the allegations and said others had been exaggerated.

The next month, The Times reported that her campaign participated in an effort to recruit candidates into the Senate race, including Daniel J. Sullivan — a charge that Ms. Peltola had denied for months and continues to contest.

Republicans seized on the news, with the Justice Department suing to block certification in the event Ms. Peltola won. Mr. Trump suggest it amounted to voter fraud, though no illegal activity had been alleged.

Ms. Peltola sought to dismiss the controversies as unwanted distractions coming from the Lower 48. Even so, as the state’s round-the-clock summer sunlight gave way to snowfall in the final weeks, she remained locked in a competitive battle with Mr. Sullivan.

“I don’t think there was ever any moment where it’s like, ‘Oh yeah, we’ve got it,’” said Martha McKenna, a longtime political consultant for Ms. Peltola. “This felt like an underdog race every single day.”

By the end, Mr. Sullivan was openly acknowledging high prices in his stump speeches, and national Republicans were swooping in to help his campaign. “Too many families are having a real hard time making ends meet,” he said at an early October rally with Vice President JD Vance in Fairbanks.

Mr. Sullivan argued that Democratic control of Congress would worsen Alaska’s economic woes by squeezing the oil industry. But like many other Republicans on the ballot this year, he struggled to find a response that resonated with voters who were angry about prices in Mr. Trump’s second term. Unlike some Republican lawmakers who voted for a resolution to curtail the president’s ability to continue to the war with Iran, which drove up oil prices, Mr. Sullivan largely supported the president on the conflict.

For more than a year, Ms. Hall, a Peltola ally, had worried that the president would show up and deliver an October surprise that could give Mr. Sullivan a final boost. Mr. Trump did just that, announcing at a rally in Wasilla last month that South Korea would invest $54 billion in a long-delayed natural gas pipeline in the state.

But as Ms. Hall saw it, Mr. Trump’s credibility had become so damaged that voters weren’t interested.

“By that point, Alaskans were like, ‘You know what, this guy’s full of it,” she said.

On election night, as the Democratic landslide swept many of his Republican colleagues out of office, Mr. Sullivan predicted that his state would defy the trend.

Two weeks later, he was swept out, too.

Christine Zhang contributed reporting.

Kellen Browning is a Times political reporter based in San Francisco.

Grand Theft Auto VI Will Steal Your Heart

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Grand Theft Auto VI

Advertisement

Supported by

Critic’s Pick

The series matures beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups with a game about love, relationships and nurturing your partner.

By Yussef Cole

Grand Theft Auto VI’s romantic leads, the vivacious Lucia Caminos and the gravel-voiced country boy Jason Duval, can hold hands with the press of a button.

The prompt appears while walking down a busy downtown street, before reps at the gym, or after pulling on ski masks to rob an armored truck. This simple interaction, perhaps more than any of the innumerable things you can get up to in this immense experience, distinguishes the latest G. T. A. from what came before. This is a game about love and relationships, their joy and heartache, and the work required to make them successful.

The surprising depth to which these themes are explored makes for a memorable and endearing experience in Grand Theft Auto VI, which largely lives up to its sky-high expectations by inverting the series’s reputation for destruction.

The 70-hour story concerns itself with Lucia and Jason’s adventures around a geographically condensed pastiche of South Florida. The first chapter is set in the game’s version of the Florida Keys, and the couple will also visit versions of the Everglades, the Gulf Coast and the national parks of North Florida before finally winding up in Vice City, the glitzy facsimile of Miami.

Events move slowly at first as the pair start off apart. Lucia is in lockup for petty theft and Jason is bumming his way around the Keys, doing small-time drug trafficking jobs and playing shockingly elaborate in-game video games with his burnout friend. But even in these early hours, there are magical, smart moments of interaction that point to the specialness of the game’s romantic core.

Instead of doing doughnuts in the middle of intersections or getting into fistfights with passers-by, Jason can opt to fix up his run-down bachelor pad in preparation for Lucia’s imminent release. There are numerous tasks around the house, like putting up drywall, painting and fixing the roof, that take up the player’s time and the character’s in-game resources, but they aim toward a productive and satisfying goal: a better relationship.

This reflects a maturation of a series that has generally only told stories about men solipsistically chasing after their own success. Here, whether you’re controlling Jason or, eventually, Lucia, much of what you can do — apart from activities routine to G. T. A. like stealing cars and robbing banks — is taking action to care for and nurture your romantic partner.

In “All About Love,” bell hooks argues that “we would all love better if we used it as a verb” instead of a noun. In our loving relationships, she writes, the “choice must be made to nurture growth.” This idea finds shape in the romantic interactivity of Grand Theft Auto VI, where players must actively choose closeness and intimacy.

It’s entirely possible to play separately from your in-game partner, and there are plenty of activities, like rescuing Lucia’s friend from a yoga cult and going hunting with Jason’s Army buddy, that can only be done individually. But, more often than not, I find myself choosing to spend the day with my partner, whose presence enriches most activities. You can have silly little conversations as you drive around, hug, exchange a quick kiss, go on dates, dance and work out at the gym together. These are all actions the player must choose to take. Playing the game like past G. T. A. s, favoring violence and chaos and nihilistically going it alone, hurts the relationship and potentially destroys it.

Choosing romance is the easy part, thanks to the chemistry and human characterization of the two leads. Lucia and Jason’s relationship builds on itself and becomes a constant, supportive presence. It gets reflected in the story missions too, as your characters make scripted choices that reflect how you behaved toward each other in the idle moments in between.

But the world puts its pressures on the relationship. Grand Theft Auto VI is a dense game filled with friction: Its cops are more savage and much smarter than before, sending dogs to sniff you out as you cower in a dead-end alley, or telling a helicopter overhead to watch out for your description or your car’s paint job. The nature of the narrative is less one of rags to riches than a story about desperation and survival, and the tension of throwing in one’s lot with untrustworthy allies.

Even when it comes to driving, the series’s bread and butter, this friction is evident. The idea of obeying traffic laws and keeping under the speed limit always seemed like outlier behavior in past games, but zooming freely down highways and blasting through red lights is noticeably more risky in Grand Theft Auto VI. While some of my favorite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit, I have just as many memories of clipping the bumper of a merging car, spinning out of control and flipping onto the median. Car crashes are serious here, challenging the idea of a clean getaway with duffel bags of marked bills and stolen jewelry.

Acquiring these ill-gotten goods is one of the game’s more interesting repeatable activities. Jewelry stores and pawn shops are the plentiful targets for stickups, but the big money, and risk, is in banks. Going in the front with guns out is a quick solution. Alternatively, you can sneak in through the back door, subdue guards quietly, erase the security footage and break into bigger safes. Inevitably, though, someone will hear something and the scene will descend into chaos. It’s a scramble to scoop up as much cash as you can carry, dashing back to your ride and tearing away from the approaching heat.

The world of Grand Theft Auto VI is a loud place, jam-packed with Rockstar’s take on American culture. Conversations among strangers are easily overheard. Jason and Lucia’s journey takes them through dramatically different environs, and introduces them to a wide variety of comic archetypes. There are sun-baked retirees on mobility scooters, leather-clad bikers, low-rent strippers and more than one drug dealer getting high on their own supply.

Many of these characters are introduced via scripted missions but countless others can be found while simply wandering around. I was in the middle of boosting a minivan when a woman walked up to me and offered bad life advice for a price. At another point, I pulled over at a highway overpass to keep a vlogger from falling to his demise while doing parkour. Vignettes like these are buried all over the place, making the world feel alive with teeming humanity.

The frenetic nature of the game’s world hits its fever pitch in Vice City. I found myself missing the more deliberate and digestible pace of the boonies. Gone were the slow, reflective moments where Jason could spend some quality time fishing, shooting pool at the bar, or helping his neighbor go on liquor runs. Vice City offers up an overwhelming amount of stuff, and fills the map with icons and activities.

Whenever things calm back down, it comes as a relief. The main story rarely slows but there are plenty of side activities to busy yourself with. Lucia’s character-specific missions are a joy. She can help her mother sell run-down houses while withstanding relatable snipes about her body. There’s also a memorable arc around rescuing a friend from a multilevel marketing scheme. Simply moving through the world as Lucia is a pleasure. She’s self-possessed and charming, but quick to throw down when the situation demands it. Her outfits and hairstyles are inspired, making her a brilliantly realized counterbalance to Jason’s white-bread personality.

In light of the previous game’s band of unlikable misanthropes, it’s a pleasant surprise to play a version of G. T. A. with characters whose entire existence isn’t some puerile joke. That’s no guarantee despite the breadth and scope of the game, its gargantuan budget and a work force often pushed to its limits. G. T. A. has always represented a certain pinnacle when it comes to video game production.

But where the dollars are most felt isn’t in the intricate skylines or the typically bombastic missions, which take liberal inspiration from decades of crime movies in the vein of Mann, Scorsese and Bay. It’s all impressively done and rendered with technological aplomb, but it isn’t anything we haven’t seen before. Instead, the game’s artistry is felt most in its Bonnie and Clyde duo.

Partway through the game, Lucia and Jason take a walk down their hotel’s sandy-white beach. They, naturally, lock hands. The foaming surf laps at their feet with hyper-realistic verisimilitude. Above is not just a skybox, but fluffy cumulus clouds hanging in volumetric space. There’s nothing to do here. The gunfights and car chases and cartoonish gangster shenanigans can wait. They’re distractions from the game’s true achievement: the well-earned satisfaction of an authentic human bond.

Grand Theft Auto VI, which will be released on Thursday, was reviewed on the PlayStation 5. It will also be available on the Xbox Series X|S.
